description:
Glenvale State School No. 727 opened on 30 October 1865.

Between 1881 and 1886 the school worked part-time with Upper Plenty State School No. 1244, before becoming full-time from 1 March 1886.

This primary school closed a number of times. The first period of operation was from its establishment in 1865 to 1895. It reopened between 1902 and 1925, and again in 1927 until its permanent closure in 1946.
name.official_title.title: Glenvale (Primary School No. 727)
title: Glenvale (Primary School No. 727)

description:
Darlington State School No. 777 opened on 14 April 1865.

It was located in the small town of Darlington on the Mount Emu Creek in Western Victoria. The primary school was established in the old Presbyterian Church building.

Ownership of the land and building was transferred from the Presbyterian Church to the Department of Education in 1868.

By 1886 the school operated on a part-time basis due to low enrolments, but regained full-time staffing in 1890. 

Darlington Primary School closed in 1977.
name.official_title.title: Darlington (Primary School No. 777)
title: Darlington (Primary School No. 777)

description:
Edenhope Common School No. 817 was established in 1865 with the construction of a three-room school building, replacing what was known as the ‘Bark School’, a single room building of bark slabs which had operated since about 1863.

In 1868 a rival Church of England school was established in the town. The two schools amalgamated when the teacher at the Common School left Edenhope. The primary school was gazetted as State School No. 817 in 1873 and relocated to a site on the corner of Elizabeth Street and Wallace Street.

In 1946 Edenhope Primary School became a Higher Elementary School, with classes for the older students held at the Showgrounds Pavilion. Bus routes from the Apsley, Goroke and Harrow districts were established to transport students to the school.

Edenhope then also became a Consolidated School and in 1956 the school moved again to the eastern shore of Lake Wallace. In 1959 Edenhope High School was also established in these buildings. A new block for primary classrooms was constructed further along the lake shore. The Consolidated and High Schools shared some facilities such as the bus service. 

The High School became Edenhope College which now educates children from Foundation to Year 12.
name.official_title.title: Edenhope (Primary School No. 817; Higher Elementary School from 1946)
title: Edenhope (Primary School No. 817; Higher Elementary School from 1946)

name.official_title.title: Kolora (Primary School No. 883; previously known as Glenormiston 1870-1892)
title: Kolora (Primary School No. 883; previously known as Glenormiston 1870-1892)

description:
Murroon State School No. 940 began as a Common School in 1868. 

The primary school operated continuously until its first closure in 1934. The school then reopened in 1946, and the Department of Education built a new school in 1964. 

However, by 16 December 1966 the primary school was permanently closed. The building was relocated to Elliminyt in March 1969.
name.official_title.title: Murroon (Primary School No. 940)
title: Murroon (Primary School No. 940)

description:
Graytown State School No. 1005 was established on 1 July 1869.

By 1877, the primary school was housed in a room at the local hotel, as the new school building first proposed in 1869 wasn’t constructed until 1878. The new building was vandalised with bullets in 1887, and then severely damaged in 1906 by a storm.

Within the first year of Graytown Primary School’s existence, enrolment had reached 100 students. However, the population of the former goldfields settlement decreased to the point that there were only 10 students enrolled by 1903.

The school closed in the 1920's, and the school building was transferred to another town along with the Catholic Church building in about 1960.
name.official_title.title: Graytown (Primary School No. 1005)
title: Graytown (Primary School No. 1005)

name.official_title.title: Waurn Ponds School
title: Waurn Ponds School (Primary School No. 1040)

description:
Chatsworth State School No. 1382 was first established in Chatsworth township in 1874. 

It was originally located in the old Presbyterian Church, with a new school building opening in 1902. A second classroom was added in 1958.

Many of the students came from families who worked on local stations, in particular Chatsworth House.

Chatsworth Primary School closed in the 1970's.
name.official_title.title: Chatsworth (Primary School No. 1382)
title: Chatsworth (Primary School No. 1382)

description:
Emberton State School No. 1450 opened on 17 September 1874.

Land including part of Allotment 9D of Section 1, in the Parish of Emberton, was gazetted as a school reserve in December 1873 in preparation for construction of the school. 

Residents were anxious that a primary school should be built, anticipating that the local Emberton Catholic School No. 1140 would close. However, the Catholic school didn’t close and so attendance at Emberton Primary School was lower than expected. Because of this, between 1884 and 1885 the school operated on a part-time basis with Edgecombe State School No. 277 (VA 4588).

In 1886 Emberton Primary School closed, and Edgecombe continued on as a full-time school. 

In 1892 the site was revoked as a school reserve.
name.official_title.title: Emberton (Primary School No. 1450)
title: Emberton (Primary School No. 1450)

description:
Durham Ox State School No. 1483 opened on 28 January 1875.

The primary school at first met in rooms previously used as a store and post office. In 1876 the school building was constructed.

Durham Ox Primary School closed in July 1945.
name.official_title.title: Durham Ox (Primary School No. 1483)
title: Durham Ox (Primary School No. 1483)

description:
Heathcote South State School No. 1520 was proposed in 1873 and established in 1875, when the Department of Education purchased an existing school (Heathcote Catholic School No. 315). The school was also known as Argyle.

By 1892, attendance at Heathcote South Primary School had fallen to the point at its amalgamation with the other local primary school, Heathcote State School No. 300, was proposed.

Heathcote South became an adjunct of Heathcote School in 1893 and the school grounds were not used.

In 1902 the school reopened, but then closed permanently in 1946.
name.official_title.title: Heathcote South (Primary School No. 1520; also known as Argyle)
title: Heathcote South (Primary School No. 1520; also known as Argyle)

description:
This school was opened on 29 November 1875 as Kellalac State School No. 1536. The primary school was located on land owned by Head Teacher Alexander Kennedy in the Werrigar district.

The school was later known as Werrigar, and then changed in 1909 to Ailsa, the name that Kennedy had given the area.

Due to the financial crisis of the 1890s the school operated on a part-time basis with Kellalac State School No. 1945.

The school closed in 1948 due to low enrolment. It reopened in 1957. Ailsa Primary School closed permanently in 1971.
name.official_title.title: Ailsa (Primary School No. 1536; previously known as Kellalac 1875-1876 and Werrigar 1911-1909)
title: Ailsa (Primary School No. 1536; previously known as Kellalac 1875-1876 and Werrigar 1911-1909)

description:
Both Foxhow and West Bank schools No. 1600 were opened in 1875, designed to operate as a pair of part-time primary schools under the same head teacher.

West Bank closed in 1883. Foxhow Primary School operated until 1971.
name.official_title.title: Foxhow (Primary School No. 1600; also known as Foxhow and West Bank)
title: Foxhow (Primary School No. 1600; also known as Foxhow and West Bank)

description:
Originally called Redruth, Wannon State School No. 1685 opened on 1 January 1876. As Redruth it also had two other school numbers, 768 and 1196.

In 1885, the school was worked part-time with Salt Pans State School No. 1041. In the early 1930s, the school was again worked part-time, this time with North Byaduk.

Wannon Primary School was closed for the duration of World War II. It closed permanently in 1976.
name.official_title.title: Wannon (Primary School No. 1685; previously known as Redruth)
title: Wannon (Primary School No. 1685; previously known as Redruth)

description:
Lake Rowan State School No. 1705 was opened on 24 April 1876.

The primary school was originally called Karrabumet, the name of the parish, but was soon after changed to Lake Rowan. The school was built on a site gazetted in Allotment 29.

In 1947, due to low enrolment, Lake Rowan became part-time with Pelluebla South State School No. 1929.

Lake Rowan Primary School closed on 27 November 1950 and arrangements were made for the local children to travel to Tungamah State School No. 2225.
name.official_title.title: Lake Rowan (Primary School No. 1705; previously known as Karrabumet 1876-1876)
title: Lake Rowan (Primary School No. 1705; previously known as Karrabumet 1876-1876)

description:
Gooram State School No. 1755 opened in August 1876. The primary school was originally called Upper Castle Creek; however the school came to be known as Gooram and the name was officially changed in 1897.

The original school building required repairs only a few months after opening, and it continued to deteriorate to the point that parents didn’t send their children in bad weather. When the local Presbyterian Church was built in 1887 the school moved there. In 1930 the school moved to a new site on Mansfield Road.

By 1923, Gooram was operating part-time with Seven Creeks State School No. 1815 until that school closed in 1929. 

Gooram Primary School closed in the 1970s.
name.official_title.title: Gooram (Primary School No. 1755; previous known as Upper Castle Creek 1876-1897)
title: Gooram (Primary School No. 1755; previous known as Upper Castle Creek 1876-1897)

description:
Rupanyup North State School No. 1758 opened on 22 September 1876. 

It was located in a building leased from the Primitive Methodist Church, located on Block 145 in the Parish of Rupanyup.

In 1890, the primary school moved to a new location at the north-west corner of Block 140 in the Parish of Lallat.

From 1884 to 1889 the primary school operated on a part-time basis with Burrereo State School No. 2180.

Rupanyup North Primary School closed in 1971.
name.official_title.title: Rupanyup North (Primary School No. 1758)
title: Rupanyup North (Primary School No. 1758)

description:
Lake Marmal State School No. 1827 opened around 1877 but the exact date is uncertain. 

In 1886 a fire destroyed the school building and the children had to travel to a neighbouring school until 1889. A public hall was then built in which the primary school reopened. 

A new school building was requested by parents in 1934, which opened in 1938. 

Due to insufficient enrolment, Lake Marmal Primary School closed in 1959.
name.official_title.title: Lake Marmal (Primary School No. 1827)
title: Lake Marmal (Primary School No. 1827)

description:
Tallangower State School No. 1871 opened in the 1870s, circa 1877.

The primary school was located west of Chetwynd, on the Tallangower Road.

The school sometimes operated on a part-time basis with Chetwynd East State School No. 2975 – first from 1899 to 1901, and again from 1903 to 1906. The school then closed, reopening in 1907 as a part-time school with Powers Creek State School No. 2217 until it closed again. 

Tallangower Primary School reopened again in 1920, but closed permanently in 1945.
name.official_title.title: Tallangower (Primary School No. 1871)
title: Tallangower (Primary School No. 1871)

description:
Catumnal State School No. 1977 opened on 28 January 1878. 

The primary school operated originally out of the Wesleyan Church in Marmal Parish in the County of Gladstone. Land on the west side of the church was gazetted in 1877 as land for a school building, which opened on 1 February 1881.

Catumnal Primary School first closed on 31 March 1910. The local parents subsequently leased the school building and opened a private school on 1 July the same year.

The school building was sold in 1919, but after requests that the school reopen, a new school was built and opened on 10 August 1924. 

By the beginning of 1945 the school was unstaffed, and it officially closed again on 20 March 1946. It reopened for the last time on 4 February 1948.

With only two pupils attending, Catumnal Primary School closed permanently on 4 March 1952.
name.official_title.title: Catumnal (Primary School No. 1977)
title: Catumnal (Primary School No. 1977)

description:
Ondit State School No. 2106 had opened by 1878, possibly as early as 1872. It was also known as Calverts’ Reserve.

The primary school was originally located on a site between Meredith Park Road and Coad’s Lane. It later moved to a new site approximately 2.4 kilometres north of the original location.

This was the second school opened in the area called Ondit. The first was State School No. 482, but the name of that school was changed to Beeac not long after it opened in 1862. 

For a number of years from August 1894, Ondit operated on a part-time basis with Turkeeth State School No. 3133.

In the 1920s the Irrewarra Soldier Settlement Scheme resulted in a sharp increase in the number of pupils. However, this didn’t last and the school closed briefly in 1945 and again for the final time in 1951.
name.official_title.title: Ondit (Primary School No. 2106; also known as Calverts' Reserve)
title: Ondit (Primary School No. 2106; also known as Calverts' Reserve)

description:
This primary school was originally opened as Wychitella South State School No. 2113 on 17 March 1879. 

When the school was known as Wychitella South, a schoolhouse was built in 1882 on a site in the south-east corner of Allotment 54, Parish of Wychitella. 

In about 1908, the Department had the school relocated to the north side of Allotment 47, Parish of Buckrabanyule. It was at this point the school became known as Wychitella North. 

Wychitella North Primary School closed in 1945.
name.official_title.title: Wychitella North (Primary School No. 2113; previously known as Wychitella South 1879-circa1908))
title: Wychitella North (Primary School No. 2113; previously known as Wychitella South 1879-circa1908))

description:
Originally known as Irrewarra State School No. 2218, this primary school opened on 25 November 1879.

Warncoort at first operated out of the local Methodist Church. The name of the school was changed from Irrewarra to Warncoort in 1904.

Warncoort Primary School closed in 1972.
name.official_title.title: Warncoort (Primary School No. 2218; previously known as Irrewarra 1879-1904)
title: Warncoort (Primary School No. 2218; previously known as Irrewarra 1879-1904)

description:
Minmindie State School No. 2289 opened in January 1881.

The primary school first opened with 62 enrolments. However, between 1904 and 1926 enrolment was low enough that the school operated on a part-time basis with Leaghur State School No. 2592, sharing the same teacher.

Minmindie Primary School closed on 2 January 1956.
name.official_title.title: Minmindie (Primary School No. 2289)
title: Minmindie (Primary School No. 2289)

description:
Murra Warra State School No. 2344 opened in 1881.

The primary school was located on Blue Ribbon Road. The original school building was used until 1963, when it was demolished and a new one constructed on the same site.

Murra Warra school closed in 1979.
name.official_title.title: Murra Warra (Primary School No. 2344)
title: Murra Warra (Primary School No. 2344)

description:
Gymbowen State School No. 2356 opened on 27 March 1881. 

The primary school was located at the east end of Lot 29B in the Parish of Gymbowen, County of Lowan. The same building was used for the entire life of the school with only minor alterations. 

Gymbowen Primary School closed on 31 August 1951. Students moved to Goroke School No. 2680, which at this time became a Consolidated School.
name.official_title.title: Gymbowen (Primary School No. 2356)
title: Gymbowen (Primary School No. 2356)

description:
Lallat North State School No. 2388 opened on 14 June 1881.

Lallat North Primary School first closed in 1902, and then reopened and closed several more times. 

The school operated as a part-time school with Lallat Plains State School No. 1686 between 1903 and 1909.

Lallat North Primary School closed permanently in December 1950.
name.official_title.title: Lallat North (Primary School No. 2388)
title: Lallat North (Primary School No. 2388)

description:
Langley Primary School opened on 30 August 1882 as Green Hill State School No. 2489. Shortly after the name was changed to Langley, as the school was quite far from Greenhill.

The school was opened because three existing schools in the area – Green Hills No. 277, Barfold No. 703, and Black Hill No. 1275 – were deemed too far away for the students.

The school was built on a site on the north-east corner of Allotment 41 in the Parish of Metcalf. Langley replaced Barfold school, which closed not long after Langley opened. 

Due to low enrolment, Langley Primary School closed permanently on 8 July 1902. 

School No. 1275 still operates and is now known as Langley Primary School.
name.official_title.title: Langley (Primary School No. 2489; previously known as Green Hill Emberton 1882-1885)
title: Langley (Primary School No. 2489; previously known as Green Hill Emberton 1882-1885)

description:
Dinyarrack State School No. 2556 opened on 14 August 1883 with an annual attendance of 26 students.

The school originally opened in a temporary location, until a school building could be constructed on part of Allotment 2 in the Parish of Dinyarrak, County Lowan. The site adjoined the Cove Station. A new school building opened in October 1885, and was also used for Sunday school, community gatherings, and as a receiving house for mail.

From 19 June 1905 Dinyarrack operated on a part-time basis with Leeor State School No. 2565. However, with attendances decreasing the school closed on 5 February 1909.

The school reopened as Serviceton North State School on 10 March 1919, but closed permanently on 20 October 1948.
name.official_title.title: Dinyarrack (Primary School No. 2556; known as Serviceton North 1919-1948)
title: Dinyarrack (Primary School No. 2556; known as Serviceton North 1919-1948)

description:
Lima State School No. 2561 opened on 1 October 1883.

From the beginning, the primary school was worked on a part-time basis with Swanpool State School No. 1310 from 1883, Rothesay State School No. 1438 from 1886, then Samaria West State School No. 2830 from 1888.

From 1889 Lima was full-time until it closed on 29 February 1892. On 2 July 1894 it reopened, again going part-time this time with Lima East State School No. 2889.

A school building was constructed on a new site in Allotment 46, Section A, Parish of Lima, and opened on 1 June 1897. Previously the school had operated out of a leased building. 

In 1938 Lima Primary School was made part-time again, first with Lima South State School No. 2658, then Tarnook State School No. 2833, and Samaria State School No. 893. In 1945, Lima went full-time again. 

In 1968 the school was unstaffed, and Lima School closed permanently on 18 June 1971.
name.official_title.title: Lima (Primary School No. 2561)
title: Lima (Primary School No. 2561)

description:
Yando State School No. 2580 opened on 21 July 1884.

The primary school originally operated out of a bark building with a dirt floor. A permanent school building was constructed in 1890.

Yando Primary School closed on 15 October 1957.
name.official_title.title: Yando (Primary School No. 2580; also known as Lake Leaghur)
title: Yando (Primary School No. 2580; also known as Lake Leaghur)

description:
Sandmount Primary School opened as Naringaningalook North State School No. 2595 on 10 December 1884.

It was located on Sandmount Road in the Parish of Yarroweyah, and eventually came to be known as Sandmount.

Sandmount Primary School closed permanently by 1978.
name.official_title.title: Sandmount (Primary School No. 2595; previously known as Naringaningalook North)
title: Sandmount (Primary School No. 2595; previously known as Naringaningalook North)

description:
Lima South State School No. 2658 opened on 16 February 1885.

From the beginning the primary school operated on a part-time basis with Barjarg State School No. 2169. By the end of 1887, Lima South was closed for the first time.

Though a site had been gazetted in 1880, there was no school building constructed and the school operated out of a leased building. The school reopened in the same building on 3 October 1889, but closed again on 26 July 1895.

In 1902 it was recommended that the school reopen, but only if the residents provided a building. WC Williams had a school built on freehold property at his own expense, which was then leased by the Department. Lima South reopened in 1903 part-time with Swanpool State School No. 1310. The original site that had been gazetted was then revoked.

Lima South State School became full-time on 2 June 1915, until it again closed on 10 June 1935. It reopened on 11 January 1938 part-time with Lima State School No. 2561, went full-time again on 3 June 1949, but was unstaffed by 1964.

Lima South Primary School closed permanently on 17 March 1970.
name.official_title.title: Lima South (Primary School No. 2658)
title: Lima South (Primary School No. 2658)

description:
Lawloit State School No. 2673 opened on 14 July 1885.

The primary school was located on a gazetted site on the south-west angle of the Lawloit township reserve.

From November 1893 the school was worked part-time with Lawloit North State School No. 3015. Then in 1900, Lawloit worked part-time with Lawloit West State School No. 3367 with both schools going back to full-time operations in 1904.

Lawloit Primary School closed on 17 March 1943.
name.official_title.title: Lawloit (Primary School No. 2673)
title: Lawloit (Primary School No. 2673)

description:
Lemon Springs Primary School opened as Mortat State School No. 2723 in June 1886. The name of the school was changed to Lemon Springs in 1887.

The school was located on Goroke-Kaniva Road.

It closed in 1924, reopening in the 1930s. Later that decade the school building burnt down, school lessons were conducted in a shed until a new building could be constructed in 1941. 

Lemon Springs Primary School closed by 1952, along with several other primary schools in the area due to the establishment of Goroke Consolidated School No. 2680.
name.official_title.title: Lemon Springs (Primary School No. 2723; previously known as Mortat 1886-1887)
title: Lemon Springs (Primary School No. 2723; previously known as Mortat 1886-1887)

description:
Nurcoung State School No. 2768 opened on 11 September 1886.

The primary school was located on Spring Hill sheep station. The original school building burnt down in 1916. The school occupied a leased building until a replacement was moved from Gravel Pits onto the original site in 1918. This building also burnt down several decades later, a replacement was built in 1945.

Due to decreasing enrolment, Nurcoung Primary School closed in 1955.
name.official_title.title: Nurcoung (Primary School No. 2768)
title: Nurcoung (Primary School No. 2768)

description:
Cororooke State School No. 2819 opened in 1887 or 1888.

The primary school was situated on the west side of the main road.

In 1952 Alvie State School No. 3038 was re-established as Alvie Consolidated School causing the closure of several primary schools in the area. One of these schools was Cororooke which closed in 1953.
name.official_title.title: Cororooke (Primary School No. 2819)
title: Cororooke (Primary School No. 2819)

description:
Duchembegarra Primary School was opened as Polkemmet State School No. 2851 on 27 January 1888.

The school was originally situated in the Bible Christian Church on the Polkemmet side of the Wimmera River. In 1889, the District Inspector suggested relocating the school to the Duchembegarra side of the river, and so the Church Trustees had the building moved. Reflecting the change in location, the school’s name was changed to Duchembegarra North in 1893.

In 1901 residents petitioned for a better school building, a new site was obtained and the new school opened in 1906.

The school closed and reopened twice more; in 1920 and 1927. Duchembegarra North Primary School closed permanently on 12 July 1955.
name.official_title.title: Duchembegarra North (Primary School No. 2851; previously known as Polkemmet 1888-1893)
title: Duchembegarra North (Primary School No. 2851; previously known as Polkemmet 1888-1893)

description:
Lochiel Bridge State School No. 2880 opened on 23 July 1888.

The primary school first operated out of the Lutheran Lions Church. Soon after, John Bushby donated a site on the south-east corner of his block in the Parish of Gerang Gerung for a permanent location. Once it was gazetted, a new school was built in 1889.

By 1946 the school was unstaffed, the students were then transferred to Dimboola State School No. 1372.

Lochiel Bridge school closed permanently on 5 June 1947.
name.official_title.title: Lochiel Bridge (Primary School No. 2880)
title: Lochiel Bridge (Primary School No. 2880)

description:
Lima East State School No. 2889 opened on 22 October 1888.

The primary school was located on a site in Allotment 5, Section C of the Parish of Lima. The school was originally housed in a temporary bark hut as the Department had not yet constructed a permanent school building on the gazetted site. In 1892 a closed school building from Moornang State School No. 2125 was transported to the Lima East site.

In 1897 the school operated part-time with Lima State School No. 2561.

In 1917 the school was moved to a new site in Allotment 5A, Section C of the Parish of Lima. This was due to frequent flooding around the old site. The reservation of the original site was revoked the following year. 

Due to low enrolment of only 4 students, the school was closed on 25 July 1945. It reopened on 10 March 1948.

Lima East Primary School closed permanently on 26 April 1971.
name.official_title.title: Lima East Primary School No. 2889)
title: Lima East Primary School No. 2889)

description:
Broughton State School (School No. 3094) (VA 795) was a coeducational primary school located in the Wimmera region of western Victoria.

The school first opened in 1889 under the Victorian Education Department (VA 714). 

The school closed on 22 March 1957, and the students were transported by bus to Kaniva Consolidated School (School No. 2531).
name.official_title.title: Broughton (Primary School No. 3094)
title: Broughton State School (School No. 3094)

description:
This primary school first opened as Tarranyurk State School No. 3121 on 18 August 1891. The name of the school was later changed to Pepper’s Plains.

The school originally operated out of a building used for Baptist church services and other community meetings. 

The Department had a permanent school building constructed in 1921, situated a few hundred metres west of the original building. 

From 1928 to 31 March 1929, the school operated part-time with Tarranyurk South State School No. 3087, after which it went full-time again. In 1951, the school was unstaffed.

Pepper’s Plains Primary School closed permanently on 31 May 1955.
name.official_title.title: Pepper's Plains (Primary School No. 3121; previously known as Tarranyurk North)
title: Pepper's Plains (Primary School No. 3121; previously known as Tarranyurk North)

description:
Nurcoung South State School No. 3157 opened on 14 June 1892.

The primary school operated out of a leased room on a farm owned by J Buffman.

In 1904 the school closed due to low enrolment. On 13 July 1936 the school reopened with 11 students on a new site.

In January 1944 the school was partially destroyed in a bushfire, the surviving building was relocated to its final location on the main road.

Nurcoung South Primary School closed permanently in November 1955.
name.official_title.title: Nurcoung South (Primary School No. 3157)
title: Nurcoung South (Primary School No. 3157)

description:
This primary school opened as Cororooke West State School No. 3189 in August 1893. It was also known as Nalangil.

The school was situated on the north-west corner of the junction of McGrath’s Road and Nalangil Road.

In 1952 Alvie State School No. 3038 was re-established as Alvie Consolidated School, causing the closure of several primary schools in the area. One of these was Nalangil Primary School which closed in 1953. 

Students were then transported by bus to Alvie. The Nalangil school building was also incorporated into the Alvie Consolidated School.
name.official_title.title: Nalangil (Primary School No. 3189; also known as Cororooke West)
title: Nalangil (Primary School No. 3189; also known as Cororooke West)

description:
Glenormiston State School No. 3207 opened in 1898. 

In 1908 the original school building fell into disrepair and a new building was constructed and used for the remaining years of the school’s existence.

Although it was unstaffed from the end of 1977, Glenormiston Primary School officially closed in 1979.
name.official_title.title: Glenormiston (Primary School No. 3207)
title: Glenormiston (Primary School No. 3207)

description:
Ullswater State School No. 3231 opened on 25 May 1895.

In 1878 a site in Allotment 74 of the Parish of Awonga was gazetted for establishment of a school, but there was not a sufficient number of students to enrol and so the site was never used. At this time a part-time private school was being operated in the town. 

When the state primary school opened it operated out of a leased building belonging to Thomas Dixon. 

In 1898 the school was run part-time with Jallakin State School No. 2780, and then closed in 1899. In 1902 Thomas Dixon had a new building constructed on his property and the school reopened there on 27 February 1903. A permanent site was purchased from him and a school building from Bringalbert North State School No. 2569 was relocated to the new Ullswater site in 1914.

In 1933 the school again ran part-time with Jallakin, before becoming full-time on 27 January 1937.

Ullswater Primary School closed permanently on 17 November 1949.
name.official_title.title: Ullswater (Primary School No. 3231)
title: Ullswater (Primary School No. 3231)

description:
Beech Forest Primary School originally opened as Weeaproinah State School No. 3235 on 29 July 1895.

The school closed in 1900 when the leased building it was operating in was no longer available. The Department acquired another building the following year and the school reopened on a part-time basis with Moorbanool State School No. 3247.

In 1909 or 1910 the school was destroyed in a fire. Shortly after this a new building was made available on the Colac Road, and the school reopened as Beech Forest. It was also known to locals as Ditchley, likely after the nearby Ditchley Park Estate. 

In the 1950s a number of students left the school when Lavers Hill State School No. 3569 was reconstituted as a Consolidated School. However, some students stayed on and the school didn’t close at this time. 

Beech Forest Primary School closed permanently in 1981.
name.official_title.title: Beech Forest (Primary School No. 3235; previously known as Weeaproinah 1895-1910; also known as Ditchley)
title: Beech Forest (Primary School No. 3235; previously known as Weeaproinah 1895-1910; also known as Ditchley)

description:
Humevale Primary School opened as Scrubby Creek State School No. 3300 on 18 February 1898.

A representative of the residents of Scrubby Creek petitioned the Minister to establish a school on an existing reserve site in 1894. In 1897 residents built a hall themselves on the reserve for the school to operate in when it opened the following year. 

In the 1920s the school’s name was changed to Humevale. 

Humevale Primary School was unstaffed in July 1968 and closed permanently.
name.official_title.title: Humevale (Primary School No. 3300; previously known as Scrubby Creek 1898-1920s)
title: Humevale (Primary School No. 3300; previously known as Scrubby Creek 1898-1920s)

description:
Tullyvea State School No. 3310 opened on 3 May 1898. 

The primary school originally operated in a mud brick building that was also used for church services and various entertainment activities. This was later replaced with a weatherboard building that was destroyed by fire in 1934, the school then relocated to a local church building until a new school building could be opened the following year. 

Due to low enrolment, Tullyvea Primary School closed permanently on 4 March 1953.
name.official_title.title: Tullyvea (Primary School No. 3310)
title: Tullyvea (Primary School No. 3310)

description:
Nalinga State School No. 3333 opened on 20 June 1899.

The primary school was originally housed in an old leased hotel. A permanent building was constructed on a site in the north-east corner of Block 17A, which had been gazetted in 1878. It opened in January 1903. 

The school was worked on a part-time basis with Upotipotpon South State School No. 2913 from 20 September 1909. On 15 March 1915 it became part-time with Gowangardie State School No. 2873, until it closed only a few months later on 19 August. The school building was later removed. 

On 29 January 1934 the school opened again, this time on a new site in Allotment 6A in the Parish of Gowangardie, with the old building from Youarang North State School No. 2301 being transferred onto the site.

Nalinga Primary School closed permanently on 16 October 1967.
name.official_title.title: Nalinga (Primary School No. 3333)
title: Nalinga (Primary School No. 3333)

description:
Eurack State School No. 3448 opened in 1903.

The primary school was opened after the Eurack Estate was subdivided for settlement, and was located on what is now known as Eurack Road in the small township. 

In May 1916 the schoolchildren planted the trees for the Eurack Avenue of Honour in front of the school. This project was initiated by the head teacher George Pentreath, who enlisted two months later. It was the first known Avenue of Honour in Victoria. 

Eurack Primary School closed around 1976.
name.official_title.title: Eurack (Primary School No. 3448)
title: Eurack (Primary School No. 3448)

description:
Meatian West Primary School (School No. 3464) (VA 807) first opened in February 1904 as Meatian State School. The co-educaitonal primary school was located approximately 10km south of Ultima in the Rural City of Swan Hill, Victoria, the school initially operated from a leased building purchased by local residents from the former Kaneira School (School No. 3246) and erected on the school site in 1903.

At its opening, Meatian State School operated part-time with Ultima State School (School No. 3426), sharing a single teacher who divided their time between both sites. Average attendance was around 13 students at the time. Further information on when Meatian State School was made full time is subject to further research.

The building was extended in 1907 to almost double its original size, but by 1920 it had fallen into disrepair despite ongoing maintenance efforts. In January 1925, a permanent wooden school building was opened west of Meatian in the Parish of Murningin, and the school was relocated and the lease on the earlier site was terminated. A shelter pavilion was added in 1927.

In July 1930, the school was renamed Meatian West State School to reduce confusion with Meatian Railway Station School (School No. 3761) (VA 819) and to reflect its location west of the railway station and township.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Meatian Primary School around this time.

Meatian West Primary School likely ceased operation around 1974, with the site possibly remaining as a “ghost school” (destaffed but not formally closed) until it was permanently closed in March 1976.  The site was sold by public auction in September 1983.
title: Meatian West Primary School (School No. 3464; previously known as Meatian State School 1904 – 1930; Meatian West State School 1930 – c.1970)

description:
Eden Park State School No. 3477 opened on 20 April 1904.

The primary school started in a leased building; by the end of 1914 a permanent school building had been constructed.

Eden Park Primary School closed in 1942.
name.official_title.title: Eden Park (Primary School No. 3477)
title: Eden Park (Primary School No. 3477)

description:
Kelvin View Primary School opened as Kelvin View State School No. 3480 on 1 August 1904.

The school originally operated out of a disused house. In 1906 locals met to establish a permanent school and John Nelson donated a new site for a school building. When the new school opened the name changed to Kelvin Grove. 

Kelvin Grove Primary School closed in 1970.
name.official_title.title: Kelvin View (Primary School No. 3480; also knowm as Kelvin Grove)
title: Kelvin View (Primary School No. 3480; also knowm as Kelvin Grove)

description:
Stonyford State School No. 3506 opened on 24 April 1906.

The primary school was located about one kilometre off the Princes Highway in the Stony Rises. The town was spelled both as Stonyford and Stoneyford.

Stonyford Primary School closed in the 1970s.
name.official_title.title: Stonyford (Primary School No. 3506)
title: Stonyford (Primary School No. 3506)

description:
Strathkellar State School No. 3536 opened on 9 January 1907.

A primary school was needed when in 1906 the large property, Strathkellar, was divided for closer settlement causing an influx of families to the area.

The school was quite successful, with a peak of around 100 enrolments in 1916. However, in later decades enrolments declined significantly along with the population.

Strathkellar Primary School closed at the end of 1970.
name.official_title.title: Strathkellar (Primary School No. 3536)
title: Strathkellar (Primary School No. 3536)

description:
Waitchie State School No. 3568 opened on 18 January 1908.

The primary school was originally located in a public hall. In 1916 a permanent school building was constructed west of Waitchie station on what was known at the time as the Swan Hill Road.

Waitchie Primary School closed around 1974.
name.official_title.title: Waitchie (Primary School No. 3568)
title: Waitchie (Primary School No. 3568)

description:
Booroopki State School No. 3607 opened on 1 March 1909.

From its opening day, it operated on a part-time basis with Morea State School No. 3285. Prior to Booroopki opening, some local children had already been attending Morea, and others Minimay State School No. 2600. Its establishment resulted in reduced enrolments at Morea. 

Booroopki was established on the Lemon Springs Estate, south-west of Goroke. The primary school originally operated in a leased room in a private house owned by Daniel Carrucher. 

Due to low attendance, the school closed on 18 May 1916. On 27 January 1937 the school reopened and was worked part-time with Jallakin State School No. 2780.

By 11 September 1951, Booroopki Primary School was unstaffed. When the school closed permanently, the students were sent to Goroke State School No. 2680, which had just been reconstituted as a Consolidated School. This caused the closure of several primary schools in the area.
name.official_title.title: Booroopki (Primary School No. 3607)
title: Booroopki (Primary School No. 3607)

description:
Noorat Estate State School No. 3609 opened in 1912.

The primary school was located in Noorat East, and was established due to overcrowding in nearby schools such as Glenormiston State School No. 3207.

Noorat Estate Primary School closed in 1956.
name.official_title.title: Noorat Estate (Primary School No. 3609)
title: Noorat Estate (Primary School No. 3609)

description:
Berrybank State School No. 3639 opened on 1 February 1910.

The primary school originally operated out of a leased shearer’s hut, but soon moved to its permanent location on the Hamilton Highway. 

In 1911 an existing school building from Cressy State School No. 731 was transferred to the site, and was used until destroyed by fire in 1944. Another second-hand school building was brought in to replace it, this time from Dereel State School No. 748. 

Before the school was established, local children had travelled to either Lismore State School No. 1293 or Foxhow State School No. 1600.

Berrybank Primary School closed in 1976. Many of the students then transferred to Lismore primary school. The school building still exists on the Hamilton Highway and is now the Berrybank Hall.
name.official_title.title: Berrybank (Primary School No. 3639)
title: Berrybank (Primary School No. 3639)

description:
Metcalfe East State School No. 3658 opened on 1 September 1910.

The primary school was opened specifically to be worked part-time with Black Hill State School No. 1275, which had previously closed down. It reopened and the schools shared a teacher who taught at one in the morning and the other in the afternoon. 

In 1915 the Department decided to replace both schools with a new school in a more central location.
This became Langley State School No. 1275.

Metcalfe East Primary School closed on 17 July 1915.
name.official_title.title: Metcalfe East (Primary School No. 3658)
title: Metcalfe East (Primary School No. 3658)

description:
Meatian State School No. 3761 opened in 1912.

It was originally located in Meatian Hall. In 1924 the school moved to a new site adjacent to the railway station, and a new school building was constructed. It was destroyed in 1954, requiring a building from Jeffcott to be moved to the site to replace it.

The school was also known as Meatian Railway Station School.

Meatian Primary School closed around 1976.
name.official_title.title: Meatian (Primary School No. 3761)
title: Meatian (Primary School No. 3761)

description:
Vite Vite State School No. 3781 opened on 31 March 1913. 

The primary school was originally located in a leased hall. This continued until 1949, when a new site facing Skipton Road was donated by CO Fairbairn and the old building from Mingay State School
No. 3773 was moved there. 

In 1935 the name of the school was changed to Banongill. Then on 18 March 1952 the name was changed again, this time to Vite Vite North. 

Vite Vite North Primary School closed in 1970.
name.official_title.title: Vite Vite (Primary School No. 3781; subsequently known as Banongill 1935-1952 and Vite Vite North 1952-1970)
title: Vite Vite (Primary School No. 3781; subsequently known as Banongill 1935-1952 and Vite Vite North 1952-1970)

description:
Carranballac State School No. 3876 opened on 1 December 1914.

The primary school originally operated out of a hall, one end set up as a school and the opposite end containing a pulpit and organ. The hall was located on the corner of Glenelg Highway and Darlington Road.

Initially the school had only 14 students enrolled in grades 1-4.

On 23 April 1921 the school opened on a new site on the south-west corner of Glenelg Highway and Darlington Road in a purpose-built school building. 

In 1953 a bus route to the school was established. 

Due to the soldier settlement scheme rolling out in the area, enrolment increased significantly in the 1950s. In 1956 enrolment reached 47 so a new prefabricated building was added to the school; in 1959 another was added.

By 1969 enrolment was again decreasing, due to soldier settlers leaving the area and their children aging out of the primary school.

Carranballac Primary School closed in 1978.
name.official_title.title: Carranballac (Primary School No. 3876)
title: Carranballac (Primary School No. 3876)

description:
Pullut State School No. 3912 opened on 23 November 1915.

The primary school was located on a site on the south-east corner of Allotment 57, Parish of Pullut in the County of Karkarooc. The site and the building were offered for free by JT Sleep. 

Pullut State School closed on 30 June 1917 when the lease on this building was terminated and an alternative location could not be found.

The school reopened on 24 April 1922, on a new site in Allotment 17, Parish of Hindmarsh in the County of Borung. The site was given to the Department by A McKenzie and a new school building was constructed.

From 21 April 1942 to 22 September 1942 Pullut was worked part-time with Werrap State School 
No. 3287 due to low enrolment, before reverting back to full-time when Werrap closed.

Pullut Primary School closed permanently on 19 October 1951.
name.official_title.title: Pullut (Primary School No. 3912)
title: Pullut (Primary School No. 3912)

description:
Fairholme Primary School opened as Whoorel State School No. 3972 on 29 July 1918.

The school was located on what was known then as Barwon Downs Road. H Lidgerwood and AJ Brien both provided an acre each for the site.

Before the school was established, local children had attended Murroon State School No. 940. Whoreel opened with 12 enrolments, 8 of those from the same family.

On 4 October 1918 the school’s Committee changed the name of the school to Fairholme, likely after Brien’s Fairholme estate. 

Due to low enrolment, Fairholme Primary School closed permanently on 23 August 1968.
name.official_title.title: Fairholme (Primary School No. 3972; previously known as Whoorel 1918-1918)
title: Fairholme (Primary School No. 3972; previously known as Whoorel 1918-1918)

description:
Wilgul State School No. 3980 opened on 15 November 1918.

Due to low enrolment, Wilgul Primary School closed permanently in 1965. The school building was transferred to the Colac Technical School.
name.official_title.title: Wilgul (Primary School No. 3980)
title: Wilgul (Primary School No. 3980)

description:
Gowanford Primary School opened on 1 July 1920 as Gowan State School No. 4026.

The school was located on a site donated by J Conway. In 1926 the name was changed to Gowanford. 

In October 1944 the school building was destroyed by a fire. The school didn’t reopen until 1946 when a building from Swan Hill West State School No. 4553 was transferred to the Gowanford site.

The school closed again from 1947 to 1951. 

Gowanford Primary School closed permanently in 1977.
name.official_title.title: Gowanford (Primary School No. 4026; previously known as Gowan 1920-1926)
title: Gowanford (Primary School No. 4026; previously known as Gowan 1920-1926)

description:
Ripple Vale State School (School No. 4125) (VA 830) was a co-educational primary school located in the town of Rickett’s Marsh, near Birregurra. 

The school first opened in 1922 as Ripple Vale State School, named after the Ripple Vale property on which the school was located. It was situated on Conns Lane, near the corner of Cape Otway Road. The school building provided had previously been used for Armytage State School (School No. 3775), which had operated in the same region from 1913 to 1921, and was relocated for use at Ripple Vale. 

On 22 February 1964, a new building was opened and the original building was demolished. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Ripple Vale Primary School. 

Ripple Vale Primary School became unstaffed in 1979 and subsequently closed. 

The school and area may sometimes be stylised as Ripplevale instead of Ripple Vale.

description:
Bradvale State School No. 4134 opened on 6 November 1922.

The primary school originally operated from an old church building that had been brought in to the town from Smythesdale. The church was destroyed in a fire in 1944. 

The school’s permanent location was 715 Crawford Road, where the old school building that replaced the church remains. 

Bradvale Primary School closed in the late 1970s.

title: Bradvale (Primary School No. 4134)

description:
Drung Drung South State School No. 4179 opened on 13 January 1924.

The primary school was required after several families moved into what was the Ballyglunin Park Estate east of Horsham, a soldier settlement area. The school opened with 32 students enrolled.

The school was located on the Western Highway.

Drung Drung South Primary School is now closed.
name.official_title.title: Drung Drung South (Primary School No. 4179; also known as Drung South)
title: Drung Drung South (Primary School No. 4179; also known as Drung South)

description:
Mount Camel State School No. 4288 opened in 1926.

The primary school originally operated in the local public hall. On 10 May 1927 it opened in a new school building.

In 1946 the school was unstaffed, due to both a shortage of teachers and low attendance. In July the same year, the local District Inspector recommended that the school remain closed permanently.

Mount Camel Primary School officially closed on 17 September 1946.

The school buildings were relocated to the Higher Elementary School Heathcote State School No. 300.

description:
Peronne State School No. 4335 opened in 1928.

The primary school was located on Allotment 24A, Parish of Mortat in the County of Lowan. This site later became the location of the Peronne Memorial Hall. 

The school was originally proposed to be worked part-time with Morea State School No. 3285, but it closed in 1928. The following year, the building from Morea was moved to Peronne to be used as a shelter shed. 

In the 1940s enrollments declined, and in 1947 the school was unstaffed until June. Peronne Primary School closed permanently on 19 December 1950 due to low enrollment.

From the following year local students travelled by bus to Goroke State School No. 2680 which had become a Group School in 1950 and then a Consolidated School in 1955.

title: Peronne (Primary School No. 4335)

description:
Dalcross State School No. 4381 opened on 27 April 1928.

The primary school was located in what had been a soldier settler’s home which had been converted to function as a school building. 

The school was named for the local Dalcross Station, which had been partly used for soldier settlement allotments. 

Dalcross Primary School closed in 1946.
name.official_title.title: Dalcross (Primary School No. 4381)
title: Dalcross (Primary School No. 4381)

description:
Ozenkadnook South State School No. 4397 opened in June 1928.

The primary school was located in a building provided by J. Pahl of Ullswater. He had earlier proposed that the school be opened to work part-time with Ullswater State School No. 3231, while the local District Inspector had proposed that the school should be opened to work part-time with Jallakin State School No. 2780. 

Ozenkadnook South only operated for two years before it first closed. Residents suggested that the school be reopened on a new, more central site. When a building was provided, the Department had the school reopened on 18 August 1932. 

Ozenkadnook South Primary School closed on 2 September 1948, with all of the students being transported to Edenhope State School No. 817. Edenhope became a Consolidated School just a few years later in 1952.

description:
Chesney Vale State School No. 4403 opened on 22 July 1928.

On 14 April 1930 the primary school relocated from its original temporary site to a new site where the building from the closed Mokoan West State School No. 2501 had been re-erected. 

Due to attendance falling to 3 students, Chesney Vale closed in 1944. It reopened the following year but closed again in 1949. 

In 1955, the building was relocated to a site on Allotment 69A in the Parish of Mokoan, at the intersection of McGann Hill Road and Old Lake Mokoan Road, and the school reopened there on 3 March 1958. However, it was later realised that this site would be inundated by the soon to be constructed Lake Mokoan.

In 1969 the school relocated again, this time to a site on Allotment 90, and the building from closed Wilby State School No. 2288 was moved there. 

Chesney Vale Primary School closed around 1973.

description:
Nullawil South West State School No. 4452 opened on 23 October 1929. 

The primary school originally operated out of a hut on a property belonging to E. Ryan. On 8 April 1934 the school moved to a site belonging to A. Murray in a new weatherboard school building. 

Nullawil South West Primary School closed in 1971.
name.official_title.title: Nullawil South West School (Primary School No. 4452)
title: Nullawil South West School (Primary School No. 4452)

description:
Whitlands State School (School No. 4536) (VA 842) was a coeducational primary school located on the Whitlands High Plateau, above the Western side of the King Valley in North-East Victoria. 

Whitlands State School first opened in 1935, after local parents organised the construction of a suitable building at Big Hole Creek, which was leased by the Department of Education (VA 714). 

Attendance at the school declined, however, and Whitlands was too remote to be worked part-time with another school, so the school closed in 1946. It reopened at the end of 1962 but was unstaffed by the end of 1969.

Whitlands State School closed permanently in 1971. Following the closure, students were transported by bus to Whitfield State School (School No. 2441).
title: Whitlands State School (School No. 4536)

description:
King Parrot Creek State School No. 4591 opened on 13 March 1941.

The primary school was located in a building that the local residents had had constructed. The school was opened after a request for a new school between Flowerdale and Kinglake West, the District Inspector had also recommended the opening of a full-time school.

The school was unstaffed in 1944 and 1945, before gaining a teacher again in 1946.

King Parrot Creek Primary School closed permanently on 7 July 1947.
name.official_title.title: King Parrot Creek (Primary School No. 4591)
title: King Parrot Creek (Primary School No. 4591)

description:
Benalla Aerodrome State School No. 4651 opened on 16 November 1949.

The primary school was located in the Benalla Migrant Camp, a Commonwealth Immigration Department residential facility for new migrants who were not from a British or English-speaking background. The school buildings were the former instruction huts used for training by the Royal Australian Air Force. The school buildings also housed the camp library.

The students who attended the school generally had very little English when they started. The school had a focus on preparing the children to assimilate into the Australian community by teaching them to speak English and involving them in community engagement activities such as raising money for the local hospital. Some students did continue to speak their native languages to each other, wear European-style clothing and play European games.

The length of attendance varied, with some students staying only a few months before their family moved into the Australian community. Others attended the school for years as their parents didn’t or couldn’t leave the Migrant Camp.

Some students would continue their education after leaving the Benalla Aerodrome school by attending Benalla High School. 

Benalla Aerodrome Primary School closed on 11 September 1963. The students moved to Benalla East State School No. 2256.

The Benalla Migrant Camp closed in 1967, and was added to the Victorian Heritage Register in 2016.
name.official_title.title: Benalla Aerodrome (Primary School No. 4651)
title: Benalla Aerodrome (Primary School No. 4651)

description:
Warrambeen Primary School opened as Wurrook South State School No. 4793 in February 1957.

The school opened in an annexe to the Leigh Shire Hall at Warrambine Creek. The name of the school was changed to Warrambeen in September 1957. 

There had previously been a school in the Warrambine Creek area, Warrambine State School No. 1793, which had closed in 1882. Soldier settlement in the Wurrook South area necessitated the opening of a new school in the 1950s as the population increased.

In 1959, a new site adjacent to the Hall was provided by Leigh Shire for the school, and the old school building from closed Duverney State School No. 3970 was relocated there. 

Warrambeen Primary School closed in 1971.

description:
Horsham East State School No. 4799 opened on 4 February 1958.

The primary school opened in a single room on the School Road, at a site on property selected by
AB White in the Parish of Horsham, County of Borung. 

The school was required due to several families moving into a soldier settlement area in Drung in 1955.

The school was proposed by the Soldier Settlement Commission to cater for these families. 39 students were enrolled on opening day.

Horsham East Primary School closed in 1972.

description:
The Melbourne Branch of the Royal Mint was established by Order-in-Council on 10 August 1869 and was opened for coinage in 1872. It was intended by its operation to stabilise the price of gold by providing a local market and to convert gold into a legally acceptable form. The Mint was under the sole control of the United Kingdom Treasury and its employees were classed as officers of the British Civil Service. Only as a branch of the Royal Mint could it mint sovereigns and half-sovereigns which were Imperial coins. Gold coins were minted until 1931. After that, gold refined was cast into fine gold bars for export.

After Federation a demand developed for a distinctive Australian currency and this was authorised by the Australian Coinage Act 1909. Australian silver coin minted in London was issued between 1910 and 1915 and bronze coin minted in England and India was issued from 1911 to 1919. During World War I, this local token coinage was undertaken by the Australian branch mints and the first issues of silver minted at Melbourne were made in 1916 and issues of bronze were made in 1919.

For many years the major activity of the Melbourne Mint was the production of coin for the Commonwealth Government with all the silver coin and a large part of the bonze produced in Melbourne. The original functions of the purchase and refining of gold continued though their importance was relatively reduced by the decrease in gold production. Gold and silver in various forms and alloys was prepared and supplied to manufacturers and others with medals of gold, silver or bronze being struck for various bodies.

In May 1970 Queen Elizabeth II issued a Proclamation discontinuing the Melbourne Branch of the Royal Mint from July 1 1970.

Other records relating to the establishment of the Royal Mint, Melbourne Branch may be found in VPRS 1099 Files on the Royal Mint.

title: Royal Mint, Melbourne Branch

Camberwell was first incorporated as the Boroondara Road District on 11 July 1854, which became the Shire of Boroondara on 17 November 1871.

The shire was renamed to the Shire of Camberwell and Boroondara on 16 May 1902.

It became a Borough on 28 April 1905, a Town on 15 May 1906, and was proclaimed a City on 20 April 1914.

description:
Appointment of Colonial Secretary

Charles Joseph La Trobe remained Superintendent of the Port Phillip District until 1850 when he was re-appointed Lieutenant-Governor in the new Crown Colony which came formally into existence on 13 January 1851. The Colonial Secretary was the chief official of Government during the period 1851 to 1855.

Functions Administered by the Colonial Secretary

Functions inherited from the Superintendent and administered directly through the Colonial Secretary's Office included:
  • census and statistics
  • education
  • goldfields administration, including the Chinese on the goldfields
  • health
  • immigration
  • libraries
  • police administration and prisons
  • ’protection’ of Aboriginal Victorians
  • management and sale of Crown Lands
  • public works and buildings
  • roads and bridges
The Colonial Secretary also came to have responsibility for the care and treatment of psychiatrically ill patients ("lunatics"), recording births, deaths and marriages, the registration of theatre licences, and the Colony's first art gallery and museum. In 1854 and 1855 the Colonial Secretary also was responsible for the Gold Office.

Aboriginal Victorians
Note: These records contain words, descriptions and information used in the past that may be insensitive or offensive and can be upsetting.

The Protectorate system established in 1839 under Chief Protector George Robinson (VA 512) continued until 1849 when The Guardian of Aborigines (VA 513) was appointed following a Select Committee report which recommended the abolition of the Protectorate. The Guardian was solely responsible for providing "protection to Aborigines" and the Crown Land Commissioners were appointed as honorary protectors, their duties being to visit reserves, report on the condition of Aboriginal Peoples and supply Aboriginal Peoples with food and clothing "in cases of extreme emergency".

Census and Statistics, Registration of Births, Deaths and Marriages

Collection of statistics and periodic census taking was at first the responsibility of the Statistics Branch of the Colonial Secretary's Office. In 1853 compulsory registration of births, deaths and marriages was introduced under the Births, Deaths, and Marriages Act 16 Vic., No.26 and the Registrar-General's Department (VA 2889) was established to administer this function. It also took over responsibilities relating to census and statistics. Prior to 1853 the births, deaths and marriages records were maintained by the churches. 

Education

Early schools were run by religious organisations. In 1848 a Board of National Education (VA 920) and a Denominational School Board had been established in New South Wales to regulate denominational schools and provide for government funded education. In the Port Phillip District a Denominational School Board (VA 703) had been set up in the same year to regulate and inspect the secular aspects of denominational schools supported by public funding. In 1852 the Victorian National Schools Board (VA 919) was established with responsibility for regulating government schools, appointing teachers and maintaining school buildings.

Health
Note: These records contain words, descriptions and information used in the past that may be insensitive or offensive and can be upsetting.

A small general hospital had been established in Melbourne in 1841 under Assistant Colonial Surgeon Cussen. By 1851, following separation from New South Wales, the civil establishment for the Medical Department, which was responsible to the Colonial Secretary, included the Colonial Surgeon, Melbourne, who was also Surgeon to the Gaol and Surgeon to the Lunatic Asylum, the District Surgeon, Geelong, a Dispenser and the Superintendent and staff of the Lunatic Asylum at Yarra Bend (VA 2839). By 1852 there were also Assistant Colonial Surgeons in Melbourne, Geelong, Williamstown and Ovens and by 1854 District Surgeons had also been appointed to Portland, Belfast, Castlemaine, Sandhurst, Ballarat, Avoca, Beechworth, Kyneton and Kilmore. Other medical staff were based at Pentridge and at the hospitals established on the goldfields at Castlemaine, Sandhurst and Ballarat.

The Chief Medical Officer and the Medical Officers in Melbourne were responsible for immigrants from the time of their landing until their departure from the Immigration Depot, for the police, and for the officers and prisoners in gaols and stockades. In the seaport towns and the goldfields they were responsible for immigrants, police, military, prisoners and officers of the gold commission.

The Health Officer, who was primarily concerned with quarantine, was Superintendent of the Sanitary Station which had been established in 1852 at Ticonderoga Bay, Point Nepean, until 1853 when he was transferred to Queenscliff and ordered to board every inward bound ship and ascertain the state of health of its passengers and crew and where necessary to place the ship in quarantine.

In 1855, under the provisions of the Public Health Act 18 Vic.,No.13 (1854), the Central Board of Health was established and became responsible for the prevention, containment and treatment of infectious and contagious diseases; the construction and maintenance of adequate drains and sewers; the regulation of noxious trades; the enforcement of standards of proper sanitation; regulation of the preparation and sale of food and drink; the compulsory vaccination of children; and the registration and control of common lodging houses. Local Boards of Health, which were effectively the municipal councils, also had a significant role in the administration of public health. 

Prior to 1848 psychiatric patients were detained in the District's gaols or sent to the asylum in New South Wales. The first permanent asylum in Victoria was built at Yarra Bend in 1848 (VA 2839). When it first opened it was officially a ward of the Asylum at Tarban Creek in New South Wales. However responsibility for the administration of the asylum was shared between the Superintendent of the Asylum and the Colonial Surgeon as part of his general responsibility for Health. They reported to the Colonial Secretary.

Immigration

The Colonial Secretary's Office was responsible for administering immigration in conjunction with the British Emigration Agent in London, who supervised the selection of applicants and arranged for their passage. In carrying out this function the British Emigration Agent and the Colonial Secretary's Office were assisted by locally appointed Immigration Agents. Between 1851 and 1855 over 350,000 migrants arrived under Government funded and sponsored schemes, as well as unassisted. During the Gold Rush period, 1851 to 1861, most migrants paid their own way and Government Schemes were largely eclipsed. The responsibilities of the Colonial Secretary's Office included local administration of Government funded assisted immigration schemes, reception and initial settlement of immigrants, as well as monitoring immigrant arrivals including inspection of ships and certification of passenger lists, and regulating alien (non-British of foreign) immigration.

Management and Sale of Crown Lands

Commissioners of Crown Lands were appointed to regulate the use of Crown Land under licence, manage Crown Lands and supervise their sale. The Commissioners reported to the Colonial Secretary and received administrative support from the Land Branch of the Colonial Secretary's Office until 1853 when the Department of Crown Lands (VA 2878) was established 
Public Works and Buildings, Roads and Bridges

The first public works and road building were undertaken by convict labourers overseen by the military detachment responsible for guarding them. The first Clerk of Works was appointed in mid 1837 and the first Overseer of Roads in September. Plans for the settlement's early public buildings were prepared by the Colonial Architect in Sydney but the locally appointed Clerk of Works took direction from the Police Magistrate and subsequently the Superintendent.

A Superintendent of Bridges was appointed in 1844 with responsibility for overseeing a range of public works, including roads and bridges. In May 1846, Henry Ginn was appointed Clerk of Works and by 1850, the civil establishment for public works included the Clerk of Works, Superintendent of Bridges, six overseers and clerks, a clerk and a messenger.

The period between separation from New South Wales in 1851 and the achievement of responsible government in 1855 was characterised by a large expansion in revenue, population, the size of the colonial administration and the need for public works and buildings. During this period the structure of the administration was re-organised a number of times. In 1851 the Colonial Architect was responsible for the construction, maintenance, rental and furnishing of public buildings while the Superintendent of Bridges was responsible for roads and bridges and other public works. By October 1852 a Colonial Engineer had been appointed at a salary twice that received by the other two officials and appears to have exercised joint responsibility with them. By 1854 there had been an amalgamation of the functions of the Colonial Engineer and the Colonial Architect, the latter position having been abolished, and while the position of Superintendent of Bridges remained, it was clearly subordinate to that of the Colonial Engineer. Each of these officials was responsible to the Colonial Secretary.

In 1853 under the provisions of An Act for making and improving Roads in the Colony of Victoria, the Central Roads Board (VA 2803) was established and assumed responsibility for the construction and maintenance of proclaimed main roads and bridges. The Act also provided for municipal responsibility for local roads and bridges, subject to the general superintendence of the Board, and District Road Boards were established. Under the provisions of their own Acts, the towns of Melbourne and Geelong were also responsible for the construction and maintenance of local roads and bridges.

The Returns of Public Works, Civil Establishment lists (see VPRS 943 Blue Books) and Finance Statements for the years 1851 to 1854 give some indication of the very rapid expansion in the administration of the public works function. In 1851, the civil establishment for public works was thirteen and by 1854 the combined establishment of the Colonial Engineer and the Central Roads Board was seventy-four. Appropriations for the six months from July to December 1851 totalled 13,372 pounds and by 1853 the appropriations for public works and buildings and roads and bridges had risen to 1,314,056 pounds for the year.

On the achievement of responsible government in 1855, the Public Works Department (VA 669) assumed responsibility for all public works functions and the Central Roads Board (VA 2803) continued to be responsible for roads and bridges until its abolition in 1858.

Theatre Licences

Under the provisions of An Act to amend the Law for regulating places of exhibition and entertainment 1850 14 Vic., No.23, the Colonial Secretary's Office was responsible for all theatrical and artistic performances involving profit or gain, or to which admission was charged. The Superintendent (VA 473) may have administered theatrical licences prior to 1851.

Functional and Agency Groupings 1851-1855

The Lieutenant Governor (later Governor) remained head of Government until the proclamation of the new constitution conferring full responsible government in November 1855. 

During the years 1851 to 1855 chief executive authority rested with the Governor advised by the Executive Council. The main departments of government were those of the Colonial Secretary and the principal colonial officials or principal officers of government, including the Treasurer, Auditor-General, Surveyor-General, Collector of Customs (later the Commissioner of Trade and Customs) and Postmaster-General. The Colonial Secretary was the chief official and all other colonial officials communicated with the Lieutenant-Governor (later Governor) via his Office.

A number of agencies covering the responsibilities of the principal colonial officials have been dated from 1851. The Superintendent (VA 473) is shown as passing responsibility for the functions listed below directly to these Agencies. They are:
  • VA 2921 Surveyor General's Department Survey and Mapping
  • VA 2825 Attorney-General's Department Crown-Solicitor's Services
  • VA 2872 Postmaster-General's Department Post Offices
  • VA 606 Department of Trade and Customs Trade, Customs, Ports and Harbours
  • VA 865 Department of the Treasurer Finance and Revenue Collection
Responsible Government 1855

The majority of functions administered by the Colonial Secretary's Office passed to the Chief Secretary's Department (VA 475) in 1855, notable exceptions being immigration, inherited by the Department of Trade and Customs (VA 606), geological survey which passed to the Surveyor General's Department (VA 2921) and the Gold Office, resumed by the Department of the Treasurer (VA 865).

title: Colonial Secretary's Office

description:
The municipal district of Sandridge was proclaimed on 11 July 1860 in response to a petition from the ratepayers of Macarthur ward of the City of Melbourne for the separation of the ward from the city and the erection thereof into a distinct municipal district.

By the same proclamation, all existing and future piers, jetties and wharves were specifically excluded from the municipal district of Sandridge.

The name, the Borough of Sandridge, was changed to the Borough of Port Melbourne by proclamation published in the Government Gazette 25 January 1884 in accordance with Act No.762 (1883) which gave the Governor-in-Council power to change the names of towns, cities, etc., by proclamation.

Local Government Reform 1993-1995

This council was abolished on 22 June 1994 as part of a statewide program of local government reform enacted between 1993 and 1995. The reform process reduced the number of councils from 210 to 78. The City of Port Phillip (VA 3716) has been appointed as the successor in law of the City of Port Melbourne and has assumed its rights, assets and liabilities.
