description:
Addington Primary School first opened as Ercildoune Presbyterian School on 23 July 1860.

The school was located on a site in Allotment 3, Section 36 in the Parish of Ercildoune, donated by Thomas Learmonth. The school was required to cater for the children of the squatters who had settled the area following the establishment of Ercildoune Station by the Learmonth brothers.

It was established as a Common School and given number 226 in 1963 when the Board of Education began the numbering system. In 1873 the school was sold to the Minster of Public Instruction for £70, whereupon it became a State School.

In 1912 the name of the school was changed to Addington, as it was closer to Addington than to Ercildoune.

In 1969 Glen Brae State School No. 3752 closed, resulting in an increase of student numbers at Addington, however this didn’t last, and from 1974 the school was unstaffed.

Addington Primary School was closed officially at a public meeting on 30 January 1981.
name.official_title.title: Addington (Primary School No. 226; previously known as Ercildoune 1863-1912)
title: Addington (Primary School No. 226; previously known as Ercildoune 1863-1912)

description:
This primary school originally opened as Adelaide Lead Common School in late 1863 or 1864.

The school was located on Sanders Road near the intersection with Possum Gully Road, Adelaide Lead, in a building constructed from locally handmade bricks.

It was reconstituted as State School No. 25 in 1873.

Adelaide Lead Primary School closed in May 1954, due to low attendance and the presence of a close by school bus to Maryborough. The building was then purchased by the Tullaroop Shire Council and became the local Shire Hall.
name.official_title.title: Adelaide Lead (Primary School No. 25)
title: Adelaide Lead (Primary School No. 25)

description:
Ainsbury State School No. 4100 opened by 1923.

It first operated out of a building on Summering’s paddock. A government-constructed school building opened in 1923.

The school closed in 1938. It was later moved to Bryon’s paddock and reopened in 1941.

Ainsbury Primary School closed in 1954. The school building was later relocated to Sea Lake High School.
name.official_title.title: Ainsbury (Primary School No. 4100)
title: Ainsbury (Primary School No. 4100)

description:
Allendale State School opened in August 1881 and was located in Parkin Street, Allendale.

The school was well attended, at the end of the first year 176 students had enrolled; by the end of the second year, enrolments were up to 319.

A school building which consisted of five main rooms with another portable room was moved to the school site in 1893.

Also in 1893, the three senior school classes (grades 4, 5 and 6) from Broomfield State School No. 1719 were transferred to Allendale. Broomfield was made an adjunct school of Allendale with the Allendale Head Teacher in charge of both schools.

Allendale Primary School is now closed. The building still remains, but is now a private residence.
name.official_title.title: Allendale (Primary School No. 2420)
title: Allendale (Primary School No. 2420)

description:
Amherst State School opened on 9 October 1874.

The primary school was located on a site on Queen Street and Church Street, Amherst that was gazetted on 15 August 1873.

Prior to its opening two other Amherst schools existed:

  • State School No. 9, originally a non-vested Denominational School established by the Church of England (1856-1874)
  • State School No. 15, originally a non-vested Denominational School established by the Presbyterian Church (1860-1874)

Amherst Primary School closed on 10 March 1946. The site including the school building was later sold.
name.official_title.title: Amherst (Primary School No. 1459)
title: Amherst (Primary School No. 1459)

description:
Wyelangta Primary School originally opened as Amiets’ Track State School No. 3577 on 4 April 1908. It was originally located in a private house leased from Pettit Bros. Sawmillers.

In 1912 the Department gazetted a permanent site on the main road in Wyelangta – now called Amiets Road – where a school building was constructed to accommodate up to 66 students.

The school was well-attended, and for a time the local Mechanics Hall was also used as a classroom.

In 1920 Stalker State School No. 4028 was established to relieve overcrowding at the school, which became known as Wyelangta.

However, by 1948 there were only 8 students in attendance, Wyelangta Primary School closed in December of that year.

The local children were transferred to Lavers Hill State School No. 3569, which not long after became a Consolidated School.
name.official_title.title: Wyelangta (Primary School No. 3577; previously known as Amiets Track)
title: Wyelangta (Primary School No. 3577; previously known as Amiets Track)

description:
Antwerp Primary School was originally opened as Antwerp West on 13 May 1897. The school was first located in the limestone Church of England in Antwerp.

By 1891 the school was known as Antwerp South, and was worked part-time between 1891 and 1893 with Katyil State School No. 2766.

The Department of Education gazetted a site for the school in Allotment 5 Section B Township of Antwerp, Parish of Kaytil. In 1902 a building was relocated from Dart Dart to what was then known as Antwerp School.

In 1909 a new building was constructed after parents kept their children home as a protest to the Department that the school was overcrowded.

Antwerp Primary School closed permanently in 1981 due to decreasing enrolments.
name.official_title.title: Antwerp (Primary School No. 3104; previously known as Antwerp South, Antwerp West and Tarranyurk North)
title: Antwerp (Primary School No. 3104; previously known as Antwerp South, Antwerp West and Tarranyurk North)

description:
Arcadia State School opened on 1 May 1877.

The primary school was originally located on the east side of the Goulburn Valley Highway. In 1917 the school was relocated to a new site on the south side of Euroa-Arcadia Road.

While the school opened with an enrolment of 34 in its first year, and had up to 55 students in 1924, by 1955 enrolments had dropped to just 11 students.

Arcadia Primary School closed permanently in 1982.
name.official_title.title: Arcadia (Primary School No. 1880)
title: Arcadia (Primary School No. 1880)

description:
Areegra State School opened in January 1880.

The primary school was first located on a site reserved by the Lands Department in July 1879. The school opened on a part-time basis, sharing a teacher with Dunmunkle North State School No. 2170 from the beginning of the year until 31 July 1880.

Areegra State School and Dunmunkle North State School shared the same school number – 2170 – until Areegra became a full-time school on 1 August 1880 under its own number 2314.

In 1900 the school was relocated after parents petitioned the Department. In 1962 a new school building was constructed and opened on 5 October.

Areegra Primary School closed in the 1980s.
name.official_title.title: Areegra (Primary School No. 2314)
title: Areegra (Primary School No. 2314)

description:
Armata Primary School No. 4965 opened on 19 September 1967.

The school was located on a site purchased by the Department bordered by Brunning and Armata Crescents and Alpina Street in Frankston North.

The school was opened to relieve enrolment pressure on other primary schools in the north east area of Frankston – Frankston Forest Primary School No. 4872 and Monterey Primary School No. 4939. They had all opened in the 1960s due to the establishment of Frankston North as a suburb and the construction of new housing estates by the Housing Commission (VA 508).

Enrolment at Armata Primary School was high. Six new classrooms were added in 1968, and another six classrooms were added at the beginning of 1970.

Armata Primary School closed in 1986.
name.official_title.title: Armata (Primary School No. 4965)
title: Armata (Primary School No. 4965)

description:
Arnold State School No. 1664 opened on 1 June 1876.

District Inspector Bolan had recommended a new school, and the parents collected £20 towards its construction in June 1873. By July the following year work had not commenced and they demanded action – the Education Department (VA 714) selected a site but construction didn’t begin until June 1875.

Between 1892 and 1920 the school was known as Arnold’s Bridge.

Arnold Primary School closed in the 1980s.
name.official_title.title: Arnold (Primary School No. 1664; also known as Arnold's Bridge 1892-1919)
title: Arnold (Primary School No. 1664; also known as Arnold's Bridge 1892-1919)

description:
Avoca Primary School opened around 15 June 1857.

The school was originally the Avoca National School. Construction began in 1856, after £90 17s was collected from local families and sent to the National Board of Education in 1854. Attendance was high – by 1867 there could be as many as 125 students in the schoolroom at one time.

In 1878 a new school building was constructed at 118 Barnett Street in Avoca. The school was built to accommodate up to 324 students, and it opened with an initial enrolment of around 250 students. It was designed by the Chief Architect and Surveyor of the Victorian Department of Education, Henry Robert Bastow. The building was added to the Victorian Heritage Register in 1982.

The original building was sold to the Church of England to use as a parish hall.

As of 2020 Avoca Primary School is still operating.
name.official_title.title: Avoca (Primary School No. 4)
title: Avoca (Primary School No. 4)

description:
Ayr Primary School No. 5041 opened on 19 October 1971.

The school was located in Doncaster.

While the school was originally constructed with fourteen classrooms, it was anticipated that this would only be enough to house enrolled students until 1973 so provision was made for the north and south wings to be extended if and when required.

Ayr Primary School closed in the 1980s.
name.official_title.title: Ayr (Primary School No. 5041)
title: Ayr (Primary School No. 5041)

description:
Back Creek State School No. 2025 opened 1 May 1877.

The primary school was located in a gazetted reserve site in the Parish of Yackandandah, Allotment 17A in Section B7. The school was on the Back Creek Road, south of Yackandandah township.

Between 1882-1883 and 1887-1888 Back Creek was worked on a part-time basis with Twist’s Creek State School No. 837.

In 1968 the school building was condemned, and the 7 students enrolled at the time attended Yackandandah State School until a portable classroom was erected. School resumed with 8 students enrolled.

Back Creek Primary School closed in the 1970s.
name.official_title.title: Back Creek (Primary School No. 2025)
title: Back Creek (Primary School No. 2025)

description:
Ballapur State School No. 3193 opened on 17 October 1893.

The primary school was located on Allotment 20, Parish of Ballapur.

In 1934 the school closed, and the school building was relocated to Watchem West. When Ballapur Primary School reopened in 1944, it then had to operate out of Ballapur Hall.

Ballapur Primary School closed permanently in 1945. The students were transferred to Birchip State School No. 2602.
name.official_title.title: Ballapur (Primary School No. 3193)
title: Ballapur (Primary School No. 3193)

description:
Bambill State School No. 4300 opened in 1926.

The primary school originally operated out of a local resident’s shed. In 1927, buildings were transported from Werrimull State School No. 4254 and Pirlta State School No. 4252 to accommodate the students.
They were relocated to the school reserve site in Bambill township, Parish of Werrimbull. 

From an initial enrolment of 45, by 1942 the number of students had declined to just 5.

Bambill Primary School closed on 23 September 1946. The teacher’s residence was relocated to Koorlong State School No. 3470, and the school building to Irymple State School No. 3174.
name.official_title.title: Bambill (Primary School No. 4300)
title: Bambill (Primary School No. 4300)

description:
Banyena State School No. 1753 opened on 9 August 1876.

The primary school was located on a Reserve site, Allotment 3 in the township of Banyena, Parish of Burrum Burrum. The school building was a portable classroom.

The school closed in 1946, and the students were transferred to Banyena South State School No. 4188. 

By 1959, enrolment at Banyena South had increased and a committee was formed to have Banyena reopened. On 2 February 1965 teaching recommenced out of the Banyena Hall while a new school building was constructed. It was occupied on 1 February 1966, but not officially opened until 20 September 1967 by the District Inspector.

Banyena Primary School closed permanently in 1976.
name.official_title.title: Banyena (Primary School No. 1753)
title: Banyena (Primary School No. 1753)

description:
Banyena South State School No. 4188 opened in February 1923.

The primary school was originally located in a two-room house in a paddock. It also served as the church and Sunday school.

In 1927 the original building from Marnoo State School No. 1554 was transported to Banyena South and positioned on a new site. This building was destroyed by fire in 1957; the building from Riachella State School No. 2674 was later moved to Banyena South to replace it.

Banyena South Primary School closed around 1974.
name.official_title.title: Banyena South (Primary School No. 4188)
title: Banyena South (Primary School No. 4188)

description:
Barfold Primary School (School No. 3424) (VA 3176) was a co-educational primary school opened in 1902 on the site of the former Watchbox Gully State School (School No. 2375) (VA 5601) in Barfold, Central Victoria. The school moved to its permanent location along Heathcote-Kyneton Road in 1904.

In 1945 Barfold Primary School was temporarily closed and students were offered conveyance or tuition by correspondence. The school re-opened three years later, in 1948, operating on a part-time basis with Redesdale State School (School No. 2571) located six miles away, with each school to be open for two and three days alternately each week.

Following a bushfire in 1949, outoffices from the former Edgecombe Primary School (School No. 277; previously known as Green Hills 1859-1877) (VA 4588) were transferred and re-erected on the Barfold Primary School site.

The part-time arrangement with Redesdale School was ceased with Barfold Primary School officially operating full time from 1951 although the school remained unstaffed until 1952.

Barfold Primary School permanently closed in 1976.
name.official_title.title: Barfold Primary School (School No. 3424)
title: Barfold Primary School (School No. 3424)

name.official_title.title: Barnawartha North (Primary School No. 1202; previously known as Dry Creek 1870-?1877)
title: Barnawartha North (Primary School No. 1202; previously known as Dry Creek 1870-?1877)

name.official_title.title: Barrabool (Primary School No. 73; previously known as Barrabool Hills)
title: Barrabool (Primary School No. 73; previously known as Barrabool Hills)

description:
This primary school opened as Serpentine Creek State School No. 1388 in 1874.

It was located in a building provided by a Mr Moffat, owner of the Serpentine Estate, and primarily catered to students living on the station.

In 1875 the school was relocated to Bears Lagoon.

Bears Lagoon Primary School closed in 1951. The remaining students transferred to East Loddon Consolidated School, as did the Bears Lagoon school building.
name.official_title.title: Bear's Lagoon (Primary School No. 1388; previously known as Serpertine Creek 1874)
title: Bear's Lagoon (Primary School No. 1388; previously known as Serpertine Creek 1874)

description:
This primary school opened as Beaufort Common School No. 60 in 1869.

The school was originally located on a Reserve site in Hill Street, comprising allotments 2-8 of section 41 and allotment 20A of section 4 in the Township of Beaufort. A stone school building was constructed on the site.

In 1925, the existing building was remodeled and a new building was added to allow Beaufort to become a Higher Elementary School. It remained so until 1959, when the secondary classes were split off to become a new High School and relocated to a new building in 1960.

In 2014 Beaufort Primary School relocated to a new site on Park Road, Beaufort to be closer to Beaufort Secondary College. As of 2020, the original site still contains the 1869 stone school building, the 1925 Higher Elementary building, as well as the building from the former Mt Rowan State School No. 757 which was relocated to Beaufort in 1952 for use as a cookery centre. The site is no longer used by the school.

Beaufort Primary School continues to operate.
name.official_title.title: Beaufort (Primary School No. 60 1864-?1973: Higher Elementary School 1925-1959)
title: Beaufort (Primary School No. 60 1864-?1973: Higher Elementary School 1925-1959)

description:
Beeac State School No. 482 first opened as Ondit State School in 1862.

This primary school originally operated in the Methodist Church at 97 Main Street Ondit, before becoming a Common School and moving to the Presbyterian Church on Main Street near the corner with Lang Street in 1865.

When the school first opened the town was known as Ondit, but by 1865 it was more commonly known as Beeac. In the 1870's another school known as Ondit opened, State School No. 2106.

In February 1923 the school moved to a new permanent site on Lang Street. Enrolment at this time was strong, with students coming from the township as well as walking or coming on horseback from surrounding farms.

Beeac Primary School is still operating on the same site on Lang Street.
name.official_title.title: Beeac (Primary School No. 482; previously known as Ondit)
title: Beeac (Primary School No. 482; previously known as Ondit)

description:
This primary school opened as Beremboke Common School No. 1017 in 5 September 1870.

The school was located on Blacks Road, Beremboke.

Between 1919 and 1926 Beremboke was worked part-time – from 1919 to 1920 with Bungeeltap State School No. 1751, from 1920 to 1922 with Mt Wallace State School No. 1018, and from 1923 to 1926 with Bungal State School No. 1155. It returned to full-time operations from 1926 until 1943, when it closed.

Beremboke Primary School closed officially in 1949.
name.official_title.title: Beremboke (Primary School No. 1017)
title: Beremboke (Primary School No. 1017)

description:
Bet Bet State School No. 1661 opened on 18 March 1876.

The primary school was originally run out of the Bet Bet Inn, located on the north side of the Bet Bet Creek.

A permanent location on Cambridge Street was gazetted in 1877, consisting of Allotments 2 and 3 of Section 5, Township of Bet Bet. However, there was no building on the site until 1887, when the portable school from Walmer North State School No. 2264 was relocated there. It was used from the beginning of 1888. 

A new, permanent building was constructed and first used on February 1913. This was necessitated by increasing enrolments. 

Bet Bet primary school closed permanently at the end of 1948. The students were transferred to Maryborough State School No. 404.
name.official_title.title: Bet Bet (Primary School No. 1661)
title: Bet Bet (Primary School No. 1661)

description:
This primary school opened as Middle Bridge No. 774 on 2 January 1865.

The school was located on a Reserve site, Allotment 31 of Section 1A, Township of Betley. The site was extended in 1877 and was on the north side of Bet Bet Creek on what is now Middle Bridge Road.

The town was originally known as Middle Bridge in reference to its bridge over the Bet Bet Creek. The name of the town was changed to Betley in 1910, and the school name changed in August of that year.

In the early twentieth century several gold mines opened in the surrounding area, causing increasing enrolments and additions to the school buildings. Enrolment decreased steadily when the mines closed after the First World War.

Betley Primary School was unstaffed in 1969 and closed permanently in 1971.
name.official_title.title: Betley (Primary School No. 774; previously known as Middle Bridge 1865-1910)

description:
Beulah East State School (School No. 3619) (VA 3188) was a co-educational primary school in the Mallee region of south-west Victoria. The school was located on Birchip-Rainbow Road, about 7 kilometres from the Beulah township.

The school officially opened on 15 February 1910 and was known as Beulah Central State School. Prior to its official opening, however, it may have been worked for a short period of time with the nearby Kerewichip State School (School No. 3212; also known as Beulah East State School). Approximately 40 students were thought likely to attend across the two schools.

In late 1928, Beulah Central State School’s name was formally changed to Beulah East State School. This was done primarily to distinguish the school from the nearby Beulah State School (School No. 3109), reducing confusion and better reflecting the name of the district in which the school was situated. 

In 1954, Beulah East State School officially closed and the students were likely transferred to Beulah State School.

Beulah East State School may have been known as Coliban Upper State School when it was first opened, subject to further research.

description:
This primary school first opened as Wirmbirchip State School No. 3066 on 1 December 1890.

The school was originally located on Allotment 108 in the Parish of Warmur, in a building constructed by the local residents as a Presbyterian and Methodist Church. The Department leased the building for the school until it first closed in 1908.

In 1920 the school opened in a new building on a site in Allotment 114.

Birchip West Primary School closed permanently in 1943. Students were transferred to Birchip State School No. 2602, which had become a Higher Elementary School.

description:
Boort State School (School No. 1796) first opened on the 15th of February 1877 in the township of Boort, approximately 250 km Northwest of Melbourne.

The school was first proposed in 1874, and a site of 2 acres at 13 King Street was gazetted in March 1876. Upon opening, school was held in an old portable building with teacher’s quarters attached ‘perched on the side of a bald sand hill in a very exposed position’. Average attendance during the first year was 19, from an enrolment of 41. Attendance had fallen to 11 the following year, prompting the school to operate half-time with Woolshed Lake (School No. 1885). In November 1881 Woolshed Lake closed and Boort became a full-time school once more.

In 1882 attendance rose to 20. In 1883 it rose again to 30, and the partition to the unused teacher’s quarters was removed to provide additional space for students. The following year a new school building was erected, and the original building was converted back into a teacher’s residence. By 1891, however, attendance had risen to 80, resulting in severe overcrowding and children under 6 being excluded from schooling. Later the same year the situation was temporarily relieved through the opening of a new private school, and in 1892 the local Mechanics Institute was leased to provide additional accommodation. By 1895 attendance had reached 117 and subsequent overcrowding over the following years resulted in an additional classroom extension in 1902.

The school became a Higher Elementary School in 1915. A proposal to establish a consolidated school in 1946 failed due to reluctance of neighbouring communities and doubts about the capabilities of the district roads in wet weather. In 1963 the school was split, with higher elementary students moving to the newly opened Boort High School (later Boort Secondary College, School No. 7625).

By 1970, the school had been renamed ‘Boort Primary School’. It continued to operate until 2012, when it merged with Boort Secondary College to form Boort District P-12 School (School No. 8882). The Secondary College campus on Malone Street was redeveloped to house the newly combined school. The Primary School campus was closed in 2013, and the buildings were demolished in June 2017. The site was being prepared for sale by the Victorian Government as of 2024.

description:
Brunswick West State School (School No. 2890) (VA 3207) opened on 16 July 1888.

Located at 490-492 Victoria Street, Brunswick, the school building was the only Melbourne-based example of the ‘Horsham type’ of architectural school design, which incorporated verandas. Only twenty-five were built in Victoria, between 1877 and 1904. The school included four classrooms designed to accommodate 348 students, who would be largely made up of children of mining families from the nearby clay pits.

The school opened with an enrolment of 210, which grew rapidly to reach 505 within the first year, necessitating the addition of two extra rooms in 1889. Two more classrooms were built in 1891 as the number of pupils continued to grow. Overcrowding was eased somewhat by the development of nearby Moonee Vale State School (School No. 3585) (VA 3585) in 1908, however by 1910, net enrolment had reached 900. Four new classrooms and an assembly hall were constructed to allow for the creation of an Infants’ School.

Immediately following the additions to the school, a timber caretakers' residence was built in Victoria St to the west of the school building adjacent to a laneway. In 1995 this residence was relocated to 46 Hunter St to the south-west corner of the then school site.

Enrolments continued to increase steadily over the following decades, with new rooms constructed or leased to cope with the numbers until several more schools opened in Brunswick by 1930. Buildings at the school began to deteriorate, and in 1939 the school was subject of an article in The Argus declaring it ‘The Worst School in Victoria’.

In April 1940, plans were commissioned for a major renovation and facelift for the building. This included the removal of all verandas including the internal courtyard verandas, removal of fireplaces, modernisation of the roofline and windows, demolition of the northernmost original classroom and its replacement with a low office building, addition of concrete verandas in the courtyard, rendering and painting of all brickwork and upgrade of all outbuildings. Building works took place between April 1941 and February 1942, during which time the school was closed. Students temporarily attended other local primary schools.

The school reopened as Brunswick Boys School in 1942, as part of an initiative of the Education Department (VA 714) to provide pathways for boys who couldn’t gain admission to high schools or technical schools. This lasted until 1970, when the school returned to its co-educational primary school status, and was re-named Brunswick West Primary School. The school number was retained. Enrolments at the time reached 321 and gradually decreased over the following two decades.

Brunswick West Primary School permanently closed in 1990. In 1992, the site was briefly used as a private school. In 1993, the site, including the former school building, was purchased by the community venture WestWyck Pty Ltd.

description:
Bunding State School (School No. 1693) (VA 3214) opened in January 1876 as Keating’s Cross State School. The school was located in the locality of Bunding, approximately 34 kilometres north-east of the regional city of Ballarat, in central Victoria.

The school was first established beside the Mineral Springs Reserve on the west side of the Ballan–Daylesford Road. Early enrolments were strong, with between 30 and 45 students attending in 1878.

By 1887, attendance had declined significantly. The school then operated part time with Spargo Creek State School (School No. 2848). The two schools shared a single teacher, who divided time between both sites, until Spargo Creek closed in 1890.

In 1888, the head teacher requested a change of name to Bunding, after the nearest post office.

In 1907, the school building was relocated about 2.5 kilometres south of the original site, to a position just north of the intersection with Kennedys Lane.

By 1919, enrolment had fallen to only two students, and the school closed from January that year. In January 1925, following requests from local parents, the school building was moved again and re-erected on a third site at the corner of Ballan–Daylesford Road and Hunt’s Lane, where the school reopened.

Bunding State School became unstaffed in February 1971 and closed permanently in early 1972.

description:
Cascade State School (VA 3237) was a co-educational primary school in the Upper Murray region of northeastern Victoria.  The school opened in 1921 on land donated by local resident James Mullins. The school accommodation building having been removed from the former Annandale State School (School No. 3534) site was re-erected for use at Cascade State School. 

From 1940, Cascade State School began working part-time with Spring Creek State School (School No. 2777), operating three days and two days in alternating weeks. Cascade State School was permanently closed in 1948.

Some years after the school’s closure, in 1959, out-offices were removed and re-erected at Koeting State School (School No. 3068). The demolition and removal of the remaining school buildings was completed by the Public Works Department (VA 669) in 1966.

description:
Cheshunt South Primary School (School No. 3076) (VA 3240) was a coeducational primary school located in the rural village of Cheshunt, along the King River in north-eastern Victoria. Throughout its existence, the school went through several periods of closure and part-time operation.

The school first opened in 1891 as Glenmore State School, following a request for a school on the “Glenmore” Estate, Cheshunt. It operated out of a room in a private residence. It is likely the school was worked half-time with Whitfield State School (School No. 2441) for a period in 1899, but was later closed in May 1899. 

Glenmore State School reopened in 1905 on a part-time basis with Degamero State School (School No. 2553; later known as Cheshunt State School) (VA 3820), out of a rented room before a weatherboard school building was rented from 1906. Glenmore State School may have closed briefly in 1917 while Degamero State School went full-time, however the two schools were once again working part-time together from September 1917 until April 1919, when Glenmore was closed due to low attendance. 

Glenmore State School was reopened full-time from 1922 with 12 students, however it was closed once more in 1925 under the system of conveyance, which likely indicated low average attendance. 

In 1956 the school was reopened on a new site on the west side of Upper King River Road, under the new name of Cheshunt South State School.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Cheshunt South Primary School. 

Cheshunt South Primary School closed for the final time in 1985.

Cheshunt South Primary School (School No. 3076) should not be confused with Cheshunt Primary School (School No. 2553) (VA 3820), which operated from 1883 to 1993.

description:
Cudgee Primary School (School No. 105) (VA 3252) is a co-educational primary school situated in the Moyne Shire Southwest Victoria, approximately 10km east of Warrnambool.

Cudgee Primary School opened in 1862 as Brucknell Creek School, a Church of England school. The school name may have been changed to Cudgee Creek Common School when it was registered as a Common School with the Board of Education (VA 713) in 1864, however exact details and dates of name changes in the school's early history are unclear.

Following the introduction of the Education Act of 1872, which established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714), the school name was likely changed to Cudgee Creek State School in 1874.

A railway line was constructed through the school grounds in the late 1880s, resulting in the relocation of the school to a new site. A brick school building was completed on the new site in 1891. The name was simplified to Cudgee State School likely in 1903. An additional classroom was added in 1910, with a folding partition installed between the two rooms in the main building, and a teacher’s residence was constructed in 1928.

Student enrolments have varied over time. Enrolment was 57 students in 1930, increasing to 71 by the middle of 1932, before decreasing to 34 by 1942. Enrolment increased to 55 students during the 1950s. Additional rooms were added in 1965, and enrolment reached 86 students by the late 1960s. Enrolment was down to 37 in 1976.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Cudgee Primary School around this time. 

Enrolment was 25 students in 1980. At that time, the school comprised two classrooms, a general-purpose room, an office, and a storeroom. In 1986, enrolment was 14 students.

In late 2009, part of the original building was damaged by fire. During 2010, the school operated from a portable classroom and a shipping container while awaiting replacement facilities and repairs. In June 2010, two replacement classrooms were installed on site.

Enrolment was 22 students in 2014 and 27 in 2024. As of 2026, the school remains in operation, and the brick building constructed in 1891 continues to be in use.

description:
Darriman State School (School No. 3013) was a co-educational primary school in the Giffard area of West Gippsland, south of Sale. During its years of operations, the school was closed and re-opened multiple times, and on several occasions was worked part-time with nearby schools, reflecting the changing population of the rural area.

Applications for a new school at Darriman were first made from 1889; later that year Darriman State School opened, utilising the Giffard Public Hall. In 1892, however, enrolments had reduced to the point that the school was closed. 

Darriman State School re-opened in 1896, at which time it was worked part-time with the nearby Darriman West State School (School No. 3070) (VA 4455). 

Darriman State School was closed from 1907 to 1911. It re-opened to work part-time with Darriman West from 1911 to 1918 and then with the newly re-opened Giffard West State School (School No. 2979) (VA 3258) from 1918 to early 1921. At that time, Darriman State School was closed under the conveyance system due to low enrolments, however it seems the school was re-opened part-time with Darriman West State School just a few months later in the year. 

In 1925, it seems that Darriman State School and Darriman West State School were both made full-time schools again. Darriman continued as a full-time school until 1940, when it was closed once again.

From 1950, Darriman State School was re-opened on a part-time basis with Giffard West. When the enrolments in the area dropped once more with the removal of a family at the end of Term 1 from Giffard West to Sale, Giffard West State School closed while Darriman State School continued as a full-time time school.

From 1954, there were calls within the community to have a dedicated school building erected for Darriman State School, which had until this time been worked variously out of the Giffard Public Hall, Darriman Hall and the local Mechanic’s Institute Hall. A school building was subsequently erected and occupied in 1956, with a shelter pavilion and woodshed added to the site in 1958.

While enrolments appear to have remained relatively steady over this time, Darriman State School became unstaffed for a period in 1967, and then again from 1971. The school permanently closed in 1972.

description:
Diggora South State School (VA 3261) opened in January of 1880 on a 2 acre site which was purchased from J. Small in 1879. The school was located on the corner of Wharparilla and Settlement Roads in the former village of Diggora, approximately 14km north-west of Elmore and 35km south-west of Echuca in the County of Bendigo.

The school initially operated out of a standard portable building with two additional rooms as accommodation quarters for up to 30 people. 

Diggora South State School was closed in 1905. in 1909, the school building was transported to Warragamba State School (School No. 2939) (VA 5328) to accommodate the growing number of students there. 

In 1922 a new school building was constructed on the original Diggora South State School site, and the school was reopened there that year. Diggora South State School closed permanently in 1963.

Diggora South State School should not be confused with either Diggora West State School (School No. 2304; previously known as Warragamba State School 1880 – 1903) (VA 5327) which was located nearby and operated for a similar period from 1889 - 1966, or Warragamba State School (School No. 2939; previously known as Diggora West State School 1889 – 1903) (VA 5328) which was also located nearby and closed in 1922.

description:
Dixie Primary School (School No. 891) (VA 3264) opened as Ecklin Common School No. 891 in May 1868.  The school was located in the small rural locality in the Corangamite Shire, southwest Victoria, Australia, approximately 190km southwest of Melbourne.  The school was originally located near Timboon Road and had an average attendance of 20 students. 

The school burnt down in 1900 and was rebuilt in weatherboard on a new site on Timboon Road.  

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked changes to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Dixie State School in 1907.

A pine plantation was established for the school in 1931, which was likely later milled for school profit as part of the School Endowment Pine Plantation to generate school funds. The school building was again destroyed by fire in October 1939 and was rebuilt in 1940 as a new weatherboard building on Dixie School Road.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Dixie Primary School around this time. 

Dixie Primary School was permanently closed in 1992.  The school building was relocated to the grounds of Terang College (School No. 6236) to become the Museum for the Terang & District Historical Society and the former school site on Dixie School Road was closed.

description:
Evansford Primary School (School No. 801) (VA 3276) opened in 1867 as Evansford Common School on a 3-acre site in the rural village of Evansford, central-west Victoria. The schoolhouse was a bluestone building with brick windowsills and an iron roof, while the teacher’s residence was a four-room timber house with shingle roof. Average attendance for the first year was 35.

In 1872 a fifth room was added to the residence. In 1873 the school’s name was changed to Evansford State School and it came under the control of the Education Department (VA 714). Minor renovations including a porch for the school building were completed in 1877, and further minor additions were made in 1901 and 1907. The school was then remodelled in 1913.

In 1911 average attendance had been 48; by 1945 it had fallen below the number required to keep a school open, and the school was subsequently closed. The residence was demolished.

The school was able to reopen in 1956, in large part due to the establishment of a soldier settlement in nearby Mt Michel providing a population boost.

The school’s name was likely changed to Evansford Primary School in 1970. The average attendance for this year was as low as 11.

The school permanently closed between 1973 and 1975. The original bluestone building remained in place and is used as a community centre as of 2026.

description:
Fawkner Primary School (School No. 3590) (VA 3278) is a coeducational primary school located in the northern suburbs of Melbourne, 12km from the CBD. 

The school first opened in 1908 as North Coburg State School, on a site on Lynch Rd. The school name was changed to Fawkner State School some time in the following years. The name change may have aligned with the erection of a new school building following a fire in 1922, but this remains subject to further research. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Fawkner Primary School. 

In 1987, the nearby Fawkner East Primary School (School No. 4864) (VA 3279) was closed, and Fawkner Primary School moved its operations to the former Fawkner East school site on Lorne St. The original Fawkner Primary School site on Lynch Rd was later purchased for a Buddhist Temple which opened in 2003.

As of 2026, Fawkner Primary School continues to operate at the Lorne St site. 

Fawkner Primary school should not be confused with Fawkner Church of England School (School No. 47) which operated from 1854 to 1892, Fawkner East Primary School (School No. 4864) (3279) which operated from 1961 to 1987, or Fawkner North Primary School (School No. 4779) (VA 3581) which operated from 1957 to 1993.

description:
Giffard West State School (School No. 2979) was a co-educational primary school in the Giffard area of West Gippsland, south of Sale. During its years of operations, the school was closed and re-opened multiple times, and on several occasions was worked part-time with nearby schools, reflecting the changing population of the rural area. 

The first formal application for a school in Giffard was made in 1887, anticipating an average 12 students to attend. Giffard State School (School No. 2979) was accordingly opened in 1889. In May 1901, the school was ordered to be closed due to low enrolments, with furniture and supplies removed to the nearby Sale State School (School No. 545). 

Giffard State School re-opened in 1918, at which time it was worked part time with the nearby Darriman State School (School No. 3013) (VA 3258). In 1921, Darriman State School was closed under the conveyance system due to low enrolments, and Giffard West became a full-time school.

In approximately 1923, the name of the school was changed to Giffard West State School, better reflecting the exact location of the school. 

In 1948, Giffard West State School was closed again due to low enrolments, however it appears that almost immediately there were calls for it to be re-opened, which were successful for the 1949 school year. This period of operation was short-lived, however. To manage the small number of school-age students in the area, Giffard West and Darriman State Schools were worked part-time together from the commencement of the 1950 school year. When the enrolments dropped once more with the removal of a family at the end of Term 1 from Giffard West to Sale, Giffard West State School closed while Darriman State School continued as full-time. 

Giffard West State School re-opened for the final time in 1961, with a net enrolment of 11 students. Although enrolments stayed relatively stable over the following years, Giffard West State School permanently closed in 1972.

description:
Goongerah Primary School (School No. 4545) (VA 3298) was a co-educational primary school located in East Gippsland, between Orbost and Bendoc. The area was used for cattle runs from the 1860s and saw a ‘gold rush’ from roughly 1872 to 1876. The school, known as Goongerah State School, opened in 1936.

From 1952, Goongerah State School was worked part-time with Lower Bendoc State School (School No. 3267), before returning to full-time in 1954. During that period, it may have also been worked part-time with Delegate River State School (School No. 2809).

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Goongerah Primary School.

In 2010, the decision was made to close Goongerah Primary School and merge it with Tubbut Primary School (School No. 4593) (VA 5645) to form a new multi-campus school. Goongerah Tubbut P-8 College (School No. 5547) (VA 5631) was opened accordingly from 1st January 2011, with the Goongerah School site used as Campus 1 of the new school.

description:
Hexham Primary School (School No. 296) (VA 3312) was a coeducational primary school located in the rural village of Hexham, in western Victoria.

The school was first opened in 1858 as Hexham National School, operating under the National School Board (VA 919). The school ran initially out of a shepherd’s hut, before a bluestone building was erected on a two-acre site west of the Hamilton Highway in 1884.

In 1862, through the Common Schools Act, the Victorian Parliament abolished the two existing centralised boards and created a single Board of Education (VA 713).  With the passing of this act, the school was re-named Hexham Common School and was given the number 296.  

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Hexham State School.  

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Hexham Primary School. 

Hexham Primary School closed in 1981.

description:
Hunter State School (VA 3315) was opened in 1923 on a 3 acre site on the corner of Lockington and Drummartin Roads in the Parish of Minto, County of Bendigo. The site was purchased from Alex Hunter in 1922 in response to a petition received by the Education Department (VA 714) which was signed by 8 soldier-settlers in the area. The petition requested the establishment of a new school to accommodate students in the vicinity of the new Hunter railway station, which opened on the new Cohuna railway line in 1915. 

Hunter State School would be the third site for the school building, having originally served Diggora South State School (School No. 2237) (VA 3261) from 1880 and then moved to Warragamba State School (School No. 2939) (VA 5328) in 1909. In 1922 the building was removed from the Warragamba site, re-erected on the new school site and renovated before Hunter State School began operations in 1923. 

In 1929, a shelter shed was erected on the site. In 1954, the region was linked to electric power by The State Electricity Commission (VA 2740), and the installation of electric power on the school premises was completed in late 1956. 

Hunter State School was closed in 1967 and the site was listed for sale by the Education Department (VA 714) in 1971. The Hunter railway station and Cohuna railway line were closed in 1981.

description:
Maude Primary School (School No. 1426) (VA 3364) was a coeducational primary school located in the rural locality of Maude, between the Moorabool River and Sutherland Creek, approximately 28 kilometres north-west of Geelong.

The school first opened in 1874 as Maude State School, replacing Glen Darriwell Church of England School (School No. 271). 

A new residence was built in 1914, and a new school building was erected in 1969, with the original building demolished the following year. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Maude Primary School. 

Maude Primary School closed in 1989 and in 1993, the site was purchased by Golden Plains Shire (VA 3688) for community use, opening as a Recreation Reserve in 1997.

description:
Morrisons’ State School (School No. 2086) (VA 3384) opened in September 1878 as Dolly’s Creek State School following the consolidation of the former Dolly’s Creek School (School No. 194) and Tea Tree School (School No. 815). The co-educational primary school was located in the rural locality of Morrisons in Central Victoria. The school was established on a new site situated south of the former Dolly’s Creek School, on the tableland west of the Moorabool River. Instruction was conducted in a new wooden school building, with an adjoining four-room teacher’s residence. In its opening year, the school had an average attendance of 78 students but by 1895, average attendance had declined to 25.

In 1903 the school was renamed Tableland State School. In 1904 the school building was relocated to a new two-acre site approximately one mile to the southeast, between the Moorabool River and the cricket ground.

By 1915 the school was overcrowded, and the teacher’s residence could no longer be used as a schoolroom, as the head teacher had since married. In 1929 the teacher’s residence was sold and removed. From the late 1920s the school was commonly referred to as Morrisons, and it appears likely that the official name change occurred around 1932; however, some reports indicate that the change was not made official until August 1951.

During the following period, the school was subject to arrangements for part-time working with a number of different schools, usually due to low attendance rates. Under these arrangements, the schools shared a single teacher, who divided their time between both sites. Morrisons’ State School worked part-time with Bungeeltap State School (School No. 1751) (VA 5718) from May 1933 to May 1935, with Mount Doran State School (School No. 1914) from January to April 1939, and with Bungal State School (School No. 1155) (VA 3215) in 1948.

Morrisons’ State School was permanently closed in December 1951.

description:
The Government House Committee was established by the Premier in 1985 to advise the Government on the long and short term renovation, conservation and maintenance requirements of the buildings and grounds of Government House. Mr F. Honan , the Deputy Secretary of the Department of Premier and Cabinet was the Chairman of this Committee.

The terms of reference of the Government House Committee were to :

(1) advise the Government on -

the long and short term renovation, conservation and maintenance requirements of the buildings and grounds of Government House.
the standards of services, facilities, furniture and fittings desirable for Government House.
the accommodation needs of the Governor and official guests.
the opportunities of putting Government House and its grounds to additional uses which would be for the benefit of the State of Victoria.
the estimates of annual expenditure in relation to the renovation, conservation, maintenance and efficient operation of the buildings and grounds, services, facilities, furnishings and fittings of Government House.
any other matter concerning Government House referred to it by the government.

(2) direct the annual program of renovation and maintenance to maintain Government House in a serviceable state.

The Committee ceased to exist as of July 1987.

description:
Nirranda Primary School (School No. 1130) (VA 3406) was a coeducational primary school located in the rural locality of Nirranda, along the Great Ocean Road in western Victoria.

The school was first opened in 1870 as Nirranda Rural School (School No. 9), but a year later increasing enrolments led to its status being raised. It was renamed Nirranda Common School and assigned the number 1130 in December 1871.

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Nirranda State School.  

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed once more to Nirranda Primary School. The school celebrated its centenary the same year.

In 1986, Nirranda Primary School was closed and merged with Nirranda South Primary School (School No. 4496) (VA 3407) and Nullaware Primary School (School No. 1652) (VA 3416) to form Nullaware and District Primary School (School No. 1652).

Nirranda Primary School should not be confused with Nirranda South Primary School (School No. 4496) which operated from 1932 to 1986 or Nirranda East Primary School (School No. 2475) (VA 3864) which operated from 1882 to 1988.

description:
Patho Primary School (School No. 1994, previously known as Gunbower Creek State School (1877 – 1888), Patho State School (1888 – c.1970) was a coeducational government school located in Gunbower Creek, North-West of Echuca.

The school was first opened by Mr John Maher on 13th of August 1877, in the leased Union Chapel (also known as the Methodist Church) on Patho Creek. Maher commenced the school without departmental authority or renumeration and taught over 40 students upon opening. A departmental officer later visited the school and recommended it to be taken over by the Education Department (VA 714), which was done by 1878.

On 10 January 1881, the school (then known as Gunbower Creek State School) moved to a new timber building with teacher’s quarters built adjacent to the Chapel grounds.

The name of the school was changed to Patho in 1888, due to long-standing confusion between it and Gunbower Creek (School No. 1790), though this school had closed in December 1877.

In 1944 tentative plans were made to establish an area school with Gunbower Island, Welton, and Torrumbarry, as the district didn’t have enough pupils for a consolidated school. This plan was not realised.

The school had a small enrolment size, with a net enrolment of only 17 in 1949, and an average attendance of 12. Its name likely changed to Patho Primary School in 1970, when there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than exclusively primary-level ones.

By April 1979 the school was no longer staffed, presumably not having had students attending. It was officially closed on the 24th of April the following year.

The school building was shifted to Echuca Primary School (No. 208). The school site was later sold to Vebsell Investments Pty. Ltd. in 1987.

The school building was later relocated to Torrumbarry circa 2019 - 2023 to serve as a meeting and resource room for the Torrumbarry Community Club.

description:
Rosebrook State School (School No. 526) (VA 3447) was a small rural school located in Rosebrook, Shire of Moyne, in Western Victoria.

It was first opened as a Church of England School in 1854 with aid from the Denominational Board (VA 703). It became Rosebrook Common School (No. 526) in 1863, and in circa 1873 was renamed Rosebrook State School, following the establishment of the Education Act 1872.

The Education Department leased a building to serve as the schoolhouse until 1874, when it completed the purchase of a new school site. A bluestone schoolhouse was built in 1878, with the previous schoolhouse converted to the teacher’s residence.

In 1946, the school had only 6-11 pupils in attendance, and there was debate as to whether it should be kept open. It later closed in 1949 as part of the government’s consolidation policy for rural schools. This policy established consolidated schools in various parts of the state during the 1940s and early 1950s. The schools were large central regional schools to which children in surrounding districts were conveyed and replaced small one-teacher schools. A school could not be established in a district unless a minimum of 200 pupils could be assured. All students from Rosebrook State School were moved to Port Fairy Consolidated School (No. 6247) (VA 5456), which opened in February 1949 and is still in operation as of 2024.

description:
Sandford Primary School (School No. 1654) (VA 3451) originally opened as Sandford State School, in 1875. A brick building with attached residence of three rooms was built on a triangular site on the Casterton-Portland Road in Sandford, replacing the town’s existing Common School No. 576. Enrolments for 1875 was 56 students. 

An additional room was added to the residence in 1879. The building for State School Kaladbro (School No. 2397) (VA 5633) was moved to the site in 1898 and used as a infants’ room. Two detached wooden rooms were added to the teachers' residence in 1908, and in 1909 another weatherboard classroom was added to the school, allowing for 67 children to be accommodated.

A fire damaging the school in 1963 resulted in classes being held in the single remaining room until a second classroom was built in 1965. The old single room was purchased and removed locally.

In approximately 1970, the school’s name changed to Sandford Primary School.

Sandford Primary School was permanently closed in 1980.

description:
Strangways Primary School (VA 3468) opened in 1875. It replaced two earlier institutions: School No. 705, which operated from 1864 to 1870 and School No. 1065, which operated from 1870 to 1875, both also named Strangways School.

Located approximately 15km southwest of Castlemaine in Central Victoria, the co-educational primary school operated out of a brick building with a square porch at each end. It was approximately 1.2km southwest of Strangways Railway Siding. 

Enrolment at the school fluctuated, ranging from over 100 students to as few as 5. These population changes were predominantly due to the rise and fall of alluvial mining and the operation of a gold mining dredge, which ran for seventeen years before closing in June 1954.

In 1935, due to low attendance rates, the school began to operate part time with Metcalfe State School (School No. 851). Strangways shared its only teacher with Metcalfe and the teacher split their time between both schools.

Strangways Primary School temporarily closed in June 1936 and reopened in August 1938, trailing a full time schedule. 

It seems likely Strangways Primary School remained unstaffed from 1964, and permanently closed in February 1971. The building was sold in June 1997.

description:
Sutton Grange Common School (School No. 798) (VA 3472) opened on the 2nd of January 1865 on a two-acre site in Sutton Grange, approximately 20 kilometres from Castlemaine. The original school building was made of weatherboard with a shingle roof.

Enrolment in its first year was 20 students. Plans by architect Thomas Muntz for a stone building were drawn up in 1869, and in November 1870 the new one-room granite-brick schoolhouse was opened. The original weatherboard building was converted into a teacher’s residence.

In approximately 1915, a wooden building was erected for use as a store and sloyd (woodworking and textiles) room. Bushfires in 1944 destroyed the teacher’s residence and part of a plantation on school grounds, but the granite-brick school building remained intact. The following year the residence from Faraday State School (School No. 797) (VA 3277) was transferred to Sutton Grange. In 1967 the wooden sloyd building was lined and used as an additional classroom.

In 1970, there were 34 students in attendance and two teachers. The school’s name changed this year to Sutton Grange Primary School, in keeping with a state-wide change to naming conventions.

Sutton Grange Primary School permanently closed in 1989 and was sold to a private owner. Over the following decades the site underwent extensive renovations and groundwork to transform into a residence; the stone schoolhouse was incorporated into the design. The property was last sold in 2024.

description:
Swan Hill Primary School (School no. 1142) is located on the traditional land of the Wamba Wamba people in Swan Hill, in the Loddon-Mallee region of Victoria. It is a co-education school serving children in years Prep-6, with approximately 500 students enrolled as of 2020.

First established as Rural School No. 60 in 1871, approximately 15 pupils were enrolled during the first year of operation. The school building at the time was a vacant timber hotel with six rooms, which was leased for £24 pounds per year and served as a schoolroom, teacher’s residence, and Presbyterian place of worship. The school became Swan Hill State School No. 1142 on 1st February 1872, however in November it closed for several months due to the resignation of the Head Teacher. It re-opened with a new Head Teacher and 35 pupils in another temporary building in April 1873; the local weatherboard Court House.

By June the following year, a report from the District Inspector stated that a new school building was “urgently needed” as the current site was too small and attendance at the school was declining “on account of having no proper building”. Many parents refused to send their children to the “discomfort of the Court House” during periods of bad weather or high temperatures.

A new brick school house with attached teacher’s residence was built and opened in 1876, with 57 pupils attending. The school population continued to rise, with 185 pupils by 1897 – however, there were no further accommodations provided to cater for the growing numbers, and overcrowding became an issue once again. In 1900, the main brick building was badly damaged in a fire that destroyed much of the school, compounding the issue. Classes were held in the nearby skating rink, which had had to have ‘a few tons’ of barley removed to accommodate the school. Some classes began moving back into classrooms over the following weeks, but not before parents protested and once again refused to send their children to school in a ‘cold, inhospitable area’.

Three new buildings were established in 1901, then in 1913 a new teacher’s residence was built to free up more space in the original brick schoolhouse; another rise in attendance in 1915 prompted the erection of an additional building. In 1917, the school began offering higher elementary classes, and in 1919 these became a higher Elementary School with a full program. During the 1920s, the school ran special evening classes in Domestic Science in the cookery centre. Overcrowding was once again an issue, however, with further extensions not meeting the increasing number of pupils.

On 23 September 1938, a new school building was opened on McCrea Street, and at the beginning of 1950 the former State School 4053 Haysdale was moved to Swan hill to provide further accommodation for classes. In 1954 and 1961 further additions were added to relieve overcrowding, which was further resolved with the opening of Swan Hill North Primary School in 1958.

By 2009, the school had 550 students enrolled, spread across 25 classes. As of 2024 it remains in operation.

description:
Toolong Primary School (School No. 3595) (VA 3491) was a small rural primary school located near Port Fairy, in south-western Victoria.

It first opened in 1909 as Toolong State School, out of a newly built wooden schoolhouse. 

In 1948, there was a move to consolidate a number of small rural schools in the area into one large school. While Toolong State School was one of those schools considered for merging, there was enough support for it to stay open when Port Fairy Consolidated School (School No. 6247) (VA 5456) was established in 1949. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Toolong Primary School. 

Toolong Primary School closed in 1983.

description:
Traynor’s Lagoon Primary School (School No. 1832) was a co-educational school located in the Northern Grampians region, west of St Arnaud. 

In 1876, the Education Department (VA 714) erected a portable wooden weatherboard building with two attached rooms for teacher’s quarters. The school opened in 1877 with 25 pupils. Enrolment fluctuated, reaching 30 students by 1889.

The school temporarily closed from 1894 to 1909. 

By 1937, the building was deemed unfit for schooling. The school building from the former Swanwater West State School (School No. 1262) was relocated to Traynor’s Lagoon. The school began operating in the new building on June 6, 1938 and the old school building was demolished.

In early 1955, the School Committee requested that a teacher’s residence from St Arnaud North (School No. 2622) be relocated to the school. Initially, this was denied due to low enrolment, as only 12 students were enrolled at the time. Although the school was selected for a new residence under the building program, the Education Department required 20 students for approval. After further communication from the Committee, it was shown that sufficient enrolments were expected the following year, and the project was approved by the Minister of Education on November 11, 1955. Due to funding issues, the residence was not relocated until 1957.

Following the permanent closure of the school in February 1966, the land was officially revoked and gazetted on 23 December 1970.

description:
Wood Wood State School opened in April 1900 as a co-educational primary school, initially operating out of the hall attached to the Wood Wood Wine Shades. Located near Swan Hill in northwestern Victoria, the school opened with an enrolment of 21 students.

In October 1909, the school opened in a new building on a reserved acre block, approximately half a mile South of the original site.   The previous building was removed and re-erected on the site of Nyrraby State School (School No. 3961).

A teacher’s residence was added to the site in 1934.

In 1970, a statewide directive was introduced to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include primary, secondary, and technical schools. As part of this change, all primary schools were encouraged to adopt ‘Primary School’ in their names. It is therefore possible that the school became known as Wood Wood Primary School around this time, although further research is required to confirm whether this change in name occurred officially.

Wood Wood State School was permanently closed in June 1975.

description:
Establishment and Function

The Natural Resources and Environment Committee was established under the Parliamentary Committees (Joint Investigatory Committees) Act 1982 (No. 9765). The purpose of the committee was:

" to inquire into, consider and report to the Parliament on -

(a) any proposal, matter or thing concerned with the natural resources of the State;
(b) how the natural resources of the State may be conserved;
(c) any proposal, matter or thing concerned with the environment;
(d) how the quality of the environment may be protected and improved; and
(e) any works or proposed works reasonably capable of having a significant effect upon the resources of the State or the environment-
where the Committee is required or permitted to do so by or under this Act." [S.4C].

Joint investigatory committees

The Committee is a joint investigatory committee of the Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council. The Committee comprised 12 members of which no more than six members could be appointed by the Council and no more than ten appointed by the Assembly.

As a joint investigatory committee, the Natural Resources and Environment Committee can inquire into matters referred to it by a joint resolution of both Houses or by order of the Governor-In-Council. It could also inquire, consider or report to Parliament on any annual report or document relevant to its functions laid before either House. Recommendations made by the Natural Resources and Environment Committee (and any other joint investigatory committee other than the Public Bodies Review Committee) were not automatically accepted by Parliament. The appropriate responsible Minister, however, was required to table a report stating action to be taken regarding these recommendations within 6 months of the tabling of the report.

Location of Records

Records of the Natural Resources and Environment Committee are listed below.

**Special Access Conditions**

Although records transferred from this agency are available for public inspection, special access conditions apply. The records have been transferred to the Public Record Office on the understanding that they remain the property of the Parliament of Victoria. Parliamentary records are transferred on condition that all requests for access will be referred to the Clerk of the Legislative Council/Legislative Assembly as appropriate, for determination in each case.

Application to inspect the records should be made to the appropriate officer and written authorisation must be presented at the Public Record Office Search Rooms before records can be made available for inspection.

description:
Establishment and Function

The Environment and Natural Resources Committee was established under the Parliamentary Committees (Amendment) Act 1992 (No.64). The purpose of the committee was to inquire into, consider and report to the Parliament on -

- any proposal, matter or thing concerned with the environment;
- any proposal, matter or thing concerned with natural resources;
- any proposal, matter or thing concerned with planning the use, development or protection of land - if the Committee is required or permitted so to do or under this Act. " [S.4EA].

The Committee effectively replaced the Natural Resources and Environment Committee (VA 3544).

This committee and Rural and Regional Committee were merged to form the Environment , Natural Resources and Regional Development Committee on 21 April 2015.

Joint Investigatory Committees

The Environment and Natural Resources Committee is a joint investigatory committee of the Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council. As such it may comprise no more than nine members of which no more than two members could be appointed by the Council and no less than two appointed by the Assembly.

As a joint investigatory committee, the Environment and Natural Resources Committee can inquire into matters referred to it by a resolution of either House or by order of the Governor-In-Council. It may also inquire, consider or report to Parliament on any annual report or document relevant to its functions laid before either House. Recommendations made by the Environment and Natural Resources Committee (and any other joint investigatory committee other than the Public Bodies Review Committee) are not automatically accepted by Parliament. The appropriate responsible Minister, however, is required to table a report stating action to be taken regarding these recommendations within 6 months of the tabling of the report.

description:
Originally named ‘Dana Street’, this school was the first National School established in West Ballarat. The school’s original bluestone building was built on Dana Street in 1856, and opened in 1857 with 50 pupils in attendance. By the end of the year this number had more than doubled.

The first teachers at the school were Charles Martin and his wife; during this time the school was colloquially known as “Mr Martin’s School”.

In 1862 it became a Common School, and in 1876, a State School. A new, larger brick building with fireplaces in each room was built the same year to house the then 1,100 pupils enrolled. An influx of students came from four local church schools that had closed due to lack of funding.

The original bluestone building remained at the school and held evening classes until 1907, when it was used by Ballarat High School until 1910. The Ballarat Junior Technical School then used the building while their own new school was built.

In 1927 the Ballarat Teachers College moved into the bluestone building for one year while the Ballarat East Town Hall was renovated. The College closed in 1931 due to the Great Depression, but re-opened in the bluestone building in 1946 and stayed there until 1958.

Sometime in 1970 the school was renamed Ballarat Primary School, also known as Dana Street Primary School. In 1977, Jubilee gates were built at the school for the 25th anniversary of the reign of Queen Elizabeth II.

Several major building projects were completed in the 1990s. The school was remodelled, and the old bluestone building was converted into a multipurpose room. In 2012 it once again became a classroom.

As of 2025, the school is still in operation with an average yearly enrolment of 250 students.

Barker's Creek State School (No. 1607) opened on 1 July 1875 on Lighthorse Road, Barker's Creek. It replaced the Wesleyan primary school which had been operating in the town since 1858.

The school building was brick with a shingle roof, measured 14 m x 6 m and sat on 5 acres of land. The school enrolled 59 pupils in 1875. By 1965 enrolled pupils dwindled to 35 and by the time the school closed in 1993, student numbers had dropped to just 14.

The red-brick school building was used by Castlemaine Secondary College until it was damaged by fire in 2008.

description:
Barwon Downs Primary School (No. 2866) was established in 1888 at 1595 Birregurra-Forrest Road, Barwon Downs and initially enrolled up to 20 students.

In 1914, a new building was erected to replace the original building that was built in 1887. The new timber school was officially opened by the Hon. J.F. Rossiter MLA on the 20 March 1965.

In 1969 there were 39 students enrolled at the school.

Barwon Downs Primary School was closed in 1993 with the school site becoming the District Fire Brigade headquarters of the Country Fire Authority.

description:
An unofficial primary school had been in operation at East Bellarine since 13 October 1873. An application was made for official recognition of the school in December 1873, the application was granted on the 1 April 1874. In 1874 the total number of enrolments was 36 pupils. 

The original school was initially housed at a building called the English Church which stood opposite the eventual site of the school. A piece of land was purchased adjoining the East Bellarine Post Office and a new school was opened on this site on Portarlington Road on 1 July 1877.

In 1915 the school dropped ‘East’ from its title and became Bellarine. 

The school was closed in 1993.

The Berriwillock Primary School opened on 21 November 1895 at the town's Mechanics Institute. In 1907 a school site was purchased on Woomelang Road (now McClelland Street), a single room school was built and 35 pupils were enrolled by July 1907.

In 1927 there were 75 students and by 1960 the school had 95 students enrolled. A new classroom was added in 1962.

Berriwillock Primary School was closed in 1993 with the school being merged in 1994 with Nandaly Primary School, Sea Lake Primary School and Sea Lake High School to form the Tyrrell P-12 College.

The Blackburn East Primary School was established in 1958 on a 5 acre site between Bindy and Vicky Streets, South Blackburn and initially enrolled 199 students. 

Enrolments continually increased until in 1971 where they numbered 727 students. This increase in pupil numbers necessitated more classrooms being built. However, numbers plateaued from that time and then declined in line with demographic changes in the area.

The school was closed in 1993 with the school site becoming a new housing estate.

Bookar Primary School (No. 3578) was established on the edge of Lake Bookaar on Darlington-Camperdown Road, Bookaar in 1908.

An extension to the school building was made in 1962 and enrolments in 1970 totalled 21 but subsequently declined.

The school was closed in 1993 with the remaining students transferred to the Camperdown Primary School. The school site became a part of the Lake Bookaar Wetland Reserve.

description:
Box Hill Primary School (no. 2838) was established on Whitehorse Road, Box Hill in 1887. 

The original school was a brick building with three rooms housed on 2 acres of land. Enrolments steadily increased during the turn of the 20th century; in 1889 enrolments numbered 211, in 1896 enrolments reached 314 and by 1914 student enrolments climbed to 600.

Additions were made to the original building in 1909, however the site proved unsuitable for the growing number of enrolments. A new school site was purchased in Station Street alongside Box Hill Gardens with a new double storey brick building built. This new building was officially opened on 13th February 1920.

Enrolments reached 946 in 1953 but numbers had declined significantly by 1993 when the school was closed.

description:
Brewster Primary School was established at Kayleys Lane, Brewster in 1924. 

In 1923, a school building on the site that had been moved from Malakoff blew off its blocks. This building was replaced by a timber classroom which still exists today.

In 1935 enrolments had peaked at 43 pupils. With student numbers increasing, the school building was extended in 1936 by 1.8 metres on the south side.

The school served as the district centre for church services, entertainment and activities until the local hall was built in 1936.

When enrolments fell below 12 in 1993, the school was closed. The school was then sold with the original timber building restored and converted into a café and residence.

description:
Crowlands Primary School (School No. 756) was a primary school located along the Wimmera Rover, approximately 24 kilometres northeast of Ararat.

The school first opened in 1863 as the United Episcopalian and Presbyterian Church. From 1864 the school was recognised as a Common School under the Board of Education (VA 713), and the name was changed to Crowlands Common School. 

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Crowlands State School.  

A new school building was erected in 1910.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Crowlands Primary School.

Crowlands Primary School closed in 1993 due to low enrolments. The former school site was sold to private interests in 2015.
