description:
Ecklin South Primary School (School No. 2647) (VA 3577) was a coeducational primary school located approximately 12 kilometres south of Terang, in western Victoria. 

The school first opened in 1885 as Ecklin South State School, on the Timboon-Terang Road. It was moved back from the main road in 1936 and a new building was erected. An additional room was added in the 1940s to meet growing enrolments, however they then dropped significantly with the opening of Timboon Consolidate School in 1941. A teacher’s residence was erected in 1950.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Ecklin South Primary School. 

In 1993, Ecklin South Primary School closed, likely due to declining enrolments.

Ecklin South Primary School should not be confused with Dixie State School (School No. 891) (VA 3264), which was known as Ecklin Common School from 1868 to 1907.

A new school building was built in Aire Street, Kirkstall in 1961.

description:
An official school was established at Korweinguboora in 1878. Prior to this, a bark and slab school had been operating in the area. Not much is known about this early school.

The school was built on Ballan-Daylesford Road, Korweinguboora. The township is located on the Daylesford-Ballarat Road, south of Daylesford.

In 1906 the school and residence were nearly destroyed by a bushfire. Around the time of World War 1, the school and residence had been separated. With the deterioration of the original building, a new building was constructed in 1964 and the old building was moved opposite the school and made into a farm shed. An additional classroom was added to the school building in 1968 to cater for a larger student population.

With a decline in enrolments, the school was closed in 1993.

description:
Leichardt Primary School was opened in a leased building on 23rd February 1874. Due to a population shift, in 1876 the Education Department provisioned a new school site with a portable school and attached residential quarters.
 
In 1877 the portable school was converted into a residence and a new detached school of timber was built suitable for 60 pupils.

During 1878 the school’s enrolment reached 86 pupils, by 1934 enrolments had fallen to 26 and they fell further in the 1960’s to just 15 students.
 
The school was closed in 1993.

description:
The Long Gully Primary School (School No. 2120) was first opened in the Bendigo region by the Minister of Public Instruction on the 15th January 1879, as Long Gully State School.

The school was built on the site of the Long Gully Common School (No. 372) that closed in 1867 and was later demolished to make way for the new school. The common school had been bought by the state from the Church of England, who opened the school in January 1856.

Between 1926 and 1928, Long Gully State School was closed and the site was used by the Education Department to house the Bendigo Teachers College. The school resumed again at the site in 1928.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Long Gully Primary School. 

Although the school was eventually closed in 1992, the red brick school building built in 1878 still stands and is listed on the Victorian Heritage Register.

description:
Merlynston Primary School opened on 23 June 1928 on a three acre block of land on Bakers Road, Coburg North. The three-storey red brick school building was built to house up to 500 students.

In 1949 the then Head Teacher, Mr. Spriggins died in an accident. In his honour, a bell tower was erected at the school.

In the 1950s, Merlynston Primary School became a training school for the Melbourne Technical College and later it housed students from Coburg Technical College.

By 1969, enrolments had reached 450 pupils.

The school was closed at the end of 1993 and the property was sold.

The property was later used as a school under the auspices of the Australian International Academy.

description:

In its first year, the school had an annual attendance of 30 students. By 1971, attendance numbers had dropped to 14.

Dwindling enrolments led to the school’s closure in 1993.

description:
Plenty Primary School (School No. 4093) (VA 3640) was a small rural primary school located in the suburb of Plenty, in Melbourne’s north-east. 

It first opened in 1922 as Plenty State School, to provide an alternative to other schools in the area experiencing overcrowding at the time. It initially operated out of a small unlined structure, until 6 acres of land were acquired and students could move into a new building there in 1924.

During the 1950s and 1960s, additional classrooms, storerooms and a staffroom were added to the school building to meet the needs of increasing enrolments. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Plenty Primary School. 

Plenty Primary School closed at the end of 1993. The site was sold to become the Plenty School of Health and Eastern Studies until 2013, when the school buildings were demolished to make for a future housing estate.

description:
The Sebastian Common School was a non-vested school which opened on 1 July 1872. The school was housed in a rented building and had an annual attendance of 39 pupils.

The school was named after Mr Sebastian Schmidt who discovered the ‘Sebastian’ goldfield, south of Raywood by Myers Creek in May 1863.

The Common School was closed on 31 January 1875.

Sebastian State School was opened in 1875 to serve the goldrush population that arrived to work the ‘Frederick the Great’ mine. It had an initial enrolment of 100 pupils which grew to 200 pupils by 1900.

When the mine closed in 1912, the number of enrolments fell to under 60 pupils. By 1939 the number of enrolments declined to 30 and by 1970 there was only 7 students enrolled.

The school was closed in 1993 and the property was sold to the City of Greater Bendigo and was converted into a Community Hall which still exists at the time this was written (June 2021).

Later the school was renamed Stewart after the Right Honorable P.J. Stewart, MLA.

In 1993 the school was closed and merged with Red Cliffs Primary School.

description:
The Department of Agriculture, Energy and Minerals was established on 1 February 1995 by amendment to Schedule One of the Public Sector Management Act 1992. The amendment removed the Department of Energy and Minerals (VA 3035) from Schedule One and replaced it with the Department of Agriculture, Energy and Minerals. The change was published in the Government Gazette Special No. 11 (S11) on 1 February 1995. The new Department was assigned all Acts from the Department of Energy and Minerals (VA 3035) and the Department of Agriculture (VA 2649), under Administrative Arrangements Order No. 143 (Victorian Government Gazette No. S 11, 1 February 1995).

The Department of Agriculture, Energy and Minerals assumed responsibility for all functions from the former Department of Energy and Minerals (VA 3035) and the Department of Agriculture (VA 2649). The Department reported to the Minister for Agriculture and the Minister for Energy and Minerals.

Structure and functions of Department

Agriculture Victoria
Agriculture Victoria was responsible for all agriculture-related functions in Victoria, including provision of guidelines and standards relating to agriculture; veterinary services; animal welfare; quarantine and animal and plant inspection; development of sustainable agriculture; and development of policies relating to agriculture and rural affairs in Victoria. Agriculture Victoria was divided into five Regions to allow co-ordination of integrated agricultural services and to facilitate research, enquiries and regulatory activities within that Region.

Energy and Minerals Victoria
Energy and Minerals Victoria was responsible for the development of Victoria's energy and minerals markets through exploration, administration and regulation. The Energy Policy Division was responsible for the development of policies which assisted the restructuring and privatisation of public sector utilities (such as the Gas and Fuel Corporation; VA 1040, and the State Electricity Commission; VA 1002) which commenced in 1993. The Resources Development Division was responsible for the regulation and development of Victoria's mineral, petroleum and other earth resources. It was responsible for the administration of the Mineral Resources Development Act 1990.

Following significant machinery of government changes after the re-election of the Kennett Government in April 1996, the Department of Agriculture, Energy and Minerals was abolished under amendment of Schedule One of the Public Sector Management Act 1992. This amendment was published in the Victorian Government Gazette No. S 33, 3 April 1996. Most functions were transferred to the new Department of Natural Resources and the Environment (VA 3972) by Administrative Arrangements Order No.150 (Victorian Government Gazette No. S 33, 3 April 1996). Acts relating to the privatisation of the energy industry were assigned to the Treasurer (VRG 23); other Acts relating to energy were assigned to the Minister for Industry, Science and Technology (VRG 124) and were administered through the Department of State Development (VA 3973). These Acts were transferred by Administrative Arrangements Order No. 150 (Victorian Government Gazette No. S 33).

description:
The Department of Treasury (VA 3007) and the Department of Finance (VA 3016) merged formally on 31 March 1995 to form the new Department of Treasury and Finance (DTF) (VA 3745) (Victorian Government Gazette 752 G12, 30 March 1995).

The Department's initial name was Department of the Treasury and Finance until 6 June 1995, when it changed slightly and became the Department of Treasury and Finance (Victorian Government Gazette, 1390 G 22, 8 June 1995).

The newly created DTF's main responsibilities were to:

- ensure responsible and contemporary financial management
- prepare, manage and monitor the State's budgetary statements
- manage the public account
- initiate effective financial and economic reforms
- achieve progressive upgrading of Victoria's credit ratings
- generate and collect revenue
- monitor, manage and identify opportunities to restructure the State's debt and liabilities
- ensure that Victoria has a value for money capital works program
- implement structural reforms of Victoria's government businesses
- develop and manage intergovernmental financial relations
- provide advice on valuation and survey matters
- manage state owned and leased property and the Government's sales of surplus property
- develop and guide budget sector wide information technology policy and strategy
- develop superannuation policy on behalf of the State
- develop and monitor the Government's vehicle fleet policies.

The Department of Treasury and Finance provided the Government with economic, financial and resource management policy advice.

Following the machinery-of-government changes made by the newly elected Labor Government under the leadership of Premier the Hon Daniel Andrews MP, which reduced the number of existing State departments from nine to seven, DTF assumed responsibility of CenITex, the whole-of-government ICT shared services agency (Statement from the Premier, Thursday 4 December 2014).

After the machinery-of-government change, implemented 1 January 2015, DTF oversaw the following groups:

- Shareholder Advisory Services
- Financial Assets and Liabilities
- Infrastructure Advice and Delivery (High Value/High Risk)
- Construction Code Compliance
- Financial Reporting
- Budget Strategy
- Portfolio Analysis
- Finance and Technology Services
- Corporate Services
- Strategic Sourcing
- Economic Policy
- Social Policy
- Cost Control and Efficiency
- Macroeconomic and Revenue Forecasting
- Tax and Intergovernmental Relations
- Gambling Policy and Litigation
- Shared Services Provider.

On 1 March 2016, DTF acquired responsibility for the following Acts, as per the Victorian Government Gazette, No. S 44, 8 March 2016:

- Audit Act 1994 - Sections 8-10, 16A, 16B, 16D, 16E and 16G (responsibility was transferred from the Department of Premier and Cabinet (VA 1039)).

Under the same Gazette notification (No. S 44, 8 March 2016), DTF lost responsibility for the following Acts:

- Housing Act 1983 - Division 6 of Part VIII (responsibility was transferred to the Department of Health and Human Services (VA 5037)).

In December 2018, machinery of government changes transferred parts of the Transport Accident Commission and WorkSafe Victoria to the Department of Transport (VA 5250) and Department of Justice and Community Safety (VA 5252).

In November 2018, a new Economic Development Division was created (Victoria Government Gazette, S 551 29 November 2018).

Following further machinery of government changes in June 2020, the new portfolio Regulatory Reform was established within DTF (Victoria Government Gazette S 314, 30 June 2020, p 13). 

Under the same Gazette notification (S 314, 30 June 2020), DTF lost responsibility for the following Act:

- State Owned Enterprises Act 1992 – Division 2 of part 2 in so far that it relates to the CenITex.

From 1 January 2023, as part of machinery of government changes that occurred following the re-election of the Labor Andrews Government in November 2022, Invest Victoria moved from DTF to the Department of Jobs, Skills, Industry and Regions (Victoria Government Gazette S 673, 5 December 2022).

DTF assumed additional responsibilities for WorkSafe from Department of Justice and Community Safety (DJCS) (VA 5252) and Transport Accident Commission (TAC) from the former Department of Transport III (VA 5250) (Victorian Government Gazette S717, 19 December 2022).

DTF along with the Department of Premier and Cabinet, participated in a shared corporate services arrangement with the new Department of Government Services (DGS) (VA 5282)

As of 1 January 2023, the Department supported the following Ministers:
•    Treasurer
•    Assistant Treasurer
•    Minister for Worksafe and the TAC

As of February 2023, the Department comprised of the following divisions:

description:
History

According to the Secretary's report of 1972 (which may be found in VPRS 9595/P1, unit 1, Outward Letter Books) the Secretariat was formed on a trial basis in 1962 with the costs of the Secretariat to be shared among the capital cities of Australia. At the Lord Mayors' of Capital Cities Conference in 1963 the value of the Secretariat (in research, and to facilitate representations to governments on matters of mutual interest to the capital cities of Australia) was acknowledged, and it was resolved that a Secretary should be appointed, and that the Secretariat should be based in Melbourne (in the minutes, 22-26 October 1963, item 29).

The role of the Secretariat was defined at the 1964 Lord Mayors' of Capital Cities Conference, 20-23 October 1964. The Secretary was to receive submissions in relation to the conference, to prepare papers and materials in relation to the conference and to make recommendations to the conference if desired, and to submit a report on important matters of interest to the metropolitan areas of the capital cities of Australia for the previous twelve months.

From 1966 onwards the minutes of conferences were created under the auspices of the Australian Capital Cities' Secretariat.

The most recent records of the Australian Capital Cities' Secretariat that were held by the City of Melbourne (prior to their transfer to the Public Records Office Victoria in 1995) were Outward Letter books dated December 1980. As at 1995 it is not known if the body continued.

description:
Sinclair Knight Merz (SKM) was an incorporated company that supplied consulting engineering services. It commenced in 1996 when Sinclair Knight and Partners (known as Sinclair Knight) merged with Merz Australia Pty Limited.

Sinclair Knight had commenced as a partnership in 1963, incorporated in 1972 and later merged with a number of Australian and international companies. Merz had commenced in Australia as a branch of Merz and McLelland, a United Kingdom firm of consulting engineers, in 1954. Merz Australia incorporated in 1988 as part of Merz and McLelland.

SKM was one of the companies that purchased aspects of Rural Water Corporation's (VA 4234) engineering consultancy arm, the HydroTechnology Division, when the Corporation was broken up in 1995. Under the terms of the sale agreement, the purchasers were entitled to take custody of relevant Rural Corporation Records pending completion of the relevant projects. On completion of the projects the records were to be returned to public custody. By August 2001 SKM had transferred several consignments of records to Public Record Office Victoria and at least one consignment to Goulburn-Murray Water (VA 3757). It is possible that SKM has retained other public records.

In 2013 Jacobs Solutions Incorporated purchased Sinclair Knight Merz and retired the brand.

description:
Wimmera-Mallee Rural Water Authority was a Rural Water Authority as defined by the Water Industry Act 1994. It was constituted as the by an Order-in-Council in accordance with the provisions of the Water Act 1989 to take effect from the 1 of July 1994. It was one of five Rural Water Authorities that was established to replace the Rural Water Corporation (RWC, VA 5234). The others being:
  • Goulburn-Murray Rural Water Authority (VA 3757)
  • Gippsland Rural Water Authority (VA 3754)
  • Southern Rural Water Authority (VA 3751)
  • Sunraysia Rural Water Authority (VA 3755)

At the time of constitution, all functions, land, liabilities, obligations, powers, property, rights, and employees of RWC became the responsibility of the new water authorities. Each authority became responsible for a specified area, based largely on existing districts and natural water systems. At the time of establishment, Wimmera-Mallee Rural Water took responsibility for the following districts:
  • Eastern Mallee Urban District
  • Northern Mallee Urban District
  • Southern Mallee Urban District

Establishment

The origin, history and main business activities of the Snowy Mountains Engineering Corporation Victoria Pty Ltd (now known as SMEC Holdings Limited) have not been researched by the Public Record Office.

The company is assumed to be an offshoot of the Snowy Mountains Engineering Corporation (SMEC) Ltd. According to the National Archives of Australia (NAA), SMEC was established in 1970 by a Commonwealth Act, the Snowy Mountains Engineering Act 1970 (39/1970). SMECs functions included providing engineering advice in relation to water transmission and hydroelectricity. SMECs predecessor was the engineering component of the Snowy Mountains Hydro-Electric Authority. SMEC became a public company in 1989 pursuant to the Snowy Mountains Engineering Corporation (Conversion into Public Company) Act 1989 (Commonwealth). SMEC Ltd, as it was known after 1989, was sold in 1993 pursuant to the Snowy Mountains Engineering Corporation Sale Act 1993 (Commonwealth).

The company purchased the Dams Design, Dams Surveillance and Project Management businesses from Rural Water Corporation (VA 2338) in 1995. The purchase occurred within the context of a restructuring of the Victorian rural water supply industry. The restructuring meant that the Rural Water Corporation was abolished, several new agencies were created and some functions were privatised.

Prior to the purchase, the Rural Water Corporation had acquired Dams Design, Dams Surveillance and Project Management services through its HydroTechnology Division. Other components of the HydroTechnology business were sold to Sinclair Knight Merz (VA 3748) and Thiess (VA 3752).

SMEC was purchased by Surbana Jurong Private Limited in 2016.

Further Information

More information about SMEC Victoria Pty Ltd and associated companies will be available from the Australian Securities Commission. Information about relevant Commonwealth government agencies is available from the NAA. The NAA Commonwealth Agency (CA) numbers are as follows:
  • SMEC Ltd: CA 3568
  • Snowy Mountains Hydro-Electric Authority: CA 75

Gippsland and Southern Rural Water Corporation, trading as Southern Rural Water (SRW) is a Rural Water Authority as defined by the Water Industry Act 1994. It was initially constituted as the Southern Rural Water Authority by an Order-in-Council in accordance with the provisions of the Water Act 1989 to take effect from the 1 of July 1994. It was one of five Rural Water Authorities that was established to replace the Rural Water Corporation (RWC, VA 5234). The others being:
  • Gippsland Rural Water Authority (VA 3754)
  • Goulburn-Murray Rural Water Authority (VA 3757)
  • Wimmera-Mallee Rural Water Authority (VA 3749)
  • Sunraysia Rural Water Authority (VA 3755)

At the time of constitution, all functions, land, liabilities, obligations, powers, property, rights, and employees of RWC became the responsibility of the new water authorities. Each authority became responsible for a specified area, based largely on existing districts and natural water systems.

The authority's appointment was later revised in 1995 and the Gippsland and Southern rural water authorities were combined, forming the Gippsland and Southern Rural Water Authority by an Order-in-Council to take effect from the 1 of July 1995. The authority retained "Southern Rural Water" as its trading name. At the time of establishment, SRW took responsibility for the following:
  • Bacchus Marsh Irrigation District
  • Macalister Irrigation District
  • Werribee Irrigation District

When the RWC was fully abolished in 1995, ownership and operation of headworks (bulk water supply reservoirs) were distributed amongst the new authorities. SRW also assumed RWC’s contractual obligations regarding the Co-operative Research Centres for Catchment Hydrology and Freshwater Ecology.

Rural Water Authorities

For rural water management, this began with the replacement of the Rural Water Commission (VA 2338) with the Rural Water Corporation in 1992, with the aim of making rural water supply commercially self-sufficient. Each new Authority was to be a body corporate, with a common seal, be capable of being sued and of suing under its corporate name, be capable of acquiring, holding, managing, and disposing of property in accordance with the performance of its functions, and was to be capable of efficiently performing its functions and lawfully exercising its powers.

There was further water industry reform in 2006. According to amendments to the Water Act by the Water (Governance) Act 2006, all regional urban water authorities and rural water authorities became corporations to be in line with changes to governance already made to the Melbourne Water Corporation (VA 1007). Authority Members were replaced with Boards of Management and the governing functions, powers, duties, and objectives of water corporations were redefined. In 2012, former licensees of metropolitan water services also became corporations, allowing for uniform governance of water services across the state.

All water corporations are required to follow the Statement of Obligations, as issued by the responsible minister under the Water Industry Act. Statements of Obligations inform strategic goals and policy development, outline pricing submissions and procedures, responsibilities of the Board, customer communications and access to information, community engagement and education, risk management, dam safety, Blue Green Algae management and responses, water services standards and operations, and compliance management. As of 2024, the most recent statement was issued 20 December 2015. An additional Statement of Obligations for Emissions Reduction was issued 23 May 2022 giving corporations a target of net-zero reportable emissions by 2035.

In addition to the functions outlined in a Statement of Obligations, responsibilities of water corporations are outlined in Part 6, Division 2 of the Water Act. All corporations are responsible for:
  • investigating, promoting and conduction research into any matter relating to their functions, powers and duties as well as educating the community about those functions
  • considering Aboriginal cultural values and uses of waterways as well as general social and recreational uses
  • ensure water resources are conserved and properly managed for sustainable use
  • facilitating and encouraging community involvement in conservation
  • integrating short and long term economic, environmental, Aboriginal cultural, social, and recreational considerations during policy development and decision making
  • conserving biological diversity and ecological integrity of waterways
  • immediately responding to threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage
  • exercising business efficiently as possible and consistently with commercial practice.

As a Rural Water Authority, SRW is also responsible for managing irrigation districts, the regulation of surface water, groundwater licensing and dams, and managing the bulk entitlements for environmental water, power generation companies and the raw water for some regional and urban water corporations to treat for drinking water.

South West Region Water Authority, trading as South West Water, was a Regional Urban Water Authority as defined by the Water Industry Act 1994. It was constituted by an Order-in-Council as the as the Hopkins Region Water Authority to take effect on 1 July 1994. The Mortlake Water Board (VA 4945) was abolished and its geographical areas, functions, land, liabilities, obligations, powers, property, rights and employees became the responsibility of Hopkins Water. The new authority also acquired the geographical areas, functions, land, liabilities, obligations, powers, property, rights and employees related to water management from the City of Warrnambool (VA 2530), Shire of Hampden (VA 2438), Shire of Heytesbury (VA 2441), Shire of Warrnambool (VA 2531), Town of Camperdown (VA 2400) as well as the responsibility for the Otway Water Supply System from the Rural Water Corporation (VA 4234). At the time of establishment, the new water authority took responsibility for the following districts:
  • Camperdown Sewerage District
  • Caramut Rural and Water Supply Districts
  • City of Warrnambool Water Supply District
  • Cobden Sewerage District
  • Mortlake Urban and Waterworks Districts
  • Derrinallum Urban District
  • Koroit Urban and Waterworks Districts
  • Lismore and Derrinallum Waterworks District
  • Lismore Rural and Urban Districts

  • Purnim Urban District

  • Warrnambool Sewerage District

On 12 January 1995 Hopkins Region Water Authority officially named South West Region Water Authority and in 1996 it acquired responsibility for the Darlington Water Supply District from Shire of Corangamite (VA 3682). In 2003 the Peterborough Sewer District was created it was appointed to South West Water to manage and control. South West Water was abolished on 1 July 2005 when it amalgamated with Portland Coast Region Water Authority (VA 4242) and Glenelg Region Water Authority (VA 4241) to form Wannon Region Water Authority (VA 4944).

Regional Urban Water Authorities

Regional Urban Water Authorities are responsible for providing water supply and sewerage services to non-metropolitan urban areas. Regional authorities work with catchment management authorities and rural water authorities to supply water to regional areas and sewerage treatment services.

Until 2006, authorities were overseen by the membership of the authority, which consisted of qualified people to be appointed in writing by the Minister as specified by the Water Act. Collectively, membership of each water authority was to hold qualifications or experience in the business of the authority, public finance or economics, engineering, business management, commerce, banking, environmental and water resource management, and law.

Industry Reform

Water authorities underwent a program of amalgamation and structural reform throughout the 1990s under the auspices of the Office of Water Reform (later the Water Bureau, established as a division in Department of Conservation and Natural Resources VA 3097). Water Boards and Sewerage Boards were gradually replaced with regional water authorities. These authorities also took over the water management responsibilities from Local Government. 

Under Division 2 of Part 6 of the Water Act, the Minister had the power to restructure existing water authorities, to create new water authorities, unite existing water and sewerage districts, and to abolish existing water authorities. By publication of an Order-in-Council in the Victorian Government Gazette, the Minister was able to constitute a new authority to take over the property, rights, liabilities, obligations, powers, staff, and functions under the Water Act of one or more authorities, so long as the terms and conditions were agreed between the affected authorities, local councils, and the Minister. The Minister was required to provide in writing to the authorities and local councils affected by the restructuring the reasons behind the decision, ensure that a copy of the document was placed before both Houses of Parliament, and liaise with the Minister administering the Local Government Act 1989 if a local council was involved.

The membership of the new water authority as specified by the Order could not included more than three people to be appointed by the Minister unless the functions of the Authority were solely related to waterway management. Each new authority was to be a body corporate, with a common seal, be capable of being sued and of suing under its corporate name, be capable of acquiring, holding, managing, and disposing of property in accordance with the performance of its functions, and was to be capable of efficiently performing its functions and lawfully exercising its powers.

description:
Aspendale Technical School opened in July 1959. The new enrolments increased steadily until stabilising at an annual figure of between 700 and 750 students. Apprentice courses began in 1968 and by 1969 there were 31 night classes.

Extensions to the humanities wing, the mathematics wing and trade block were completed in 1965. 
In 1968 the Department erected a caretaker’s cottage and parents formed the Aspendale Technical School Co-operative Society to build the assembly hall.

The school suffered a fire in 1971, destroying the science, social studies and art rooms, as well as general classrooms. The principal office was also destroyed.

The school was declared a co-educational facility in 1978.

Declining enrolments led to the school’s closure at the end of 1992. Most of the site was sold to become a housing estate. The remainder was acquired by Kingston City Council and became the Glen Street Reserve.

description:
Oakleigh Secondary College (School No. 7285) (VA 3787) was a co-educational technical high school located on the corner of Poath and North Roads, Hughesdale, in Melbourne’s south-east suburbs. It first operated as Oakleigh Technical School, providing education in trades such as wood-working, electricals, plumbing, horticulture and more. It was attended by students from Oakleigh, Dandenong, Berwick, Cranbourne and Mulgrave.

A new technical school for Oakleigh was first announced by the Minister for Education in 1941, and a 11-acre site on Poath Rd was gifted at this time to the Education Department (VA 714) by the City of Oakleigh (VA 871) for this purpose. Oakleigh Technical School, however, was not formally established by the government until July 1944, at which time contracts were raised for the erection of a brick school and workshops on the Poath Rd site.

Even though school building was not yet finished, the school was officially opened for teaching in February 1946, with classes running out of temporary accommodations rented from Oakleigh City Council, a Methodist Church, a Presbyterian Church and the Oakleigh Sub-branch of the RSL. From May 1946 the school building was completed enough to support classes on site, and it was officially opened in April 1947, with classrooms, workshops and laboratories to accommodate 600 students.

In 1952, to accommodate growing enrolments, two aluminium prefabricated buildings were added to the school site, providing four more classrooms for teaching. Further additions were added to the site in the following decades, including a masonry-veneer teaching block in 1960, a sports pavilion in 1962 and a school hall in 1964.

Oakleigh Technical School became particularly well-known for its Horticultural School. In 1970, a new glasshouse and potting shed were built, and in 1976 a new potting shed was constructed on a site used by the school on Gembrook Rd, Emerald. As of 1979, it was reported that around 700 apprentices and adults doing trade courses were undertaking three-year courses at Oakleigh Technical School in gardening, nursery, turf management and landscape gardening. At this time, it was the only place in Australia offering apprenticeships for horticultural trades. 

In 1990 the school underwent a name change to Oakleigh Secondary College, along with other technical schools in the state.

From 1991, proposals were raised to merge a number of secondary schools in the Oakleigh area. It looked likely that Oakleigh Secondary College would merge with McKinnon Secondary College (School No. 8125) and Murrumbeena Secondary College (School No. 8110) VA (4752), with those sites combining and becoming campuses of a larger McKinnon Secondary College. The final decision, however, was for Oakleigh Secondary College to close outright, which it did at the end of the 1991 school year.

The Holmesglen College of Technical and Further Education (VA 1204) ran Horticulture subjects out of the former Oakleigh Secondary College site for a short period, until a new site was acquired in Glen Waverley 1992 and all facilities were relocated there. The Poath Rd site was subsequently sold in 1993 and the buildings demolished.

description:
The Ararat Mining District was one of six mining districts established by the Governor-in-Council on 4 January 1858 under the provisions of An Act for Amending the Laws Relating to the Goldfields (21 Vic.,No.32).

The District was divided at that time into three divisions: Ararat, Pleasant Creek and Raglan. The boundaries of each of these divisions and of the whole district are described in the Governor-in-Council's proclamation printed in the Government Gazette, 5 January 1858, pages 3-5.

The Ararat Mining District was abolished and the Ararat and Stawell Mining District established in its place on 10 April 1899 (see Government Gazette, 14 April 1899).

The number, boundaries and names of the divisions within the Ararat and Stawell District changed several times throughout the nineteenth and twentieth century. Annual reports of the Mines Department and reports of the Goldfields Commissioners show that by 1890 there were four divisions within the district and that the number fell back to three by 1917, and again increased to four by 1934.

Over time the role of Mining Districts diminished as the administration of mining became more centralised. In 1975 the remaining functions of the Ararat and Stawell Mining District were transferred, along with those of all other districts, to the centralised control of the Mines Department.

For further information about the operations of mining districts and the functions of district officials see the Inventory of Agencies for VRG 25 Mining Districts.

Location of Records

In addition to those records listed below, see List of Holdings second edition, 1985, section 9.0.0. and section 4.0.0.

Ararat and Stawell District Court of Mines Records

Records attributed to the Ararat and Stawell Mining District include records created by district officials such as Registrars and Wardens. A Court of Mines also operated in each District. Although each District had only one Court of Mines, that court may have sat at several localities within the District at various times. Records of the Ararat and Stawell District Court of Mines have been determined to be court records rather than administrative records of the mining district. Accordingly they have been attributed to the local courts at which the Ararat and Stawell District Court of Mines sat.

description:
By 1873, a private school was functioning in a red-brick building erected on a half-acre of land on the corner of Queen Street and Dyte Parade, Ballarat. The same year an application was made to turn this private school a State School, and over the following years further land surrounding this original site was bought and developed until 1878, when a school able to accommodate 250 pupils was ready. Ballarat East State School—also known as Queen Street State School—(School No. 1998) (VA 3809) was officially opened the same year.

By 1882, attendance had reached 300, and a continued high attendance over the next six years necessitated repairs to the floors and galleries. In 1905 the galleries were removed, during which time students attended schools in Bakery Hill (likely Ballarat Primary School (School No. 34)) and Eureka Street (Likely Eureka Primary School (School No. 1071) (VA 3834)).

In 1909, the school began to make use of two rooms in the Ballarat East Library, and in 1926 a swimming pool was built; the first at a Ballarat school. It was chlorinated in 1963. Further works in this decade included a new tiled roof to replace the original slate in 1968, and minor renovations to classrooms in 1969.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Ballarat East Primary School around this time.

Declining enrolments led to a merger with Brown Hill Primary School (School No. 35) (VA 3816) to form Caledonian Primary School (School No. 5384) at the end of 1993. Classes were consolidated at Brown Hill’s Thompson Street site, and Ballarat East was closed. The former school was acquired by the Uniting Church.

description:
Ballarat Primary School (School No. 4981) (VA 3811) was a coeducational primary school located in Ballarat East.

The school first opened in 1969 as Ballarat State School out of six classrooms on a site on Richards Street, Ballarat East. It was often referred to as the Ballarat (Richards St), or Richards Street School, likely to avoid confusion with other schools in Ballarat at the time.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Ballarat Primary School.

At the end of 1993, Ballarat Primary School (School No. 4981) closed and merged with Golden Point Primary School (School No. 1493) (VA 3839) and Eureka Primary School (School No. 1071) (VA 3834) to form Canadian Lead Primary School (School No. 5383) (VA 5820). The Richards Street site was retained as a campus for Canadian Lead Primary School until a new school building was opened in 1997, after which the site was sold for housing.

description:
Bennettswood Primary School (School No. 4693) (VA 3812) was a government primary school located in Burwood, in Melbourne’s eastern suburbs.

The school opened in 1954 and may initially have been known as Kooyoongkoot State School before being renamed Bennettswood State School either prior to, or around the time of, opening. Opening enrolment was 352 students.

Bennettswood State School formed part of a new education precinct established in Burwood during the post-war expansion of education facilities in Victoria. The precinct also included Burwood Teachers’ College and Burwood High School (School No. 7675).

The school initially comprised a nine-room prefabricated Hawksley building arranged in two parallel blocks. Six rooms were added in 1956, two in 1957, seven in 1958, and four in 1961. An additional room was opened in 1966. The school also operated as a training school for students attending the adjacent Burwood Teachers’ College.

A new central library opened in 1970. Around the same time, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Bennettswood Primary School.

Burwood Teachers’ College underwent several administrative and institutional changes over subsequent decades and later became part of Deakin University. The former Burwood High School site was also incorporated into the expanding university campus.

In 1993, Bennettswood Primary School merged with Box Hill South Primary School (School No. 4138) to form Roberts McCubbin Primary School (School No. 5419). Bennettswood Primary School subsequently closed, and the site was absorbed into the Deakin University campus.

description:
Cheshunt Primary School (School No. 2553) (VA 3820) was a coeducational primary school located in the rural village of Cheshunt, along the King River in north-eastern Victoria. 

The school first opened in 1883 as Degamero State School, named for the Degamero Station settlement. Degamero State School was worked part-time with Glenmore State School (School No. 3076; later known as Cheshunt State South School) (VA 3240) for periods off and on between 1905 and 1919, resuming full-time operation when Glenmore State School closed for several years. 

A bushfire swept through the area in 1927, destroying the school building and all records. The school was rebuilt and reopened in 1929 under the new name of Cheshunt State School. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Cheshunt Primary School. 

At the end of 1993, Cheshunt Primary School was closed and merged with Whitfield Primary School (School No. 2441) to form the new Whitfield District Primary School (School No. 5397). The Cheshunt Primary School site was subsequently sold to private interests. 

Cheshunt Primary School (School No. 2553) should not be confused with Cheshunt South Primary School (School No. 3076; previously known as Glenmore State School) (VA 3240), which operated from 1891 to 1985.

description:
Dumbalk Primary School (School No. 3415) (VA 3828) was a coeducational primary school located in South Gippsland. 

It first opened in March 1902 as Nerrena East State School, operating out of a leased building with 22 students. A fire destroyed the school building in February 1906 however, and classes were conducted in a private house until the new school was ready in April 1909. 

In 1936, the school was again destroyed by fire, and for the next two years classes were run out of the Dumbalk Hall. Part of Jumbunna State School (School No. 2954) (VA 3850) was removed to Dumbalk to assist with the rebuilding and in 1938, when classes resumed at the rebuilt site, the school name was changed to Dumbalk State School. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Dumbalk Primary School. 

In 1994, Dumbalk Primary School merged with Meeniyan Primary School (School No. 3165) to form the new Tarwin Valley Primary School (School No. 5420; briefly known as Dumbalk Primary School). The original Dumbalk site became the administrative centre while the Meeniyan site became campus 2. Tarwin Valley Primary School changed its name in 2020 to Meeniyan Primary School.
title: Dumbalk Primary School (School No. 3415; previously known as Narrena East State School 1902 – 1938; Dumbalk State School 1938 - 1970)

description:
Eureka Primary School (School No. 1071) (VA 3834) was a coeducational primary school in Ballarat East.

The first iteration of this school was founded by the Free Presbyterian Church on Specimen Hill in Eureka Street, Ballarat, in 1854. It was vested in the Denominational School Board (VA 703), who supported the acquisition of a half-acre site for the school in 1856. 

In 1869, the school became a common school and the school property was transferred from the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church of Victoria to the Board of Education (VA 713). The school became known as Specimen Hill, Ballarat Common School at this time. 

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming a State School. The exact name of the school at this time is subject to further research, though it may have remained Specimen Hill, Ballarat State School. 

In 1930, the school was proclaimed a training school, and was referred to as Eureka Street, Ballarat State School. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. At this time, the school name was changed to Eureka Primary School. 

At the end of 1993, Eureka Primary School closed and merged with Ballarat Primary School (School No. 4981) (VA 3811) and Golden Point Primary School (School No. 1493) (VA 3839) to form Canadian Lead Primary School (School No. 5383) (VA 5820). The Eureka Street site was used as campus 2 of Canadian Lead Primary School until a new school site was completed at the end of 1997 to which all students transferred. The Eureka Street site was later sold and subdivided for housing. 

Eureka Primary School should not be confused with either Eureka State School (School No. 3707) which existed from 1911 to 1940 in the Parish of Eureka, in north-western Victoria, or with Specimen Hill Primary School (School No. 1316) (VA 5761), which has operated in Ballarat since 1857.

description:
Golden Point Primary School (School No. 1493) (VA 3839) was a coeducational primary school located in Ballarat.

The school first opened in 1875 as Golden Point State School, out of a purpose-built building erected on a site bounded by Grant, English and Dunn Streets. Initial enrolment was 920 students. From 1876, night school was offered for students aged 12 to 20. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Golden Point Primary School.

At the end of 1993, Golden Point Primary School closed and merged with Ballarat Primary School (School No. 4981) (VA 3811) and Eureka Primary School (School No. 1071) (VA 3834) to form Canadian Lead Primary School (School No. 5383) (VA 5820). In 2006, the Golden Point site was sold in two halves, the northern section of land to Ballarat Goldfields and southern section of the site with the school buildings to community groups. 

Golden Point Primary School (School No. 1493) should not be confused with Golden Point Common School (School No. 286), which operated from 1856 to 1877.

description:
Harcourt North Primary School (School No. 4043) (VA 3846) opened in January 1921 as Harcourt North State School. The co-educational primary school was located on McIvor Road in the Victorian Goldfields area within the City of Greater Bendigo. It opened with an initial enrolment of 16 students in Grades 1 to 8 and operated from a single-room wooden building that had been transported from Sandon State School (School No. 1539) and re-erected on the Harcourt North site in December 1920.

A shelter shed was added to the site in 1926, and in 1932, another school building was transported from the former Moonlight Flat State School (School No. 1486) (VA 5357) near Castlemaine to be used as a classroom. After much rallying from the school community, a 5-room teachers’ residence was erected and occupied on the school site in November 1950. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Harcourt North Primary School around this time. 

Declining enrolments led to a merger of Harcourt North Primary School with Harcourt Primary School (School No. 299) (VA 3845) in December 1993. The new school, Harcourt Valley Primary School (School No. 5404) (VA 5730), operated from the Harcourt Primary School site on Market Street, and the Harcourt North site was permanently closed.

description:
Lardner Primary School (School No. 1711) (VA 3852) was a coeducational primary school located on Burnt Store Road, Lardner, in west Gippsland. 

The school first opened in 1876 as Lardner’s Track State School, out of a bush hut with slab walls and bark room on Lardner’s Track. In 1886, the school moved into a new building on Burnt Store Road, off Lardner’s Track. 

It is likely that the school name was changed to Lardner State School in 1905, at the suggestion of then Head Teacher John Robertson, though the exact time of this change remains subject to further research.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Lardner Primary School. 

At the end of 1993, Lardner Primary School was merged with Hallora Primary School (School No. 2377) (VA 3842) and Warragul West Primary School (School No. 2938) (VA 3889) to form the new Lardner and District Primary School (School No. 5393). As of 2025, Lardner and District Primary School continues to operate out of the former Lardner Primary School site on Burnt Store Road.

description:
Port Welshpool Primary School (School No. 3375) (VA 3870) was a co-educational primary school located in South Gippsland.

The school first opened in 1900 as Port Welshpool State School. It was run out of a rented building until 1915, when a new site was established for the school North of the town. A building from another town was moved onto the site to house the 30 students enrolled. This building was burned down, however, in 1934 and schooling was moved to the nearby public hall. Another building was subsequently brought to the site and used for the next 25 years. It was replaced in 1957 by a new prefabricated school on a new site near the township, on the corner of Stewart and Dobson Streets.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Port Welshpool Primary School. 

Enrolment numbers declined and at the end of 1993, Port Welshpool Primary School was closed and merged with Welshpool Primary School (School No. 3011) to form the new Welshpool and District Primary School (School No. 5396). The new school took over the former Welshpool Primary
school site, and the Port Welshpool school building was demolished to make way for a private residence.

description:
Steels Creek Primary School (School No. 2725) (VA 3879) was a coeducational primary school located in the Yarra Ranges. 

The school first opened in 1886 as Steels Creek State School. Fire destroyed the original building in 1943. Classes were held in the local church until it was rebuilt in 1945.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Steels Creek Primary School. 

Steels Creek Primary School closed in 1992 due to declining enrolments. After its closure, the building was repurposed as the Steels Creek Community Centre.  

The name of the school is sometimes recorded with the spelling of Steel’s Creek.
title: Steels Creek Primary School (School No. 2725; previously known as Steels Creek State School 1886 – c.1970)

description:
Stony Creek Primary School (School No. 3665) (VA 5644) was a small rural primary school located in the West Gippsland region of Victoria.

The school first opened in 1910, as Stony Creek State School. A dedicated school building was designed by the Public Works Department (VA 669) and built in 1913. In 1947 a teacher’s residence was built.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Stony Creek Primary School. 

Stony Creek Primary School closed in 1989.

There have been several Victorian schools named Stony Creek over the years. Stony Creek Primary School (School No. 3665) should not be confused with:
  • Stony Creek State School (School No. 886), years active 1865 to 1916
  • Stony Creek East State School (School No. 4529), years active 1934 to 1939
  • Stony Creek, Balnarring State School (School No. 1534; later known as Shoreham), years active 1875 to 1950
  • Stony Creek, Devon State School (School No. 1662), years active 1874 to 1886
  • Stony Creek, Palmerston State School (School No. 1407), years active 1875 to 1950
  • Yarraville – Stony Creek Common School (School No. 1122), years active 1871 to 1874
title: Stony Creek Primary School (School No. 3665; previously known as Stony Creek State School 1910 – c.1970)

description:
Tottenham Primary School (School No. 4707) (VA 3884) was a coeducational primary school located on Sunshine Road, in Melbourne’s western suburbs.

The school first opened in 1953 as Tottenham State School. The first students came from the nearby Footscray West State School (School No. 3890), which up until this time had been known as Tottenham State School. The name was changed once the new School No. 4707 was established, to more accurately reflect the locations of the two schools. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Tottenham Primary School. 

At the end of 1993, Tottenham Primary School was closed and merged with Tottenham North Primary School (School No. 4703) (VA 5595) to form Tottenham Crossing Primary School (School No. 5415) (VA 5594), on the Tottenham North site. The Tottenham Primary School site was subsequently sold.

description:
Located in the Murray Valley area of Northern Victoria, this school officially opened as Baulkamaugh West State School on 28 January 1890. Classes took place in a newly built timber schoolhouse measuring 24ft x 18ft on one acre of land, purchased from J. Moncrieff in approximately 1889.

The name changed to Waaia State School (No. 2986) (VA 3887) by 1900. Another school also known as ‘Waaia’ became Waaia South State School (School No. 1950). 

In 1920 the school building underwent remodeling and repairs, during which time classes were held at the local hall. An additional acre of adjoining land was purchased in 1924 from James Moncrieff and Frederick Jorgenson.

On 12 March 1946, the school closed, and pupils were conveyed to Numurkah (School No. 2134) due to the transfer of the Head Teacher. It re-opened on 6 June 1946. 

A new prefabricated residence was erected in 1952. By this time the school was overcrowded, with an enrolment of 47 and students sitting three per desk. An unused school building from the closed Picola West school (School No. 2558) as well as outbuildings and a shelter pavilion were moved to Waaia the following year.

By 1955 enrollment was 67 and expected to rise. An additional site of 5 acres was purchased for the school, and a two-room timber building was constructed. Both the original and the new sites were then in use, providing four classrooms in total.

In 1962 the two buildings on the original site were condemned. They were demolished the following year, and an additional building was built on the new site. Enrolments fluctuated between 50-90 over the following decade. The name of the school likely changed to Waaia Primary School around 1970, following a state-wide change to naming convention.

In 1993 the school merged with Yalca South (School No. 2198) (VA 3894) to become Waaia Yalca South Primary School (No. 5401). The school was consolidated on the Waaia Primary School site, and the Yalca South site was closed and later sold.

description:
Yalca South Primary School (School No. 2198) (VA 3894) was a coeducational primary school located in northern Victoria. 

The school first opened in 1880 as Yalca South State School. In1928 it was temporarily closed due to low numbers. In February 1959 the school building was destroyed by a fire in which school and committee records were also lost. The school was rebuilt and reopened in September of that year.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Yalca South Primary School. 

In 1993, declining enrolments led to Yalca South Primary School closing and merging with Waaia Primary School (School No. 2986) to form Waaia Yalca South Primary School (School No. 5401). Students were consolidated on the Waaia Primary School site and the Yalca South site was closed and later sold to private interests.
title: Yalca South Primary School (School No. 2198; previously known as Yalca South State School 1880 - 1970)

description:
Yanakie Primary School (School No. 4842; previously known as Yanakie State School) was a co-educational school located in West Gippsland, 7km north of Wilson’s Promontory. 

Between 1959 and 1965, forty-six families arrived to the isolated and windswept district in small groups following a rigorous selection process by the Soldier Settlement Commission (VA 2270) and later the Rural Finance and Settlement Commission (VA 2273). With the influx of young families, a school at Yanakie was requested to cater for the children from the surrounding farms. 

In June 1959, a requisition for works for the erection of a school building, water tanks, lavatories and shelter shed for the new school, totalling £5,750 was approved by the Public Works Department (VA 669). The school opened near the corner of Millar and Meeniyan-Promontory Road 14th June 1960 in this new 48ft x 24ft building consisting of 2 classrooms, with an enrolment of 27 students. 

In June 1962, a school bus service was financed by parents to resolve the problem of school times coinciding with milking times.

Local farmers and school committee members came together in working bees to fence the settler blocks, for which they would receive compensation from the Soldier Settlement Commission, which would then be put towards purchasing equipment to the school or funding the construction of the local hall. 

In September 1964, 4 acres of land abutting the land reserved for the Yanakie Town Hall on Millar Road was officially purchased by the Education Department (VA 714) for the school site. The building was also used for various community gatherings, including church, Sunday school and social occasions until the completion of the town hall in 1966.

In 1965, they requested a third classroom to ease crowding. This was denied and as a result, occupation began 12th September, 1966 for a room attached to the local hall where Grade 3 classes were held. 

At some stage, the name changed from state to primary. This likely occurred in 1970, as there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Yanakie Primary School.  Whilst there was no formal announcement regarding the name change, Victoria Government Gazette notices from around this time reflect the change with both names being used interchangeably for some time. 

Fish Creek Primary School (School No. 3028) (VA 5480) and Yanakie Primary School (School No. 4842) officially merged on 31 December 1993 to form Fish Creek Primary School with a new school number, No. 5391, on the Fish Creek site. Prior to the merge, the Fish Creek School Council wrote to the Department requesting that the school retain its original school number. Thus, the merged school changed its entity number back to School No. 3028 on 1 January 1994.

The land of the school site was sold by the Department of Education, Employment and Training
(VA 4828) in December 1999.
title: Yanakie Primary School (School No. 4842; previously known as Yanakie State School 1960 – c. 1970)

description:
Box Hill South Primary School (School No. 4183) (VA 3898) was a co-educational primary school located on Birdwood St, Box Hill South, in Melbourne’s Eastern suburbs.

The school first opened in 1927, as Box Hill South State School, in a newly built red brick building. There were 90 students initially enrolled. In 1951, to accommodate increasing enrolments, an infant block was added to the site, and in 1963 a hall, canteen, and film room were also erected.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Box Hill South Primary School. 

Due to decreasing enrolments, in 1993 it was decided to merge Box Hill South Primary School with the nearby Bennetswood Primary School (School No. 4693) (VA 3812). Both schools were accordingly closed, and the new Roberts McCubbin Primary School (School No. 5419) opened for the 1994 school year. It took over the Box Hill South Primary School site, and as of 2025, continues to use the original brick school building.

description:
Framlingham Primary School (School No. 1082) (VA 3902) was a coeducational primary school located approximately 29 kilometres from Warrnambool, in Victoria’s south-west. 

It first opened on Framlingham High Street in 1872 as Framlingham Common School, with an average attendance of 38. The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and marked a change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Framlingham State School. Attendance increased rapidly to 124 by the 1890s, however enrolments were later impacted by the changing local dairy industry. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Framlingham Primary School. 

On 16 February 1983, the ‘Ash Wednesday’ fires led to the evacuation of the school.

In 1993, Framlingham Primary School was closed and merged with Grassmere Primary School (School No. 1817) to form the new Grassmere Primary School (School No. 5381), on the Grassmere site. The Framlingham site was sold to private interests.

description:
Note: These historical records contain words, descriptions and information that may be insensitive or inappropriate and that may be upsetting.

Purnim Primary School (School No. 1016) (VA 3910) was a co-educational primary school which first opened as Purnim Common School in 1871. Purnim is a small country township located approximately twenty kilometres north of Warrnambool.

The school first operated out of temporary accommodation, moving to a new site on Mortlake Road in 1876. A building was planned to accommodate 43 pupils.

Between 1872 and 1875, the school changed its name to Purnim State School. This was due to the Education Act (Vic) 1872, which established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and a subsequent change to school naming conventions.

A residence was built in 1876 and the schoolhouse was extended to accommodate an additional 20 students in 1881. In 1910, after the residence had been unoccupied by several Head Teachers, the residence was leased to a local family for approximately two years. Between 1912 and 1916, the teachers’ residence was condemned and sold, and a shelter shed was built using the proceeds.  

The school experienced fluctuations in attendance over the years, impacted by various factors such as legislative changes that affected the nearby Framlingham Aboriginal Community including the forced removal of Aboriginal children and the intermittent closing and reopening of the nearby Catholic school, St. Marcellus School.

Between 1952 and 1953, the old school building was sold for removal, and it is likely a building each from Paaratte (School No. 4493) and Lower Heytesbury (School No. 4489) schools were relocated to Purnim grounds to be used as extra classrooms.

In August 1967, the school received permission to establish a plantation as part of a school endowment program. 250 trees were planted in an unused portion of the school grounds at the rear of the school. It is not clear if or when the plantation was sold. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, it was likely at this time that the school name was changed to Purnim Primary School. Victoria Gazette notices from the period reflect this change.

Purnim Primary School closed permanently in 1993 and the site was later sold to private interests. The 1990s marked a significant era of transformation in education throughout Victoria, as the Jeff Kennett government initiated numerous school closures and mergers across the state.
title: Purnim Primary School (School No 1016; previously known as Purnim Common School 1871 – c.1875; Purnim State School c.1875 – c.1970)

The Road District of Echuca was established on 19 February 1864. It was proclaimed a Shire on 26 May 1871. Between 1878 and 1893 the Shire was redefined many times as parts were severed and annexed. On 27 October 1909 the name of the Shire was changed to Rochester (see VA 2497).

The name Echuca was also used to describe a Borough and City which existed from 1864 to 1994 (see VA 2427).

description:
Brentwood Primary School (School No. 4984) (VA 3924) was a co-educational primary school located in the eastern Melbourne suburb of Glen Waverley. Initial staff advertisements in the Education Gazette listed the school as Glen Waverley South State School, however it was later listed as Brentwood State School by the time it opened in February 1969. The name Brentwood was derived from the Brentwood Estate subdivision, named after the developer's former home near London.

The school site, originally a 20-acre market garden, allocated 5 acres for Brentwood School and 15 acres for Brentwood High School (School No. 4984). Construction began in 1968, with plans to build 16 classrooms, a library, a multi-purpose room, an office, and storerooms. Brentwood High School occupied six of the primary school classrooms during the first year of operation whilst both schools were still under construction.

Brentwood State School opened with an initial enrolment of 320 students, many transferring from Glen Waverley Primary School (School No. 2219). Rapid housing development in the area led to a quick increase in student numbers, reaching 530 by March 1970. However, the opening of nearby Cooinda State School (School No. 5018; VA 3823) in 1972 caused net enrolment to drop from 671 to 520.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, it was likely at this time that the school name was changed to Brentwood Primary School.  Victorian Government Gazette notices from the period reflect this change.

The 1990s marked a significant era of transformation in education throughout Victoria, as the Jeff Kennett government initiated numerous school closures and mergers across the state. Brentwood Primary School permanently closed in 1993 when it merged with the recently closed Cooinda (School No. 5018; VA 3823) to form Glen Waverley South Primary School (School No. 5436). The two schools were consolidated on the Brentwood site and the Cooinda Primary School site was sold.

description:
Heatherdale Primary School (School No. 4904) (VA 3928) was a coeducational government school located in Mitcham, approximately 20 kilometres east of Melbourne’s central business district. The school was opened in February 1963 on the corner of Purches and Good Governs Streets, in a newly built brick building with sixteen classrooms. By 1972, there were 21 members of staff and 600 children enrolled.

During the following decades, declining enrolments led to the merger of Heatherdale with Verdale Primary School (No. 4987) on 17 December 1993, on the Verdale site. The merged school was renamed Rangeview Primary School (School No. 5431). Rangeview Primary School (School No. 5431) was still in operation as of 2024.

The Heatherdale school site was sold and developed into the Patrick Court housing estate.

description:
Scotsburn Primary School (School No. 2176) (VA 3934) was a government primary school located in the rural locality of Scotsburn, approximately nine miles from Ballarat at the foot of Mount Buninyong. The locality was named after the Scott family, who settled in the area around 1840.

In 1879, a wooden schoolhouse with an attached three-room teacher’s residence was erected. The school officially opened on 1 September 1879 and was known as Burnt Hill State School for a short period. Enrolment in the first year was 78 students.

In 1880, the school name was changed to Scott’s Marsh, sometimes also recorded as Scots Marsh. On 12 December 1889, the school was renamed Scotsburn State School.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Scotsburn Primary School around this time.

In 1995, Scotsburn Primary School permanently closed and the site became a campus of Buninyong Primary School (School No. 1270).

description:
Turriff West State School (School No. 1071) (VA 3834) was a small coeducational rural primary school in north-western Victoria.

The school opened in 1917. In 1923 it was granted a single classroom to operate out of, as well as a 9-acre plantation. 

Turriff West State School closed in 1973, likely due to low enrolments. As of 2025, it seems that the former school plantation is managed by Parks Victora (VA 4253) as Turriff West School Bushland Reserve. 

Turriff West State School should not be confused with similarly named schools from the same region, such as Turriff Primary School (School No. 3735) (VA 3937), which existed from 1912 to 1978, and Turriff East State School (School No. 3695), which existed from 1911 to 1932.

description:
Kalianna Special School (School No. 4728) (VA 3950) is a specialist education school in North Bendigo, catering to children with an intellectual disability in the Mt Alexander, Loddon and Greater Bendigo regions.

The school was established on 15 September 1953 as Kangaroo Flat Special School, opening in the old Kangaroo Flat school building with an initial enrolment of 15 children. The first Head Teacher was Nathalie Schier and in 1959, mothers of children attending the school formed the first official Mothers’ Club in a Victorian special school, with Mrs R.A. Stewart as the President.

From 1966, the school became known as Bendigo Special School and enrolments continued to grow. In 1974, Bendigo Special School received a Building Projects Grant from the Commonwealth Government for the erection of a new school site and in February 1976, the new school opened in North Bendigo with an enrolment of 120 students. These students were transferred from both the previous Kangaroo Flat school as well as from Primary, Secondary and Technical schools around the Bendigo area.

The new school was officially opened by the Minister of Special Education on 30 June 1976 and the name of the school was formally changed from Bendigo Special School to Kalianna School. The word Kalianna was said to mean ‘to aspire to’ or ‘to go forward’, and the word ‘special’ was deleted from the name (though it continues to be frequently used in the name).

The Victorian School Building Authority commenced a project in 2015 to provide Kalianna Special School with new and upgraded facilities, including new classroom blocks with flexible learning areas to enable teachers to better support individual student needs. The works were completed in 2020.

Kyneton Special Development School (VA 3959), also known as Kyneton SDS, was a small specialist school situated on Baynton Street in Kyneton, within the Macedon Ranges in North-Western Victoria.

The school was opened in February 1986 and catered to students with additional needs and/or intellectual disabilities aged 5 to 18 years.  It appears the school had close relationships with Windarring Disability Services, Kalianna Special School (School No. 4728; VA 3950) and Kyneton Primary School (School No. 0343; VA 5272). 

Kyneton Special Developmental School closed in 1990 due to declining enrolments. 

Additional information on this school is subject to further research.
