description:
The Bayswater Boys' Home was established by the Salvation Army in 1897 at Liverpool Street, The Basin, east of Melbourne. It accommodated boys who had been placed in legal custody, on behalf of the Social Welfare Branch of the Government of Victoria. The campus included three Bayswater Boys' Homes. These Homes closed progressively from 1980. The Bayswater Youth Training Centre closed in 1987.

Initially, there were two Homes in the complex, Bayswater No. 1 and 2 Homes. In 1930, some buildings were transferred from Coode Island and set up as a third home at Bayswater to accommodate boys who had not offended, or who were not suited to the environment of No.1 Home. In 1947, Bayswater No. 3 Home closed and the boys were transferred to a rebuilt and expanded No. 1 Home.

From the 1950s, Bayswater No. 1 Home accommodated up to 48 boys on referral from Turana with fixed sentences from the Children's Court. The No. 1 Home always catered for older and more serious offenders in a minimum-security setting. Other homes in the complex dealt with younger people, less serious offenders, non-offenders, and those in need of special supervision and support.

The No. 1 Home was known as the Bayswater Farm and Vocational Training Centre as farming was its original focus. Training in vocational trades was later introduced. In 1960 it was known as the Bayswater Youth Training Centre and in the mid-1960s it introduced an apprentices' preparatory course.

Bayswater No. 2 Home was a separate junior section housing approximately 50 boys. In 1962, a cottage established for 12 boys acted as a halfway house between institutional care and return to the community, increasing No. 2 Home's capacity to 60- 65 boys.

In 1973, the Salvation Army opened Lyndon Lodge in Auburn as an aftercare hostel for boys from both Bayswater Boys' Home and Hayville Child Care Centre in Box Hill. Administration of the Bayswater Youth Training Centre and No. 2 Home was combined.

Bayswater Youth Training Centre ceased operations in 1987. Bayswater Boys Home became the Mountain Valley Youth Camp and Conference Centre, and the youth training centre became The Basin Farm, part of the Salvation Army's Bridge and Employment Programs.
name.official_title.title: Bayswater Salvation Army Boys Home
title: Bayswater Salvation Army Boys Home

description:
In 1973 the Kingsbury Training Centre commenced as a residential institution catering for patients with an intellectual disability, located in the large Mont Park site in Bundoora (along with a number of other institutions).

The following extract from the Heritage Victoria website explains:
The former Mont Park/Bundoora Psychiatric and Repatriation Hospitals Complex consisted of seven hospitals on a site of 185 hectares. The site comprising the Mont Park and Strathallen estates was consolidated by the Victorian government by purchase and transfer from the Closer Settlement Board in 1909. The Mont Park Hospital commenced in 1910 with the building of the Farm Workers Block (later part of Kingsbury Training Centre). In 1912 the landscape gardener Hugh Linaker was employed to layout the grounds of Mont Park and other State mental hospitals. The other hospitals were gradually split off from the Mont Park administration to form separate entities. These were the Macleod Repatriation Hospital (1915), the Bundoora Repatriation Hospital (1920), the Gresswell Sanatorium (1933), Larundel Mental Hospital (1938 opened 1951), the Plenty Mental Hospital (1963) and the Kingsbury Training Centre (1974).

Kingsbury was closed by c.1995. The former residents of both Janefield and Kingsbury Training Centres whose support needs were assessed as high, were sent to purpose-built facilities, Plenty Residential Services community residential houses.
name.official_title.title: Kingsbury Training Centre
title: Kingsbury Training Centre

description:
Northcote Cemetery was established in May 1861 by four local German residents, August Schwaebsch, Albert Fritsche, Moritz Heiner and Edward Hellwig.

Given there was a small but significant population of German settlers in Northcote and Preston from 1849 onwards, the Cemetery site in Northcote was also known as 'German Lane' Cemetery. Before 1901, the cemetery may have also been known as the Cawdor Town Cemetery.

The cemetery at Northcote was managed by a series of trustees, usually local businessmen, until the cemetery passed to Northcote City Council (VA 520) control in 1921. Later in 1994, City of Darebin (VA 3683) became the trustees when Northcote City Council and City of Preston (VA 976) merged.

Under the provisions of the Cemeteries Acts, trustees of public cemeteries were appointed by the Governor-in-Council. The trustees were responsible for the administration and maintenance of the cemetery, the collection of fees and expenditure of revenue (for e.g. grants, subsidies received) the registration of burials and cremations, the making of rules and regulations and determining the scale of fees.

In 2010, Northcote Cemetery was amalgamated into the Greater Metropolitan Cemeteries Trust (VA 5107).

Burials officially ceased at Northcote Cemetery in 1908 although people with the right of internment could continue to be buried in plots already purchased. The last confirmed burial was in 1971.
name.official_title.title: Northcote Cemetery (Northcote Cemetery Trust 1861-1921; Northcote City Council 1921-1994; City of Darebin 1994-2010)
title: Northcote Cemetery (Northcote Cemetery Trust 1861-1921; Northcote City Council 1921-1994; City of Darebin 1994-2010)

description:
On 9 July 1858, Trustees were appointed for the ground set apart at Templestowe as a site for a general cemetery. The first burial at Templestowe Cemetery occurred on 20 March 1860.

The cemetery at Templestowe includes a variety of monuments, lawn graves, niche walls and a chapel. Hence since the 1970s, records indicate it was also known as Templestowe Cemetery, Memorial Gardens and Chapel.

From 28 February 1967, the newly established City of Doncaster and Templestowe (VA 2422) began working with the Templestowe Cemetery Trust to administer the Templestowe Cemetery, in accordance with the Cemeteries Act 1958. The local council became involved in purchasing land for the cemetery and, later, ensuring the cemetery remained open during its period of increasing popularity. At various times, councilors were on the Templestowe Cemetery Trust.

Due to an expansion of the community in the 1960s, the Templestowe Cemetery began providing more multicultural internment services, catering to a variety of denominations and by the 1980s the cemetery began to reach burial capacity. On 8 April 1987, Templestowe Cemetery ceased offering burial services under order of Health Department Victoria (VA 2695). The cemetery would however continue to provide cremation and monument services.

The Trusteeship of Templestowe Cemetery was transferred to Manningham City Council (VA 3701) on 15 December 1994. The council administered the cemetery until 2010 when the Trust was amalgamated into the Greater Metropolitan Cemeteries Trust (VA 5107).

Cemeteries are controlled by a Trust appointed by the Governor-in-Council on the recommendation of the responsible Minister. Trustees are responsible for the administration and maintenance of cemeteries, the collection of fees and expenditure of revenue (for e.g. grants, subsidies received) the registration of burials and cremations, the making of rules and regulations and determining the scale of fees.
name.official_title.title: Templestowe Cemetery (Templestowe Cemetery Trust 1858-1994; Manningham City Council 1994-2010)
title: Templestowe Cemetery (Templestowe Cemetery Trust 1858-1994; Manningham City Council 1994-2010)

description:
In December 1864 Malcolm McLean made a deed of gift for the development of a public cemetery on Plenty Road Preston. In its early days the site was known as Darebin Creek Cemetery but became known as Strathallan Cemetery and was the burial place for many of Preston's pioneer settlers.

The Strathallan Cemetery Trust managed the cemetery at Preston until 1922 when the City of Preston (VA 976) took over the Trusteeship. City of Preston expanded the site during the 1920s and acquired a large parcel of land from the Mont Park grounds in 1925. The Trustees agreed on a new site layout which had roads radiating out from the central gates, leaving the old part of Strathallan Cemetery untouched. On January 1931, the site re-opened as the Preston General Cemetery.

During the 1960s-1970s, the City of Preston began catering to the growing number of post war Italian families in the area and also developed plans for a large Mausoleum. The council became the City of Darebin (VA 3683) in 1994 and continued management of Preston Cemetery until 2010 when the cemetery was amalgamated into the Greater Metropolitan Cemeteries Trust (VA 5107).

Under the provisions of the Cemeteries Acts, trustees of public cemeteries were appointed by the Governor-in-Council. The trustees were responsible for the administration and maintenance of the cemetery, the collection of fees and expenditure of revenue (for e.g. grants, subsidies received) the registration of burials and cremations, the making of rules and regulations and determining the scale of fees.
name.official_title.title: Preston Cemetery, also known as Strathallan Cemetery (Strathallan Cemetery Trust 1846-1922; City of Preston 1922-1994;  City of Darebin 1994-2010)

description:
The Board of Inquiry as to the Boarding Out of Neglected Children; the Administration of the Children’s Maintenance Act 1919; and Certain Other Cognate Matters was appointed on 24th March 1921 with the Board members of William Ross Anderson, Sir Aaron Turner Danks, Janet Henderson, Robert James Love, Mary Catherine Rogers. The Board held 15 public sittings and examined 42 witnesses. The terms of reference of the Board were within the whole are of governmental care for neglected children.

The Report dealt with the following problems: the rate of payment to mothers and foster mothers; the prevention of abuse of the provisions of the Act; the need for amendments to the Act; the need to insure compliance with the court orders against fathers of children committee to the care of the Department; the need to insure that maintenance payment do not fall into arrears.

The Report was presented to both Houses of Parliament by His Excellency’s Command on 15th July, 1921, and totalled 16 pages.

description:
The Board of Inquiry to Inquire into the Methods in the Public Service was presented to both Houses of Parliament by His Excellency’s Command as a Report in 1927. The Chair of the Board was James Wallace Ross, of Wilson, Ross, and Company, Public Accountants.

The Scope of the Inquiry was to investigate charges of waste, extravagance, overlapping and over-staff in the Victorian Public Service. The Report, totally 94 pages and completed on 11th December 1926, covers the whole system of Public Service organisation and methods, as well as problems of staff administration in all section of government enterprises.

description:
The Board of Inquiry Appointed to Inquire and Report upon the Most Practical Manner and Means in or by which the State of Victoria Might Assist in Reducing the Accident Rate in Industry in Victoria was appointed on 14th January 1958. The Report, totalling 29 pages, from the Board was Presented to Parliament by command of His Excellency the Governor on 14th July 1958.

The Board members were Victor Henry Arnold (chairman), Allen John Christophers and Gerald James de Mestre. The Board conducted 57 hearings in Melbourne, whereby witnesses appeared; several inspections of factories were made; and written evidence was submitted by other stakeholders.

The Report describes the statutory and other provisions governing industrial safety in Victoria. There is a review of industrial accidents in the State and a survey of the steps and procedures so far taken to reduce industrial accidents. The Report also covers the need for reorganising the Department of Labour and Industry and the Industrial Hygiene Division of the Department of Health. A brief review of existing provision and desirable changes in the workers’ compensation regulations concludes the Report. It is recommended that an Industrial Safety Bureau be established, that the Department of Labour and Industry establish an Industrial Safety Branch and that the Health Department take on the responsibility of advising on the employment of physically handicapped persons. Finally the Report suggest that the Workers’ Compensation Act be amended.
name.official_title.title: Board of Inquiry Into the Most Practicable Manner and Means by Which the State of Victoria Might Assist in Reducing the Accident Rate in Industry in Victoria
title: Board of Inquiry Into the Most Practicable Manner and Means by Which the State of Victoria Might Assist in Reducing the Accident Rate in Industry in Victoria

description:
In 1966, following the foundation of the Cato Chair of Psychiatry at the University of Melbourne, the Parkville Psychiatric Unit was opened under the auspices of the Mental Health Research Institute.

The purpose of the Unit was to provide inpatient cases for postgraduate psychiatrists in training as it was closely associated with the Department of Psychiatry at Melbourne University. In its first year the Unit had 36 admissions with an average number of 13 residents during the year. A wide range of research was conducted at the Unit.

In 1970, the Research Institute formerly acknowledged their role at the Parkville Unit by renaming itself the Institute of Mental Health Research and Postgraduate Training.

The Parkville Unit continually developed. By 1975, facilities included inpatient treatment (36 beds), day patient attendance, outpatient care and individual and group therapy. It continued, however, to provide a facility for teaching of post-graduate doctors and medical students.

Due to its teaching role, patients admitted to the Unit have represented the whole spectrum of psychiatry. Excluded, however, are children and adolescents, demented elderly patients, chronic alcoholics and patients with certain types of drug addictions.

Parkville Psychiatric Unit services have since changed. As of 1984, it was a 12 bed psychiatric hospital providing inpatient and outpatient care, especially for adolescents from the North-West zone. In fact, its title was changed to Parkville Adolescent Unit. The Parkville Unit ceased functioning as an inpatient service in 1991.
name.official_title.title: Parkville (Psychiatric Unit 1966-1984;  Adolescent Unit 1984-1991)
title: Parkville (Psychiatric Unit 1966-1984;  Adolescent Unit 1984-1991)

description:
Electricity Supply Board of Inquiry for Victoria was appointed on 16th May 1949. The inquiry was set up in terms of the sixth recommendation of the VA 5176 Royal Commission into Electricity Supply (from 1947). The terms of reference included inquiring into and reporting on the most economical way to supply electricity to all of Victoria; and the most suitable form of organisation to undertake the task. The Board members were Balfour Staines Woodfull (chairman), K.C. Fraser and Roy Liddelow.

The Report was presented to both Houses of Parliament by His Excellency's command in 1950. The report totalled 59 pages, including appendices of graphs and maps; and also includes the Interim Report. The Report analyses the economic and technical aspects of the extension of electricity supply to rural districts, quoting an estimated cost of about £100m to do the job for the whole of Victoria.

The Report’s findings are that the cost of electrification of rural areas should be borne from the Consolidated Revenue until the rural areas can pay their way. It also suggests that fuel winning, briquette making, generation and main transmission of power must be centralized, but that the distribution of electricity should be decentralized. The recommendations detail the establishment of District Electricity Boards and their relation to the State Electricity Commission, and the establishment of a Rural Electricity Grants Committee to organize the financing of the District Boards and their activities.

See also VA 5176 Royal Commission into Electricity Supply (from 1947).
name.official_title.title: Board of Inquiry into Electricity Supply
title: Board of Inquiry into Electricity Supply

description:
The Library Service Board appointed by His Excellency the Governor to inquire into and make recommendations regarding the adequacy of Library Service in Victoria, was appointed on 13th September 1940. Its members were Ernest Roland Pitt, Colin Robert Badger, William Charles Baud, Kenneth Stewart Cunningham and Alfred Ernest McMicken.

The Board’s terms of reference were: to inquire into the adequacy of the service provided by the Public Library of Victoria, departmental libraries, free libraries, mechanics’ institutes and similar libraries; to prepare plans for the development and organisation of library services in Victoria; and to recommend the extent to which the Government of Victoria and its Municipalities should financially assist in the establishment and maintenance of library services and the conditions which would apply to any subsidies.

The Board held 81 sittings and evidence was given by 29 witnesses. A short progress report was presented to Government after 12 months, in 1941. The final Report, totalling 63 pages, was presented to both Houses of Parliament by His Excellency's command in 1944.

title: Board of Inquiry into Library Services I

description:
The Railway Inquiry Board was appointed on 25th February 1895. Its members were James Joseph Casey (chairman), William Cain, Charles Henry Grant and David Whitley. It examined 107 witnesses, and most of the evidence was taken in Melbourne.

The scope of the investigation was to inquire into the ways to reduce the annual deficit of the Railway Department; to give relief to producers without burdening the general revenue; and to generally report on the working of the Victorian Railways.

The Railway Inquiry Board: Report of the Board Appointed by His Excellency the Governor in Council to Inquire into the Working and Management of the Victorian Railways was presented to both Houses of Parliament by His Excellency's command in 1895. The Report consists of 30 pages of the Final Report, and 463 pages of appendices, including transcripts, maps, drawings and financial tables.
name.official_title.title: Board of Inquiry into the Working and Management of the Victorian Railways
title: Board of Inquiry into the Working and Management of the Victorian Railways

description:
The Royal Commission Appointed to Inquire into Certain Allegations Regarding the Administration of the Licensing Laws of Victoria was constituted by Letters Patent on 7th September 1942. Thomas Stuart Clyne was appointed the sole Royal Commissioner. The Royal Commission was to inquire into the truth or falsity of certain serious allegations of the administration of Licensing Laws of Victoria made during a debate in the Legislative Assembly by the Honourable Member for Hawthorn, Leslie Henry Hollins.

The Report, totalling 8 pages, was presented to both Houses of Parliament by His Excellency's command on 17th November 1942. The Royal Commission sat for 12 days in September and October 1942. Evidence was given by 20 witnesses and 174 documents were produced as exhibits.

The numerous charges made against the Licensing Police all related to laxity in the enforcement of the law. The Report found no evidence to support Hollin’s allegations. However, the Royal Commission added that the Licensing Police should adhere more closely to the letter of the law.
name.official_title.title: Royal Commission into Licensing Laws
title: Royal Commission into Licensing Laws

description:
The Royal Commission appointed to inquire into and report upon the effects of the organization and practices of the bread industry in Victoria was appointed on 14th April 1949. The sole Commissioner was Leonard Edward Bishop Stretton.

The Report of the Royal Commission, totalling 38 pages, was presented to both Houses of Parliament by His Excellency's command on 30th July 1949. The terms of reference include reporting on the organisation and practices of bread industry in Victoria, and the conditions affecting the cost of production and distribution of bread; price and quality; whether any practices are disadvantageous to bakers, shopkeepers and consumers; the effect of recent decrease of hours of labour and any increases of the cost of manufacture and distribution of bread.

The chapter headings indicate the scope of the Report: The structure of the organization of the industry; How the protective mechanism of the industry works; The miller-baker relationship; Why the industry has been organized; Practices of the industry; General consideration of industrial combinations; Suggested forms of control; The effect upon the price and quality of bread of the decrease of hours of labour and increase of costs.
name.official_title.title: Royal Commission into the Organisation and Practices of the Bread Industries in Victoria
title: Royal Commission into the Organisation and Practices of the Bread Industries in Victoria

description:
On 20th September 1878 land was gazetted for the purposes of a cemetery in the township of Goornong (Government Gazette, No. 53, 10th June 1881). The first burial occurred in the Goornong Cemetery on 4th August 1884. The site is known as Goornong Public Cemetery.

Under the provisions of the Cemeteries Acts, trustees of public cemeteries are appointed by the Governor-in-Council, upon recommendation of the Minister for Health. The Trustees are responsible for the administration and maintenance of the cemetery, the collection of fees, expenditure of revenue (e.g. grants and subsidies received), the registration of burials and cremations, and the making of rules and regulations to determine the scale of fees.

The Trustees are responsible for keeping accounts of receipts and expenditure. The Cemeteries and Crematoria Act (2003) requires a cemetery trust to report annually to the Secretary (of Department of Health as at 2014) in respect of the exercise of its powers and functions under the Act. The Trustees were also required to permit free burials of destitute persons (paupers).
name.official_title.title: Goornong Cemetery Trust
title: Goornong Cemetery Trust

description:
The Geelong Female Refuge was established in 1868 to accommodate unmarried pregnant woman and to care for babies unable to stay with their mothers.  The home was nondenominational and administered by a committee of management.

In 1928, the Refuge was renamed Bethany Babies' Home. Bethany also operated as a mothercraft training school and maternity hospital.  After World War II, Bethany became known as a babies' hospital treating premature and frail babies awaiting return to their parents.  

By the late 1950's, Bethany provided residential care to wards of state, infant life protection placements and privately placed children.  Bethany was also an approved adoption agency.

In 1977, it ceased to operate as a babies' home and became Bethany Community Support which functioned as a child and family care agency.
name.official_title.title: Bethany Babies' Home [Previously known as Geelong Female Refuge 1868 - 1928]
title: Bethany Babies' Home [Previously known as Geelong Female Refuge 1868 - 1928]

description:
The Victorian Institute of Teaching was created on 18 December 2001 under the Victorian Insitute of Teaching Act 2001, to replace the Standards Council of the Teaching Profession (VA 4088).

The Victorian Institute of Teaching (VIT) was an independent statutory authority for the teaching profession, whose primary function was to regulate members of the teaching profession in Victoria in the public interest, by enforcing high ethical and professional standards for teachers.

VIT's 2015 Annual Report states the following information: "The Council of the Institute oversees and sets policy directions for the Secretariat, which is structured into an Executive and four operational branches who report to the CEO. The council appoints committees to provide strategic policy advice to guide their deliberations or to administer, upon delegation, certain Institute functions.

"The Secretariat carries out the work of the Council in relation to its functions under the Education and Training Reform Act 2006. Two branches, the Registration Branch and the Standards and Professional Learning Branch, administer the business areas of registration, accreditation, standard setting and professional
learning.

"The Corporate and Communications Branch manages the Institutes finances, facilities and information systems, human and physical resources, and the Institutes communications, including the telephony service, website, email correspondence, print communications and publications such as the annual report.

"The Professional Conduct Branch administers the Institutes disciplinary function."

The Education and Training Reform Act 2006 amalgamated all of the relevant education and training Acts (including the Victorian Institute of Teaching Act 2001) and was proclaimed 1 July 2007.
name.official_title.title: Victorian Institute of Teaching
title: Victorian Institute of Teaching

description:
The Royal Commission on the State Public Service (Victoria) (also known as the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Working of Public Departments) was asked to investigate the whole public service administration of the State of Victoria, exclusive only of Railways Department which was investigated by a separate Royal Commission (VA 5174) in the same year. This Royal Commission was specifically asked to include in its survey the “officers of Parliament”. It was entered in the Records of Patents Book Number 24, page 440, on 17th February, 1916.

The Commission’s members were Alexander Cooch, William Ross Anderson and Joseph Thorton Tweddle. The Final Report, totalling 131 pages, was presented to both Houses of Parliament by His Excellency’s Command, and addressed to His Excellency the Honourable Sir Arthur Lyulph Stanley, Governor of the State of Victoria, in 1917. The Commissioner’s examined 109 public sector officials for the Final Report.

The Final Report sets out the history of public service legislation and the conditions, regulating entrance to the public service. Then follows a close analysis of the performance of Government Departments in this order: Treasury, Chief Secretary’s Department, Department of Public Instruction, Law Department, Department of Lands and Survey, Public Works Department, Mines Department, Department of Public Health, Agriculture Department, State Forest Department, Department of Labour. A final chapter discusses the officers of Parliament, fire insurance and fire prevention, amalgamation of State Laboratories, employment of women.

The recommendations of the First Progress Report (originally published on 30th June 1916) are summarised at the end of the Final Report, which ends with a “Summary of conclusions and recommendations with an estimate of resulting economics and proposed new revenue”. The Final Report also contains an appendix titled “The Department Record System”, a Report authored by Mr. Henry Octavius Allan, from the Department of Crown Lands and Survey.
name.official_title.title: Royal Commission on the State Public Service
title: Royal Commission on the State Public Service

description:
The Royal Commission on the Geelong Harbor [Harbour] Trust was established and entered on record in the Registrar of Patents Book 24, page 389, on 1st March 1912.

The Commissioner’s appointed were Donald Mackinnon (chair), Henry Angus, Samuel Barnes, John Gray, Martin Hannah and Robert Henry Solly. Their task was to inquire into and report as to the policy adopted by the Geelong Harbour Trust Commissioners regarding the development of the Port of Geelong and four specific factors; and complaints and charges that were made; and to advise on reducing costs associated with the Geelong port.

A Progress Report, totalling 22 pages, was presented on 24th July 1912. The Final Report, totalling 58 pages, was presented to both Houses of Parliament by His Excellency’s Command, Sir John Michael Fleetwood Fuller, Governor of the State of Victoria on 13th October 1912. The Commission held 30 public sittings and took sworn evidence from 89 witnesses in Geelong and Melbourne and from three unsworn witnesses in Adelaide.

The Royal Commission reported on all aspects of the Trust, the history and development of the Geelong port, its dependence on its own hinterland, accessibility to shipping through Hopetoun Channel and development projects such as freezing works and the Trust’s own farm. Other parts of the Final Report deal with accounts, charges, and future policy. There are three appendices included in the Final Report.
name.official_title.title: Royal Commission on the Geelong Harbour Trust
title: Royal Commission on the Geelong Harbour Trust

description:
The Royal Commission into the Railways and Tramways Systems of Melbourne and Suburbs was entered in the Register of Patents, Book 24, pages 361-362, on 17th November 1910. Its Terms of Reference included an investigation of the existing public transport system, the desirability or otherwise of placing the railway and tramway systems under one ownership and management, the terms of compensation for municipalities and private companies if the Victoria Railways took over the whole transport system, the terms under which inner and outer Suburban Municipalities could join in a greater metropolitan transport system, etc.

The Commission’s members were Sir John Emanuel Mackey (chair), Henry Vine Champion, David Henry Dureau, James George Membrey, Robert Henry Solly and Joseph Sternberg. George Edwin Emery was also a Commissioner, but did not sign the Report.

The Report, titled the Report of the Royal Commission Appointed to Inquire Into and Report Upon the Railway and Tramway Systems of Melbourne and Suburbs, was presented to both Houses of Parliament by His Excellency’s Command on 12th September 1911. The Report examines the existing transport system and shows details of use and of service, including financial statements. The various suburban services are analysed and the possibility of electrification is discussed at length. Recommendations are covered for suburban railways, and for tramways and cable trams of Greater Melbourne.

description:
The Royal Commission on the Acquisition of Certain Estates by Sir Thomas Bent, as a Minister of the Crown, was entered on record in the Register of Patents Book, no. 24, page 339, on 8th April 1909. The Commission was to inquire about: circumstances connected to acquisition of land at Maribyrnong, Mont Park, Thornbury, Pender's Grove; and the connection or interest Sir Thomas Bent, former Treasuer and Premier of Victoria, had with the St. Kilda and Brighton Electric Street Railway or Tramway and the surrounding area. An Order in Council extending the scope of the inquiry to include Werribee was gazetted on 12th May 1909.

The Commission members were William Hutchinson (chairman), Hugh John Munro Campbell, George Alexander Elmslie, James George Membrey, Robert Henry Solly, Robert Stanley and Thomas Tunnecliffe. A total of 19 sittings were held between 2nd June 1909 and 8th July 1909, examining 62 witnesses.

The full Report, totalling 323 pages, was named ‘Report on Maribyrnong, Mont Park, Thornbury, Pender's Grove, and Werribee : also Sir Thomas Bent's interest in certain lands adjacent to the St. Kilda-Brighton electric street tramway : with findings and minutes of evidence’, which was presented by the Commissioners to His Excellency Sir Thomas David Gibson-Carmichael, and both Houses of Parliament, on 23rd July 1909. The Minutes of Evidence makes up the bulk of the Report.
name.official_title.title: Royal Commission on the Acquisition of Certain Estates by Sir Thomas Bent, as a Minister of the Crown

description:
The Royal Commission’s (title shortened to ‘Royal Commission on the Extension of Melbourne Westward’) terms of reference sought a report on the proposed removal of the railway station from Spencer Street and on the best means of connecting the city with the proposed docks to be constructed on the West Melbourne swamp. It was entered on record in the Register of Patents, Book 22, page 369, on 18th January 1887.

The Commission’s members were Albert Edwin Elworthy Lee Tucker (Chairman), William Anderson, Robert Burrowes, William Cain, George Selth  Coppin, David Mortimer Davies, Clement Hodgkinson, John Laurens, Walter Madden, William Robertson, Sir Frederick Thomas Sargood, Alexander John Skene, James Cooper Stewart, Nathan Thornley, John Alston Wallace, James Henry Wheeler, Peter Wright. Note of these, William Cain, George Coppin, John Laurens, James Cooper Stewart and William Robinson declined to sign the report; details of why are included in the Report. The Commissioner’s held 15 meetings, and examined 27 witnesses.

The Report was named ‘Extension of Melbourne Westward. Report of The Royal Commission in Regard to Proposed Removal of the Spencer-Street Railway Station to Allow of the Extension of Melbourne Westward, also in Regard to the Best Means of Connecting the City with the Proposed Docks, West Melbourne Swamp; together with Appendices, Minutes of Proceedings, and Minutes of Evidence.’ It totals 153 pages, including five appendices, and was presented to both Houses of Parliament by His Excellency’s Command; the Governor of Victoria was Sir Henry Brougham Loch, and the Premier was Duncan Gillies. The Report was submitted on 18th August 1887. The Royal Commission examined the financial implications of these schemes and the Report sets out in some details what pecuniary benefits would accrue to the city from the sale of some land and development of new sites.

description:
Creswick Public Cemetery commenced operations in 1858, with the first burial taking place on 20 December 1858. The cemetery was first mentioned in the Victoria Government Gazette on 7 April 1858, with the official appointment of trustees for the cemetery under the authority of the Governor-in-Council.

The cemetery was established in Creswick in response to requests for a permanent cemetery site. On 7 November 1856, Alexander Lewers wrote to the Colonial Secretary following a meeting of Creswick residents, asking for advice on how to obtain a permanent cemetery for the township. In the letter, Lewers observes that up until the time of writing, burials were taking place 'on a piece of ground within two hundred yards of the township boundary' and that the ground had 'since proved to be on a lead of gold'. Lewers further observed that the 'crowded state' of the small parcel of land used for burials made it 'dangerous in the highest degree'. This older cemetery, now adjacent to Calembeen Park, had no appointed trustees, was never gazetted, and no records of burials at this location remain extant.

By March of 1858, trustees had been elected for the new cemetery, and a plan of the subdivision of ground for the new cemetery site had been produced. The new cemetery site of twenty acres was located on the Clunes Road to the north of the Creswick township. An additional triangular area of land adjacent to the cemetery and the Clunes Road was approved in 1868, and the entire area of 'twenty-five acres one rood thirty-three perches' was officially gazette on 12 March 1869.

Cemeteries are controlled by a Trust appointed by the Governor-in-Council on the recommendation of the responsible Minister. Trustees are responsible for the administration and maintenance of cemeteries, the collection of fees and expenditure of revenue (for example: grants, subsidies received) the registration of burials and cremations, the making of rules and regulations and determining the scale of fees.
name.official_title.title: Creswick Cemetery (Creswick Cemetery Trust)
title: Creswick Cemetery (Creswick Cemetery Trust)

description:
On 28th March 1861 six acres of land was gazetted for the purposes of a cemetery for the township of Woodend (Government Gazette No 49, 28th March 1861). Trustees of the Cemetery were gazetted in April 1861, with a Plot Purchase register commencing in 1864. The official Burial Register commenced in November 1931. The first burial in the lawn section of the Cemetery was in 1975, and in 1978 the Columbarium Wall was completed.

Under the provisions of the Cemeteries Acts, trustees of public cemeteries are appointed by the Governor-in-Council, upon recommendation of the responsible Minister (as at 2017 it was the Minister for Health). The Trustees are responsible for the administration and maintenance of the cemetery, the collection of fees, expenditure of revenue (e.g. grants and subsidies received), the registration of burials and cremations, and the making of rules and regulations to determine the scale of fees. The Woodend Cemetery Trust comprises of 6 members and the Secretary as at 2017. The Trustees are responsible for keeping accounts of receipts and expenditure.
name.official_title.title: Woodend Cemetery (Woodend Cemetery Trust)
title: Woodend Cemetery (Woodend Cemetery Trust)

description:
The Coburg Teachers' College was established by the Education Department (VA 714) in 1959 as a teaching training institution. The College was under the direct control of the Department.

Classes at Coburg Teachers' College commenced in February 1959 and December 1960 saw the college's first graduation.

Initially the College offered two-year courses for the Trained Primary Teacher's Certificate and three-year course for the Trained Infant Teacher's Certificate. A three-year course for the Diploma of Teaching (Primary) was introduced in 1968. By 1969 the three-year Diploma course remained as the only course offered to intending primary teachers by the College and was a basic qualification for employment in the state's education system.

In July 1973, the College became the State College of Victoria at Coburg [VA 5188] having been admitted as a constituent member of the State College of Victoria [VA 437] in accordance with the State College of Victoria Act 1972.

description:
The Nunawading Youth Residential Centre was established on 17 September 1991, on the former site of Winlaton Youth Training Centre (VA 5093), as a facility for 10 to 14 year-old male and female offenders. The centre was located at 186 Springvale Road Nunawading.

The Children and Young Persons Act 1989 required that the provision of services for children and young people on protective orders be separated from those provided to young offenders in custody. The Nunawading Youth Residential Centre functioned as a youth training centre for young people sentenced to detention, and not for children placed on protection orders.

Baltara Youth Reception Centre closed in 1992 and the children were transferred to the Nunawading Youth Residential Centre. A decrease in referrals as a result of diversion programs and community-based sentencing saw the permanent closure of the Nunawading Youth Residential Centre on 3 August 1993. Its residents were sent to the Parkville Youth Residential Centre (VA 5166; see also VA 5086), a new facility built on the site of the former Baltara Reception Centre (VA 5090).

The Nunawading Youth Residential Centre comprised residential sections within the compound (including Warrina and Karringal), Wimbirra Remand Centre and the Leawarra Hostel. In 1992, Wimbirra closed and the Warrina residential section took over the remand function. The Leawarra Hostel closed in 1992.

In 1993, the Nunawading Youth Residential Centre had a population of about 25 sentenced youth at the time of its closure. These residents were relocated to Parkville Youth Residential Centre.

Legislation and record keeping:

The Children and Young Persons Act 1989 required that the provision of services for children and young people on protective orders be separated from those provided to young offenders in custody. The Act established different divisions in the Childrens Court to completely separate child protection matters from criminal custodial matters.

The Children and Young Persons Act 1989 also replaced the terms ward of state (introduced by the Neglected Childrens Act 1887) and trainee (introduced by the Social Welfare Act 1960), with the new term, children in need of protection. The old terminology was phased out in the 1990s. After this, both child protection cases and sentenced young people were classified as clients, the term used today for all Victorian care leavers.

Young people who entered into the youth justice system before implementation of the 1989 Act, kept their trainee case history files, and not the later Client Relationship Information System institutional files (JJ CRIS prefix). This explains why the older records continued until the late 1990s, well after the terminology had changed.

The term client is still used for all care leavers in Victoria.

Also see:
- Winlaton Youth Training Centre (VA 5093) is the predecessor agency, situated on the same site at 186 Springvale Road, Nunawading.
- Nunawading Youth Residential Centre, Education Centre No.4794 (VA 3962) represents the education function of Winlaton/Nunawading.
name.official_title.title: Nunawading Youth Residential Centre (also known as Nunawading Youth Training Centre)
title: Nunawading Youth Residential Centre (also known as Nunawading Youth Training Centre)

description:
Family Safety Victoria was established as an administrative office by an Order in Council on 22 June 2017 (Vic. Gazette Notice No: G 25, 22 June 2017). It commenced on the 1 July 2017 as an independent administrative office within the Department of Health and Human Services (VA 5037) portfolio, with the Special Minister of State as the responsible minister.

The establishment of Family Service Victoria was in response to recommendations from the 2016 Victorian Royal Commission into Family Violence (VA 5075) and as a part of Victoria's Family Violence Rolling Action Pan 2017-20. It is Victoria's first government agency solely dedicated to delivering family violence reform.

At the time of its establishment, the responsibilities of Family Safety Victoria were to:

- Lead the establishment of Support and Safety Hubs in the Department of Health and Human Services regions across Victoria which are to provide women, children and young people experiencing family violence access to coordinated support from justice, health and social services,
- Lead the implementation of family violence information sharing reforms,
- Establish and operate a Central Information Point to enable information to be shared between police, courts and government services so that perpetrators can be tracked and victims kept safe,
- Lead the redevelopment of the Family Violence Risk Assessment and Risk Management Framework, and
- Establish a Centre for Workforce Excellence to help develop workforce capabilities of the services involved in family violence.
name.official_title.title: Family Safety Victoria
title: Family Safety Victoria

description:
Victorian Ports Corporation (Melbourne) (VPCM) was the statutory authority created by the Victorian Government following the successful completion of the lease of the commercial operations of the Port of Melbourne. Victorian Ports Corporation (Melbourne) (VPCM) began operating on 1 November 2016 as the successor agency to the Port of Melbourne Corporation (VA 4028).

Established under the Transport Integration Act 2010 (Vic) the VPCM was responsible for the management of commercial shipping in Port Phillip, towage regulation, waterside emergency and marine pollution response, and the management of Station Pier cruise ship terminal.

The agency was also responsible for the State-retained business and activities resulting from the leasing of the Port in 2016 as well as the work of the Harbour Master.

VPCM was abolished as it merged with Victorian Regional Channels Authority (VA 5237) to create Ports Victoria (VA 5257) on 1 July 2021.

description:
The Victorian Pharmacy Authority (VPA) is the successor in law to the Pharmacy Board of Victoria II (VA 4877). The Act was proclaimed on 30 June 2010.

The VPA is established in accordance with section 81 of the Pharmacy Regulation Act 2010 with the Minister for Health as the responsible Minister. The Act provides for the regulation of pharmacy business, pharmacy departments and pharmacy depots.

The Act requires:
- the owners of pharmacy businesses, pharmacy departments and pharmacy depots to be registered,
- to license a person to carry on a pharmacy business or a pharmacy department,
-to issue standards in relation to the operation of pharmacies, pharmacy businesses, pharmacy departments and pharmacy depots,
- to keep a public register

Note:
The registration of pharmacists and the handling of complaints about the conduct or health of a pharmacist is the responsibility of the Pharmacy Board of Australia which has its services administered by the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency.

description:
The Economic Development, Infrastructure and Outer Suburban/Interface Services Committee is a former Joint Investigatory Committee of the 57th Parliament of Victoria.

On the 1st August 2013, pursuant to the Parliamentary Committees Amendment Act 2013, the Joint Investigatory Committees known as the Economic Development and Infrastructure Committee [VA 3139] and the Outer Suburban / Interface Services and Development Committee [VA 4776] were abolished.

The Economic Development, Infrastructure and Outer Suburban Interface Services Committee was established as successor committee [VA 5220, this agency].

On the 21 April 2015 it merged with the Education and Training Committee

The functions of the Economic Development, Infrastructure and Outer Suburban/Interface Services Committee are, if so required or permitted under this Act, to inquire into, consider and report to the Parliament on any proposal, matter or thing concerned with:

- economic development, industrial affairs or infrastructure
- the provision of services to new urban regions
- the development or expansion of new urban regions.

In subsection (1), urban regions means any part of Victoria developed for urban purposes that is not within regional Victoria as defined in section 16(2).

description:
The Law Reform, Drugs and Crime Prevention Committee was constituted under the Parliamentary Committees Act 2003.

The Law Reform, Drugs and Crime Prevention Committee is a former Joint Investigatory Committee of the 57th Parliament of Victoria. On the 21 April 2015 it merged with the Road Safety Committee and became the Law Reform, Road and Community Safety Committee.

The functions of the Law Reform, Drugs and Crime Prevention Committee are, if so required or permitted under this Act, to inquire into, consider and report to the Parliament on any proposal, matter or thing concerned with

(a) legal, constitutional or parliamentary reform
b) the administration of justice
c) law reform
d) the use of drugs, including the manufacture, supply or distribution of drugs
(e) the level or causes of crime or violent behaviour.

It is not a function of the Law Reform, Drugs and Crime Prevention Committee to inquire into, consider and report to the Parliament on any proposal, matter or thing concerned with-

(a) the joint standing orders of the Parliament
b) the standing orders or rules of practice of the Council or the Assembly.

description:
Guildford Primary School (School No. 264) (VA 5225) was opened in September 1861 as Guildford School, gaining official recognition by the National School Board (VA 919) some months later in November 1861. Located in Guildford, Victoria, approximately 124 kilometres north-west of Melbourne, the school was a co-educational and non-denominational primary school.

When Guildford School first opened, it operated out of a single-roomed timber building lined with calico, which had been erected with private funds. The exact site of the original school is subject to further research.  

In 1862, through the Common Schools Act, the Victorian Parliament abolished the two existing centralised boards and created a single Board of Education (VA 713). With the passing of this act, the school was renamed Guildford Common School and was given the number 264. A new school site of 2 acres fronting Franklin Street was selected, and a brick T-shaped building was completed on the site in 1868. Additions were made to the building in 1870 and 1873 and major alterations carried out between 1877 and 1912.

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Guildford State School at some stage between 1873 and 1878. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term “State school” to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use “primary school” in the name. Accordingly, the school’s name was changed to Guildford Primary School.

Guildford Primary School closed in 2017. Three years later, in October 2020, the Minister for Education James Merlino and State Member for Bendigo West Maree Edwards announced that due to local demand, the Guildford School would be reopening as a campus of Campbells Creek Primary School (School No. 120).  The Guildford Campus of Campbells Creek Primary School was officially opened in 2022.
name.official_title.title: Guildford (Primary School No.264)
title: Guildford Primary School (School No. 264; previously known as Guildford Sate School c.1875 – 1970; Guildford Common School 1862 – c.1875; Guildford School 1861 - 1862)

description:
The Moorabbin Justice Centre opened on 29 October 2007 as part of a Victoria State Government commitment to increase access to justice in the south-eastern suburbs. It is located at: 1140 Nepean Highway, Highett, Victoria 3190.

The Justice Centre includes a Magistrates' Court, Children's Court, Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal, Corrections Victoria, Sherriff's Office and Police Prosecutions Unit. The Centre draws cases from the municipalities of Kingston, Glen Eira, Bayside and parts of Monash.

Children's Court criminal matters were heard from the opening of the Moorabbin Justice Centre in October 2007. Moorabbin Children's Court, Family Division commenced in June 2009.

Children's Courts in Victoria are specialist courts with two divisions dealing with cases involving children and young people.

The Family Division hears applications relating to the protection and care of children and young persons at risk, and applications for intervention orders.

The Criminal Division hears matters relating to criminal offending by children and young persons.

By 2011 Judicial registrars had begun operating at the Moorabbin Justice Centre. Appointed by the Governor in Council, judicial registrars are independent judicial decision makers who assist the Magistrates' Court in dealing with a variety of matters that come within the court's criminal and civil jurisdictions. Their responsibilities in criminal matters include, but are not limited to:

- hearing and determining all criminal offences where the maximum penalty is not imprisonment, and all offences for which an infringement notice can be issued
- licence restoration and interlock removal applications
- consider and determine applications to adjourn criminal proceedings to allow offenders to undertake the court's diversion program.

For civil matters responsibilities include:

- exercise powers under the Magistrates' Court Civil Procedure Rules with some exceptions
- hear and determine civil arbitrations where amount sought is less than $5000
- determine civil interlocutory, rehearing and other
- applications, both in chambers and in open court and
- industrial mediations.

The Magistrates' Court carries out a number of functions including hearing criminal and traffic offences, civil disputes, family law, family violence and intervention orders, committal hearings and fines and penalties.

The Magistrates' Court is established by Section 4 of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989. Its civil and criminal jurisdictions place it below the County Court and Supreme Court to which all of its decisions may be appealed.

The Magistrates' Court has no appellate jurisdiction related to the decisions of another Court or Tribunal.

Moorabbin Magistrates' Court moved from the Melbourne region to the Frankston region, effective July 2011.

title: Morrabbin Justice Centre

description:
The Alexandra Babies' Home was established c.1909 at 187 Scott Parade, Ballarat East. 

The Home had a capacity of 36 children, most of which were wards of the state. When children reached the age of four they were typically transferred to the Ballarat Orphanage.

The Babies’ Home was located next to the Ballarat Female Refuge (VA 5829) in Scott Parade.

The Home was initially run by a committee of management before the Ballarat Town and City Mission (VA 5830) took over management of the Home in 1921. The Mission had closed the Ballarat Female Refuge and George Street Children’s Home and opened Ballarat Town and City Mission Rescue and Children’s Home in their place. It was also operated by the Mission alongside Alexandra Babies’ Home.

The Rescue Home closed in 1941, but the Babies’ Home continued operating, still run by the Mission.

The Babies’ Home was renamed to the Alexandra Toddlers' Home in 1964 to reflect that the children cared for at the Home were aged from eighteen months to five years.

The institution ceased to be registered by the Social Welfare Department as a Children's Home upon its closure on 8 November 1973. The Home had been experiencing financial difficulties. Some children who were living at the Home when it closed were returned to their parents; others were placed in alternative institutions.

description:
The site for Numurkah Cemetery was temporarily reserved from sale by order of the executive council on 22 May 1882 (Government Gazette, 26 May 1882, No. 58, p. 1170). The first trustees were appointed by the Commissioner of Crown Lands on 17 July 1882 (Government Gazette, 21 July 1882, No. 75, p. 1780).

The trustees of the cemetery resigned on 31 December 1974 and the appointment of the council of Numurkah II Shire (VA 2482) as trustees took place in March 1975, from which time the cemetery came under shire management. During this period, the lawn cemetery was reserved in 1977.

Local government administration of the cemetery trust continued after Numurkah Council was amalgamated into Moira Shire (VA 3705) in 1994. Moira Shire administered the trust until 2001 when new trustees were appointed under a new amalgamated cemetery trust (VA 5234 Numurkah-Wunghnu Cemetery Trust) administering both Numurkah and Wunghnu cemeteries.

Cemeteries are controlled by a Trust appointed by the Governor-in-Council on the recommendation of the responsible Minister. description:
The site for the Wunghnu Cemetery was temporarily reserved from sale by order of the executive council on 22 April 1879 (Government Gazette, 25 April 1879, No. 45, p. 928). The site was 6 acres and located south west of the township centre. The first trustees were appointed by the Commissioner of Crown Lands on 27 May 1879 (Government Gazette, 30 May 1879, No. 56, p. 1195).

This was the second site chosen for a cemetery in Wunghnu. Earlier, in 1876, another site (of 10 acres to the north of the Wunghnu township centre) was gazetted under the land parish name of Mundoona (Government Gazette, 30 June 1876, No. 45, p. 1223). This reserve was eventually revoked in 1888 (Government Gazette, 24 February 1888, No. 19, p. 614).

After the resignation of all members of the trust, the council of Numurkah II Shire (VA 2482) was appointed as trustees of the cemetery on 24 August 1982, from which time the cemetery came under shire council management.

Local government administration of the cemetery trust continued after Numurkah Council was amalgamated into Moira Shire (VA 3705) in 1994. Moira Shire administered the trust until 2001 when new trustees were appointed under a new amalgamated cemetery trust (VA 5234 Numurkah-Wunghnu Cemetery Trust) administering both Numurkah and Wunghnu cemeteries.

Cemeteries are controlled by a Trust appointed by the Governor-in-Council on the recommendation of the responsible Minister. Trustees are responsible for the administration and maintenance of cemeteries, the collection of fees and expenditure of revenue (for example: grants, subsidies received) the registration of burials and cremations, the making of rules and regulations and determining the scale of fees.

description:
The Victorian Regional Channels Authority (VRCA) began operations on 1 April 2004. The VRCA was established to manage the commercial navigation of the channels in Geelong port waters and to oversee the Channel Management for the Port of Portland and Hastings. The Authority was established by the Victorian Government under the Port Management Act 1995 and the Transport Integration Act 2010.

In managing the Geelong channels, the VRCA's key responsibilities include:
* Management of shipping control
* Provision of navigation aids
* Channel management
* Marine environment protection
* Safety and security

VRCA was abolished as it merged with Victorian Ports Corporation (Melbourne) (VA 5216) to create Ports Victoria (VA 5257) on 1 July 2021.

description:
On 1 January 2019, the Department of Transport (DT) (VA 5250) was created by Order of the Governor-in-Council under section 10 of the Public Administration Act 2004 (Victoria Government Gazette, S 552, 29 November 2018). This was part of machinery of government changes made by the re-elected Labor Government under the leadership of Premier the Hon Daniel Andrews MP. .

As a result of these machinery of government changes, the Department of Economic Development, Jobs, Transport and Resources (DEDJTR) (VA 5034) was split into two departments - the Department of Transport as the on-going department and Department of Jobs, Precincts and Regions (VA 5251) assuming the responsibilities of the non-transport portfolios.

The DT is responsible for ongoing operation and coordination of the state’s transport networks as well as the delivery of new and upgraded transport infrastructure.

The DT supported the Minister for Fishing and Boating; Minister for Ports and Freight; Minister for Public Transport; Minister for Roads and Road Safety; Minister for the Suburban Rail Loop; and Minister for Transport Infrastructure. The portfolios of Transport Infrastructure, Public Transport, Ports and Freight and Roads and Road Safety had been transferred from DEDJTR. 

Following machinery of government changes in June 2020, the portfolios of Roads, and Road Safety and the TAC, merged to form the new portfolio Roads and Road Safety (see Victoria Government Gazette, S 314, 30 June 2020, p 3).

The Department of Transport had five divisions: Investment and Technology; Network Integration; Network Planning; People and Business Services; Policy and Innovation; and Transport Operations.

Other bodies administered by the DT included Chief Investigator, Transport Safety; Commercial Passenger Vehicles Victoria; Port of Hastings Development Authority; Public Transport Victoria; Suburban Rail Loop Authority; Transport Accident Commission; Transport Safety Victoria; V/Line; VicRoads; Victorian Ports Corporation (Melbourne); Victorian Rail Track (VicTrack) and Victorian Regional Channels Authority.

On 1 January 2023, the Department of Transport was renamed the Department of Transport and Planning (VA 5286) by Order of the Governor in Council under section 10 of the Public Administration Act 2004 (Victorian Government Gazette, S 673 Monday 5 December 2022). The name change was part of machinery of government changes made by the re-elected Labor Andrews Government following the November 2022 State election.

Responsibility for Acts was transferred from Department of Transport (VA 5250) to the Department of Transport and Planning (VA 5286) under Administrative Arrangements Order No. 251 (Victorian Government Gazette, No. S 717, 19 December 2022).

description:
The Department of Jobs, Precincts and Regions (DJPR) was established on 1 January 2019 through an administrative order under Section 10 of the Public Administration Act 2004 (Victoria Government Gazette, S 552, 29 November 2018).

This was part of machinery of government changes made by the re-elected Andrews Labor Government, which changed the number of existing state departments from to seven to eight. The Department of Economic Development, Jobs, Transport and Resources (VA 5034) was split into two departments - the Department of Transport III (VA 5250) as the on-going department and DJPR assuming the responsibilities of the non-transport portfolios.

In addition, through the machinery of government changes, the DJPR assumed responsibility for the following: Office of the Suburban Development from the Department of Environment, Land, Water and Planning (VA 5036); Office of Racing and the Office of the Racing Integrity Commissioner from the Department of Justice and Regulation VA 5038 (which at that time was renamed the Department of Justice and Community Safety VA 5252); Sport and Recreation Victoria from the Department of Health and Human Services (VA 5037); Latrobe Valley Authority, Biomedical Precincts and Cities, Precincts and GovHubs from the Department of Premier and Cabinet (VA 1039).

On its establishment, the following portfolios were transferred from other departments to the DJPR: Priority Precincts (moved from DPC VA 1039); Racing (moved from DJR VA 5038); Suburban Development (moved from DELWP VA 5036); Tourism (moved from DEDJTR VA 5034); Sport and Recreation (moved from DHHS VA 5037); Major Events (moved from DEDJTR VA 5034).

The machinery of government changes on 22 June 2020 resulted in a number of changes to DJPR portfolios: Priority Precincts was renamed to Business Precincts; Community Sport was added as a new portfolio; and Local Government moved from DELWP (VA 5036). The previous portfolio of Jobs, Innovation and Trade ceased and was split into four new portfolios: Employment; Industry Support and Recovery; Innovation, Medical Research and the Digital Economy; and Trade.

As of April 2022, the DJPR was organised into the following administrative groups:  Agriculture; Corporate Services; Jobs, Innovation and Business Engagement; Creative, Sport and Visitor Economy; Employment and Inclusion; Forestry and Climate Change; Global Victoria; Industry Coordination and Recovery; Local Government and Suburban Development; Rural and Regional Victoria; and Strategic Communications and Marketing.

As of April 2022, the DJPR was responsible for the following portfolios: Agriculture; Business Precincts; Community Sport; Creative Industries; Employment; Industry Support and Recovery; Innovation, Medical Research and the Digital Economy; Local Government; Racing; Regional Development; Resources; Small Business; Suburban Development; Tourism, Sport and Major Events; and Trade.

Following the announcement that the 2026 Commonwealth Games will be held in Victoria, two new ministerial portfolios were added to DJPR on 27 June 2022 (Victoria Government Gazette, No. S 319, 27 June 2022): Commonwealth Games Delivery; Commonwealth Games Legacy.

On 1 January 2023 DJPR was renamed the Department of Jobs, Skills, Industry and Regions (DJSIR) (VA 5284) by The Governor in Council by Order made under section 10 of the Public Administration Act 2004 (Victorian Government Gazette, No. S 673, 5th December 2022). This name change was part of machinery of government changes made by the re-elected Labor Government under the leadership of Premier the Hon Daniel Andrews MP following the November 2022 State election.

Responsibility for Acts was transferred to the new DJSIR from DJPR, as well as some other Departments, under Administrative Arrangements Order No. 251 (Victorian Government Gazette, No. S 717, 19th December 2022).

On 1 January 2019, the Department of Justice and Regulation (VA 5038) was renamed to Department of Justice and Community Safety (DJCS) (VA 5252) by Order of the Governor-in-Council under section 10 of the Public Administration Act 2004 (Victoria Government Gazette, S 552, 29 November 2018). It replaced the Department of Justice and Regulation. The name change was part of machinery of government changes made by the re-elected Labor Government under the leadership of Premier the Hon Daniel Andrews MP. 

Its primary functions were reform, administration and enforcement of the law in Victoria including all police and prosecution functions; administration of the Court system; provision of the prison system; administration of various tribunals established to protect citizens' rights; provision of emergency services; drafting of legislation; business and non-business licenses; births, deaths and marriages certificates; and provision of legal advice to Government.

At its establishment, the Department supported the Attorney-General; Minister for Consumer Affairs, Gaming and Liquor Regulation; Minister for Corrections; Minister for Crime Prevention; Minister for Police and Emergency Services; Minister for Victim Support; Minister for Workplace Safety; and Minister for Youth Justice.

DJCS had thirteen divisions: Aboriginal Justice; Community Safety Building Authority; Consumer Affairs, Liquor, Gaming and Dispute Services; Corporate Governance and Support; Corrections and Justice Services; Emergency Management Victoria; Fines, Registration and Crime Prevention; Justice Policy and Data Reform; Legal and Integrity; People and Workplace Services; Police, Community Safety and Communications; Service Delivery Reform, Coordination and Workplace Safety; and Youth Justice.

DJCS’s authorities included the Business Licensing Authority, Country Fire Authority, Emergency Services Telecommunications Authority, Residential Tenancies Bond Authority and Victorian State Emergency Service Authority. DJCS also held partnerships with over 40 statutory entities.

DJCS operated over seven areas, comprising the Northern Metropolitan, South East Metropolitan, Barwon South West, Gippsland, Grampians, Hume and Loddon Mallee regions.

From 1 January 2023, DJCS gained and lost some responsibilities as part of machinery of government changes that occurred following the re-election of the Labor Andrews Government in November 2022. DJCS gained the Racing portfolio from the Department of Jobs, Precincts and Regions (VA 5251). Responsibility for Consumers Affairs Victoria and Registry of Births, Deaths & Marriages was transferred from DJCS to the newly established Department of Government Services (VA 5282). description:
Following the machinery of government changes announced on 30 November 2020, the Department of Health and Human Services (VA 5037) was separated into two new Departments – the Department of Health (DoH) (VA 5255) and Department of Families, Fairness and Housing (DFFH) (Victoria Government Gazette - Special Gazette No. S684, 22 December 2020). The name of the Department of Health and Human Services was changed to the Department of Health, while the Department of Families, Fairness and Housing was established as a new office.

The two departments came into operation on 1 February 2021.

DFFH includes the former Department of Health and Human Services (VA 5037) ministerial portfolios of:
  • Child Protection  
  • Prevention of Family Violence 
  • Housing 
  • Disability, Ageing and Carers (both DFFH and DH provide some support to this portfolio)
The Department is also responsible for the following portfolios that were previously served by the Department of Premier and Cabinet (VA 1039):
  • Multicultural Affairs
  • Equality
  • Veterans 
  • Women 
  • Youth
(Victoria Government Gazette - Special Gazette No. S41, 27 January 2021)

The DFFH departmental structure also supported:
  • Family Safety Victoria 
  • Homes Victoria 
  • Respect Victoria

The Fairer Victoria division, which had been part of the Department of Premier and Cabinet (VA 1039), was also incorporated into DFFH. 

A range of portfolio entities sat under DFFH including the Victorian Multicultural Commission, Respect Victoria, Queen Victoria Women’s Centre Trust, Public Sector Gender Equality Commissioner, Gender Equality Commissioner, Language Loop, the Shrine of Remembrance, Victorian Veterans Council and Family Violence Reform Implementation Monitor. 

The Family Violence Branch in DPC’s Social Policy Group also transferred to DFFH to continue the implementation of family violence reforms. 

There were no Ministerial portfolio changes to DFFH following the machinery of government changes that occurred after the November 2022 State election and the re-election of the Andrews Labor Government.

description:
Ports Victoria began operations on 1 July 2021. Its establishment merged the Victorian Regional Channels Authority (VA 5237) and Victorian Ports Corporation (VA 5216), to bring the responsibility for all of Victoria’s commercial ports and waterways under one agency. Prior to this, the port of Melbourne and regional port waters were managed by separate agencies. This amalgamation was part of the government’s response to the 2020 Independent Review of the Victorian Ports System.

Ports Victoria was established under the Transport Integration Act 2010, the details of which were published in the Victoria Government Gazette Special Gazette Number S296 on 17 June 2021. All the functions of VPC and VRCA at that time were transferred to Ports Victoria.

The functions of Ports Victoria, as outlined in pages 21-23 of Victoria Government Gazette S296, include:
•    To promote and market the port of Melbourne
•    To manage, or enable management by others, stevedoring operations 
•    To establish, manage, dredge, and maintain channels in the port of Melbourne and regional port waters
•    To provide and maintain navigation aids
•    To publish information on the depths and configurations of channels and berths
•    To provide and maintain systems of navigation in the port of Melbourne and regional port waters
•    To direct and control the movement of vessels in the port of Melbourne and regional port waters
•    To plan, develop, and operate Station Pier and West Finger Pier
•    To support and develop the Port Capacity Project as part of the port of Melbourne.

On its commencement, operations of Ports Victoria were headquartered in Geelong.

description:
On 1 July 2020 the new agency Fire Rescue Victoria (FRV) assumed all of the functions of the Melbourne Fire and Emergency Services Board (VA 4363) as well as career Country Fire Authority (VA 482) firefighters. While the MFEB was abolished at this time, the CFA continued as a body for volunteer firefighters only.

Fire Rescue Victoria is the successor in law to the Metropolitan Fire and Emergency Services Board under Section 99 of the Fire Rescue Victoria Act 1958.

FRV serves metropolitan Melbourne and major regional centres, operating 85 stations across the state as well as supporting volunteer responses where required.

Co-located FRV and CFA stations include both career and volunteer firefighters. They were formerly run by the CFA; under the legislation these stations have become FRV responsibility. CFA is now a community-based, solely volunteer firefighter organisation.

FRV is a statutory body within the Department of Justice and Community Safety (VA 5252).

description:
On 1 July 1995 the Bendigo Health Care Group was established through the merger of the Bendigo Hospital (VA 1264) and the Anne Caudle Centre (VA 1275) (see Victoria Government Gazette G 24, 22 June 1995, pg. 1531). In line with the Department of Health and Community Services (VA 3092) guidelines, Bendigo Psychiatric Services joined the group. Prior to the merger, Bendigo Psychiatric Services had been operating as an independent entity from around 1972.

In May 2010, the Brumby Government announced that a new hospital would be built in Bendigo. In January 2017, patients and staff were moved from the old site to the new Bendigo Hospital.

description:
The Western Health Care Network (WHCN) was created on 1 August 1995 by an order of the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister for Health under Section 65c of the Health Services Act 1988.  The WHCN was an aggregation of the Royal Melbourne Hospital (VA 1048), North West Hospital (see VA 5265), Altona Hospital, Western Hospital, and Williamstown Hospital. Additionally, Werribee Mercy Hospital joined later that financial year. The aggregation of the hospitals was part of the Kennett Government’s policy for health services in metropolitan Melbourne.  As a result, the individual hospital boards of management were replaced by one Network Board of Management (see Victoria Government Gazette G29, 27 July 1995, page 1981 and to s65(c) of the Health Services Act 1988 for legal effect of aggregation. Refer to s65(c) and s65(d) of the Health Services (Metropolitan Hospitals) Act 1995 which provided for the aggregation of metropolitan hospitals and succession in law.)

In August 1996 North Western Health Mental Health (NWMH) was established as a Western Mental Health program.

In February 1997 the Victorian Infectious Diseases Reference Laboratory (VIDRL) came under the control of the WHCN. 

On 3 November 1997, WHCN merged with part of the former North Eastern Health Care Network into the newly named North Western Health Care Network (NWHCN). This occurred under an order of the Governor in Council dated 28 October 1997, acting under section 8(1) of the Health Services Act 1988, and amending Schedule 3 to the Health Services Act, as published in Victoria Government Gazette s139, 3 November 1997, page 1. The NWHCN comprised those hospitals and services previously under WHCN as well as Preston and Northcote Community Hospital (PANCH), Northern Hospital and Bundoora Extended Care Centre.

NWHCN was disaggregated on 30 June 2000 and Melbourne Health (see The Royal Melbourne Hospital VA 1048) was proclaimed.  Melbourne Health was created and incorporated as a Metropolitan Health Service pursuant to the Health Services (Governance) Act 2000 and an associated Order by the Governor-in-Council dated 22 June 2000 (Victoria Government Gazette s88, 23 June 2000, page 11). 

Melbourne Health comprised of the RMH (VA 1028), Melbourne Extended Care and Rehabilitation Service (previously known as North West Hospital 1991 - 1999) (VA 5265), North Western Mental Health (NWMH), North West Dialysis, and the Victorian Infectious Diseases Reference Laboratory.

The WHCN, NWHCN and Melbourne Health head offices were located on the RMH site in Grattan Street, Parkville. Network records which relate only to The Royal Melbourne Hospital’s operations and functions during the time of WHCN, NWHCN and Melbourne Health are attributed to the RMH.  Records created at the Network executive level which relate either to overall Network strategy and management, or solely to other hospitals within the WHCN and NWHCN are attributed to the WHCN / NWHCN.

Records created during the Melbourne Health period are treated as records created by The Royal Melbourne Hospital (VA 1048) as the hospitals and services that comprised Melbourne Health were eventually subsumed under the RMH umbrella, and Melbourne Health itself rebranded as The Royal Melbourne Hospital on 1 July 2020, although Melbourne Health remained the legal name used for statutory purposes.

Note that some records relating to WHCN, NWHCN and Melbourne Health activities are also to be found in VA 5265 Melbourne Extended Care and Rehabilitation Service (previously known as North West Hospital 1991 - 1999).

description:
The Melbourne School of Nursing (MSN) was formed in 1950 when the Royal Melbourne Hospital’s (VA 1048) School of Nursing joined with those of the Queen Victoria Hospital, Fairfield Hospital (VA 1231) and the Royal Women’s Hospital (VA 1241). It was established by the Hospitals and Charities Commission and was located in the Mayfield Centre Malvern with Miss Jean Headberry as the Dean of the School. The Royal Children’s Hospital (VA 1239) provided paediatric experience. 

The MSN was both an effort to overcome the shortage of nurse trainees, and a response to concerns to lift standards of nurses' training in Australia following World War Two and developments overseas, including increased experience of Australian nurses abroad. It enrolled 2452 students and produced 1693 graduates.

In 1954, the Queen Victoria Hospital (VA 1254) withdrew its association from the MSN. Following this, in 1955, the name of the School was changed to The Royal Melbourne Hospital and Associated Hospitals School of Nursing. However, in May 1960, the Committee of Management of the RMH wrote to the MSN advising them of their intended withdrawal effective October 1960 to re-establish its own nursing school and after this no further enrolments were accepted. The name remained The Royal Melbourne Hospital and Associated Hospitals School of Nursing until its closure, even after the withdrawal of the Royal Melbourne Hospital in 1960. The School closed on 30 September 1963. 

In 1954, a Melbourne School of Nursing Past Trainees Association was formed with one of their responsibilities being the administration of various grant funds to further nursing training and research activities. This Association folded around 2001.
