description:
The Southern Health Care Network was created on 1 August 1995 by an order of the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister for Health under Section 65c of the Health Services Act 1988 (Vic) to aggregate the Dandenong Hospital (VA 1246), the Hampton Rehabilitation Hospital (VA 1237), the Kingston Centre (VA 1278), the Monash Medical Centre (VA 2823), the Mordialloc-Cheltenham Community Hospital (VA 1251), the Sandringham and District Memorial Hospital (VA 1256), and the Westernport Memorial Hospital (VA 1748). 

As a result, a new Board of Directors was constituted with eight members appointed overseeing all the aggregated hospitals. Refer to the Victoria Government Gazette G29, 27 July 1995 and s65(c) of the Health Services Act 1988 (Vic) for the legal effect of aggregation as well as the names of the first appointed Board members, and s65(d) of the Act for the succession in law. 

The Southern Health Care Network became one of many networks across metropolitan Melbourne formed as part of the Kennett Government’s policy for health services.
 
At the end of December 2001, the Governor in Council on recommendation of the Minister for Health, announced a number of incorporations of metropolitan hospitals to be cancelled, including the Southern Health Care Network. This took effect on the 1st of January 2002 (Victoria Government Gazette, Gazette 51, 20 Dec 2001).
 
At the same time, under s208 of the Health Services Act 1988 (Vic), all the property, rights and liabilities of the Southern Health Care Network were allocated to the newly formed Southern Health. Southern Health was established under s181 of the Health Services Act 1988 (Vic), which allows for the establishment of a metropolitan health service. This took effect on the 31st of December 2001 (Victoria Government Gazette, Gazette 51, 20 Dec 2001).
 
On the 30th of May 2013, Southern Health was renamed Monash Health (Victoria Government Gazette, Gazette S191, 30 May 2013). 

Monash Health as of 2021 oversees many hospitals and health care facilities and services, including but not limited to, mental health services, aged care services and community health services. Their existing hospitals and medical centres include many with long history’s including the Monash Medical Centre (VA 2823) and the Kingston Centre (VA 1278) which can be traced back to the 19th Century. Over the years Monash Health has established new medical facilities, including the Casey Hospital in 2004 and the Monash Children’s Hospital in 2017.

description:
On 1 July 1991, Mount Royal Hospital (VA 1280) merged with the Greenvale Centre (VA 1277) to form the North West Hospital under the Health Services Act 1988 s65(1). The North West Hospital operated at two sites, one at the previous Mount Royal Hospital site in Parkville and the other at the previous Greenvale Centre in Greenvale. The Greenvale site was decommissioned in 1998. 

On 1 August 1995, North West Hospital legally became part of VA 5262 Western Health Care Network (WHCN), although it continued to operate under its own name. The WHCN was created by an order of the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister for Health under Section 65c of the Health Services Act 1988 to aggregate the Royal Melbourne Hospital (VA 1048), North West Hospital, Altona Hospital, Western Hospital, and Williamstown Hospital (VA 1262).

In 1998, the rehabilitation program from The Royal Melbourne Hospital’s Essendon campus moved to the North West Hospital’s Parkville site. 

On 15 July 1999, North West Hospital was renamed Melbourne Extended Care and Rehabilitation Service (MECRS). 

On 30 June 2000, MECRS became a part of Melbourne Health. Melbourne Health was created and incorporated as a Metropolitan Health Service pursuant to the Health Services (Governance) Act 2000 and an associated Order by the Governor-in-Council dated 22 June 2000. 

On 24 January 2005, the MECRS site changed its name to The Royal Melbourne Hospital – Royal Park Campus when it was effectively taken over by the Royal Melbourne Hospital (VA 1048).

description:
Greenvale Village for the Aged was established on the site of the Greenvale Sanatorium in 1955. Although sanatorium patients continued to be treated at the site until February 1956, expansion of the Greenvale site commenced in 1955 to facilitate new elderly patients by the end of the calendar year. Greenvale was inaugurated on 22 August 1955 and registered as a Benevolent Home by the Hospitals and Charities Commission (VA 694) 19 September 1955. (Annual report 1956)

In July 1962 it was re-registered as a Hospital for the Aged with the objectives of providing care for the elderly as well as establishing a geriatric research centre. The centre studied disabilities of aged people, enabling their treatment and rehabilitation, and the social and medical problems associated with such disabilities. (Annual report 1963).

Greenvale Village for the Aged changed its name to Greenvale Geriatric Centre, by Order-in-Council made 27 March 1973 under the Hospitals and Charities Act 1958, Section 5(3), (Victoria Government Gazette 4 April 1973, page 742). The Hospitals and Charities Commission approved the name change on 26 February 1973, effective 1 March 1973 (VGG 28 February 1973, page 449). A new centre for rehabilitation, Sir William Upjohn House, was opened in 1974. 

The corporate name Greenvale Geriatric Centre changed again to Greenvale Centre by Order-in-Council made 25 June 1986 under the Hospitals and Charities Act 1958, Section 50 (VGG 2 July 1986, page 2452). The Department of Health approved the name change on 12 May 1986 (VGG 21 May 1986, page 1448).

On 1 July, 1991, the Greenvale Centre amalgamated with the Mount Royal Hospital (VA 1280) located in Park Street, Parkville, under the Health Services Act 1988 s65(1) and became the North West Hospital (VA 5265) by Administrator in Council (VGG 26 June 1991, page 1712-13). The site became known as North West Hospital – Greenvale Campus.

description:
Kyneton Primary School (School No. 343) (VA 5272) is a coeducational government school located in Kyneton in the Macedon Ranges Shire.

The school first opened as a National School on 24 March 1856 on the corner of Ebden and Baynton Streets. The original school building consisted of two rough bluestone rooms built by Towell, Burton and Thirkettle. Attendance upon its opening was 30 students, which quickly increased to 80. A period of dissention among the school community regarding the condition of the school resulted in a dramatic drop in attendance in the late 1850s, but numbers increased once this was resolved.

In September 1862 the school was renamed Kyneton Common School. Following the Education Act 1872 it was again renamed, becoming Kyneton State School. In 1873 an additional room was added to help accommodate the rapidly expanding school population. In 1877 a further two classrooms, a bell tower, and an office were added by George Piggin and William Wall.

A cadet corps was established within the school at the end of the 19th century, and a rifle range built. It was then abolished in 1911. The school interior was completely remodelled and additions made in 1907, necessitating classes to be held within the School of Mines, the Salvation Army Hall, and the drill hall. The school was reopened by the Minister of Public Instruction on the 5th of July the same year, and no further additions were made until the years 1958-1960.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than exclusively primary-level ones. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name, and school number 343 became Kyneton Primary School.

During the 1980s, further additions were made to the school, and then in 2018 a new school building was built on a larger site next to Kyneton High School (School No. 936) at 49-79 Edgecombe Street. The project was completed in April for $11.5 million, and the school relocated to the new site later the same year. The school remains in operation as of 2024, with approximately 338 students enrolled.

The original school was heritage listed and classified as part of the Victorian National Trust (Property No. B1273) in 2000. In the 2020-21 Victorian Government Budget, $12 million was allocated to restore and redevelop the heritage site into a creative community zone with a gallery, exhibition space, and function room. The project is a collaboration between Development Victoria, Creative Victoria and Working Heritage, who was selected in 2021 to be the site’s operator. In 2022 Development Victoria appointed the construction firm McCorkell to carry-out the works.
title: Kyneton Primary School (School No. 343, previously known as Kyneton National School (1856 – 1862), Kyneton Common School (1862 – c.1872), Kyneton State School (c.1872 – 1970)

description:
Wallan Primary School (School No. 664) (VA 5273) is a coeducational government school situated in Wallan, regional Victoria.

The school was first opened as Wallan Wallan Scots School by Reverend Thomas Craig in 1858, with 34 students enrolled. Classes were taught in a weatherboard school building built on Queen Street, with Thomas Noble as Head Teacher. Noble’s wife was employed as the Sewing Mistress.

An additional brick building was added in 1862 after enrolments increased. The school became a Common School (No. 664) the same year. Following the Education Act 1872, the Education Department (VA 714) purchased the premises and replaced the weatherboard section with a brick building. A small playing area situated across the road from the school was acquired around the same time. Between 1873 and 1878 the school was renamed Wallan Wallan State School.

In 1908 a teacher’s residence was bought. It was then sold and vacated in 1959.

Due to an increase in enrolments, the school was renovated, with new buildings added. These were officially opened in 1958 by Hon. J.S. Bloomfield, the Minister of Education. In 1970 the school was renamed Wallan Primary School.

Wallan Primary School had approximately 650 students enrolled in 2021, and 724 by 2023. The school was still in operation as of 2024.

Please note that the traditional name for the area is ‘Wallan Wallan’ in the Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung language. The school is found to be referred to as both ‘Wallan Wallan’ or ‘Wallan’ Common/State School up until approximately 1940, when the second ‘Wallan’ appears to have been dropped.
title: Wallan Primary School (School No. 664; previously known as Wallan Wallan Scots School 1858 – 1862; Wallan (Wallan) Common School 1862 – c.1873; Wallan (Wallan) State School c.1873 – 1970)

description:
Woodend Primary School is located in Woodend, on the northwest side of the Macedon Ranges and 70 kilometres from Melbourne.

Established as a National School on 28 June 1855, the school had an enrolment of 22 in its first year. The school building at the time was likely made of timber, with a wooden bell tower that had fallen into disrepair by 1917.

Following the Common Schools Act of 1862, the school’s name changed to Woodend Common School. The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Woodend State School in 1873. The school number was retained.

From 1913 – 1914 classes were held in a leased building while the school was remodelled. It may have been at this time that the timber building was replaced with brick, as shown in site plans from 1941 onwards. A teacher’s residence was built on Forest Street, Woodend, sometime after 1920.

The school purchased 21 acres of land in 1963. A school building from the closed Chanters Lane State School (No. 923), was moved to Woodend and used as a general-purpose room.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term “State school” to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use “primary school” in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Woodend Primary School.

By 1979 the school had 7 classrooms, inclusive of the brick schoolhouse with 4 classrooms and additional detached portable buildings. Enrolment at the time was 247.

In 1984 the closed Carlsruhe Primary School (No. 115) site became part of the Woodend Primary School campus. The site is now known as the Carlsruhe Annex, where Year 4 students spend four days per week, engaging in a curriculum focusing on sustainability, environmental awareness and animal husbandry.

A major upgrade to the school was completed in 2019. This included a new music facility with practice and meeting rooms, the conversion of a multi-purpose room into a gym, and landscaping.
From 2016 enrolment at the school has fluctuated, in part due to a large amount of people moving to rural areas during COVID-19. At its peak in 2021, 460 students were enrolled. By 2024 this had dropped to 391.

As of 2025, this school is still in operation.
title: Woodend Primary School (School No. 647; previously known as Woodend Common School 1855–1862; Woodend National School 1862–1873; Woodend State School 1873-1970)

description:
Taradale Primary School opened as Taradale National School on 1 April 1855. There were 27 students initially enrolled at the school with an average attendance of 18 students.

Additions to the schoolhouse were made in 1874. By 1877 the average student attendance grew to 205.

As mining was the predominant occupation in the region, the school provided night classes for pupils aged between 12 to 35 years of age.

The original timber residential building was replaced in the early 1900s.

During the period of the first World War, 1914 – 1918, the school’s population had fallen to approximately 75 students, and this number remained steady until the 1930s.

Due to the decline in mining and commerce in the 1930s, the population of Taradale dropped. During this time school enrolments averaged between 20 to 30 students. By 1967 the enrolments stood at 31 pupils.

In 1968, much of the flooring in the original bluestone and brick building was replaced, and in 1970 the school named was changed to Taradale Primary School.

In 1995, the building from the closed Metcalfe Primary School No. 851 was moved to Taradale and used as a multi-purpose room.

In 2005, Taradale Primary School celebrated its 150th anniversary with a plaque being dedicated at the entrance of the school building. The original school building is still in use today [2022].
title: Taradale Primary School (formerly Taradale National School, Taradale Common School, Taradale State School)

description:
Castlemaine Primary School (School No. 119) (VA 5276) is a coeducational government school located in Castlemaine, a Gold Rush town established in the mid-19th century on the traditional lands of the Dja Dja Wurrung people in central Victoria. 

The school was originally a National School, opened in 1855 with 72 students enrolled. Classes were held in a tent that was erected on the corner of Urquhart and Mostyn Streets. Population growth soon made a larger and more permanent school necessary; the foundation for which was laid on 15 April 1856. The school was built in the Norman style and included two large classrooms.

In 1862, the Victorian Parliament abolished the two existing centralised boards and created a single Board of Education (VA 713) through the Common Schools Act. With the passing of this act, the school was re-named Castlemaine Common School. Later, the Education Act 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and introduced free, compulsory and secular schooling for Victorian children. Subsequently, school naming conventions once again changed and the school was renamed Castlemaine State School. The school number was retained. Attendance at this time rose to 210.

With an ever-increasing population, the local community requested a larger more suitable school building be built. The new two-storey stone building was opened by the Hon. Angus Mackay, MLA, Minister of Public Instruction on the 5 July 1875, and is still in use as the school's main building as of 2026.

In 1876, the school was designated a ‘Training School’; the first teachers' training school to be established in Victoria. By 1878, 900 students were enrolled. Castlemaine North State School (School No. 2051) opened the same year, gave relief from overcrowding.

In 1968, the school became a training school for students from the Bendigo Teachers College.

Enrolments decreased significantly over time, with approximately 237 students in attendance in 1969. Following a statewide change to school naming convention in 1970, the school’s name was changed to Castlemaine Primary School.

In 2003 a new ‘L’ shaped building was completed beside the 1875 schoolhouse. The new building provided five classrooms, a multi-purpose room, a canteen and student amenities. In addition, it created disabled access to both the new facility and the old building, and a courtyard between the two. The 1875 building was refurbished and contained administration, the principal’s office, library, art room, staff lounge and amenities and two classrooms.

In 2019 and 2025, funds allocated by the State Government allowed for multiple upgrades and modernisation of school classrooms and toilet facilities. In 2023, enrolment was 170.

The school is still in operation as of 2026.
title: Castlemaine Primary School (School No. 119; previously known as Castlemaine Common School 1855-1862; Castlemaine National School 1862-1872; Castlemaine State School 1872-1970)

description:
Mount Macedon Primary School (School No. 415) (VA 5277) is a coeducational primary school located in the Macedon Ranges, north-west of Melbourne. 

The school was first established under the Denominational School Board (VA 703) in 1858 by the Reverend R.T. Cummins, out of a single room timber building. 

In 1862, through the Common Schools Act, the Victorian Parliament abolished the two existing centralised boards and created a single Board of Education (VA 713). With the passing of this act, the school became Mount Macedon Common School.

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked a change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Mount Macedon State School.
 
In 1874, a new brick school building was built. A memorial drinking fountain was established in the school grounds in 1919 to celebrate and commemorate peace following the end of the First World War.

The school celebrated its centenary in 1958. As part of the celebrations ornamental entrance gates were erected, and a time capsule containing several documents and letters was sealed into a post on the righthand side of the gates. The school grounds also featured a bell tower in memory of the School Committee Chairman, Vernon Turnbull, who passed away in 1967.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Mount Macedon Primary School.

The community of Mount Macedon suffered significant losses during the Ash Wednesday bushfires in 1983, including damage to the original Mount Macedon Primary School buildings. The school bell remained standing, and stones from the original buildings were used to construct a new entrance to the school.

In 2019, a new STEAMM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Art, Mathematics and Music) Centre was constructed; it was a finalist for ‘Best School Project Under $5 million’ in the 2020 Victorian School Design Awards. In 2025, a new outdoor inclusive learning space was also completed. 

As of 2025, the Mount Macedon Primary School is still in operation with the original brick building still in use.
title: Mount Macedon Primary School (School No. 415; previously known as Mount Macedon Denominational School 1858 – 1862; Mount Macedon Common School 1862 – c.1873; Mount Macedon State School c.1873 - 1970)

description:
Carlton North Primary School (School No. 1252) is a co-educational primary school located in the inner-northern suburbs of Melbourne, that has been operating since its establishment in 1873.

The school first opened on 28th July 1873 as Carlton Stockade School, on the site of the former Collingwood Stockade (VA 4608), on Lee Street, North Carlton.  The Collingwood Stockade had been established in 1853 to house convicts working in nearby bluestone quarries. The building was repurposed in 1866 as the Collingwood Asylum (VA 2851) until 1873, when the school was handed over to the Education Department (VA 714). Before the school was able to be opened, it underwent sulphur fumigation due to the dilapidated and unhygienic state of the building. 

Upon opening in 1873, the school had an enrolment of 276 students and by 1874 it was reported that it would accommodate up to 600 students. After only four years, however, the buildings were deemed unsuitable, and the school building was almost entirely demolished and replaced by a building which is still standing, as of 2024. The building was based on a standard design, which had been produced as part of a competition by the new Education Department (VA 174) in 1873. When the new school building was opened 1879, the school name was also changed to Lee Street State School. 

In 1913 the former caretaker’s house was demolished and an infant school was built on the site, opening in 1915.   

Student enrolments reached 980 in the 1930s and in 1937, the building was extensively remodelled as part of a large building programme undertaken by the Public Works Department (VA 669). 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Carlton North Primary School around that time, though it continued to be referred to as Lee Street Primary School on occasion. 

The original Carlton North Primary School building was listed on the Victorian Heritage Register in 1982, as an example of the 1870s ‘competition school’ building in the Gothic Revival style, with the listing amended in 2023 to include additional land.
title: Carlton North Primary School (School No. 1252; previously known as Carlton Stockade School 1873 – 1879; Lee Street State School 1879 – c. 1970)

description:
Nagambie Primary School (School No. 1104) (VA 5279) is a coeducational primary school located in the Goulburn Valley region of northern Victoria. 

It first opened as Goulburn Valley School in 1870, just outside the township of Nagambie in a post and bark building. A new school building was built and was officially opened on 1 October 1871, and the school became recognised as a Common School by the Board of Education (VA 713).

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming known as Nagambie State School.

In 1885 a new school building was built and was opened by Mr G. Hall, MP for Moira. An unused school building from Prairie State School (School No. 1981) was moved to the Nagambie in 1904 to provide extra accommodation but this building was eventually destroyed by fire. In July 1910, two new rooms were added to the school building. By 1910 enrolments had reached 201 students.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Nagambie Primary School.

In 2021 the school celebrated its 150th anniversary. As of 2026, it continues to operate
title: Nagambie Primary School (School No. 1104; previously known as Goulburn Valley School 1870 – 1871; Goulburn Valley Common School 1871 – c.1872; Nagambie State School c.1873 – 1970)

description:
Ararat Primary School (School No. 800) (VA 5280) opened as Ararat Common School on 15 May 1865. The school was created from the amalgamation of the Church of England and Presbyterian Schools.

The denominational school buildings were used for a short period of time, but with a school population of 230 students by October 1865, a new school building was built on High Street, Ararat to accommodate the students.

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked a change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Ararat State School.

By 1873 the school was inadequate for the enrolment of new students, so the Board of Advice requested the Minister of Public Instruction to reserve 5 acres of land at the intersection of Moore and King Streets for a new school site.

The Hon. W. McLennan MLA laid the foundation stone for the new school, and it was officially opened in November 1875 with 509 new enrolments. By 1877 enrolments had reached 831 students.

By 1902, structural changes were needed to the school buildings to implement the new policy of reduced class sizes. Changes included the improvement of lighting, classroom re-arrangement with windows in internal walls and larger external windows to let in more natural light.

The Public Works Department (VA 669) drew up plans for further changes to the school buildings in 1912 to accommodate its 632 students. These changes meant the removal of the bell tower and spire, and the erection of wooden offices at the front of the school. This work was completed in 1914.

On 11 June 1965, a central school library was opened by the Premier of Victoria, the Hon. Henry Bolte MLA. This event marked the occasion of the centenary of the school.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Ararat Primary School.

The school has seen further upgrades over the years, but the biggest refurbishment happened in 2010 which included the construction of a new front entrance and earth façade.

As of 2025, Ararat Primary School continues to operate. 

Ararat Primary School should not be confused with the following primary schools that also operated in the area:

  • Ararat Church of England School (School No. 10), operating from 1857 – 1865
  • Ararat Presbyterian School (School No. 13), operating from 1860 – 1865
  • Ararat Catholic School (School No. 20), operating from 1857 – 1875
  • Ararat Dam State School (School No. 2364), operating from 1881 - 1893
  • Ararat West Primary School (School No. 4720), operating 1955 – present
title: Ararat Primary School (School No. 800; previously known as Ararat Common School 1865 – c.1873; Ararat State School c.1873 – c.1970)

description:
Essendon Primary School (School No. 483) (VA 5281) is a coeducational primary school located in the inner north-west of Melbourne, within the City of Moonee Valley (VA 3707). 

The school was originally established in 1850 as the Pascoe Vale National School No. 483, under the National School Board (VA 919). The original wooden building, located on a two-acre block of land close to the junction of Five Mile and Moonee Ponds Creek, had three rooms and accommodated twenty-six boys. In the 1860s the school property and building were sold, and a new school was built on Fletcher Street, Essendon.

In 1862, through the Common Schools Act, the Victorian Parliament abolished the two existing centralised boards and created a single Board of Education (VA 713).  With the passing of this act, in 1863 the school was re-named Essendon Common School, retaining the school no. 483. 

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked a further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Essendon State School.

Due to the increase in population and overcrowding over the following decades, a new school building was built in 1875, on the corner of Raleigh and Nicholson Streets, Essendon. Further extensions were made to the building in 1877, but by November 1914 enrolments totalled 1026 students while the school only had room enough for 792 students. In 1917 an infant block was built on the school property, and three pavilion classrooms and two nearby churches were also used as classrooms. Additions were added to the school in 1921 and 1922, and a monument was erected in the school gardens in memory of the victims of the first World War in 1923 by the Old Boys’ Association of the school. In 1933, a school bell was presented to the school by the Mothers’ Club, School Committee, Old Girls’ Association, and the Old Boys’ Association. A weatherboard art classroom was added to the school in 1955, however it burnt down that same year. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Essendon Primary School.

In 2018, a large upgrade and modernisation program was completed, resulting in new administration and senior primary learning facilities. 

As of 2025, Essendon Primary School continues to operate, and is the oldest school still operating in Melbourne.
title: Essendon Primary School (School No. 483; previously known as Pascoe Vale National School 1850 – 1863; Essendon Common School 1863 – c.1873; Essendon State School c.1873 - 1970)

description:
The Department of Government Services (DGS) (VA 5282) was established on 1 January 2023 by the Governor in Council by Order made under section 10 of the Public Administration Act 2004 (Victorian Government Gazette, No. S 673, 5th December 2022). This occurred as part of machinery of government changes made by the re-elected Labor Government under the leadership of Premier the Hon Daniel Andrews MP following the November 2022 State election. The new Department increased the total number of State Departments from nine to ten.

Upon its establishment DGS brought together Digital Victoria and Service Victoria from Department of Premier and Cabinet (DPC) (VA 1039). Local Government Victoria moved into DGS from the former Department of Jobs, Precincts and Regions (DJPR) (VA 5251). Consumer Affairs Victoria (VA 3084); Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages (VA 983); and Working with Children Check moved into DGS from Department of Justice and Community Safety (DJCS) (VA 5252).  

DGS assumed oversight of Public Record Office Victoria (VA 683) as well as Cenitex, the whole of government shared information and communications technology (ICT) services state-owned enterprise, from DPC.

DGS was also responsible for Victorian Public Service (VPS) accommodation management, grant administration and the procurement of whole of government goods and services.  

A corporate shared service arrangement was established between DGS, DPC and Department of Treasury and Finance (DTF) (VA 3745).  

The Department supported the following Ministers:
•    Minister for Government Services (jointly with DPC)
•    Minister for Consumer Affairs
•    Minister for Local Government.

Responsibility for Acts was transferred to DGS from various other Departments under Administrative Arrangements Order No. 251 (Victorian Government Gazette, No. S 717, Monday 19 December 2022).

As of 1 January 2023, DGS was responsible for or provided oversight to the following entities:

•    Cenitex
•    Public Record Office Victoria (VA 683)
•    Victorian Government Purchasing Board
•    Service Victoria
•    Digital Victoria
•    Consumer Affairs Victoria (VA 3084)
•    Business Licensing Authority (VA 4213)
•    Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages (VA 983)
•    Commissioner of Residential Tenancies
•    Domestic Building Dispute Resolution Victoria (overseen by Chief Dispute Resolution Officer)
•    Dispute Settlement Centre of Victoria (overseen by Chief Dispute Resolution Officer)
•    Estate Agents Council (VA 4214)
•    Motor Car Traders Claims Committee
•    Residential Tenancies Bond Authority
•    Local Government Victoria
•    Victorian Local Government Grants Commission
•    Working with Children Check.

description:
On 1 January 2023, the Department of Education and Training (II) (DET) (VA 5035) was renamed the Department of Education (III) by the Governor in Council by Order made under section 10 of the Public Administration Act 2004 (Victorian Government Gazette, No. S 673, 5th December 2022). The name change was part of machinery of government changes made by the re-elected Labor Government under the leadership of Premier the Hon Daniel Andrews MP following the November 2022 State election. 

As part of the machinery of government changes, the Training and Skills and Higher Education portfolios moved from Department of Education and Training II (VA 5035) into the Department of Jobs, Skills, Industry and Regions (VA 5284).

The primary functions of the Department were to deliver education and development services for children and young people, while maintaining links to the Skills portfolio to support Victorians to transition between school and further education and training.

Responsibility for Acts was transferred to the Department of Education (DoE) from DET under Administrative Arrangements Order No. 251 (Victorian Government Gazette, No. S 717, 19th December 2022). 

At its establishment the Department supported the following ministerial portfolios:
•    Minister for Education
•    Minister for Early Childhood and Pre-Prep. 

As of 1 January 2023, the Department was organised into central groups and regions. The groups included:

•    Financial Policy and Information Services
•    People and Executive Services
•    Policy, Strategy and Performance
•    Early Childhood Education
•    School Education Programs and Support
•    Victorian School Building Authority
•    Schools and Regional Services
•    Schools Workforce
•    Senior Secondary Pathways Reform Taskforce.

The regions of the Department were North Eastern Victoria, North Western Victoria, South Western Victoria and South Eastern Victoria.

The Department’s authorities and entities included: 

•    Adult, Community and Further Education Board
•    AMES (Adult Migrant English Service) Australia
•    Children’s Services Coordination Board
•    Disciplinary Appeals Boards
•    Merit Protection Boards
•    Victorian Academy of Teaching and Leadership
•    Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority
•    Victorian Institute of Teaching
•    Victorian Registration and Qualifications Authority.

description:
On 1 January 2023, the Department of Jobs, Precincts and Regions (DJPR) (VA 5251) was renamed the Department of Jobs, Skills, Industry and Regions (DJSIR) by Order of The Governor in Council by Order under section 10 of the Public Administration Act 2004 (Victorian Government Gazette, No. S 673, 5th December 2022). The name change was part of machinery of government changes made by the re-elected Labor Government under the leadership of Premier the Hon Daniel Andrews MP following the November 2022 State election.

As part of the machinery of government changes, the Invest Victoria and Economic Development portfolios moved from the Department of Treasury and Finance (VA 3745) to DJSIR.  Policy oversight for the Breakthrough Victoria Fund moved from Department of Premier and Cabinet (VA 1039) to DJSIR.  The Training and Skills and Higher Education portfolios moved from the former Department of Education and Training II (VA 5035) to DJSIR.  The Department also supported the new portfolio of Outdoor Recreation which brought together hunting, fishing and boating. The previous Fishing and Boating portfolio sat under the former Department of Transport III (VA 5250).

The primary functions of the Department were to support economic development, trade and investment attraction, industry and innovation, training and skills and higher education, employment, the delivery of the 2026 Commonwealth Games, outdoor recreation, community sport, creative industries, manufacturing sovereignty, regional and suburban development, small business and tourism, sport and major events.

On 1 January 2023, the Department of Environment, Land, Water and Planning (DELWP) (VA 5036) was renamed the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DEECA) by Order of the Governor in Council under section 10 of the Public Administration Act 2004 (Victorian Government Gazette, S 673,5 December 2022). The name change was part of machinery of government changes made by the re-elected Labor Government under the leadership of Premier the Hon Daniel Andrews MP following the November 2022 State election.

As part of the machinery of government changes, the agriculture and resources portfolios moved from the former Department of Jobs, Precincts and Regions (VA 5251) into DEECA.  

The planning portfolio moved from the former DELWP (VA 5036) into the renamed Department of Transport and Planning (DTP) (VA 5286). Land Use Victoria (VA 862) also moved from DELWP into DTP.

description:
Omeo was appointed a Court of Mines for the Beechworth Mining District (VA 3145) in 1858, however a Court of Petty Sessions was not appointed there until March that year. This was somewhat unusual as Courts of Mines usually required a County Court registrar and judge. As such it is unclear if the court actually sat in Omeo until 1869, when a County Court was appointed there. A Court of Mines was appointed at Omeo again, this time for the Gippsland Mining District (VA 3804) in 1870.

A Court of Insolvency for the Eastern Insolvency District, as well as a Court of General Sessions were appointed in Omeo in 1891. The Licensing Court heard liquor license proceedings for the surrounding districts until 1917, when the Bairnsdale Licensing Court (VA 4337) assumed responsibility for the district. The County Court, Court of Mines and Court of General Sessions were discontinued in 1931. The brick courthouse, completed 1893, heard Magistrates’ and Children’s Court proceedings until hearings ceased sometime after 2017. Omeo sits within the Magistrates’ and Children’s Gippsland Court Regions.

Omeo Courts includes:
  • Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1858 – by 2025)
  • Children’s Court (1907 – by 2025)
  • Licensing Bench/Licensing Court (1865 – 1917)
  • County Court (1869 – 1931)
  • Court of Mines (?1858 – 1931)
  • Court of Insolvency (1891 – 1928)
  • Court of General Sessions (1891 – 1931)

District and Circuit Court Systems

In the mid-19th to early 20th century, courts and court districts were established across Victoria of various levels. This practice remained until either the court was abolished, or a state-wide court entity was established. Once a statewide court was established, hearings continued in regional centres using a circuit court system.

Under the district system, courts largely administered themselves, with major decisions such as the appointment of judicial officers and court locations, as well the development of court rules, procedures and jury lists passed down by Governor in Council. Additionally, judicial officers, registrars and clerks were appointed to specific court locations. These functions were largely taken over by the primary court and their respective chief judicial officer once the primary court was established. Likewise, judicial officers were no longer appointed to specific court locations, but rather to the primary court then assigned to hearings according to the scheduled circuit.

Both district courts and circuit courts commonly used their own recordkeeping systems to manage cases until centralised recordkeeping systems were gradually introduced from the late 20th century. Administrative resources were often shared between the different levels of court when operating from the same location.

Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1838 – Present)

Courts of Petty Sessions were established to hear criminal and civil cases of minor offences and disputes. Courts of Petty Sessions were appointed to be held in population centres. These courts were renamed Magistrates’ Courts in 1971. Under the Magistrates’ Court Act 1989, the Magistrates’ Court of Victoria (VA 5113) was constituted as the primary body, while the various courts were grouped into regions with the largest in each appointed as a headquarter venue. Magistrates and other Judicial Officers were assigned to regions to hear cases in each location according to the scheduled circuit. Each region is managed by a regional coordinating magistrate and a senior registrar. Individual Magistrates’ Courts continue to maintain their own case registries. As of 2023, there are 51 courts in 13 regions. The Court has several divisions including Koori Court, Drug Court, Assessment and Referral Court as well as several specialist family courts. These divisions are appointed to locations within regions, usually the headquarter court.

Children’s Court (1907 – Present)

Children’s Courts were established to hear and to inquire into charges against children. During the 1930s, these courts also began hearing other cases involving children such as child neglect. Children’s Courts were appointed to be held at locations that already held Courts of Petty Sessions or Magistrates’ Courts and operated as a division of the Magistrates’ Court until the Children's Court of Victoria (VA 4190) was established in 2000. As such, Children’s Courts operated under the Magistrates’ Court district system until 1989 and continue to mirror the Magistrates’ Court’s regional system. Like the Magistrates’ Court, when the Children’s Court of Victoria was constituted as the primary and independent body, courts were grouped into regions, and Judicial Officers and Support Services staff were assigned to these regions. Judicial officers were assigned to hearings according to each region’s circuit schedule. Individual courts continue to maintain their own case registries and often share administrative resources with the Magistrates’ Court registries. As of 2025, there are 33 courts in 6 regions. The Court has a Family division, and Criminal division, as well as a Children’s Koori Court for criminal matters.

Licensing Court (1885 – 1968)

Licensing Courts were first established to grant and transfer liquor licences. From 1865 to 1885, this function was administered by Licensing Benches of the Court of Petty Sessions. Licensing Courts were established in licensing districts under The Licensing Act 1885 at courts appointed to hold Court of Petty Sessions hearings. Other kinds of licences, such as Auctioneer and Hawkers licences, were granted at annual Licence meetings at Courts of Petty Sessions. This practice continued until 1916 when the Licensing Court of Victoria (VA 2955) was constituted, and a circuit system was introduced. Under the circuit system, 3 magistrates were appointed to the primary court who then held annual hearings at each appointed Licensing Court location according to the circuit schedule. When the court was replaced with the Victorian Licensing Court (VA 2905) in 1954, this was changed to one Judge of the County Court as Chair, and 2 magistrates. The court was abolished in 1968 and liquor licensing functions were transferred to the Liquor Control Commission (VA 1110). See also Licensing Courts (VA 2870).

County Court (1852 – Present)

County Courts were established to hear civil matters and assumed the functions of the Courts of Request, which had operated prior to Victoria’s separation from New South Wales. Regional County Courts operated under the district court system until 1957, when the County Court of Victoria (VA 686) was constituted under the County Court Act 1958 (Vic). Under the circuit court system, County Courts continued to maintain their own case registries until centralised recordkeeping systems were gradually introduced from the late 20th Century. As of 2023, the court is made up of a criminal division, criminal appeals division, commercial division, common law division, adoption division and a County Koori Court. There are 11 circuit locations outside of Melbourne, 6 of which also hold County Koori Court hearings. 

Court of Insolvency (1871 – 1928)

Courts of Insolvency were established in each proclaimed Insolvency District across Victoria according to the Insolvency Statute 1871. Courts of Insolvency were appointed at places that held County Courts hearings, and Insolvency Districts generally mirrored County Court Districts. All County Court judges outside of Melbourne were also appointed judges of the Court of Insolvency. Although the clerks of the District Courts of Insolvency were required to send a copy of the Order of Sequestration (Bankruptcy/Insolvency Order) to the Chief Clerk at Melbourne, these orders were not incorporated into the Register of Insolvencies (VPRS 757) created by the Court of Insolvency at Melbourne (VA 2304). Courts of Insolvency continued to operate under the County Court District system until the function of Bankruptcy and Insolvency hearings was transferred to the Commonwealth in 1928.

Court of Mines (1855 - 1969)

Courts of Mines were established to hear mining-related cases such as disputes over entitlements of partners, shareholders, and employees of mining enterprises. Between 1855 and 1857, proceedings relating to mining rights were heard within designated Gold Fields Local Court Districts at the largest court in the district, known as a Local Court, and presided by a Justice of the Peace. This system was refined in 1858 when Courts of Mines were appointed within Mining Districts at locations where County Courts operated. Unlike Local Court or County Court districts, Mining Districts usually had multiple court locations. This system continued until the Court of Mines was abolished under the Mines (Abolition of Courts) Act 1969 (Vic) and the County Court (VA 686) assumed responsibility for hearing mining-related cases.

Court of General Sessions (1853 – 1968)

Courts of General Sessions were established to hear criminal cases of a more serious nature than the Court of Petty Sessions, excluding the most serious crimes such as murder and treason. The Court of General Sessions continued to operate under the district court system until 1968, when the County Court of Victoria (VA 686) assumed responsibility for Criminal Cases and the Court of General Sessions was abolished under the County Court (Jurisdiction) Act 1968 (Vic).

A Court of Petty Sessions was appointed in Bruthen in July 1883. Hearings were heard in the Bruthen Mechanics Institute, which was built in 1883. description:
A Court of Petty Sessions was first appointed in the Bendoc area (often spelled Bendock prior 1940) at Wagra (Upper Bendock) in 1869, however this was later revoked in 1886 and a court appointed to Buchan in lieu thereof. A Court was later appointed at Bendoc proper in December 1889 and the court in Buchan was revoked in 1890. A new courthouse was built and opened for the township on 1 December 1966, despite the decision already being made that a Magistrate should only visit the court in special circumstances. The court was last visited by a Magistrate in 1975, and only 29 cases were processed between 1976 and 1981. The Bendoc court was closed on 1 January 1983 and its records were directed to be delivered to Bairnsdale Magistrates’ Court (part of Bairnsdale Courts - VA 4337).

Bendoc Courts includes:
  • Court of Petty Sessions, Wagra (Upper Bendock) (1869 – 1886)
  • Court of Petty Sessions, Buchan (1886 – 1890)
  • Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court, Bendoc (1889 – 1982)
  • Children’s Court (1907 – 1982)

description:
A Court of Petty Sessions was appointed in Cann River in March 1949. The court was closed on 1 January 1983 and its records were directed to be delivered to Bairnsdale Magistrates’ Court (part of Bairnsdale Courts - VA 4337). The closure of the court was considered problematic at the time as it serviced a remote community, despite sitting infrequently. After its closure the Deputy Commissioner for Police reported an increase in costs due to travelling expenses, reluctance on the part of witnesses to assist with prosecutions due to the required distances to be travelled, absence of a Clerk of Courts to assist with legal matters and a lack of policing efficiency while officers were attending distant courts. Despite these concerns, a court was not reinstated in the area.

Cann River Courts includes:
  • Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1949 – 1982)
  • Children’s Court (1949 – 1982)

Administrative resources were often shared between the different levels of court when operating from the same location.

Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1838 – Present)

Courts of Petty Sessions were established to hear criminal and civil cases of minor offences and disputes. Courts of Petty Sessions were appointed to be held in population centres. These courts were renamed Magistrates’ Courts in 1971. Under the Magistrates’ Court Act 1989 (Vic), the Magistrates’ Court of Victoria (VA 5113) was constituted as the primary body, while the various courts were grouped into regions with the largest in each appointed as a headquarter venue. Magistrates and other Judicial Officers were assigned to regions to hear cases in each location according to the scheduled circuit. Individual Magistrates’ Courts continue to maintain their own case registries. As of 2023, there are 51 courts in 13 regions. The Court has several divisions including Koori Court, Drug Court, Assessment and Referral Court as well as several specialist family courts. These divisions are appointed to specific locations within regions, usually the headquarters court.

Children’s Court (1907 – Present)

Children’s Courts were established to hear and to inquire into charges against children. During the 1930s, these courts also began hearing other cases involving children such as child neglect. Children’s Courts were appointed to be held at locations that already held Courts of Petty Sessions or Magistrates’ Courts and operated as a division of the Magistrates’ Court until 2000. As such, Children’s Courts operated under the Magistrates’ Court district system until 1989 and continue to mirror the Magistrates’ Court’s regional system. Like the Magistrates’ Court, when the Children’s Court of Victoria (VA 4190) was constituted as the primary and independent body, courts were grouped into regions, and Judicial Officers and Support Services staff were assigned to these regions. Judicial officers were assigned to hearings according to each region’s circuit schedule. Individual courts continue to maintain their own case registries and often share administrative resources with the Magistrates’ Court registries. As of 2023, there are 47 courts in 6 regions. The Court has a Family division, and Criminal division, as well as a Children’s Koori Court for criminal matters. Like Magistrates' Koori Courts, Children's Koori Courts are appointed to specific locations.

description:
In 1874, a small four-roomed home in Kew owned by Margaret McCulloch (wife of Sir James McCulloch, Premier of Victoria), furnished it to operate as a convalescent home. The house was then known as the Melbourne Convalescent Home for Women.

In 1886, the convalescent home moved to larger premises in Oakleigh and was renamed the Oakleigh Convalescent Home for Women. The home was no longer operated by McCulloch as she had returned to England by this time. The Oakleigh house was officially opened by Lady Loch (wife of Governor of Victoria, Sir Henry Loch) on 18 May 1886 on an 11 acre block of land on Drummond Street. 

The Oakleigh facility was later deemed too small by the Home’s Committee, who decided to sell it and build a larger building on 20 acres of land that was purchased on what was then known as Clayton’s Road. Lady Loch laid the foundation stone on 21 November 1888. By 17 September 1889 the first patients had moved into the new home. On 1 November 1889 the Governor officially opened the home and it resumed its original name of the Melbourne Convalescent Home for Women.

The initial by-laws of the Home stated that the objective of the Institution was to afford relief to such women and children not under the age of twelve, as the Committee considered fit subjects for reception irrespective of religious belief and country of birth. The Committee was to consist of not less than fourteen members with five members to form a quorum. The Committee was to conduct the general business of the Home and to appoint the Matron. It was the Matron’s responsibility to have control of the domestic arrangements of the Home, including the comfort and well-being of the patients. Two auxiliaries were formed in 1926; one covered the Oakleigh and Murrumbeena areas; the other covered Clayton. Both auxiliary groups were later replaced by the McCulloch House Auxiliary.

In 1952, the status of the home was changed from public to private. Accompanying the change was an increase in charges in both private and public beds. In 1959, new extensions were finished to accommodate patients from the Mount Royal Geriatric Clinic (VA 1280). This work was the result of a Public Appeal made in 1956.

On 20 November 1969 the name of the home was changed to McCulloch House. The intention was to honour Lady McCulloch but also to incorporate future facilities for male patients. The Home was not being used as a convalescent home at that time and plans indicated that it was to become a geriatric rehabilitation hospital. Male patients were first admitted to McCulloch House in 1979.

It was announced in 1977 that McCulloch House would amalgamate with the Queen Victoria Memorial Hospital to become Queen Victoria Medical Centre (VA 1254). The amalgamation occurred on 1 July 1977. The Committee of Management became known as the McCulloch House Advisory Committee and tabled a report to the full Board of Management each month. 

The House's function as a nursing home ceased in 1992. As of November 2023, it functions as a supportive and palliative care unit of Monash Health (VA 5264).
title: McCulloch House (previously known as Melbourne Convalescent Home for Women 1874 - 1886, Oakleigh Convalescent Home for Women 1886 - 1889, Melbourne Convalescent Home for Women 1889 - 1969)

description:
Establishment

Development Victoria was established on 1 April 2017 under the Development Victoria Act 2003, formerly known as the Urban Renewal Authority Victoria Act 2003, and the Victorian Urban Development Authority Act 2003.

In 2016, the Urban Renewal Authority (known as Places Victoria) (VA 5005) and Major Projects Victoria (VA 2979) amalgamated to form Development Victoria, which then assumed the responsibility for delivering major property and civic projects across Victoria. Development Victoria is a Statutory Authority governed by the Development Victoria Board of Directors and was established as a Public Non-Financial Corporation.

Functions and Projects

Development Victoria’s functions under the Act include:
  • Carrying out property development and social and economic capital works projects in accordance with government policies and strategies
  • Providing advisory services
  • Developing declared projects

The Act requires Development Victoria to carry out its functions using commercial disciplines.
Development Victoria also has specified functions and powers under the Docklands Act 1991 to promote, encourage and facilitate development of the Docklands area.

Major projects managed by Development Victoria include:
  • Flinders Street Station
  • The Shrine of Remembrance
  • Palais Theatre
  • The State Library
  • Melbourne Arts Precinct
  • Ballarat and Bendigo GovHubs
  • Melbourne Park redevelopment
  • Riverwalk housing estate
  • Alfie Altona North residential housing development 
  • Urban renewal precincts such as
    • Fitzroy Gasworks 
    • Docklands
    • Fisherman’s Bend Innovation Precinct 
    • Revitalising Central Dandenong
    • Junction Place Wodonga
    • Arden

Governance

At the agency's establishment, the Minister for Major Projects had primary responsibility for Development Victoria under the Development Victoria Act 2003, as well as the Docklands Act 1991. The Treasurer was responsible for managing and monitoring the agency's financial position including its capital structure and operating performance. Debt finance for projects was approved by the Treasurer on a case-by-case basis, and the organisation’s aggregate financial assumptions and forecasts were approved annually by the Treasurer through the Corporate Plan.

Responsibility for two Acts was transferred to the Minister for Priority Precincts on 29 November 2018, while responsibility for projects in various suburban areas was shared with the Minister for Suburban Development. On 1 July 2020 the Minister for Transport Planning took primary responsibility for the Development Victoria Act, while the Minister for Business Precincts took responsibility for the Docklands Act. The administration of the Acts were transferred again on 1 January 2023 to the Minister for Transport and Infrastructure and the Minister for Planning respectively. On 10 October 2023 the Minister for Development Victoria and Minister for Precincts assumed responsibility for administration of the Acts respectively.

The Board of Directors has responsibility for strategic oversight of Development Victoria and considers projects presented by management for approval before they are presented to the Minister. Projects are managed in accordance with the Project Development and Construction Management Act 1994.

description:
Establishment

The Urban Land Council was formed in May 1975 as the result of an agreement between the Commonwealth and Victorian Governments. The agreement was made pursuant to the provision of financial assistance under the Urban & Regional Development (Financial Assistance) Act 1974 (Commonwealth).

Projects

Under the Act, programs approved for funding included:
  • Urban expansion and re-development (which may include sewerage and water supply)
  • Area improvement, being urban and regional improvement and rehabilitation
  • Sewerage
  • Water supply
  • Flood mitigation

The Council managed the funding of several major housing projects in the outer metropolitan regions, including new estates in Thomastown, Keilor, Westerngate, Westdale Park, Altona, and Deer Park, as well as the Monmia and Thornhill estates in Keilor Downs.

Functions

The primary objectives of the Council (and successor agencies) were to stabilise land prices and encourage home ownership, particularly First Home ownership.

As the Council was an unincorporated body having no legal entity it could not own land, let contracts, enter into formal agreements, nor own funds. Day-to-day operations of the Council were serviced by the Victorian Ministry of Planning (VA 600), and the Housing Commission of Victoria (HCV) (VA 508).
The HCV purchased designated lands, arranged for planning, servicing, development design, and entered into agreements with municipalities and service authorities regarding development projects. The HCV entered into and administered contracts for construction of works, supervised and administered those contracts, kept account of expenditure, and obtained individual titles to lots so that they might be offered for sale. The HCV administered the sale of lots including receipting of and accounting for monies related to those lots. 

The HCV transferred these responsibilities to the Urban Land Authority (ULA) (VA 5294) once established in 1980.

Replacement

In 1980 the Urban Land Council was replaced by the ULA, set up in accordance with the Urban Land Authority Act 1979 (Victoria), which came into operation on 12 March 1980. At this time, the land purchased for projects funded by the Council was vested in the ULA as well as the Council’s remaining cash reserves.

description:
Establishment and Governance

The Urban Land Corporation (ULCorp) was formed in accordance with the Urban Land Corporation Act 1997, which came into operation on 3 February 1988. ULCorp was established as the successor in law of the Urban Land Authority (ULA) (VA 1358), and all rights, assets, liabilities and obligations of the ULA were transferred to ULCorp.

In 2001 the act was renamed the Urban and Regional Land Corporation Act 1997 and the corporation became known as Urban and Regional Land Corporation (ULRC) from 1 July 2001. URLC's purview was extended regional development.

ULCorp was established as a statutory corporation under section 88A(I) of State Owned Enterprises Act 1992 and was initially responsible to the Minister for Planning and Local Government. It was responsible to the Minister for Planning from October 1999 until December 2002, then the Minister for Major Projects until it was abolished in 2003. As a statutory corporation, it was a public authority for purposes of reporting but did not represent the Crown. The ULCorp/URLC was managed by a Board of Directors. 

Functions

The functions of URLC, to be carried out on a commercial basis, were to develop residential land in Victoria and develop other land in Victoria where this was incidental to a residential development. It was also required to provide consultancy services in relation to the development of land whether within or outside Victoria or outside Australia.

Projects

URLC played a key role in the development of Melbourne's growth corridors. Major projects included:
  • Albion
  • Altona Village
  • Aurora
  • Epsom Park
  • Larundel
  • Lynbrook
  • Mont Park
  • Mount Cooper
  • Point Cook

Replacement

In 2003 the Victorian Urban Development Authority Act 2003 repealed the Urban and Regional Land Corporation Act 1997. URLC and the Docklands Authority (VA 5498) were merged and replaced by the Victorian Urban Development Authority (VA 5004).
title: Urban and Regional Land Corporation (previously known as Urban Land Corporation 1998 - 2001)

description:
Brentwood Park Primary School is a co-ed and non-denominational government school situated in the outer suburban area of Berwick.

The school is located on the site of a former sheep and dairy farm established around 1883 by John Samuel White. After changing hands several times, the land was purchased by the Pearson family at the beginning of the 20th century and named ‘Kippenross’. When the family moved in 1911, the farm was sold to Humphrey and Mercy Davy, and then again sold in 1920 to Moira Pennefather, who may have re-named the farm ‘Ardsley’. In 1946, Co. Cecil Mervyn Thomas bought the property, and re-named it ‘Brentwood’. Though the property has changed hands again several times since, this name is reflected in the name of the school now occupying the land.

In November 1994, the Minister for Education, Hon. Don Hayward, and the Governor-in-Council, approved and signed the Constituting Order for the School Council of Brentwood Primary School (Victorian Government Gazette No. G 47, 24 November 1994, p. 3119). In December, the Minister signed an Instrument of Appointment for the inaugural membership of the council, who’s term of office commenced this same date. By this time, the school had 198 pupils enrolled, and building and landscaping of the school grounds were in their final stages.

The school was registered for 'Intake 4 Schools of the Future’ induction program, a government initiative that provided the school with a one-off ‘implementation grant’ of $8,600 and a further one-off ‘professional development grant’ of $525 to facilitate attendance of appropriate personnel at professional development activities during the induction program.

The school opened 20 May 1995, with 323 students recorded in their census day the same year. As of 2022, this number has tripled, with a total of 964 students.
title: Brentwood Park Primary School (School No. 5308)

description:
On 26 October 1856, a public meeting was held to discuss the establishment of a new National School in Belmont, a southern suburb of Geelong, Wadawurrung Country. A Committee was appointed to establish the new school and were provided with a subsidy grant of £100 to buy a site and erect a building. By December of the same year, a notice in the Geelong Advertiser stated that the school was open for children of both sexes to attend, and a Head Teacher named Ryder was appointed by the Local Board, although he had no teaching certification. At the end of the year, ten boys and sixteen girls aged between four and fourteen years old were enrolled in the school.

The exact site of the original school is uncertain; however, it is likely that it was on or near the current site along Mt Pleasant Road. The school had two rooms and was the first ‘vested school’ in Geelong, with building costs, and part of the teachers’ salaries and book costs contributed to by the Board of Education.

In 1917, the school was renovated and painted throughout, adding three more rooms and a lavatory to the building. During the renovation process, classes were held in the Belmont Methodist Church.

The school number changed multiple times, from 34 to 21 to 18 and 23, until 1863 when Belmont became known as ‘Common School No. 26’ under Head Teacher John Quinton. The name of the school also changed over time. After 1872, it became ‘Belmont State School’, and in 1970, ‘Belmont Primary School’.

As of 2022, approximately 275 students were enrolled across 12 classes, from Prep to Grad 6.

description:
School No. 2174 opened in 1879 near Stawell, with 13 students enrolled under Head Teacher Agnes Muir. Although the region was initially named Bolangum, the Government Surveyor at the time called the district Warngar Parish, and the local post office called it Kanya. The school has likewise carried the names ‘Warngar State School’ and ‘Kanya State School’ throughout its existence. During its early years it is most often referred to as ‘Warngar’, and when it closed in 1959, it was known as ‘Kanya’.

The school was a small weatherboard building primarily serving children of farmers and labourers in the area, originally on a half-time basis. From 1888 to 1891, Warngar State School merged with Wallaloo East State School (school no. 2698). In 1914, Warngar was converted from a half-time to a full-time establishment. Between approximately 1922-1933 the school was ‘closed for some years’, reopening in May 1933.

Kanya State School closed at the end of 1959, with many of its students transferring to Wallaloo East State School.

description:
Alexandra Secondary College (School No. 7505) (VA 5300)  first opened it’s doors as Alexandra High School in 1953 on a shared site with Alexandra Higher Elementary School (School No. 912), absorbing the secondary classes of that school. A new site for a High School was purchased in 1945 and the High School relocated to a newly constructed facility in 1957. In 1978, a Technical component was established.

Alexandra Secondary College is a co-education secondary school situated in the rural township of Alexandra in North-Eastern Victoria. Students are drawn from the greater district of Alexandra which includes the townships of Marysville, Narbelthong, Buxton, Taggerty, Thornton, Eildon, Molesworth, Yarck and Merton. 

In 1990 the school underwent a name change to Alexandra Secondary College following the Change of School Name and Reclassification of Schools Executive Memorandum No 314 from the Ministry of Education (VA 1112).

description:
Lyndale Secondary College (School No. 8000) (VA 5301) is a co-education secondary school that first opened its doors as Lyndale High School in February 1961, based out of the girls’ gymnasium at Dandenong High School (School No. 7760).  After just three weeks, the school moved to portable classrooms located behind Dandenong Girls High School (School No. 7761) and later that year, in November 1961, the school relocated to a newly constructed facility. The school was officially opened in 1964 by Hon. J.S. Bloomfield, the Minister of Education.

The need for Lyndale Secondary College arose from the growing demand for education in the area north of the Princes Highway. Dandenong High School (School No. 8858) had become overcrowded, leading to the acquisition of land from Mr. and Mrs. Alfred Potts a decade earlier. The new school was intended to serve the region north of Heatherton Road and west of Stud Road.

In 1962, Noble Park High School (School No. 8813) temporarily utilised facilities at Lyndale while awaiting the completion of their own school building. Two years later, in 1964, Lyndale High School provided temporary facilities to Springvale High School (School No. 8325) after a fire partially damaged the school. 

In 1968 Lyndale High School became the first Victorian high school to introduce the Indonesian subject at the year 7 level.

Major building programmes between 1968 and 1975 were the building of the Assembly Hall in 1972, the Commonwealth Science Block in 1973, six classrooms (four in 1971 and two in 1973), an administrative upgrade in 1973, a freestanding unit of reading rooms from 1974 to 1975 and a Commonwealth Library in 1975. 

In 1990, the school underwent a name change to Lyndale Secondary College following the implementation of the "Change of School Name and Reclassification of Schools” Executive Memorandum No 314 from the Ministry of Education (VA 1112).

description:
Mount Waverley Secondary College (School No. 8105) (VA 5302) is a co-educational secondary school serving years 7-12. The school was established as Mount Waverley High School in February 1964 to meet the growing population in Victoria. The school initially operated from three portable classrooms on the grounds of Glen Waverley High School (School No. 8808) before moving to the site located on Stephensons Road, between Lechte and Gordon Roads, covering 15 acres of Housing Commission land in Mount Waverley, Victoria.  

In 1990 the school underwent a name change to Mount Waverley Secondary College following the Change of School Name and Reclassification of Schools Executive Memorandum No 314 from the Ministry of Education (VA 1112). 
The 1990s marked a significant era of transformation in education throughout Victoria, as the Jeff Kennett government initiated numerous school closures and mergers across the state.  

At the end of 1993, Waverley North Primary School (School No 4884; VA 3941) merged with Syndal North Primary School (School No 4946; VA 3935) and the site was repurposed and acquired as the Mount Waverley Secondary College Junior Campus location.  In 1996, the Stephenson’s Road site became the Senior Campus, and the Waverley Road site became the Junior Campus. 

In January 2003, a fire destroyed much of the Senior campus buildings. Staff and students were temporarily relocated to Deakin University (VA 1053) Burwood campus for three weeks. The school was rebuilt and officially reopened in December 2004.

Mount Waverley Secondary College should not be confused with Waverley Secondary College (School No. 8455; VA 4755) in Chadstone, Victoria, which closed in 1996.

title: Mount Waverley Secondary College (School No. 8105; previously known as Mount Waverley High School 1964 – 1990)

description:
Templestowe High School (School No. 8375) (VA 5303) was the first secondary school in the Shire of Doncaster and Templestowe. It was established in 1960 within temporary quarters at Greythorn High School (School No. 7875; VA 4748).  

In February 1961, the first two stages of its permanent building were completed and the school moved to its permanent location at the corner of Manningham Road and Hazel Drive in Lower Templestowe, a site once occupied by a gold mine. In 1961, Banyule High School (School No. 4746) and Watsonia High Schools (School No. 8445) temporarily shared the premises while awaiting their own permanent facilities. 

The school was officially declared open in March 1963 by The Honourable J.S. Bloomfield, Minister of Education, though it soon faced cramped conditions due to a population boom in Templestowe despite the addition of “A” Block and “C” Block in 1964. Relief came in 1969 with the opening of Doncaster High School (School No. 7776).

Sports ovals and an outdoor gymnasium were completed in 1970 and 1971 respectively and in 1972 the Commonwealth Library Building and Commonwealth Science Block were added to the school.

In 1977, the School Council and Curriculum Committee were formed, followed by the establishment of the Administrative Committee in 1983.

The 1990s marked a significant era of transformation in education throughout Victoria, as the Jeff Kennett government initiated numerous school closures and mergers across the state.  

In 1994, a decline in enrolments led to the ‘merging’ of Templestowe High School with Templestowe Technical (School no. 7372) to form the new Templestowe College (School No. 8823). Templestowe High School was closed and the site was sold to make way for the David Road housing estate.
