description:
Victoria University Secondary College (VUSC) (School No. 8891) (VA 5304) is a state co-educational secondary school catering to Years 7-12 across two campuses: a Junior Campus located in Deer Park and a Senior Campus located in Cairnlea. The Trade Training Centre is located on the Senior Campus. 

VUSC was established in 2010 by the amalgamation of Brimbank Secondary College (School No. 7340; formerly Jamieson Park Secondary College, and prior to that St Albans Technical School) and Deer Park Secondary College (School No. 7764). Additionally, in 2011, Kealba Secondary College (School No. 7942) was also incorporated into VUSC. 

As part of its international program, VUSC maintains a sister school relationship with the High School Affiliated with Yangzhou University, located in the Jiangsu Province, China.  Beginning in 2014, students have travelled to China each year as part of the Victorian Young Leaders to China program.
name.official_title.title: Victoria University Secondary College (School No. 8891)
title: Victoria University Secondary College (School No. 8891)

description:
Victorian College of the Arts Secondary School (VCASS) (School No. 7384) (VA 5305), is a co-educational selective government secondary school, with speciality in the performing and visual arts.  Instigated by the former tertiary institution Victorian College of the Arts (VCA; VA 1075), as a separate and complementary institution, VCASS was founded in 1978 by Lenton Parr and Jack Pitt and established under the direction of the Deputy Premier and Minister of Education, Lindsay Thompson as the Victorian College of the Arts Technical School (VCATS).

In 1981, the school was incorporated as a Secondary School under the umbrella of the VCA – as a fifth school of the College. The name was changed from the VCA Technical School (VCATS) to the VCA Secondary School (VCASS).  

In 1985 the building known as the Elizabeth Murdoch Building was refurbished by the Education Department and the secondary school was given an office and teaching space there. 1993 saw the removal of almost all the portables and in 1997 the secondary school was allocated an additional building, ‘I’ Block.

For most of its history VCASS shared its campus and buildings with the tertiary VCA within the Melbourne Arts Precinct, St Kilda Road in Southbank.  Under Colin Simpson's leadership the Victorian Government approved a permanent building on Miles and Moore Streets, Southbank in 2004. Architectural firm Williams Boag worked closely with the school in the design of a new purpose-built facility and the school moved from the former VCA site in June 2009.

The Dance and Music specialist programs run in parallel from Year 7 to 12. In 2013 the school added a Year 11 intake for its Visual Arts program. In 2016 a new Theatre Arts program commenced with a Year 11 intake.  The school also provides academic classes to secondary students from other institutions including the Australian Ballet School, and Gymnastics Victoria.

In 2024, VCASS is till in operation.
name.official_title.title: Victorian College of the Arts Secondary School (School No. 7384; previously known as Victorian College of the Arts Technical School 1978 - 1981)
title: Victorian College of the Arts Secondary School (School No. 7384; previously known as Victorian College of the Arts Technical School 1978 - 1981)

description:
Baringa Special School (School No. 5079) (VA 5306) was established in 1974 as Moe Special School, a regional special school for students with mild intellectual disabilities catering for students aged 5 – 18 years. It was situated on Staff Street in Moe, within the Latrobe Valley.  The school encouraged students to engage with neighbourhood primary or secondary schools on a part time basis. 

The student population is drawn from a wide geographical area incorporating Trafalgar, Yallourn North, Newborough, Moe, Rawson, Churchill, Yinnar, Hazelwood, Traralgon, Glengarry, and Toongabbie.

Initially, the school was divided into three main divisions: a primary section, secondary section and young adult group.  There was no standard grade structure in place, instead students were placed in classes according to a range of criteria which may have included age, gender, social skill, academic ability, physical size and teachers. 

The school underwent a name change circa 1979 to Baringa School (also known as Baringa Special School) and 1982 saw the establishment of a School Council. By 1994, the school had streamlined its operations, maintaining a primary section and a secondary section, which includes the transition to post school options program.  The absence of standard grade structures remained, with students organized into pastoral groups. Cooperative teaching, cross-age tutoring, and other innovative teaching and learning strategies were recognised as valuable components of the school's approach.

In the year 2000, Baringa Special School expanded by adding an annex located in Leongatha, effectively creating two campuses.  However, the annex was separated and earmarked to become part of the proposed South Gippsland Specialist School by 2004.
name.official_title.title: Baringa Special School (School No. 5079; also known as Baringa School; previously known as Moe Special School 1974 – c.1979)
title: Baringa School (School No. 5079; also known as Baringa Special School; previously known as Moe Special School 1974 – c.1979)

description:
Ewing House School for Deaf Children (School No. 4834) (VA 5307) was founded in August of 1950 by a committee made up of four parents, following a visit from Sir Alexander Ewing, a Professor at Manchester University, England, and his wife, Dr. Irene Ewing.  

Ewing House School for Deaf Children went on to provide education and some residential services for deaf children. The school was situated in Wendouree, Ballarat and operated from 1950 – 2003.

Following the Ewing visit in August of 1950, four parents came together to form what would become the Victorian Committee for the Promotion of Oral Education to the Deaf.  During the Ewing visit, a teacher was offered a scholarship to train in Manchester. Recognising the need for more trained teachers, by October of the same year, the committee had sent two more teachers to Manchester for training.

By 1952, the formation of the initial parent committee soon brought inquiries and requests for assistance and land was purchased in Wendouree, Ballarat, on the North side of Lake Wendouree. With the assistance of a treasury grant obtained by the Minister of Education, the Honourable J.G. McDonald, the school began construction of three classrooms, a playroom, a test room, and office.

In 1958, a principle was appointed, and the Victorian Committee Education Council approached the Education Department (VA 714) with a proposal to take over the school's operations. This transition led to the election of the first school committee in 1959. That same year, the school’s hostel was opened by Sir Henry Bolte, the Premier of Victoria. The event marked the arrival of the first matron, accompanied by five children and an assistant.

In 1963, additional buildings were acquired, including a house on Gregory Street, which was repurposed as a second hostel. However, by 1967, enrolments began to decline due to the introduction of the Visiting Teachers program in Victoria which allowed children who were considered capable to complete their education in "hearing schools”.

In 1968, the Education Department (VA 714) designated Ewing House School for Deaf Children as an official training school for teachers from the Glendonald School for Deaf Children (School No. 4683; VA 3955), providing them with the opportunity for practice teaching rounds. 

Ewing House School for Deaf Children closed in 2003 and the Ballarat Deaf Facility was established with the relocation to purpose-built rooms at Forest Street Primary School (School No. 4936) and Ballarat High School (School No. 7540).
title: Ewing House School for Deaf Children (School No. 4834)

description:
Maryborough Specialist School (School No. 5308) (VA 5308) was established in 1986 as Maryborough Special Developmental School and was situated on the same site as the adult centre, Asteria Services (then, Wattle Day Training Centre / Wattle Human Services).  The school was originally run out of a youth club hall and was established to cater for school aged clients of the centre. 

Located in Maryborough, Maryborough Specialist Primary School was the only such school within a radius of 70km.  It provided specialist education for students with physical and/or intellectual disabilities including secondary aged students with behavioural challenges. 

The local catchment area for the school included the townships of Natte Yallock to the north, Newstead to the east, Avoca to the west and Talbot to the south. The closest city was Ballarat, approximately 70 kilometres to the south.

The school name was changed from Maryborough Special Developmental School to Maryborough Specialist School in 1998. 

In 2005, Maryborough Specialist Primary School merged with Maryborough East Primary School (School No. 2828) and Maryborough Regional College (School No. 8825) to form the new Maryborough Education Centre (School No. 8845).
title: Maryborough Specialist Primary School (School No. 5250; also known as Maryborough Specialist School; previously known as Maryborough Special Developmental School 1986 – c.1998)

description:
Northern School for Autism (School No. 5309) (VA 5309), originally known as Preston Special Developmental School, opened on 4 February 1980.  The school is located in northern metropolitan Melbourne and provides for the educational needs of students with autism ranging in age between 5 and 18 years. Programs are designed to meet the individual students needs and interests with emphasis placed on communication, social interactions, play skills and promoting increased independence and access to the community. 

Since its establishment, the school has gone through several changes in locations, originally operating on a single campus site in Preston.

In 2006, to meet the growing needs of students in the region, Preston Special Development School expanded with the addition of the Jacana Campus to the existing Preston Campus. The school name was also changed at this time to the Northern School for Autism (NSA).  

The Jacana Campus operated from 2006 to 2012 and was situated on the former site of the Western Autistic School Annexe (School No. 5290), co-located with Jacana Primary School (School No. 4839).  In 2009, Jacana Primary School vacated this site to become part of the Broadmeadows Valley Primary School (School No. 5529).  

In 2012, the Lalor Campus of NSA was opened, in a self-contained wing of Peter Lalor Secondary College (School No. 7217).

2013 saw the Preston Campus relocate from the corner of Tyler and Crevelli Streets, Preston to the former Burbank Primary School (School No. 4917) site on Gertz Ave, Reservoir.  The Jacana Campus separated from NSA at this time to become the Jacana School for Autism (School No. 5555) and occupied the entire former NSA Jacana Campus and former Jacana Primary School site.

In 2015, NSA launched a satellite program at Norris Bank Primary School (School No. 3618), providing specialised education to students who had completed their first year at the Reservoir campus.
title: Northern School for Autism (School No. 5219; previously known as Preston Special Developmental School 1980 - 2006)

Rosamond School (School No. 5310) (VA 5310) is a co–educational specialist school for primary and secondary aged students that has operated since 1943 for young people with a clinically diagnosed mild or mild/moderate intellectual disability.  The school caters to students who live in the inner west of Melbourne including Brimbank, Hobsons Bay, Maribyrnong and Moonee Valley City. The school claims to be the first purpose-built school of its kind in Victoria. 

The school began operations as Footscray North Special School on Rosamond Road, West Footscray, which was adjacent to Footscray North Primary School (School No. 4160). The Education Department (VA 714) assumed responsibility for the school in September 1957 and the name was changed to Rosamond Special School in 1977. Further research is required to explore the period preceding the Education Department’s involvement. 

Campus 2, Olympia Street Campus was opened in 2007 and closed in 2009.

In July 2013, Rosamond School relocated to a new purpose-built premises in Braybrook, on the former site of Sunshine Harvester Primary School (School No. 5526; previously known as Braybrook Primary School, School No. 1102), which closed following an arson attack in 2010. 

The school provides an approved curriculum framework differentiated to meet student needs. Students are grouped into four sections—early years, primary, secondary and post–compulsory. 

Specialist programs include visual and performing arts, environmental science, physical education, food and nutrition, horticulture and information and communications technology.

Allied health services available to support students (and their families), in 2019, include speech pathology, occupational therapy, and a psychologist consultant—as well as access to the visiting teacher service and Student Support Services (SSS).
title: Rosamond Special School (School No. 4792; also known as Rosamond School; previously known as Footscray North Special School 1943 - 1977)

description:
Note: These historical records contain words, descriptions and information that may be insensitive or inappropriate and that may be upsetting.

The Victorian College for the Deaf (School No. 3774) (VA 5311) provides programs for deaf and partially deaf students as well as for deaf students with disabilities and a limited number of hearing students who experience communication disorders. The co-educational school provides programs for both primary and secondary age students. 

The Victorian College for the Deaf opened as the School for the Deaf and Dumb in November 1860 and first operated from a brick house on Peel Street, Windsor in Melbourne. The College became a state school when the Education Department (VA 714) became involved in 1913. The College comprises a unique partnership between the government and the independent organisation, VSDC-Services for Deaf Children. A formal agreement exists between the Education Department, VSDC (Victorian School for Deaf Children)-Services for Deaf Children and the School Council.

The College was founded because of a letter which was published in the Melbourne Argus deploring the lack of facilities for educating the deaf in the Colony. The letter was written in February of 1859 by Mrs Sarah Lewis, the mother of a deaf child. The letter spurred a response from Sandhurst resident Mr. Frederick John Rose, a deaf man who had come from England in 1852 and had been educated at the Old Kent Road School for the Deaf in London. Mr Frederick J Rose opened the School for the Deaf and Dumb in 1860 and Mrs Lewis’ daughter, Lucy, became the first student. 

Enrolments increased rapidly, and the school moved in 1861 to the corner of Henry and Upton Streets, Windsor; in 1862 to Nelson Street, Windsor; and in 1864 to Leal House, Commercial Road, Prahran. It was in Nelson Street, the Committee was formed and applied to the government for land on which to build a permanent school for the deaf. The block was granted, an area of about six acres on the corner of St Kilda Road and High Streets, Prahran. The central edifice and southern wing were opened as the Victorian Deaf and Dumb Institution in 1866 to provide both classrooms and residential accommodation. The north wing of the building was completed in 1871 and a cottage hospital was erected on the site in 1887.  

The Committee took responsibility for the school in 1869. In 1913, the Education Department (VA 714) assumed responsibility for the education of deaf children and took on the employment of the teaching staff after an amendment to the Education Act of 1910 which contained clauses making the education of deaf children compulsory. The Board of Management retained the responsibility for the provision of education support services and the residential care of students. 

In 1926 the Committee offered the Education Department some of the St Kilda Road land for the construction of classrooms at the expense of the Department. The new building was completed in 1957 and opened in May of 1928 by then Director of Education, Mr J. McRae.

During the war years, Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) occupied the St Kilda Road building and in 1942, the school moved to Marysville and were housed in Mary-Lyn. Classes resumed in school buildings from early 1944 and RAAF vacated later the same year. 

The corporate name was changed to Victorian School for Deaf Children in 1949 under the provisions of section 50 of the Hospitals and Charities Act 1948. 

In 1950 the Victorian School for Deaf Children built and operated the Princess Elizabeth Kindergarten for Deaf Children (School No. 4822) on Elgar Road, Burwood. Responsibility for staffing the kindergarten was transferred to the Education Department (VA 714) in 1958.  In 1976, the kindergarten was re-named the Princess Elizabeth Junior School for Deaf Children and was closed in 2002. 

Throughout the 1950s the Education Department sent several teachers to Manchester to study the latest method of teaching the deaf. In 1951 enrolments peaked, mainly due to the rubella epidemic some years previously. Temporary accommodation was provided in army huts until a second storey was erected on top of the west wing of the school in 1953.  

The W.D. Cook Pre-School Centre was opened and built by the Board of Management in 1957 on the grounds of the school. In 1971, the H.P. Green Wing was built by the Education Department (VA 714). 

In 1974 the school established two family group homes for deaf children in Stott Street, Box Hill. By the late 1970s students in residence from the school and kindergarten were accommodated in three on-campus family group homes. The school and kindergarten closed on weekends and any children not able to go home stayed at the Stott Street family group homes.

In 1983 a decision was made to phase out boarding school style accommodation in favour of family group homes. Homes were located in Atkinson Street, Oakleigh, Jasper Road and Shrewsbury Street, Bentleigh

In 1995, the Victorian School for Deaf Children became the Victorian College for the Deaf after the Department of Education (VA 3098) entered into an agreement with the Board to guarantee operation of the school for another thirty years. 

In 2024, the school is still in operation.
title: Victorian College for the Deaf (School No. 3774; previously known as School for the Deaf and Dumb 1860-1866; Victorian Deaf and Dumb Institution 1866-1949; Victorian School for Deaf Children 1949-1995)

description:
Wangaratta District Specialist School (WDSS) (School No. 5226) (VA 5312) is a multi-mode specialist school catering for students with mild to severe intellectual and associated disabilities from 5 to 18 years of age.

WDSS is located in the rural city of Wangaratta and services the Benalla, Myrtleford, Ovens and King Valleys, Rutherglen, Wahgunyah, and Wangaratta districts.

It appears the school was established in 1984 with the establishment of the school council. Further research is required to confirm if the school was operating prior to the establishment of the school council. 

An additional school campus in Benalla is due to be opened in late 2024.  The school was allocated funding for the planning and construction of the new campus from the 2020-21 Infrastructure Planning and Acceleration fund and the 2020-21 State Budget.
title: Wangaratta District Specialist School (School No. 5226; also known as WDSS)

description:
The first school for the residents of Mooralla and Geerak in the Southern Grampians Shire was held in the local Methodist Hall in 1877. The Education Department (VA 714) rented the hall for approximately 2 pounds, 10 shillings per quarter, and supplied a teacher to educate the approximate 27 children expected to attend the school at the time. By 1887, the residents pushed for the construction of a purpose-built school, as the conditions of the church hall was no longer adequate.

Two acres of land in the Parish of Mooralla was reserved for the construction of a new school building and gazetted on 14th February 1888. The new building had three rooms, with one used as a classroom, and two for the teacher's residence. As attendance the school increased, one room of the teacher’s quarters was used for lessons.

This building was condemned in 1930, and the school functioned in the Mooralla Public Hall while a new one was built. The construction of a one-room timber schoolhouse with a corrugated roof was completed in 1932 and declared open on 24 January 1933. Soldier settlement after World War II increased enrolment, and in the 1950s a 6ft extension was added. By 1962, a larger building entirely was needed, and this new school was opened by the Minister of Education on the 10th of May 1963.

Education continued in the new building until October 1975, when the school was left unstaffed. The Education Department (VA 714) removed the 1963 building shortly afterwards, leaving the 1933 school as the only building on the land. The school seems to have closed sometime in 1978.

This 1933 schoolhouse was part of a complex of civic buildings which once formed a community hub in East West Road. It was listed on the Victorian Heritage Database as ‘State School No. 1835 (Former)’ (Place ID 23416) in 2002, due to its historical significance as an ‘expression of the early community's struggle for education’, and for ‘its association with 100 years of schooling in the area’. The building is of particularly significant for the local community as the last surviving building in the former village of Mooralla. 

Approximately 235 pupils attended Mooralla State School throughout its history.
title: Mooralla State School (School No. 1835; also known as Mooralla Primary School)

description:
Approximately 5 kilometres south-east of Shepparton and situated amongst local orchards, Orrvale is a rural primary school for prep – grade 6, with approximately 400 students as of 2023. It is closely connected with the history of the region’s fruit growing industry and influenced by waves of migration from various parts of the world since 1913.

The school was originally known as ‘Shepparton Estate’ and was opened in the leased Orrvale Presbyterian Church in 1913. Eight grades were taught in the one room, forty-five students having enrolled the same year, many transfers from School No. 1713 Shepparton East. The school’s first and long-standing permanent teacher was Northern Irishman Mr. William McCleary, commonly known as ‘Old Boss’ or ‘Boss’ by the community.

As the region’s population grew, a new school building became necessary. Two local men rode on horseback to collect signatures for a petition to the government, who authorized the erection of a new State School Building at the end of 1914. The new building, that consisted of two schoolrooms, an office, and a veranda, was first used on the 4th of February 1916.

The school was re-named Orrvale State School after the district, both named for the local member of parliament, Hon. William Orr. A school residence was erected on the site in 1928, and was still in use by the Head Teacher/Principal and their family until 1986, when it was torn down to make way for future school developments.
title: Orrvale Primary School (School No. 3805; also known as Shepparton Estate; Orrvale State School)

description:
In July 1898, School No. 3313 – known as Rainbow Rise or Rainbow State School - was established in a public hall in Rainbow, North-West Victoria. It functioned on a half-time basis alongside Werrap State School until 1901, when Rainbow Rise moved to a recently completed hall within the township and began operating as a full-time school.

In 1905 the school moved to a new site, and in 1919 became Rainbow Higher Elementary School in response to growing demand for higher education. In 1959 the school split, becoming Rainbow Primary School and Rainbow High School (later Rainbow Secondary College, School No. 8255).

Rainbow Primary School continued to develop and expand as the town grew. In 2011 the primary school was co-located with Rainbow Secondary College (School No. 8255), before the schools merged in 2014 to become Rainbow P-12 College (School No. 8256).

Rainbow P-12 College officially opened in 2015, with 120 students coming from Rainbow and the surrounding districts, including Jeparit, Yaapeet and Beulah.
name.official_title.title: Rainbow Primary School (also known as Rainbow Rise, Rainbow State School, Rainbow Higher Elementary School, School No. 3313)
title: Rainbow Primary School (School No. 3313; also known as Rainbow Rise; Rainbow State School; Rainbow Higher Elementary School)

description:
Tinternvale Primary School (VA 5316) is a co-educational Prep to Grade 6 primary school located on Tintern Ave, Ringwood East in the Maroondah City Council area in north-east Melbourne. It opened in February 1976, at which time it was listed as being situated in the suburb of Bayswater North, though the school site has not changed over time. The school catchment area includes parts of Ringwood East, Bayswater North and Croydon South. 

In 2008, a proposal was made to merge Tinternvale Primary School with the nearby Croydon South Primary School (School No. 4890). While Croydon South Primary School, located only 1.5km away from both Tinternvale and Dorset Primary Schools, had been experiencing declining enrolments for some years, the primary motivation in seeking a merger at this time was an opportunity to secure funding through the Victorian Government’s Building Futures: Better Schools Today Program. In the program, newly merged schools would receive priority funding, and would allow the schools to improve opportunities and facilities for students. After a period of community consultation, the Minister for Education approved the proposed merger in September 2008, to take effect 1 January 2009. The merger was completed in due course with both school councils formally dissolved by the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development (VA 4840) in February 2009, and a new council constituted for Tinternvale Primary School. Students commenced the 2009 school year at the existing Tinternvale Primary School campus, leaving the Croydon South Primary School site vacant.

In 2020, Tinternvale Primary School secured Minor Capital Works funding to upgrade school site security and to create a clear boundary to the adjacent public bike path and bushland. The works were completed in 2022.
title: Tinternvale Primary School (School No. 5075)

description:
Wangaratta Primary School (VA 5317) is a co-educational Prep to Grade 6 primary school located near the junction of the Ovens and King Rivers in Wangaratta, North-Eastern Victoria. 

The school was first established in 1850 following a visit to the region from George Rusden, an agent for the National School Board of New South Wales (VA 920), as part of a tour promoting the benefits of government-assisted education. Land for the school was granted to the National School Board in July and the school was officially opened on 22 August 1850 as Wangaratta National School, with Henry Howard as the first Head Teacher. In 1851 the National School Board (VA 919) was established in Victoria, taking over the administration of Victorian schools including Wangaratta National School. By 1853, there were 59 students recorded to be enrolled, with an average actual attendance of 25, growing to 111 enrolments by 1857. 

In 1862, the Commons Schools Act established the Board of Education in Victoria (VA 713). The school became known as Wangaratta Common School at this time and was given the number 643 in 1863, when a new numbering system for schools was introduced. Ten years later, the Education Act 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and introduced free, compulsory and secular schooling for Victorian children. The Wangaratta school became known as Wangaratta State School from 1 January 1873, with Edward P. Date as Head Teacher.

In 1970, there was a statewide change in the use of the term “State school” to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use “primary school” in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Wangaratta Primary School. 

The buildings and grounds of the school have undergone significant changes throughout the years. A new school building was commissioned by the Education Department in 1876 and completed in 1877, at which time the school could accommodate 422 students. There was also a detached, four-roomed teacher’s residence on the site and the new building was officially opened by the Hon. W. Collard Smith, the Minister of Public Instruction. Further major extensions and renovations to the school site took place in 1914, then able to accommodate around 500 students.  In 1927 the River Red Gum School Plantation was established on 18 acres along the banks of the Yellow Creek 2 miles from the school. A concrete swimming pool was constructed in 1939, diagonally opposite the main school ground, which was then replaced 30 years later by a modern School Learner Swimming Pool in 1969.
title: Wangaratta Primary School (School No. 643; previously known as Wangaratta National School 1850 – 1862; Wangaratta Common School 1862 – 1872; Wangaratta State School 1873 – 1970)

description:
Woori Yallock Primary School (VA 5318) is a co-educational Prep to Grade 6 school located in the Upper Yarra Valley. 

It was first established as Woori Yallock State School in 1874, with schooling commencing on 19th January 1874 out of a tent leased by the Education Department (VA 714). 21 students were enrolled for instruction by the Head Teacher M. O’Halloran at this time. A wooden portable schoolroom was first used from 1876 and a permanent site of 5 acres was established in 1877. 

The school has on occasion been known as Woori Yallock and Hoddle’s Creek, but it doesn’t seem that the schools were ever formally combined. From 1884, however, Woori Yallock State School was worked half-time with the Don River School (School No. 2599; also known as Launching Place Primary School) until it resumed full-time independent schooling in 1886.

In 1889, a half-acre plot was planted with white mulberry trees at the direction of the Head Teacher James Murphy, who had an interest in silk production. 

In 1915, a new building was built and opened by the Minister of Public Instruction, with the original school building moved in 1917 to another portion of the school site and converted into a teacher’s residence. Various repairs and site upgrades were made with government funding over the years, from periodic repainting and repairs, through to the provision of sewerage in 1962, and the building of an additional classroom in 1972.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term “state school” to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use “primary school” in the name. Accordingly, the school’s name was changed to Woori Yallock Primary School. 

In 2019, Woori Yallock Primary School received state government funding for infrastructure upgrades and a new relocatable building. In 2020, the school was allocated a further $10.5 million for upgrades and modernisation of its facilities and buildings, with these works due to be completed in 2024.
title: Woori Yallock Primary School (School No. 1259; previously known as Woori Yallock State School 1874 - 1969)

description:
Auburn High School (VA 5319) is a co-educational secondary school located in Hawthorn East. It opened in 2014 on the site of Hawthorn Secondary College (School No. 7934), immediately following its closure in December 2013.

Hawthorn Secondary College had been having a period of low enrolments, with many students from local public primary schools attending private schools for their secondary education. Following consultation with local principals and parents, it was identified that it would be desirable to have a government high school in the area that offered aspirational academic programs, such as the International Baccalaureate and language immersion, to follow on from language immersion programs already running in nearby primary schools. In March 2013, the Hawthorn Secondary College School Council unanimously agreed to request that the Education Minister close Hawthorn Secondary College and reopen a new school on the same site the following year.

Accordingly, Auburn High School commenced operations at the start of the 2014 school year, with the new name officially registered in December 2015. In its first year enrolments were reported to be just under 300, with many students continuing from the former Hawthorn Secondary College; by 2022 enrolments had grown to almost 700. 

Since 2016, Auburn High School has been accredited with the Agency for French Education Abroad (AFEA) to offer French Immersion and French Binational programs, where students can study the same curriculum and sit the same end of cycle examination (Diplôme National du Brevet) as in France. As of 2023, it is the only Victorian government high school to be offering the Binational French program. It offers the International Baccalaureate curriculum alongside the Victorian Certificate of Education (VCE), and also runs an International Student Program at Years 10-12.
title: Auburn High School (School No. 7526)

description:
Eaglehawk Secondary College (VA 5320) is a co-educational Year 7 to Year 10 secondary school located in the Greater Bendigo region of North-Western Victoria. As of 2023, it has around 650 enrolled students and services Eaglehawk, Bendigo and the surrounding areas.

There were calls in the community for a post primary school in the Borough of Eaglehawk from as early as 1949, with repeated requests made to the Education Department (VA 714) throughout the 1950s, however it took some time for a suitable site to be determined and acquired. Accordingly, the school first opened as Eaglehawk High School in 1964, and at this time operated out of five portable classrooms at Camp Hill State School (School No. 1976) in Bendigo, with 122 students enrolled. In November 1964 the Education Department acquired 17 ½ acres of land at Reserve Street, Eaglehawk, and students commenced the 1965 school year in newly constructed buildings on the Reserve Street site.

From 1973, Eaglehawk High School established technical components in the curriculum, in response to requests to the Education Department for increased access to technical education in the country area. Technical components were established jointly by the Secondary Schools and Technical Schools Divisions of the Department, with resourcing provided gradually according to the needs of the school and community. By 1975, Eaglehawk High School was officially listed as a technical school and was offering technical subjects, with further physical facilities in development. It seems the school became known as Eaglehawk High Technical School around 1981 and in 1989 celebrated 25 years of secondary education in the borough.

In 1990 the school underwent a name change to Eaglehawk Secondary College following the Change of School Name and Reclassification of Schools Executive Memorandum No 314 from the Ministry of Education (VA 1112).
title: Eaglehawk Secondary College (School No. 7790; previously known as Eaglehawk High School 1964 – c.1981; Eaglehawk Technical High School c.1981 - 1990)

description:
Eumemmerring Secondary College (VA 5321) was a multi-campus secondary school located in the south-eastern suburbs of Melbourne. It was sometimes referred to as a district college, as it provided secondary education over a larger area than a single school would otherwise. It was at one point the largest secondary school in Victoria. Its name came from the district over which the school existed, from Doveton to Narre Warre, which had been previously named Eumemmerring.

Eumemmerring Secondary College was first established in 1991, from what used to be Hallam High School (School No. 7883). The area had been struggling for facilities to support a growing number of secondary age students, and while there had been proposals to establish new schools at Fountain Gate and Endeavour Hills, it was decided instead to form a single multi-campus college. This decision was also driven by the introduction of the Victorian Certification of Education (VCE) at the senior secondary level, as it was thought that having more students enrolled would support the teaching of a greater range VCE subjects.

From 1991, the school ran on two campuses: Hallam Campus, on the former Hallam High School site on Frawley Road in Hallam, and Fountain Gate Campus, on Josephine Avenue in Narre Warren. In 1992, Endeavour Hills Secondary College (School No. 7133) amalgamated with Eumemmerring to become a third campus of the school, on Amalfi Drive in Endeavour Hills. At this time, there was already an idea to open a fourth campus, which culminated in the opening of the Gleneagles Campus in 1996 on Reema Boulevard in Endeavour Hills. With the establishment of the fourth campus, the structure became embedded as Hallam Campus teaching senior secondary, or Year 11 and 12, and the remaining three teaching Years 7-10. 

In 2008, after a period of community consultation, it was decided to disaggregate Eumemmerring Secondary College into four independent schools, though they would continue to be linked by an Alliance. Accordingly, new schools were established from 2009 at each of the former Eumemmerring Secondary College campuses: Hallam Senior Secondary College (School No. 8868), Gleneagles Secondary College (School No. 8869), Fountain Gate Secondary College (School No. 8870) and Endeavour Hills Secondary College (School No. 8870). The Eumemmerring Secondary School Council was formally dissolved in March 2009.
title: Eumemmering Secondary College (School No. 8496)

description:
Flinders Peak Secondary College (VA 5322) was a co-educational secondary school. It first opened in 1978 under the name Corio North High School, and the original site consisted of 43 acres of land bounded by Plantation Road and Hendy Street in the Corio Shire (VA 2410). Upon opening, the school operated out of portable classrooms with 120 students enrolled.

Development of the site commenced in 1979. Notably, Corio Shire contributed $18,000 to the construction of sporting facilities at the school site to facilitate community use, which included two ovals, two hockey fields, a soccer field, six tennis courts, two basketball courts, two netball courts and a children’s playground. Various formal and informal arrangements between the school council, Corio Shire and later, the City of Greater Geelong (VA 3149) dictated the administrative and maintenance obligations of the parties regarding the facilities.

In December 1979, new buildings became available for use. One of them, Block ‘F’, was built primarily to house the school’s boiler room and toilet facilities, with additional change facilities added at the request of council to increase its suitability for community sporting use. In September 1981, further school buildings were opened for geography and science, art and craft and home economics, and a cafeteria. In 1983, the Corio Shire contributed $80,000 toward the Education and Community Activity Centre (i.e. stadium). Works were undertaken by the Geelong Council on the internal space of Block ‘F’ in 2006 and 2007 to create a social room for community sporting use, which in 2007 became the sole responsibility of the Greater Geelong City Council. 

In 1990, Corio North High School underwent a name change to Flinders Peak Secondary College following the implementation of the "Change of School Name and Reclassification of Schools” Executive Memorandum No 314 from the Ministry of Education (VA 1112).           

In 2007, the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development (DEECD) (VA 4840) commenced planning for the Corio-Norlane Education Regeneration Project under the Building Futures policy framework. This multi-staged project involved the re-configuration of 9 government schools in Corio and Norlane into one prep to year 12 college across five campuses, to be called Northern Bay College (VA 5358). 

Accordingly, Flinders Peak Secondary College was permanently closed in December 2010, along with Corio Bay Senior College (School No. 7105), Norlane West Primary School (School No. 4880), Corio Primary School (School No. 124), Corio West Primary School (School No. 5031), North Shore Primary School (School No. 4301), Norlane High School (School No. 8175), and Corio South Primary School (School No. 4927) to form the new Northern Bay P-12 College (School No. 8901; VA 5358). The Flinders Peak school site continued to be used as an education facility by Nelson Park School (School No. 4768) and other organisations for a short time after the school’s closure.

In 2013, DEECD signaled its intention to sell the site. The site was subsequently sold in 2016, and all school buildings have since been demolished, with the exception of the former ‘F’ block, which is occupied by the Geelong Rugby Union Club as their sporting clubrooms.
title: Flinders Peak Secondary College (School No. 7744; previously known as Corio North High School 1978 – 1990)

Opening in 1976, Bulleen Heights – then named Bulleen Special School – is a co-ed and specialised government school for students with Autism Spectrum Disorder and/or severe language impairment.

In its early years, the school provided students regular visits by a speech therapist, a teacher for the deaf, a music teacher, and a physiotherapist. Rather than be divided into traditional class structures based on age, students were divided into three ability streams, further separated into class groups according to ‘academic, social, physical, emotional and dependency maturational factors’. The streaming was flexible, with students able to move between them when ready.

In 1989, the school’s name changed to Bulleen Heights School (Victorian Government Gazette 50, 20 December 1989, 3293). The school’s class structure was also changed, with students placed in groups according to several interacting factors that included their stage of educational development, peer group interaction, student/teacher relationship, and the student’s age.

As of 1998, the school was comprised of three main buildings and a three-bedroom brick house in extensive grounds. The house, called ‘Yungaburra’, was used as a centre for independent living skills. The school had three main departments serving students aged between 5 – 20 years old – Primary, Intermediate/Secondary and Transition.

Currently, Bulleen Heights School teaches students aged 5 – 18 across two campuses in the North-Eastern suburbs of Melbourne – Pleasant Road, Bulleen (Primary campus), and Manningham Road, Lower Templestowe (Secondary campus). Classes follow the Victorian curriculum, supplemented by a multi-disciplinary team of speech therapists, occupational therapists, and a psychologist who provide additional therapy and educational service to the students.
name.official_title.title: Bulleen Heights School
title: Bulleen Heights School (School No. 5099; previously known as Bulleen Special School 1976-1989; also known as Bulleen Heights Specialist School)

description:
A Court of Petty Sessions was appointed in Lakes Entrance, in the township then known as Cunninghame, in 1895. In 1888 the Lakes Entrance township was extended to border Cunninghame. Although never officially renamed, development in the area grew Lakes Entrance’s town centre–effectively engulfing Cunninghame–and the township’s various amenities were gradually renamed. The Cunninghame Court of Petty Sessions became commonly known as the Lakes Entrance Court of Petty Sessions sometime between 1912 and 1929. The court heard Magistrates’ and Children’s Court proceedings and was situated in the Gippsland court region until it was removed from the Magistrates’ Court circuit. The last hearings scheduled at the court were held in 1999. As no order was given to officially close the court, it is unclear where the courts records were located after its closure, however, the nearby Bairnsdale Court (VA 4337) is likely.

Lakes Entrance Courts include:
  • Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1895 – 1999)
  • Children’s Court (1907 – 1999)

District and Circuit Court Systems

In the mid-19th to early 20th century, courts and court districts were established across Victoria of various levels. This practice remained until either the court was abolished, or a state-wide court entity was established. Once a statewide court was established, hearings continued in regional centres using a circuit court system.

Under the district system, courts largely administered themselves, with major decisions such as the appointment of judicial officers and court locations, as well the development of court rules, procedures and jury lists passed down by Governor in Council. Additionally, judicial officers, registrars and clerks were appointed to specific court locations. These functions were largely taken over by the primary court and their respective chief judicial officer once the primary court was established. Likewise, judicial officers were no longer appointed to specific court locations, but rather to the primary court then assigned to hearings according to the scheduled circuit.

Both district courts and circuit courts commonly used their own recordkeeping systems to manage cases until centralised recordkeeping systems were gradually introduced from the late 20th century. Administrative resources were often shared between the different levels of court when operating from the same location.

Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1838 – Present)

Courts of Petty Sessions were established to hear criminal and civil cases of minor offences and disputes. Courts of Petty Sessions were appointed to be held in population centres. These courts were renamed Magistrates’ Courts in 1971. Under the Magistrates’ Court Act 1989 (Vic), the Magistrates’ Court of Victoria (VA 5113) was constituted as the primary body, while the various courts were grouped into regions with the largest in each appointed as a headquarter venue. Magistrates and other Judicial Officers were assigned to regions to hear cases in each location according to the scheduled circuit. Individual Magistrates’ Courts continue to maintain their own case registries. As of 2023, there are 51 courts in 13 regions. The Court has several divisions including Koori Court, Drug Court, Assessment and Referral Court as well as several specialist family courts. These divisions are appointed to specific locations within regions, usually the headquarters court.

Children’s Court (1907 – Present)

Children’s Courts were established to hear and to inquire into charges against children. During the 1930s, these courts also began hearing other cases involving children such as child neglect. Children’s Courts were appointed to be held at locations that already held Courts of Petty Sessions or Magistrates’ Courts and operated as a division of the Magistrates’ Court until 2000. As such, Children’s Courts operated under the Magistrates’ Court district system until 1989 and continue to mirror the Magistrates’ Court’s regional system. Like the Magistrates’ Court, when the Children’s Court of Victoria (VA 4190) was constituted as the primary and independent body, courts were grouped into regions, and Judicial Officers and Support Services staff were assigned to these regions. Judicial officers were assigned to hearings according to each region’s circuit schedule. Individual courts continue to maintain their own case registries and often share administrative resources with the Magistrates’ Court registries. As of 2023, there are 47 courts in 6 regions. The Court has a Family division, and Criminal division, as well as a Children’s Koori Court for criminal matters. Like Magistrates' Koori Courts, Children's Koori Courts are appointed to specific locations.

A Court of Petty Sessions was appointed in Lorne in November 1939. The court heard Magistrates’ and Children’s Court proceedings until the court was closed on 1 October 1984 and its records were directed to be delivered to clerk of the Colac Magistrates’ Court (VA 4323).

Lorne Courts include:
  • Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1939 – 1984)
  • Children’s Court (1939 – 1984)

District and Circuit Court Systems

In the mid-19th to early 20th century, courts and court districts were established across Victoria of various levels. This practice remained until either the court was abolished, or a state-wide court entity was established. Once a statewide court was established, hearings continued in regional centres using a circuit court system.

Under the district system, courts largely administered themselves, with major decisions such as the appointment of judicial officers and court locations, as well the development of court rules, procedures and jury lists passed down by Governor in Council. Additionally, judicial officers, registrars and clerks were appointed to specific court locations. These functions were largely taken over by the primary court and their respective chief judicial officer once the primary court was established. Likewise, judicial officers were no longer appointed to specific court locations, but rather to the primary court then assigned to hearings according to the scheduled circuit.

Both district courts and circuit courts commonly used their own recordkeeping systems to manage cases until centralised recordkeeping systems were gradually introduced from the late 20th century. Administrative resources were often shared between the different levels of court when operating from the same location.

description:
Establishment 
The Office of the Special Investigator (OSI) was an independent statutory body that was established out of the recommendations of the Royal Commission into the Management of Police Informants (VA 5254). 

The Royal Commission recommended that the Victorian Government establish a Special Investigator to investigate whether there is sufficient evidence to establish the commission of criminal offences (connected with Victoria Police's use of Ms Nicola Gobbo as a human source) by Ms Gobbo or the current and former police officers named in the Royal Commission's final report delivered in November 2020 or in the complete and unredacted submissions of Counsel Assisting the Royal Commission. The Royal Commission also recommended the Special Investigator investigate Victoria Police officers for disciplinary offences in relation to the same conduct.

As at the 1 December 2021, the Special Investigator Act 2021 established the Office of the Special Investigator and the Hon. Geoffrey Nettle AC QC was appointed by the Governor in Council as the Special Investigator.

Purpose
The OSI’s purpose was to investigate potential criminal conduct and breaches relating to the recruitment, management and use by Victoria Police of Nicola Maree Gobbo as a human source.

Where the OSI determined relevant offences may have been committed, its role extended to compiling briefs of evidence that were filed alongside recommended charges for determination by the Victorian Director of Public Prosecutions. 

As outlined in the Special Investigator Act 2021, the functions of the OSI were as follows:
a) to access, receive, assess and deal with Royal Commission records to determine whether
    i     evidence of the commission of one or more relevant offences or offences exist; 
    ii    or evidence of a breach of discipline exists.
b)    to investigate and gather further evidence to determine whether -
    i    a relevant offence or an offence may have been committed; 
    ii    to compile briefs of evidence to give to the DPP for the purposes of determining whether charges should be filed; 
    iii    to commence any criminal proceedings.
c)    to investigate, and (if appropriate) charge, any police officer with the commission of a breach of discipline by the police officer arising from, or out of, the conduct of persons involved in the use of Nicola Maree Gobbo as a human source;
d)    to access, receive, assess and deal with IBAC records provided to the Office of the Special Investigator
e)    to receive public interest disclosures and investigate public interest complaints;
f)    to provide reports to the Implementation Monitor;
g)    to cooperate, coordinate and consult with the IBAC at the request of the IBAC for the purposes of a coordinated investigation within the meaning of section 72 of the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission Act 2011 in accordance with that Act to determine whether a relevant offence or breach of discipline has been committed;
h)    to report to Parliament on any matter relating to the functions and duties of the Office of the Special Investigator.

The OSI investigated whether there was sufficient evidence to establish - 
a)    the commission of a relevant offence by Nicola Maree Gobbo; and
b)    the commission of a relevant offence by any police officers and former police officers named in the following documents -
    i    in the complete and unredacted submissions of Counsel Assisting the Royal Commission into the Management of Police Informants; 
    ii    the Royal Commission's final report
c)    the commission of a breach of discipline by any police officers named in the following documents in connection with the use of Nicola Maree Gobbo as a human source by Victoria Police -  
    i    the complete and unredacted submissions of Counsel Assisting the Royal Commission into the Management of Police Informants; 
    ii    the Royal Commission's final report.
 
Conclusion and Reporting
On the 21 June 2023, Special Investigator Geoffrey Nettle tabled a special report in Parliament. 

Following advice from the Special Investigator after none of the investigations conducted by the Office of the Special Investigator resulted in any criminal or disciplinary proceedings being commenced, the Victorian Government announced on 27 June 2023 that the Office of the Special Investigator should be decommissioned.

In November 2023, the Special Investigator Repeal Act 2023 was passed. The Act repealed the Special Investigator Act 2021 and abolished the Office of the Special Investigator. On the 19 Dec 2023, the Proclamation of Commencement was published in the Victorian Government Gazette S687 and fixed the 2 February 2024 as the day on which the Act comes into operation.
title: Office of the Special Investigator

description:
Diggora West State School (VA 5327) opened in 1880 as Warragamba State School, later renamed Diggora West in March of 1903.  

The school was likely located on Dingee Road in the former village of Diggora, approximately 16 kilometres west of Rochester in the Parish of Pannoomilloo, County of Bendigo. The exact location is unknown and subject to further research. The school and residence were set on 1.5 acre grounds and were equipped with three water tanks. 

In 1912 Diggora West State School was closed due to low student numbers. Despite the closure of the school, the building remained in good condition and served as a venue for regular church services and as a post office.  

The school was reopened in 1918 due to the 1915 construction of the Elmore and Cohuna railway line, bringing the population closer to the railway station.  

The school was permanently closed in 1966 and the Elmore and Cohuna railway line was closed in 1981. 
 
Diggora West State School should not be confused with either Warragamba State School (School No. 2939; previously known as Diggora West State School 1889 - 1903) (VA 5328) which was located nearby and closed in 1922, or Diggora South State School (School No. 2237) (VA 3261) which was located nearby and operated for a similar period from 1880 – 1963.
title: Diggora West State School (School No. 2304; previously known as Warragamba State School 1880 - 1903)

description:
Warragamba State School (VA 5328) opened in 1889 as Diggora West State School and was renamed Warragamba in March of 1903.

The school was located on the corner of Lockington and Settlement Roads in the former village of Diggora, approximately 14km north-west of Elmore and 35km south-west of Echuca in the County of Bendigo.

In 1909, the school building on the former Diggora South State School (School No. 2237) (VA 3261) site was transported to Warragamba State School to accommodate the growing number of students, following the (temporary) closure of Diggora South in 1905.

By 1910, the land for a residence had been purchased from Thomas, Jane and Roger Shotton. The residence, along with a kitchen and veranda added by the Head Teacher, was constructed and occupied.

Warragamba State School closed permanently in 1922 in response to a petition requesting the establishment of a school closer to the new Hunter Railway Station and low average attendance. The school building was then moved approximately 2 miles south to the new Hunter School (School No. 4133) (VA 3315) in preparation for its opening in 1923.

The Education Department (VA 714) sold the land of the former Warragamba State School and teachers’ residence sites in 1923.

Warragamba State School should not be confused with either Diggora West State School (School No. 2304; previously known as Warragamba State School 1880 – 1903) (VA 5327) which was located nearby and closed in 1966, or Diggora South State School (School No. 2237) (VA 3261) which was located nearby and closed permanently in 1963.
title: Warragamba State School (School No. 2939; previously known as Diggora West State School 1889 - 1903)

description:
Porepunkah Primary School (VA 5329), established in January of 1873 as a Common School, is one of Victoria’s oldest public schools and is located in the Shire of Bright in northeast Victoria.  

Initially proposed as a Rural School (No. 106), the Board of Education (VA 713) went on to acquire land from William Hooper in 1861. However, the Board realising the community’s preference for a Common School issued an Order in 1872, assigning the school number 1144.  

Led by James Duncan, the local Committee commissioned a single room building which was completed in December 1872. The structure was unlined and unpainted but had a ceiling. In 1874 a four-room teacher’s residence was added to the site. 

The Porepunkah Common School became a State School in 1875 and formed its first Official Committee in 1911.  

In 1912, the construction of a new wooden school was completed and formally opened by Minister Hon A. A. Billson and Director Frank Tate. A new wooden residence of five rooms was completed by 1913. In 1914, the original school building which had since been repurposed as an Infant Room, underwent renovations. A shelter shed was also constructed in 1914, with half of the costs covered by the Department.

In 1924, Porepunkah Primary School purchased over 40 acres of Crown land for a School Endowment Pine Plantation fundraising initiative.  In 1925, the first trees were planted, and the land was milled in 1955 with the school receiving a cheque for £750 which led to the construction of an additional classroom that year.

In 1941, the wooden building (originally constructed in 1912) was relocated to a more suitable location within the school grounds and underwent renovations, transforming it into a visual education room. Electricity was connected to the school in 1951 and an additional classroom, office and storeroom were added in 1963.  

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term “State school” to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use “primary school” in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Porepunkah Primary School. 

A major redevelopment occurred from 2010 to 2011, retaining the original 1963 development and adding four new classrooms, toilets and a multi-purpose / library area. The original school building functioned as an Outside School Hours Care room until 2021, after which it was repurposed into a Foundation classroom.

In 2023, Porepunkah Primary School celebrated 150 years of education in Porepunkah. The school is still in operation as at 2024.
title: Porepunkah Primary School (School No. 1144; previously known as Porepunkah Common School 1873 – 1875; Porepunkah State School 1875 – 1970)

description:
The Accountability and Oversight Committee was a Joint Investigatory Committee of the Parliament of Victoria. The committee was established under the Parliamentary Committees Act 2003 according to amendments specified in s. 48 and 49 of the Freedom of Information Amendment (Freedom of Information Commissioner) Act 2012. The Committee was also granted powers and responsibilities under the Ombudsman Act 1973.

The committee has a number of functions, including:
  • monitoring, reviewing, and reporting to Parliament on the performance of the Victorian Information Commissioner
  • examining the annual report, and any other reports, of the Victorian Information Commissioner
  • inquiring into freedom of information matters referred to the committee by Parliament
  • monitoring, reviewing, and reporting to Parliament on the performance of the Ombudsman
  • examining reports by the Ombudsman that are tabled in Parliament
  • monitoring, reviewing, and reporting to Parliament on the performance of the Victorian Inspectorate regarding Ombudsman officers and the Judicial Commission.

The Committee’s function was to monitor, review and report to the Parliament on the overall performance of the Victorian Ombudsman (VA 1037), the Victorian Information Commissioner, and the Victorian Inspectorate regarding Ombudsman officers. The Committee was not an alternative review body and as such, it could not review any individual decision, finding or determination by these bodies. Where evidence was presented that a complaint or review was not handled in a correct and fair manner, the Committee could make further enquiries, but the original decision could not be changed as a result. 

The committee was merged with the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission Committee (VA 5333) to form the Integrity and Oversight Committee (VA 5790) according to amendments specified in s. 189 of the Integrity and Accountability Legislation Amendment (Public Interest Disclosures, Oversight and Independence) Act 2019. The committee ceased at the end of the 58th Parliament.

Joint Investigatory Committees

Joint Investigatory Committees are groups of members appointed by the Legislative Council and Legislative Assembly to conduct investigations and make recommendations about topics of particular interest to Parliament. Some committees have ongoing functions to scrutinise legislation and finances, and others conduct inquiries into specific subject matters. A key feature of committee work is the taking of evidence from the public and expert witnesses as part of the inquiry process. Committee investigations result in reports to Parliament.

Joint committees have between five and ten members of whom at least one is a member of the Council, and one is a member of the Assembly. Joint committees can inquire into matters referred to it by a resolution of either House or by order of the Governor-In-Council. They may also inquire into, consider, or report to Parliament on any annual report or document relevant to its functions laid before either House. Recommendations made joint investigatory committees are not automatically accepted by Parliament. The responsible Minister must however, table a report stating action to be taken regarding the recommendations within six months of the tabling of the Committee’s report.

The Economy and Infrastructure Committee is a Standing Committee of the Legislative Council of the Parliament of Victoria. The Committee was established following amendments made to the Legislative Council’s Standing Orders in 2010. Members were first appointed in 2011.

The committee's functions are to inquire into and report on any proposal, matter or thing concerned with agriculture, commerce, infrastructure, industry, major projects, public sector finances and transport.

Standing Committees

Standing Committees are ongoing House inquiry committees established by Standing Orders. According to section 23.02 of the Legislative Council’s Standing Orders and section 202 of the Legislative Assembly’s Standing Orders, at the commencement of each parliament, standing committees are to be appointed for Economy and Infrastructure, Environment and Planning, and Legal and Social Issues in each House of Parliament.

The three Standing Committees were introduced to the Legislative Council after amendments to the Council’s Standing Orders were made in October 2010. These Standing Committees were later established in the Legislative Assembly in the 2019 amendment of the Assembly’s Standing Orders.

Initially, each Council Standing Committee was divided into Legislative Committees and Reference Committees, although in practice these committees shared members and acted as one. While Legislative Committees were concerned with Bills, draft Bills, annual reports and estimates of expenditures, Reference Committees were concerned with matters referred to them by the Council. The Legislative and Reference committee types were removed in the 2023 amendments of the Council’s Standing Orders, mirroring the structure already introduced in the Assembly. Assembly Standing Committees differ to Council committees in that the Assembly committees are only concerned with matters relating to specific Departments.

description:
Bridgewater North State School (VA 5338) was a co-educational primary school situated on Collins Road in the town of Bridgewater on Loddon, approximately 40km northwest of Bendigo in central Victoria.  

Bridgewater North State School opened originally as Rural School No. 133 and was registered as a State School with the Education Department (VA 714) in 1874. The names “Bridgewater North” and “Bridgewater on Loddon” appear to be used interchangeably at this time. The original opening date of the school is unknown but is estimated at around 1860.  In 1872 the Committee was formed and in 1877, a teacher’s residence was completed on the site. 

In 1895 Bridgewater North Primary School was closed under the system of conveyance, which likely indicated low average attendance. 

The school was re-opened in 1906 and experienced some years of low average attendance and Bridgewater North was almost closed again in 1910 with complaints the buildings were unfit for school purposes. Around this time attendance began to increase as students from Salisbury West (School No. 1773) had begun to attend Bridgewater North due to difficulties crossing the nearby Loddon River at times.

Bridgewater North was closed again in 1929 on account of low attendance numbers and reopened again in 1939 due to petitioning by local community.  

Bridgewater North was permanently closed in 1954 and the buildings were demolished in 1967.

Bridgewater North Primary School (School No. 1387) should not be confused with either:
Bridgewater Primary School (School No. 1097; previously known as Bridgewater Common School, Bridgewater State School) which opened in 1871 and is still in operation; or
Cape Bridgewater State School (School No. 741; previously known as Cape Bridgewater School, Bridgewater School, Cape Bridgewater Common School) which opened in 1862 and is still in operation; or
Lower Cape Bridgewater State School (School No. 32; previously known as Bridgewater Common School, Bridgewater Peninsula, Bridgewater State School, Lower Cape Bridgewater, Bridgewater Lower) which opened in 1856 and closed in 1946.
title: Bridgewater North State School (School No. 1387; also known as Bridgewater on Loddon State School; previously known as Rural School No. 133 C. 1860 – 1874)

description:
Eskdale Primary School (School No. 2318, previously known as Leased School No. 2318, Eskdale (1881 – c.1883), Eskdale State School (1883 – c.1950s) (VA 5339)) is located 60 kilometres east of Wodonga in the Mitta Valley, north east Victoria.

As early as 1876 the residents of Tallandoon and Stockyard Flat on the Mitta Mitta had petitioned for a school in the area. Initially two half-time schools were planned; Tallandoon could provide a schoolhouse in a leased shepherd’s hut with slab floor and bark roof, however Stockyard Flat required a building to be supplied. While a site for this was gazetted in 1878, financial difficulties delayed providing both building and the furnishings for both schools. In 1880, residents in Tallandoon glazed and re-roofed the shepherd’s hut, a portable building was provided for Stockyard Flat, and furniture was precured for both schools by December.

The Tallandoon school was officially opened in January 1881 as Leased School No. 2318, Eskdale. The Stockyard Flat school was named Tallandoon and ran half-time with Eskdale under the same school number until 1883, when both schools operated full time; Eskdale under School No. 2318, and Tallandoon as School No. 2533. The same year, Eskdale obtained a new site 14 miles from Eskdale township, and a new school building was erected, a portable wooden building with accommodation for 30, with two tiny ‘lean-to’ rooms attached for teacher’s quarters. A decline in attendance in the late 1880s resulted in both Eskdale and Tallandoon resuming half-time operation, and by the early 1990s attendance at Eskdale had fallen to 20.

By 1907, attendance had doubled, and the school resumed full-time operation, however a disagreement emerged between the Eskdale townsfolk and the Eskdale farming community. Those in the township wanted the school either removed to or re-built within town, as their children had to walk a long way to attend, and more children in town who were not yet enrolled would otherwise attend if the distance were not so great. The farming community preferred the school remain in the south. Petition and counter petition were presented to the Department of Education regarding the site of the school, but no changes were made. The school building was at this point overcrowded and run down, with poor conditions for students and teachers alike resulting in further discontent. The local School Board of Advice had condemned the building and made complaints about it to the Department, but it wasn’t until 1912 that action was taken. Classes were temporarily run in the town’s public Hall while a new building was erected, opening in 1913.

In 1934 a residence was erected on a corner site facing the Omea Highway, and in 1949 a Bristol prefabricated unit was supplied for further school accommodation. The school was run at this site until 1977, when it was again moved to a new building within the township, opening with 50 pupils, two teachers and one part-time librarian. The old school building was demolished.

Eskdale merged with Mitta North Primary School (School No. 3974) in 1989, retaining the Eskdale site and School No. 2318. In 2010 the school underwent a major upgrade, and as of 2023 remains in operation.
title: Eskdale Primary School (School No. 2318; previously known as Leased School No. 2318, Eskdale 1881 – c.1883; Eskdale State School 1883 – c.1950s)

description:
Jeparit Primary School (School No. 2988, previously known as Jeparit State School (1889 – c.1950s) (VA 5340), is a small co-educational primary School located in the heritage town of Jeparit, within Hindmarsh Shire. Notably, the town was home to former Prime Minister Robert Menzies, who attended Jeparit State School.

The school was first proposed in a letter from Arthur Scott to the Education Department (VA 714) in May 1889, and opened on 18 November the name year in a building on the Hindmarsh Station homestead. Enrolment upon its establishment was 11 boys and 19 girls, with Sophia McDonald as Head Teacher. Average attendance was 11.

In May 1891, the Jeparit Presbyterian church was built and leased to the Department for Jeparit State School, which moved to the church building in October that year. The primitive building was made of lime-washed pine sapling with a corrugated iron roof and wooden floor, and measured 35ft x 15ft x 12ft.

In 1894 a school building with teacher's quarters was removed from Woolshed, near Dimboola, to Jeparit. The Department later purchased a site of one acre from Mr John Scott Peterson and others on 22 December 1900 for use by the school. In March 1914 the School Committee and the local MLA, James Menzies, wrote to the Department concerning the poor seating accommodation in the upper school room, and asking that the long desks be replaced with modern dual ones.

During 1922 plans were made to have the school enlarged, extending room two and adding a third room. In May 1923, classes were moved to a local hall while the renovations took place. The new school site officially opened in September 1929.

In 1948, 6 acres were bought from G. Livingston and the following year 9 acres of Crown land were reserved for school purposes, with the hope that a consolidated school would later be established. A new house for the Principal was built on the new site and first occupied in 1966. Plans for a secondary school site were underway until the late 1970s, however never eventuated.

Jeparit State School was re-named Jeparit Primary School in the 1950s. As of 2024, 22 students were enrolled, split between a grades Prep-2 and 3-6.
title: Jeparit Primary School (School No. 2988; previously known as Jeparit State School 1889 – c.1950s)

description:
Pootilla State School (School No. 2095) (VA 5341) first opened on the 9th of October 1878, with Sam Trend as Head Teacher and Miss Cope as Work Mistress. A wooden portable building measuring 24 ft x 16 ft with an iron roof and attached teacher’s quarters was erected on a site chosen by the Bungaree District Inspector of Schools, within a water reserve near Ballarat.

In 1879, the school’s name was officially changed from Fellmonger’s Road School to Pootilla State School, although it was still referred to as the former until mid-1880. The net enrolment for the year was 83, with average attendance being 50. This occasionally rose to 63. At the time, the school contained 6 desks that could sit 5 students each and a gallery which could hold 20 children, thus having a seating capacity of 50. The school’s Board of Advice and the Head Teacher wrote to the Education Department (VA 714) requesting additional accommodation, as finding space for a further 12 or 13 children was difficult and impacted schoolwork. In 1881, the school room was lengthened by 10 ft.

From 1883 into the early 20th century, there were several complaints made to the Department about the state of the Head Teacher’s residence, which was described as ‘disgustingly dirty and in unsanitary condition’ in 1901. It is unclear if repairs were made, but in the School Inspector’s report of 1934, the residence was declared as ‘condemned’. It was nevertheless rented out to a new Head Teacher the following year, garnering further complaints.

In 1946 the school closed, and its pupils were transferred to Brown Hill State School No. 35. Locals petitioned to have the school reopened as late as 1950, when the Public Works Department (VA 669) had begun dismantling the building to move it to Bungal, where a schoolhouse had burnt down years earlier. A petition was submitted to have the building remain at Pootilla, naming 17 children in the area either approaching school age or already attending schools in the area. A vote was held on 13 October 1950, determining the building would stay in Pootilla, however it did not reopen as a school. Three years later, it was moved to Grenville State School No. 1153.
title: Pootilla State School (School No. 2095; previously known as Fellmonger’s Road School 1878-1879)

description:
Galaquil State School (VA 5342) was first opened as Batchica North in January 1891. The primary school was situated on a 5 acre block in the town of Beulah, in the southern Mallee region of Victoria.  The school building, an unlined galvanised-iron room, was completed by a local committee in the months prior to its opening. 

In 1902, the school's name was changed to match the new rail-siding, Galaquil. In 1912, a new wooden school building was completed on the site as well as the addition of a shelter shed for which half the cost had been raised locally. 

Galaquil State School closed in 1928 under conveyance which likely indicated low average attendance and was reopened in 1932. 

The school building was deemed unsafe in 1949 due to sever white ant damage, and students were moved to a cottage made available by a local resident approximately one mile south. In 1950, due to the continued dangerous condition of the building, the decision was made not to rebuild Galaquil School. Instead, students were conveyed to Beulah State School (No. 3109), resulting in the permanent closure of Galaquil State School.

Galaquil State School should not be confused with Beulah State School (School No. 3109; previously known as Galaquil) which was located on the corner of Hopetoun Road and Bell Street, Beulah which opened in 1891 and is still in operation as of 2024.
title: Galaquil State School (School No. 3083; previously known at Batchica North 1891 - 1902)

description:
Minyip Primary School (School No. 2167, previously known as Minyip State School (1879 – c.1970s) (VA 5343) is a co-educational government primary school located in the small farming community of Minyip, Wimmera.

The school first opened in a portable building in September 1879 on Main Street, Minyip. Initial enrolment was 37, with 15 pupils having come from a local private school. A new brick building was erected in 1884, but by 1915 was condemned and deemed unsafe for use, with cracks running throughout and bricks on the verge of collapse. The same year, it was replaced by a new wooden building. Built to the same plan as smaller schools established in the Mallee region, this building was too small to properly accommodate Minyip’s larger numbers. Enrolment at the time was 77, whereas the new building only had seating to accommodate 72; several children instead sat on boxes. By 1919 enrolment had grown to 93, with an average attendance of 84. All nine classes were taught in the one room, with only 8 square feet of space allotted per child as opposed to the 12 ½ square feet provided by the Board of Health regulations.

The building was enlarged in 1921, and a sliding partition added. Further rooms were added as attendance increased in 1935, 1958, 1962, and 1964, when enrolment had reached 158. In 1977, the closed Lawler Primary School (School No. 3414) (VA 4544) was transferred to Minyip to provide further accommodation.

As population levels in Minyip and nearby towns decreased, dropping from 610 in 1981 to 436 in 2001, school enrolments likewise declined.
