As of 2024, there are only 40 students enrolled at Minyip Primary School, which operates with two classrooms – grades 3 to 6 in one room, and grades Prep to 2 in the other.
title: Minyip Primary School (School No. 2167; previously known as Minyip State School 1879 – c.1970s)

description:
Appin Park Primary School (School No. 5207) (VA 5344) is a co-educational primary school located in the Rural City of Wangaratta, in north-east Victoria and is part of the Benalla, Mansfield and Wangaratta (BMW) network of schools. It is located at the end of Appin Street and backs onto One Mile Creek.

The establishment of Appin Park Primary School was first raised in 1980, with the works for a new school building contracted in 1981. The school was opened for the start of the 1982 school year, with students attending from the local community and surrounding farming communities.

In the 2018-19 State Budget, the adjoining Wangaratta District Specialist School (School No. 5226; also known as WDSS) (VA 5312), was allocated $2.2 million to increase the capacity of the school, and as part of this the facilities at Appin Park Primary School were also modernised. The same thing happened in 2020, when $5.235 million was allocated to the next stage of the Wangaratta District Specialist School master plan. While a new building was constructed at WDSS, the facilities at Appin Park were modernised once more, and a new hardcourt was built.
title: Appin Park Primary School (School No. 5207)

description:
Camp Pell School (School No. 4719) (VA 5345) was a co-educational primary school established in 1954 for the families living in the Camp Pell Emergency Housing Settlement. The settlement was an army camp within Royal Park in the suburb of Parkville which became home for people experiencing the post-war housing shortage in Victoria. 

In 1952, an Attendance Officer working for the Education Department (VA 714) reported that 80% of the children residing in the camp were enrolled at one of three nearby schools but encountered difficulties in regularly attending classes. The report attributed these difficulties partly to parents’ reluctance to allow their children to cross the very busy Flemington Road.

In response to the report, the Department established Camp Pell School. The school opened in May 1954 within a converted army hut, including four classrooms, an office and storeroom.

By 1956 all families had been relocated from the settlement, prompting the closure of the school in June after only two years of operation.  The school building was relocated to Footscray Technical School (No. 7152).
title: Camp Pell School (School No. 4719)

description:
Condah State School (VA 5346) was a co-educational primary school in the town of Condah, in the Glenelg region of south-west Victoria. It first opened as a common school in 1871, subsequently becoming a state school with the introduction of the Education Act in 1872. The school operated until its closure in 1951 as part of the government's consolidation policy for rural schools which saw the closure and consolidation of a number of primary schools in the region.

Applications for a new school at Condah were raised as early as 1868, when it was proposed to establish a weatherboard school to service 28 local children. The school was officially opened on 8th April 1871.

In 1915, the school community approached the Education Department (VA 714) regarding a new school building, as the current building had been in a dilapidated state for some years. A new site on Portland Road, adjoining the Presbyterian Church grounds, was accordingly surveyed and tenders for the construction of a new building were invited in 1915. A new residence was also added to the site in 1947, with renovations to the school in 1949. 

Discussions about merging state schools in the area began from 1944, when it was represented by parents to the Minister of Public Instruction that students would benefit from communal facilities such as libraries, art rooms, cafeterias, and sports facilities, that would otherwise not be available at small, often single-teacher, rural schools. This discussion included existing schools at Heywood, Heathmere, Myamyn, Drumborg and Homerton.

In 1951, the official process of consolidation began, with schools progressively closing and students moving to the Heywood State School (School No. 297) site to join the newly established Heywood Consolidated School (School No. 5226) (VA 5369). As well as Condah, these schools included Myamyn State School (School No. 1692), Drumborg State School (School No. 1240), Hotspur State School (School No. 1260) (VA 5440) and Mount Eckersley State School (School No. 1720) (VA 5402). 

Condah State School was officially closed on 22th July 1952 and the Condah school building was moved to Heywood form part of the new school site. 
 
Condah State School should not be confused with other similarly named schools that also operated in the Condah area. These include Condah South State School (School No. 3055), Lake Condah State School (School No. 1096; previously known as Lake Condah Common School 1871 - 1872), Wallacedale State School (School No. 3217; previously known as Condah Swamp State School), Branxholme South State School (School No. 906), which was also known as Condah at one point, and Spring Creek State School (School No. 1138) which was located at Condah.
title: Condah State School (School No. 1019; previously known as Condah Common School 1871 - 1872)

description:
Doncaster Secondary College (VA 5347) is a co-educational secondary school in the City of Manningham (VA 3701) in the north-eastern suburbs of Melbourne on the lands of Wurundjeri Woiwurrung people of the Kulin Nation. Formerly an orchard, the 15-acre site was purchased by the Education Department (VA 714) in 1960 to develop into a secondary school. 

Doncaster Secondary College was opened as Doncaster High School in February 1969 with 62 students enrolled. The building structure consisted of 2 classrooms, a staffroom and an amenities block.  

The following decade was a period of rapid growth for the school with the student population reaching 1200 students. Several upgrades and changes were made to improve the school facilities. In 1970, the Commonwealth Library was completed which facilitated additional classrooms and administration office, 1974 saw the total number of portable classrooms reach 22 and in 1976 the gymnasium was completed.

In 1990 the school underwent a name change to Doncaster Secondary College (DSC) following the Change of School Name and Reclassification of Schools Executive Memorandum No 314 from the Ministry of Education (VA 1112).

Following the completion of a new food technology rooms in 2003, the VET (Vocational Education and Training) hospitality program commenced and in 2006, the DSC Sports Field was completed. New offices facing Church Road were added in 2011 and in 2012, the SBAT (School-Based Apprenticeship Traineeship) program was introduced. In 2013, the DSC Sports Stadium was officially opened with seating for 650 people. In 2017, the College self-funded to have rooftop solar installed.
title: Doncaster Secondary College (School No. 7776; previously known as Doncaster High School 1969 - 1990)

description:
Eastville Primary School (VA 5348) was first opened in 1873 as Bradford Creek State School. The school was a co-educational primary school located on Shelbourne Road in the region of Loddon, northern Victoria. In 1880, the school was renamed Eastville State School to avoid confusion with the nearby Bradford State School (No. 2153).   

The original school building was made from slab cut timber (slab hut) with a bark roof. A weatherboard school with teacher’s residence attached was completed in 1874. The shingle roof was replaced with galvanised iron in 1903, and the school building was renovated 1909. During 1924-25, extensive renovations were carried out and the students attended Laanecoorie School (No. 733) while the work was completed.  

Eastville Primary School temporarily closed in April 1894, reopening three months later in July to work part time with Bradford State School (No. 2153). It shared its only teacher with Bradford School and the teacher split their time between both schools. Eastville resumed as a full time school once enrolment reached 36 students in 1898 and the first Committee was elected in 1911. Fluctuating enrolments led to another temporary closure between 1936 and 1940.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term “State school” to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use “primary school” in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Eastville Primary School. 

Eastville Primary School permanently closed in 1996.
title: Eastville Primary School (School No. 1245; previously known as Eastville State School 1880 – 1970; Bradford Creek State School 1873 - 1880)

description:
Fountain Gate Secondary College (School No. 8870) (VA 8870) was established as a Year 7-12 school in 2009. The school is located in Narre Warren within the south-east growth corridor of the City of Casey and has a total enrolment of 1394 students as of 2022.

Fountain Gate Secondary College was established as a stand-alone school with the 2008 disaggregation of Eumemmering Secondary College (School No. 8496) (VA 5321) into four independent schools. The Eumemmering Fountain Gate Campus was changed to Fountain Gate Secondary College and the school was opened for the 2009 school year.

In 2018 the school received State funding for Upgrade and Modernisation and was redeveloped to provide the college with new, purpose-built learning spaces and a refurbished science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) centre.
title: Fountain Gate Secondary College (School No. 8870)

description:
Frankston East Primary School (School No. 4682) (VA 5350) was established in 1952 on Ashleigh Avenue, Frankston in Melbourne’s southern suburbs. The school is located within a cluster of 7 government schools within the Karingal Estate.

In 1952 the school operated from prefabricated classrooms. By 2022, the school has eight buildings consisting of permanent classrooms, teacher resource rooms, a Performing Arts Centre, Science Centre, school hall and a library.

At some stage the name changed from State to Primary. This likely occurred in 1970, as there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term “State School”. "State School" now referred to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools. And all primary schools now included "Primary School" in its name. 

Accordingly, the school name was changed to Frankston East Primary School. While there is no formal announcement regarding the name change, Victorian Gazette notices from around this time reflect the change.
title: Frankston East Primary School (School No. 4682; previously known as Frankston East State School 1952 – c.1970)

description:
Glen Alvie Primary School (School No. 3203) (VA 5351) first opened as the Wonthaggi North State School in 1893. Located in the township Glen Alvie of the west Gippsland area of Victoria, the school originally operated out of the home of the head teacher at the time, Mrs. Varco.

Initially, the school operated full time, but some months later shifted to part time operations with Almurta School (No. 2908). Increased enrolments led to the school’s return to full time operations in 1897 and relocation to a leased Mechanics’ Hall. 

In 1901, the name of the school and the district was changed to Glen Alvie and in 1902, the school moved again to Blackwood Hall. In 1918, land was acquired as a permanent site for the school, and by January the following year, the new school building was completed and opened.  The addition of a shelter shed was completed in August 1922.

In 1932, the Baptist Church purchased some of the adjoining land from the school, and in 1955 the school was wired for electricity. 

At some stage, the name changed from state to primary. This likely occurred in 1970, as there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term 'State school' to refer to all state-run primary, secondary and technical schools and for all primary schools to be referred to as 'Primary Schools'. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Glen Alvie Primary School. Whilst there was no formal announcement regarding the name change, Victorian Gazette notices from around this time reflect the change with both names being used interchangeably for some time.

In 1980, the timber classroom from the former Bass Primary School (No. 847), which closed in 1978, was dismantled and relocated to Glen Alvie Primary School. 

Glen Alvie Primary School seems to have closed permanently in 1983.

Glen Alvie Primary School should not be confused with the former Almurta State School (No. 2908), which was known as Glen Alvie State School from 1894 – 1901 and operated nearby from 1888 - 1954.
title: Glen Alvie Primary School (School No. 3203; previously known as Wonthaggi North State School 1893 - 1901; Glen Alvie State School 1901 - c.1970)

description:
Heyfield Primary School (School No. 1108) (VA 5352) was opened as Heyfield Common School in 1871. The school is located in the township of Heyfield in the eastern Victorian region of Gippsland and services the surrounding rural districts of Glenmaggie, Seaton and Denison. The traditional owners are the Indigenous Australians of the Gunaikurnai nation.

Heyfield Common School changed its name following the introduction of The Education Act of 1872 which established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714). This marked changes to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Heyfield State School at some stage between 1873 and 1878. 

The original school building was destroyed by fire in 1906, and was rebuilt in 1907.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term “State school” to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use “primary school” in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Heyfield Primary School. 

New classrooms were added in 2010 as part of the ‘Education Revolution’ and offer the opportunity to open doors between classrooms and to team-teach in larger spaces.  In 2024, the Heyfield Primary School is still in operation
title: Heyfield Primary School (School No. 1108; previously known as Heyfield State School c.1875 – 1970; Heyfield Common School 1871 – c.1875)

description:
Kangaroo Flat Primary School (School No. 981) (VA 5353) is a co-educational primary school located in the Bendigo suburb of Kangaroo Flat, Victoria. The school was opened as Kangaroo Flat Common School (No. 981) in July 1870, after a request from the Board of Education (VA 713) to merge two nearby denominational schools: the Wesleyan Kangaroo Flat Common School (No. 354) and the Church of England Kangaroo Flat Common School (No. 363).  

In 1873 the school changed its name to Kangaroo Flat State School. This was due to the Education Act 1872, which established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and a subsequent change to school naming conventions.

Since opening, the school has undergone multiple renovations and relocations. It originally operated out of a single brick building on Chapel and View Streets. In 1873, a new weatherboard building was added, followed by an additional brick building in 1883. In 1914 a pavilion classroom was added, followed by extensive remodelling of the older school buildings two years later. During these renovations, children up to grade two were accommodated in the pavilion room, and two Sunday schools were leased for the other pupils.  In 1918, an acre of land opposite the school was donated for a soldiers' memorial and playground. 

In 1953 the school relocated to a new four-acre site on Lockwood Road, with prefabricated Bristol buildings. From 1955 to 1960, several new buildings were added to the site, including another wing along Neil Street, an art room, a multipurpose room and library. 

The school’s former site became Kalianna School (then known as Kangaroo Flat Special School, School No. 4728) (VA 3950) from September 1953. In 1976, Kalianna School (by then known as Bendigo Special School) moved to a new location, leaving the original site on Chapel and View Streets vacant. This site was then reused by Kangaroo Flat State School and became known as the “Annexe”. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Kangaroo Flat Primary School. 

In 2005, the school relocated to its new site on Olympic Parade and into a new building. A gymnasium was added to the site in 2012. The buildings on the former Lockwood Road site were demolished in 2005 to make way for the purpose-built Bendigo Special Developmental School (No. 5298) which opened in 2006.

Kangaroo Flat Primary School should not be confused with the former Kangaroo Flat Common School (No. 354) which was a Wesleyan school that operated from 1854 – 1870. Nor should it be confused with Kangaroo Flat Common School (No. 363), a Church of England school that operated from 1861 – 1870.
title: Kangaroo Flat Primary School (School No. 981; previously known as Kangaroo Flat Common School 1870 – 1873; Kangaroo Flat State School 1873 – 1970)

description:
Kingower Primary School (School No. 351) (VA 5354) was a co-educational primary school located in the Kingower township near Inglewood, in central Victoria.  

Established by the Church of England, under the Denominational School Board (VA 703), the school as opened as Kingower School in March 1858. The school originally operated out of a two room wooden building on a half-acre site. 

In 1863, through the Common Schools Act, the Victorian Parliament abolished the two existing centralised boards and created a single Board of Education (VA 713). With the passing of this act, the school was assigned the number 351 and likely renamed Kingower Common School. 

The Education Act 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and introduced free, compulsory and secular schooling for Victorian children. By 1873, steps were being taken to establish Kingower as a State-vested school and the Head Teacher notified the Department that the trustees were prepared to lease the existing building until a new government building could be erected. It’s likely that around this time the school became known as Kingower State School. It was also referred to as Kingower Primary School, with both names being used interchangeably. 

In September 1873, the District Inspector proposed a 2-acre site near the Dunolly-Newbridge Road, and this site was officially gazetted in September 1874.

In December 1881, the leased school building was destroyed by fire. From January 1882, the school temporarily operated from a leased building known as Mrs. Souter’s Assembly Room. By July 1882, the new State building, a wooden school and teachers' residence, was completed and operational. In 1902, a veranda was added to the front of the residence, and in 1907 two shelter sheds were built, the Department paying half. The gallery in the schoolroom had been removed in 1905.

In 1907, a new detached kitchen was constructed, and a covered walkway connecting it to the main house was added in 1908. By 1912, funds raised from a school concert facilitated removal and re-erection of the old Kingower Mechanics Institute, along with its collection of over 1,100 books, on the school grounds to serve as a library.

The school permanently closed in 1949 due to low attendance and the building was sold in 1964.
title: Kingower Primary School (School No. 351; previously known as Kingower School 1858 – 1863; Kingower Common School? 1863 – c.1875?; also known as Kingower State School? c.1875? – 1949)

description:
Lara Lake Primary School (School No. 769) (VA 5355) was established in 1865 as Lara Lake Common School. The school is a co-educational primary school located in Lara, then also known as Duck Ponds, approximately sixty kilometres southwest of Melbourne and sixteen kilometres north of Geelong.

The original building was constructed in 1864 and designed for a capacity of 40 students. Attendance on opening, however, was 51. Between 1870 and 1873, a teachers’ residence was added, followed by a building capable of accommodating up to 120 students in 1874.  

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Lara Lake State School at some stage between 1873 and 1878.

In 1966, following the Aberfan mining disaster in South Wales, United Kingdom, Lara Lake State School raised funds and sent supportive letters to which the Aberfan community responded with gratitude and pictures of the Welsh dragon. In 1969, Lara Lake State School was completely destroyed in a large grassfire. The Aberfan school in Wales raised money to assist in the Lara Lake State School rebuild. To mark this bond, the school adopted the dragon emblem as its official insignia. Students began the new year with classes in the local hall and in the nearby Methodist Sunday school building.

In June 1970 the rebuild was completed and the school reopened. A new brick building, an administration area and 7 permanent classrooms were added. At the same time, a statewide decision was made to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary, and technical schools instead of just primary schools. Accordingly, the school was renamed Lara Lake Primary School. The opening ceremony featured an exchange of the Victorian State flag with the national flag of Wales.

Lara Lake Primary School saw further building improvements at the turn of the millennium. Main building upgrades occurred in 2004, followed by the addition of a synthetic oval and a gymnasium, featuring a music room and canteen in 2011. Further enhancements included new classrooms, a library, and a staff room in 2017, with additional classrooms added in 2019 to accommodate growing enrolments. By 2024, enrolments had passed more than 800 students.
title: Lara Lake Primary School (School No. 769; previously known as Lara Lake Common School 1865 - c.1875; Lara Lake State School c.1875 - 1970)

description:
Manningham Park Primary School (School No. 4940) (VA 5356) began as Manningham State School in 1966. The school was located on Manningham Road in in Lower Templestowe, a northeastern suburb of Melbourne, adjacent to Templestowe High School (School No. 8823).

Manningham State School was renamed Manningham Primary School, likely around 1970. This chance followed a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name.

By 1971, the school consisted of 22 classrooms and a library which had been opened in 1969.

In April 1997, Manningham Primary School merged with Doncaster Park Primary School (School no 4861) and changed its name to Manningham Park Primary School, retaining the school number 4940.

Manningham Park Primary School permanently closed in January 2010 after merging with Templestowe Heights Primary School (School No. 5004) due to declining enrolments.

In 2011, the site of the former Manningham Park Primary School became the secondary campus of Bulleen Heights School for Autism (School No. 5099).
title: Manningham Park Primary School (School No. 4940; previously known as Manningham Primary School c.1970 – 1997; Manningham State School 1966 – c.1970)

description:
Moonlight Flat State School (School No. 1486, previously No. 442) (VA 5357) was a Victorian government school located in Moonlight Flat, East of Castlemaine.

First opened by Primitive Methodists in 1858 as Moonlight Flat School, it consisted of a single low wooden building measuring 28ft x 12ft x 6ft, situated West of Colles Road on Wesley Hill. It closed soon afterwards and was reopened by Presbyterian authorities on 1st April 1861. In 1863 it became Moonlight Flat Common School, No. 442.

By 1872 the building was far too small and in poor condition. Plans were made for a new school, and a wooden shingle-roof building with living quarters attached was erected across the road in 1874. The following year it opened as Moonlight Flat State School, No. 1486, and the old School No. 442 was closed.

The school operated in this building until it closed on 30th June 1893. It was re-established on 1st April 1912 in the leased Moonlight Flat Church of England building before finally closing on 11th April 1925. In 1931, part of the school building was moved to North Harcourt State School (School No. 4043).
title: Moonlight Flat State School (School No. 1486; previously School No. 442 1858 - 1872; previously known as Moonlight Flat School 1858 – 1863; Moonlight Flat Common School 1863 – 1872; Moonlight Flat State School 1872 - 1925)

description:
Located in the Geelong suburbs of Corio and Norlane, Northern Bay College (School No. 8901) (VA 5358) is a co-educational prep to year 12 college established in 2011 as part of an agreed Regeneration Concept involving nine schools and the government.

In the early 2000s, these schools sought government support to address their aging infrastructure amid Victoria's population growth. Limited funding allocations meant significant regeneration was required, rather than smaller building updates. The Regeneration Concept was developed and led to the merging of the nine schools, forming what is claimed to be Victoria’s largest multi-campus school.

The first schools to merge were Rosewall Primary School (No. 5122) and Corio Primary (No. 124) in 2007 and in January 2011, the Northern Bay P-12 College was formed from the merger of:
  • Corio Bay Senior Secondary College (No. 7105) became the Senior Campus and administration centre
  • Norlane West Primary School (No. 4880) became the West Campus
  • Corio Primary School (No. 124) became the East Campus
  • Corio West Primary School (No. 5031) became the North Campus
  • North Shore Primary School (No. 4301) became the South Campus
  • Flinders Peak Secondary College (No. 7744; VA 5322) site was closed
  • Norlane High School (No. 8175) became Cox Road Campus
  • Corio South Primary School (No. 4927) became Corio South Primary Campus

While construction was taking place, students attended Norlane High School (No. 8175). The Flinders Peak Secondary College site was closed by 2011.

The Cox Road Campus closed in 2012, and the Corio South Primary Campus became the Vermont Campus until the rebuilding at other campuses could accommodate students from the former Corio South Primary School. Later that year, the following campus name changes became effective:
  • Campus 1 - Goldsworthy Road 9-12 Campus (Formerly Goldsworthy Road 10-12 Campus)
  • Campus 2 - Peacock Avenue P-8 Campus (Formerly Peavercock Avenue P-7 Campus)
  • Campus 3 - Hendy Street P-8 Campus (Formerly Hendy Street P-7 Campus)
  • Campus 4 - Wexford Court P-8 Campus (Formerly Wexford Court P-7 Campus)
  • Campus 5 - Tallis Street P-8 Campus (Formerly Tallis Street P-6 Campus)

In November 2014, the Vermont Avenue P-6 Campus closed.

By 2020, 75% of the planned rebuild had taken place and the final Campus rebuild commenced in 2022 at Campus 1, Goldsworthy Road 9-12 Campus.
title: Northern Bay P-12 College (School No. 8901)

description:
Note: These historical records contain words, descriptions and information that may be insensitive or inappropriate and that may be upsetting.

Leonard Street, Parkville (School No. 3522) (VA 5359) State School was established in May 1906 under the direction of the Victorian Neglected Children’s Aid Society, a non-denominational home providing longer-term care for children.

The Society was established in 1893 and by the turn of the century, had opened receiving centres in Latrobe Street, Melbourne and in Brighton. In 1902, the Society bought the property situated in Leonard Street, Parkville. The property was known by several names over time, including Ayr Cottage, Miss Sutherland’s Home, Parkville House, Swinburne House and Swinburne Lodge.

The Education Department (VA 714) undertook teaching at the Home in 1906, and it was gazetted as State School No. 3522.  Students ranged from grades 1 to 6, with a junior and senior room. Construction had begun for a new wing in 1904 and opening in 1907, provided a large school room, kindergarten classroom, dormitories and lavatories. In 1937, a wing was added to the 1907 addition, with a façade presenting to Leonard Street.

In 1920, the word ‘Neglected’ was removed from the name of the Society, changing its name to Victorian Children’s Aid Society. 

Leonard Street, Parkville school closed in 1966, when the Society sold the Parkville property. The children’s home was moved to Black Rock and became known as Swinburne House.  

The Parkville property was conveyed in February 1967 to the University of Melbourne after receiving a Federal and Victorian State Government grant funding.
title: Leonard Street, Parkville (School No. 3522; also known as Victorian Children’s Aid Society 1920 – 1966; Victorian Children’s Aid Society Home 1920 – 1966; previously known as Victorian Neglected Children’s Aid Society 1906 – 1920)

description:
Carlton Gardens Primary School (Rathdowne Street Carlton) (School No. 2605) (VA 5360) is located at 215 Rathdowne Street, Carlton, at the edge of Melbourn’s CBD.

The school’s two-storied brick building was built in Italian Gothic style in 1883 – 1884, to the designs of architect Henry Robert Bastow of the Public Works Department. It was built on land sold to the Education Department (VA 714) by Thomas O’Grady on 4 January 1879 for £2925, with 130 ft frontage to Rathdowne street and 160 ft to a right-of-way leading into Drummond Street, Carlton.

It officially opened as Rathdowne Street State School, or State School No. 2605, on 1 November 1884 with John Sergeant as Head Teacher. Enrolments for 1884 – 1885 was 817, with the average attendance being 491 (247 boys, 244 girls). Although ostensibly built to accommodate 868 pupils, the school struggled with overcrowding in its early years, with classrooms and playground overtaxed. Students were often sent to the gardens to relieve the shortage of space. As of 26 November 1886, the school staff included ten teachers and John Sergeant, Head teacher. A caretaker and his family also lived on-site, in a small two-room brick building.

The school itself was built to relieve pressure of surrounding schools within Melbourne’s densely populated inner suburbs. Most of the original intake had transferred from Carlton State School (Drummond St), No. 177 (VA 4447), which had been housed in Lygon St and two leased buildings, one at the Trade’s Hall and the other in Drummond St, Carlton.

In 1886 a portable building to accommodate 30 children was moved from Cambridge Street, Collingwood and refitted as a small practicing school for School No. 2605. In November 1887, additions were made to the building to accommodate an extra 380 pupils, and in January 1888, John Sergeant requested that a room be “fitted up” as a kindergarten.

School attendance in October 1905 was 831, of whom 150 were infants accommodated in a room 60’ x 25’ with a gallery. On 8 May 1908 the Department bought extra land on Rathdowne Street from John Keleher, and in 1913 the caretaker’s quarters were replaced by a new four-room timber structure.

During the influenza epidemic of 1919 the school building was used as a hostel for nurses working at the Auxiliary hospital housed at the Exhibition Building. During this time the school leased St Andrew’s Church Hall (St Andrew’s Presbyterian Church, Carlton), the Drill Hall on Grattan Street, the Grattan Street Orderly Room, and the Sunday School building of the Central methodist Mission in Queensberry Street to conduct classes.

The 1920s were an eventful decade for the school. From 1920, two classrooms were utilized by Melbourne High School to conduct Sloyd classes, displacing the elementary classes taught there. In 1921, a fire damaged rooms on the ground floor. During 1923-1924, the school was closed for extensive repairs and remodeling, which provided improved lighting and ventilation. During this time the children were taught in the nearby Exhibition Building and St. Andrew’s Church Hall while examinations were being conducted. From 1925 the United Jewish Education Board taught Hebrew to night classes in the school, and in 1926 a needlework centre was established to cater girls from schools in the district. Melbourne High School vacated the two Sloyd rooms in 1927, which were then converted into a kindergarten.

Up until the 1960s, school attendance continued to be over 400. When families began to move out of Carlton to the Easter Suburbs, enrolment fell to a mere 40 pupils. In the 1970s – 1980s, there were approximately 120-130 pupils enrolled.

In 1978, the Victorian Teacher’s Union requested urgent repairs on behalf of staff and students. The buildings were in poor condition, with no water or drainage in the art room, fences falling, rusted spouting on the roof that couldn’t hold water, a broken skylight panel with cracked glass, dilapidated stairs, and non-functional heaters with blown-out pilot lights and leaks. Additionally, at the time there was only one staff toilet to serve 18 adults with no working light; a kerosine lantern was used.

In 1982, the school was listed on the Victorian Heritage Register. In 2020-2023, the school completed an expansion and modernisation project, creating space to accommodate an additional 150 students. Enrolments for 2022 were 422.

During its history the school has been known by several names, sometimes concurrently. From 1884 until around the 1950s, it was called Rathdowne Street State School or Carlton State School (Rathdowne Street). From then until approximately 1980, it was known as Rathdowne Street Primary School or Carlton Primary School (Rathdowne Street). From circa 1980 it was simply Carlton Primary School, until 1999 when the name was officially changed to Carlton Gardens Primary School. Throughout its existence, members of the school community have also referred to the school with the nickname “Rathie”.
title: Carlton Gardens Primary School (Rathdowne Street Carlton) (School No. 2605; previously known as Rathdowne Street State School and Carlton State School (Rathdowne Street) 1884 – c.1950s; Rathdowne Street Primary School and Carlton Primary School (Rathdowne Street) c.1950s – c.1980; Carlton Primary School c.1980 – 1999)

description:
Stevensville Primary School (School No. 5047) (VA 5361) is a co-educational primary school located in St Albans, in the local government area of Brimbank (VA 3675). The school was opened in 1971 in a new, brick veneer building on King’s Road.

By 1995, the school was made up of 2 buildings, with some provision for double classrooms.  

As of 2024 Stevensville Primary School remains in operation.

More information on Stevensville Primary School is subject to further research.
title: Stevensville Primary School (School No. 5047)

description:
Tarrawingee Primary School (School No. 1116) (VA 5362) opened as Tarrawingee Common School in 1872.  The school was a co-educational primary school located the Tarrawingee village which was on route to the Eldorado and Beechworth gold diggings, and approximately 12 km east of Wangaratta. 

The school operated from a brick building at the intersection of the Great Alpine and Beechworth-Wangaratta Roads.  The brick building had replaced an old slab structure which was likely the former site of a Catholic School (No. 635) which operated from 1858 to 1871.

In the early 1880s, a timber teachers’ residence was relocated from Stanley Forest State School (School No. 550) to Tarrawingee. In 1883, the four-room residence with a shingle roof was expanded with a lean-to extension—a basic, shed-like structure—for the post office, which the head teacher’s wife operated.  The residence fell into disrepair by 1889, and by 1905, the Committee deemed it uninhabitable. Despite this, the Head Teacher remained in the building for several months.

Between 1873 and 1878 the school changed its name to Tarrawingee State School. This was due to the Education Act (Vic) 1872, which established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and a subsequent change to school naming conventions.

In 1920 a shelter shed was added to the site.  In 1921, the Committee gave permission to the Machine Gun Trustees to place a German model gun which had been captured in France during the first World War on the school porch.  It remained there until 1939.  By 1922 the original brick building had fallen into disrepair and a new school building was built. 

In 1930, due to low attendance rates, the school began operating part-time with Oxley Flats State School (School No. 2347). It shared its only teacher with Oxley Flats, and the teacher divided their time between both schools.

A new teachers’ residence was built in 1951.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Tarrawingee Primary School. 

The 1990s marked a significant era of transformation in education throughout Victoria, as the Jeff Kennett government initiated numerous school closures and mergers across the state.  In 1993, Tarrawingee Primary School (School No. 1116)  and Eldorado Primary School (School No. 246) merged to form Tarrawingee Area Primary School (School No. 5400) which operated from 1994 - 1998.
title: Tarrawingee Primary School (School No. 1116; previously known as Tarrawingee Common School 1872 - c.1875; Tarrawingee State School c.1875 – 1970)

description:
The School for Student Leadership originally opened as a single campus situated in Dinner Plain, in the Victorian Alps. Established in 1999 as the Alpine School, it was the first school of its kind in Victoria, offering a specialised residential educational program for Year 9 students from regional and metropolitan Victorian government schools. The program runs over one term (7 to 10 weeks) for a group of up to 45 students.

The school building was designed and built by Cas Bak Builders on land donated by BCR Asset Management sometime in late 1998 – 1999, and officially opened in 2000.

The school building consists of a large multipurpose dining room and teaching space, classrooms and communal common areas. There are two separate sleeping and bathroom facilities, with 11 rooms in each of the two accommodation wings. The school has staff supervision accommodation in each wing. The construction is made of stone, timber, and corrugated iron, and includes a fireplace in the dining room and hydronic heating throughout.

Several modifications have occurred to the building since its initial construction. This includes building an IT room with servers; construction of the vehicle sheds; creation of the basketball court; removal of urinals; and de-genderisation of accommodation wings.

Sometime between 2008 - 2010, the school’s official name changed to The School for Student Leadership, however it the original campus continued operating under the name ‘the Alpine School’.

Three further campuses have opened across Victoria over the years; the Snowy River Campus was established at Marlo in 2003, constructed in 2006 and opened in 2007. The Gnurad Gundidj Campus was constructed in Glenormiston, Western Victoria, in 2008 and opened in 2009.  The Don Valley Campus in the Yarra Valley opened in 2021.

These campuses follow a similar operational model to the Alpine School Campus. Each campus is located on extensive grounds and comprises a main building with a central open multi-purpose space with kitchen, used for dining and larger group activities. Each site also comprises a central office/reception area, classrooms, undercover and outdoor recreation areas, a meeting room, student and staff accommodation, bathroom facilities and a central laundry.

Since the opening of the school in 2000, nearly 10,000 students have participated in the program across the four regional campuses, and approximately 100 schools have been represented.

As of 2025, the school is still operational.
title: The School for Student Leadership (Alpine School) (School No. 8837; previously known as The Alpine School 1999 – c.2010)

description:
Tulkara State School (School No. 4519) (VA 5364) was a co-educational primary school established in 1933. The site, located on Greens Creek-Landsborough Road in the parish of Navarre, county of Borung, was purchased by the Education Department (VA 714) from O.W. Bibby. The single room weatherboard building and furniture were relocated from the former Woodlands Estate Lower State School (School No. 4167). The school opened with an enrolment of 10 students.

In 1941, Tulkara State School operated part-time with nearby Wattle Creek State School (School No. 2057). However, Tulkara State School permanently closed in March 1942 due to low attendance rates. In October 1947, the school building was relocated to Stawell Primary School (School No. 502) for use as a classroom, and the site was sold back to O.W. Bibby in 1953.
title: Tulkara State School (School No. 4519)

description:
Western Tyres Primary School (School No. 4603) (VA 5365) was a co-educational primary school established in Tyres Valley, a former timber logging community of the Gippsland region of eastern Victoria. 

Opened in 1942, the school catered to families employed at nearby Morgan’s and Ingram’s mills after the mill owners approached the Education Department (VA 714) to establish a school for their employees’ children. Following the District Inspector’s suggestion, plans were made for a full-time school.

Morgan and Ingram built a suitable room to be leased by the Department as Western Tyres Primary School.  Furniture and equipment were brought from the former Northern Mill School (School No. 4485) after its closure in 1941.

Western Tyres Primary School was closed in March 1968. However, the school may have been unstaffed for one or two years prior to being formally closed.
title: Western Tyres Primary School (School No. 4603)

description:
Wodonga Senior Secondary College (School no. 8480) (VA 5366) is a co-educational secondary college for students in years 10 – 12, located within the Wodonga local government area, approximately three hours northeast of Melbourne.  

The College was originally established in 1954 as Wodonga High School when the secondary classes of Wodonga Higher Elementary School (later known as Wodonga Primary School; School No. 37) separated from the primary classes to form a dedicated secondary school for students in years 7 to 12. The primary school moved out of the High Street site in 1954, allowing the high school to occupy the buildings until 1962. A new site was purchased between Woodland and Brockley Streets, and the first classes moved into the new building in November 1960. Senior forms remained at the High Street site until the end of 1962, when they joined the new school. The new school was officially opened by Hon. JS Bloomfield, Minister for Education, in 1965.

In 1967, additional land between Woodland and Brockley Streets was purchased to square the site and provide a soccer pitch. In 1968, three new classrooms were added to accommodate increasing student numbers. Wodonga High School as it was then known, was one of the foundation members of the Murray Valley Secondary Schools Association, but at the end of 1968 this sports association disbanded.

The 1970s and 1980s were a time of significant development for the school. In 1971, Galvin Hall, named after John Galvin, a teacher for 27 years at the school, was built. New facilities included four matriculation classrooms in 1972, two commercial rooms, and a boys’ sick room in 1973. The science block was completed in 1974, followed by a library and nine portable classrooms in 1975. In 1978, a metal craft room was added, and an observatory was built in 1980 to house a reflective telescope. Further expansion included the establishment of four tennis courts in 1981, followed by the addition of four more portable classrooms in 1982.

In 1987, the Acrobatic Arts Community School (School No. 6256; later known as Flying Fruit Fly Circus School) opened as an ancillary setting of Wodonga High School. Following a fire that destroyed the Flying Fruit Fly Circus School building in early 2003, the school temporarily relocated to Wodonga West Secondary College (School No. 8477; later known as Wodonga Middle Years College) until it became a permanent Campus 2 of the Wodonga West College in 2005.

In 2006, as part of a broader initiative to regenerate government secondary education in Wodonga, Wodonga High School merged with Wodonga West Secondary College (School No. 8477) and Mitchell Secondary College (School No. 7420) to form Wodonga Senior Secondary College, retaining the school number 8480, and catering to students years 10 to 12. Simultaneously, Wodonga Middle Years College (School No. 8851) was established for students in years 7 to 9, with two campuses derived from Wodonga West and Mitchell Secondary Colleges.

Between 2004 and 2015, the Seymour, Shepparton, Benalla and Wodonga Flexible Learning Centres and Choice Wodonga opened as ancillary campuses of Wodonga Senior Secondary College, and make up the North East Flexible Learning Network. These Campuses provide students who generally experience difficulties accessing mainstream school an educational pathway tailored to their needs.

In 2016, the College became part of the Wodonga Federation of Government Schools. The Federation was established in 2016 and is a strategic collaboration between eight government member schools within the local government area of Wodonga. These include:
Wodonga Senior Secondary College (including Wodonga Flexible Learning Centre)
Wodonga Middle Years College (School No. 8851)
Belvoir Wodonga Special Developmental School (School No. 5222)
Melrose Primary School (School No. 5141)
Wodonga South Primary School (School No. 5042)
Wodonga West Primary School (School No. 4814)
Baranduda Primary School (School No. 2222)
Wodonga Primary School (School No. 37)
Between 2017 and 2021, the College engaged in a formal partnership with Wellington Secondary College, New Zealand.  

As of 2022, the College comprised of a main building with teaching and learning spaces, the Trade Training Centre which provides for vocational training, a licenced restaurant and commercial kitchens, hairdressing and beauty training facilities, a sports training facility and performing and visual arts centres. In August 2023, a new dual court stadium and the renovated Galvin Hall, now a Performing Arts Centre, were officially opened.
title: Wodonga Senior Secondary College (School No. 8480; previously known as Wodonga High School 1954 – 2006)

description:
Woolshed Reef State School (School No. 1457) was a co-educational primary school by the Loddon River, near Newbridge in the Parish of Tarnagulla. It was primarily established to serve the children of mining families in the area.

The school was opened by John A. Finch on 16th June 1874, with an initial attendance of 12 boys and 11 girls. In 1876 a portable wooden schoolhouse for 30 children with quarters was authorised. By 1877 there were 43 children recorded on the role.

By 1892, however, enrolments had dropped enough that Woolshed Reef State School was closed on 23rd June 1892. Most students transferred to Laanecoorie State School (School No. 733) (VA 3611).

However, in the following years, families continued to request for there to be a school in the area. In 1907, an application for establishment of a state school was raised, saying 17 area children would attend, though due to doubts as to whether the school would be permanent, nothing occurred at this time. By 1913 however, renewed calls for a school saw School No. 1457 re-open under the new name of Poseidon State School. Despite an optimism that the opening of several new mines in the area warranted a dedicated school in the area, enrolments were low, and the school closed just three years later, at the end of 1916.
title: Woolshed Reef State School (School No. 1457; subsequently known as Poseidon State School 1913 - 1916)

description:
Yarram Primary School (School No. 693) (VA 5368) is a coeducational government school located in the township of Yarram, 220 kilometres southeast of Melbourne in the Wellington Shire.

Established at the end of 1861 as Yarram-Yarram National School, 23 students were enrolled in its first year of operation. Classes were held in a leased building on 2 acres until 1877, when the lease was refused renewal. The school moved to temporary accommodation while a new brick building was built, opening later that same year.

Enrolments steadily increased over time, from 28 in 1871 to 100 in 1900, and 144 in 1901. By 1914 it had reached 182, when only 140 students could be comfortably accommodated. The school was so overcrowded that children were being taught in the outdoor pavilion, necessitating extensions that were carried out over the following few years. The school became a Higher Elementary School in 1918, and in 1924 its name became Yarram State School – the town having also changed its name to drop the second ‘Yarram’ that year.

In addition to its existing Primary and Higher Elementary classes, Yarram became a High School in 1951. The same year a fire broke out in the building, damaging the Infant’s Block; this was replaced by a Bristol unit.

Both primary and secondary classes were held in the one building until the High School moved to its own campus in 1956, becoming Yarram High School (No. 8490). By 1963, net enrolment was 310, and expected to reach 324 the following year. The school building has been condemned by the Public Works Department (VA 669), and in 1964 work was requisitioned to erect a new school building with 10 classrooms and ancillary buildings, staffroom, and offices. This was completed by 1965, however the new building lacked a library or craft room. Instead, a double classroom had to be repurposed to house the library, and children attended art classes in box rooms and storage areas.

The school changed its name to Yarram Primary School in 1970 and continued to face issues with overcrowding into the 1970s, alleviated somewhat by the transfer of a portable classroom from Yarram High School in 1976. In 1994 the school combined with Port Albert Primary School (No. 490).

In 2016, parents of students at Yarram Primary School began a social media campaign for the school to receive much-needed repairs and upgrades. At the time, the toilets were in poor condition, the roof leaked, and children sometimes had to do classwork in the corridors. The school had been identified as in need of modernisation as far back as 1996, but work was put off for over two decades. In the 2016-17 State Budget, $4 million was allocated to the school for a major upgrade and modernization project, which was completed in 2018.

As of 2024, the school remains in operation.
title: Yarram Primary School (School No. 693; previously known as Yarram-Yarram National School 1861 – 1872; Yarram-Yarram State School 1872 – 1924; Yarram State School 1924 - 1970)

description:
Heywood Consolidated School (School No. 6225) (VA 5369) is a co-educational primary school located just outside the town of Heywood, in the Glenelg region of South-Western Victoria. It was first established in 1951 as part the government's consolidation policy for rural schools which saw the closure and consolidation of a number of primary schools in the region. 

Discussions about merging state schools in the area began from 1944, when it was represented by parents to the Minister of Public Instruction that students would benefit from communal facilities such as libraries, art rooms, cafeterias, and sports facilities, that would otherwise not be available at small, often single-teacher, rural schools. This discussion included existing schools at Condah, Heywood, Heathmere, Myamyn, Drumborg and Homerton.

In 1951, the official process of consolidation began, with schools progressively closing and students moving to the Heywood State School (School No. 297) site to join the newly established Heywood Consolidated School. Alongside Heywood State School, the schools that closed included Condah State School (School No. 1019), Drumborg State School (School No. 1240), Hotspur State School (School No. 1260) (VA 5440), Mount Eckersley State School (School No. 1720) (VA 5402) and Myamyn State School (School No. 1692).

In March 1951, approximately 80 students from Hotspur, Drumborg and Mount Eckersley were temporarily accommodated at Buffalo Hall, a building leased for teaching on Owen St, Heywood, until April when the Hotspur and Drumborg school buildings were placed on the Heywood site. They were followed by the buildings from Mount Eckersley, Condah and Myamyn in May.

The Heywood school was officially classified as a consolidated school on 11th May 1951, at which time the school number 297 was retired. Further research is required to determine when Heywood Consolidated School was assigned the school number 6225, but it was in use in Government publications from at least 1980. 

In 1954, six additional classrooms were built on the site.

In 1955 Homerton State School (School No. 1400) (VA 5438) and Heathmere State School (School No. 4526) (VA 5437) were also slated to close and merge with Heywood Consolidate School. Heathmere State School officially closed on 29th April 1955 and Homerton State School on 22nd June 1955. While it was thought to move the Homerton school building to the Heywood site, it was eventually deemed too old and instead became used as a community hall. In 1956 suggestions were made to remove buildings from the closed Heathmere & Homerton schools to Heywood for conversion to a domestic arts wing, but new buildings for this purpose were erected instead.

In 1962, Heywood and District Secondary School (School No. 7910; previously known as Heywood High School) opened using temporary classrooms on the Heywood Consolidated School site, before moving to its present location on Gorrie St, Heywood in 1963.
title: Heywood Consolidated School (School No. 6225)

description:
Clayton West Primary School (VA 5370) was a co-education primary school between Alvina Street and Scotsburn Avenue, in Oakleigh South. 

It first opened in 1962 as Clayton West State School, with approximately 280 students. The students were primarily drawn from the neighbouring Clarinda State School (School No. 3366) and Huntingdale State School (School No. 4716), who were running out of room to accommodate their student bodies.

The school was initially run out of a new eight-classroom building and a further two classrooms were added in 1963.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Clayton West Primary School. 

The school received upgraded facilities over the years, including an Administration upgrade and Hall construction in 1995, major maintenance and Library relocation in 1996, and a new “state of the art” Computer Laboratory which was purchased in 1997.

Due to the proximity of the Clarinda and Huntingdale primary schools, the enrolments at Clayton West Primary School never greatly increased, and by 1997 had reduced to around 140 students. In 2006 plans were made to merge Clayton West Primary School with Clarinda Primary School. The closure of Clayton West Primary School was effective as of 1 January 2007, with all students moving to the Clarinda school site.

The former Clayton West Primary School site was cleared and left for several years, before being rezoned and sold by the Napthine Government in 2014 for a residential development.
title: Clayton West Primary School (School No. 4840; previously known as Clayton West State School 1962 – c.1970)

description:
Eaglehawk North Primary School (School No. 1428) (VA 5371) is a co-educational primary school located in the Greater Bendigo region of North-Western Victoria. The school officially opened in July 1874 as Eaglehawk North State School, with an average attendance of 325 students.

The school was formed after the closure of the Church of England school, Sailor’s Gully (School No. 570), and the Catholic school, Myer’s Flat (School No. 433), which were struck off the State roll by the Education Department (VA 714) in June 1874. The teachers from these schools were transferred to the new nondenominational North Eaglehawk State School (School No. 1428).

A site for the new school was gazetted on July 4, 1873. Initially, the government school leased the brick building of the former Church of England school while the new school was under construction. The new building, accommodating 390 children, was completed by July 1874 and officially opened with an enrolment of 470 students. The school originally consisted of three large classrooms, each measuring 51ft x 21ft.

Over the years, the school has been known as Hodge’s School, named after the first Head Teacher, and later as Sailor’s Gully School. This name was affectionately used well into the 1960s by local residents and was often used interchangeably with Eaglehawk North.

In September 1893, Eaglehawk North State School became an adjunct of Eaglehawk State School (School No. 210). This meant that Eaglehawk North remained open for children in the 1st and 2nd classes only, while children in the 3rd and higher classes were taught at Eaglehawk State School. The schools separated In July 1909 and Eaglehawk North State School regained its separate identity.

In 1914, a shelter shed was erected by the School Committee, with the costs shared by the Education Department. In 1916, the school underwent extensive renovations, including internal alterations that divided some classrooms in half. During this time, the school leased St. Stephens Church hall for classes.

Enrolments started to decline around the time of World War II and the reduction of gold mining, averaging around 100 students.  In December 1950, a teacher's residence was purchased and occupied the following day. The last head teacher to live there left in September 1975. Afterward, teachers from other schools used the residence until it was sold in the 1980s.

In August 1960, additional land was transferred to the Education Department for further extension for playing areas. In 1966, the school was redecorated and its ceiling re-lined with board and by 1974, a central library was established.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Eaglehawk North Primary School.

In 1980, the regional office of the Education Department accepted a proposal to upgrade the school, initiating plans for a redevelopment. The final report and recommendations for this redevelopment were adopted in February 1984. By June 1986, the old shelter shed was sold for removal. The new school was officially opened in March 1990.

In 1994, Sebastian Primary School (School No. 1510) permanently closed, and many of its students transferred to Eaglehawk North Primary School.

In 2023, there was a student population of 317. Planning began for a new Early Learning and Childcare Centre, with the first intake of the four-year-old Kindergarten program scheduled for 2029.
title: Eaglehawk North Primary School (School No. 1428; previously known as Eaglehawk North State School 1874 – 1970; also known as North Eaglehawk School; also known as Hodge's School and Sailor’s Gully School)

description:
Mooroopna Primary School (School No. 1432) (VA 5372), originally known as Mooroopna State School, is located in Mooroopna, approximately 180 km north of Melbourne, on the banks of the Goulburn River, opposite the larger town of Shepparton.

The first school in Mooroopna was a private school established by William Crimp in 1873.  This school operated three days a week in a log hut with a bark roof and had an average attendance of 15 students. As the population grew due to increased settlement, public meetings were held to establish a state school and a site was chosen by the Board of Education (VA 713). 

Mooroopna State School officially opened in July 1874 in a newly constructed wooden building. However, the building was soon deemed inadequate, and within a year of opening, parents began protesting the overcrowded conditions. In response, a new brick building with a lobby and three large classrooms was completed in March 1877, and the original wooden structure was sold for removal in 1876.

Another brick classroom was added in 1929. However, by 1936, with the opening of the nearby Catholic St. Mary’s School, enrolment dropped from a high of 211 students to 175 by 1939.

Following World War II, the town’s population increased rapidly, leading to the addition of several timber classrooms: one in 1948, two classrooms and a staff room in 1954, two classrooms and a storeroom in 1957, and two classrooms and another storeroom in 1964. A canteen was built in 1968, and a library in 1970. Another wing with four classrooms and other facilities was added in 1972.

The school’s name likely changed from "Mooroopna State School" to "Mooroopna Primary School" around 1970.  At this time there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. 

The school faced significant challenges in the late 1970s due to fires. In 1978, three classrooms and other facilities in the southwest wing were destroyed by a deliberately lit fire, and portable classrooms were brought in to replace the lost rooms. A second fire in 1979 destroyed the northwest wing, which housed the library, three classrooms, and a staff room. Again, portable facilities were provided.

At this time, the school had an enrolment of around 600 students. Mooroopna Park Primary School (School No. 5088) opened on the northern side of Mooroopna in 1980. The new school, with its own staff and principal, shared the Mooroopna Primary School site until August 1980, when its own buildings were ready for occupation.

Since 1980, Mooroopna Primary School has undergone numerous changes. A new library was constructed on the site of the destroyed northwest wing and opened in August 1982. Four modular buildings were sited and linked to each other and the remaining existing buildings by covered walkways. Internal renovations of the original brick building also took place. In 1984, the adjoining Anglican Church property was purchased. The church building was dismantled and removed, and the church hall and meeting rooms were converted into a school hall, computer/music room, and canteen.

Additional classrooms were built in 1997 and opened by the Premier, Mr. Kennett, in early 1998. In March 2001, a third fire destroyed seven classrooms. An extensive rebuilding and modernisation program was completed in October 2003, providing nine new classrooms and an art room. The existing students’ toilet block was demolished, and new toilets were built. The new buildings were occupied in the last few weeks of 2003 and officially opened in February 2004.

In 2008, Mooroopna Primary School had an enrolment of around 325 students. As part of the Building the Education Revolution in 2010, the school constructed a large, modern open learning area consisting of six classrooms, a large central open learning space, meeting rooms, toilets, and office facilities. After the construction of this building, the school was able to remove all portable classrooms.

As of 2024, the school is still in operation and had an enrolment of 226 students and a total of 11 classrooms.
title: Mooroopna Primary School (School No. 1432; previously known as Mooroopna State School 1874 – 1970?)

description:
Napoleons Primary School (School No. 1072) (VA 5373) is a co-educational primary school which opened as Napoleon Lead Common School on 1 November 1870. Located in a rural residential village 14 km south of Ballarat on the road to Colac, the original colonial settlement was known as Napoleon Lead. The area was named after a local miner who either resembled Napoleon or wore a hat similar to his. Over time, the name was shortened first to Napoleon and then later to Napoleons.

Napoleon Lead Common School (School No. 1072) replaced Napoleon Lead Common School (School No. 712), a Church of England school that opened in 1864 with the same name. The original school closed on 30 October 1870 when the Bishop of Melbourne consented to vest the school in the Board of Education (VA 713). The new government school (No. 1072) opened on 1 November 1870 in the same building, with an enrolment of 207 students, although average attendance was 94.
                                                                 
Between 1873 and 1878 the school changed its name to Napoleon Lead State School. This was due to the Education Act (Vic) 1872, which established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and a subsequent change to school naming conventions.

A new 40ft x 19ft building was added to the site in the 1870s. The original weatherboard building used by the Church of England school served as an infant room until 1884, when it was replaced by a 20ft x 20ft extension to the front of the new building. The original weatherboard building was then used as a shelter shed until it was sold in 1888.

On April 1, 1915, the school was officially renamed Napoleons State School from Napoleon Lead State School. That year, the Department also acquired the police quarters for use as a teacher's residence and added a new building to the school site. The Minister approved transferring the old building to the Napoleons residents for public use, provided it was maintained, and school property was safeguarded. The old building was sold in 1953 and relocated to Crown land, where it became the foundation for a new public hall.

In 1928, an agreement was established between Elsternwick State School (School No. 2870) and Napoleons on a fifty-fifty basis to share a plantation, with an initial planting of 350. The original plantation was on a 5-acre block off Nine Mile Road, but a new block was acquired in Well’s Lane, Napoleons, in the early 1930s. Both allotments were still producing pines for the school in 1995.

In 1968, the Youth Hostels Association (YHA) of Victoria expressed interest in the site of the former teacher's residence and leased it. By 1974, the YHA considered purchasing the property but ultimately decided to close the hostel. The property was then leased by a group called Talents & Abilities Unlimited before being sold to a private buyer in 1989.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Napoleons Primary School.

In 1989, an administration block and covered walkways linking the buildings were added to the site. In 1995 a building from the Buninyong Primary School (School No. 1270) was moved to Napoleons Primary School for use as the school Library.

In 2002, the school relocated a new 5-acre site adjacent to the recreation reserve on Colac-Ballarat Road and the old site was listed for sale by auction in December 2008.

In 2019, the school had a population of 102 students. By 2023, the school had established a partnership with Qingdao University in China, offering a Chinese Mandarin language program. Additionally, a kitchen garden program, sponsored by the Golden Plains Shire (VA 3688), was introduced.
title: Napoleons Primary School (School No. 1072; previously known as Napoleon Lead Common School 1870 – c.1875; Napoleon Lead State School c.1875 – 1915; Napoleons State School 1915 – 1970)

description:
Wembley Primary School (School No. 4788) is a co-educational primary school in Yarraville in Melbourne’s Western suburbs. It is located on St Leonards Ave, Hawkhurst St and Wembley Ave, taking its name from the latter.

The idea for the future Wembley school was first raised in 1955 due to severe overcrowding at several nearby schools. The site for a new school was identified and bought by the Education Department (VA 714) and in 1957, the building of a six-classroom school block with an office, staffroom, toilets and store commenced. The school officially opened on 5 February 1958 as Wembley State School, with 265 students enrolled.

Two more classrooms were added to the school building in 1959, kicking off a significant period of development in the following decade. Over the 1960s, the main building block was extended to 10 classrooms, the grounds were fenced with boundary trees planted, a basketball court and cricket pitches were added, and the first portable classroom was erected. In 1968, two more permanent classrooms and the G R Evans Memorial Library were established. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Wembley Primary School. Around the same time, the school introduced Migrant English classes to support the growing number of children enrolling from non-English speaking backgrounds, primarily from Greece and the former Yugoslavia. 

The facilities at Wembley Primary continued to evolve over the years. These developments included the building of a new architecturally designed School Hall in 1995, a significant redevelopment of the Library and Resource Centre in 1999, installation of additional portable classrooms in 2002, and implementation of a new Master Plan from 2003 to 2005, which resulted in five new classrooms and a new canteen, as well as renovations to the administration and staff room areas. In 2008, the school celebrated its 50th year of operation by installing new gates at the main entrance on St Leonards Ave and at the school crossing entrance on Wembley Ave. In 2009, the school received $2.5 million as part of ‘Building the Education Revolution’ funding, which was used for additional classroom buildings. In the 2021-22 State Budget, it received $10.219 million for the upgrade and modernisation of the main building, due to be completed in 2024.
title: Wembley Primary School (School No. 4788; previously known as Wembley State School 1958 – c.1970)

description:
Preston West Primary School (School No. 3885) is a co-educational primary school located on Murray Road, Preston, in the City of Darebin. 

The prospect of a new school was first raised in 1910, as a response to rapid building growth in the Preston area, though it was not seen as urgent as there were already several schools in the district. The site for the new school was identified in 1913 and construction of a brick school building to accommodate 200 students commenced in 1914. It opened in January 1915 as Preston West State School. 

During its early years of operation, the school premises also served as a place of worship for West Preston Methodists on weekends and then, in 1919, as an emergency hospital during the post-first World War influenza epidemic. At this time, schooling continued for those students who were well enough in local church, library and public hall buildings. 

Enrolments increased considerably over the years, and additions made to the school buildings accordingly. This included initial expansions in 1925 and further construction in 1927 to accommodate some 900 students, and the erection of several prefabricated classrooms in the 1940s and 1950s to meet enrolments of more than 1000. The space issues were eventually eased with the building of additional schools in the area and by 1970 the enrolments had dropped to around 600. 

In 1958, Preston West State School was declared a training school for Melbourne Teachers' College before being transferred to the growing Coburg Teachers’ College in 1960. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Preston West Primary School. 

Further additions made to the school site include a gymnasium built in 2010, a double-storey building accommodating four classrooms completed in 2013 and five new buildings erected in 2016 for students in Grades 4-6.
title: Preston West Primary School (School No. 3885; previously known as Preston West State School 1915 - c.1970)

description:
Coburg East Primary School (School No. 4260) (VA 5377) was a co-educational primary school established in 1926 on Nicholson Street in Coburg, in Melbourne’s North-West.

The establishment of a new school in the area was recommended by the District Inspector to ease overcrowding at nearby Moreland Primary School (School No. 2837), which was struggling with a net enrolment of 2,400 students. Coburg East Primary School’s building and caretakers’ cottage were completed by June 1926, and classes commenced in September of the same year. By October, the school had elected its first School Committee. 

During its years of operation, Coburg East Primary School supported several different activities. From 1926 to 1932, and again from 1960 to the schools closure in 1997, it functioned as a Rural Training School (also known as Coburg East Rural Practising School B) for trainee teachers. Increased attendance of children at the primary school closed the Rural Training School for a period, as the facilities were required for the children. 

Separate from its function as a Rural Training/Practicing School, Coburg East Primary School was also classed as a Training School in 1926 for both junior teachers and students of the Melbourne Teachers’ College. From 1959, it was run exclusively for students of the newly erected Coburg Teacher’s College (VA 5211) and its subsequent iterations of teacher education until 1997, when this function moved to the Bundoora West Campus of RMIT University (VA 1046). 

Coburg East Experimental School was also established on the site in 1941. This is subject to further research.

In 1948 a converted army hut was added to the primary school site and provided space for additional classrooms. Coburg East Primary School attendance steadily decreased from the 1950s, and by 1997 this decline in enrolments led to Coburg East Primary School and Coburg-Preston Secondary College (School No. 6244; formerly Preston Technical School) merging to become Moreland City P-12 College, retaining the school number 6244. 

The school’s original Mediterranean style red-brick building was sold and reopened as the Antonine Sisters Maronite Primary School in 1998 (as at 2024, the Junior Campus of the Catholic, co-educational Antonine College). The site is protected by a Merri-bek City Council (formerly Moreland City; VA 3709) heritage overlay.
title: Coburg East Primary School (School No. 4260)

description:
School No. 3043 opened on the 16th of September 1890 as Agnes River State School in Agnes, South Gippsland. The Head Teacher was Joseph L. Aminthe from its opening until 15 May the following year. During 1890 the total enrolment was 16 (9 boys and 7 girls), and the average attendance was 9. Classes were run out of a leased building.

The school was closed on 27 July 1893 but reopened on 1 January 1905. In January 1906, the school building burnt down during a bushfire. It was replaced in June the same year by a small two-room weatherboard building constructed by John Summers.

From 18 July – 16 August 1919 the school was closed by the Health Inspector due to an influenza epidemic in the area.

A teacher’s residence was built in Toora in 1935, and in 1958 the school building underwent renovations, including the addition of a classroom. By this time, the school’s name had changed to Agnes State School, and it had an average attendance of 20.

The school was Gazetted as closed in 1976, and the school building was relocated to the Foster Museum at 9 Main Street, Foster. It now forms part of the South Gippsland Historical Society Complex, which includes a collection of historical buildings and objects from Foster and the surrounding districts.

This text is subject to further research.
title: Agnes State School (School No. 3043; previously Agnes River State School 1890 – c. 1950s)

description:
Balook State School (School No. 2719) was a co-educational primary school located in the Balook farming district, northwest of Tarra-Bulga National Park, on the Country of the Brataualung clan of the Gunaikurnai people. Previously known as Bulga, an Aboriginal work meaning mountain, the name Balook was given to the area in 1914.

An application for a new school in the area was first made in June 1885, with 20 potential students able to attend. Accordingly, Bulga State School (School No. 2719) was opened on 29 October 1885, at which point it was worked half-time with Callignee State School (School No. 2649) (VA 3228). It was run out of a leased room in an old house until 1890, when it moved into a leased space at the Mechanics Institute. This building was destroyed by fire on 13th May 1891, causing the school to be run out of a different leased room once more. On 1st July 1893 the school moved into leased premises at the newly built Public Hall. 

Due to low enrolments, Bulga State School briefly closed in 1895 before re-opening in October 1896. 

In 1913, the school community petitioned for a purpose-built school building to be erected. In 1914 a site for a school was purchased and a wooden building completed there on 25th February 1915. At the same time, the school name was changed to Balook State School in line with naming changes in the region.

Once again, by October 1925, there were only 4 students attending Balook State School, causing it to be closed. Again, it re-opened the year later, at which time it was worked half-time with the neighbouring Blackwarry State School (School No. 3427) until enrolments reached 16 and Balook was able to be worked full-time from July 1927. In 1942, bushfires destroyed fencing and outbuildings and in 1951, a teacher’s residence was erected on the site. 

From 1957, the future of Balook State School was in doubt and it was unstaffed when the Head Teacher was transferred to a neighbouring school.
