While a new teacher was appointed in 1958, due to low enrolments no guarantees were made as to the longevity of the school. In 1966, the school again became unstaffed and, as there were only two students enrolled, a successor was not appointed and the school was subsequently closed for the last time. From 1969, the former Balook State School site was granted to Westall Secondary College (School No. 8470) for use as a school camp.
title: Balook State School (School No. 2719; previously known as Bulga State School 1885 - 1914)

description:
Briagolong Primary School (School No. 1117) (VA 5380) opened as a Common School in 1871, replacing Rural School No. 71, Top Plain. The co-educational primary school is located in the rural town of Briagolong in Central Gippsland, Victoria. In the early days, the area was also known as Top Plain. Early colonial pioneers who identified sections of the Bushy Park run used names such as Top Plain and Little Plain, which became part of the language of Gippsland. By 1885, the area was known as Briagolong, from the name of the Aboriginal tribe, the Braiakaulung, who occupied the area. Members of this tribe were removed to Ramahyuck Mission Station in 1864.

In October 1871, the school was vested in the Board of Education (VA 713) and became Common School No. 1117, and tenders for a brick schoolroom were let. The change to a Common School meant more funding was available, and the school applied for the construction of a brick building. The application was approved, and the old timber buildings used by the Rural School were accepted by the Board as a teacher's residence. Upon completion of the brick building in late 1872, the two original wooden buildings were moved and altered to improve the teacher's residence, although it was unlined and of poor standard. A verandah and chimney were also added, and the building was fenced off from the rest of the school.

In 1914, a new teachers’ residence was built. The old residence was given to the School Committee for use as a shelter shed. In 1915, a large weatherboard classroom and a detached sloyd woodworking room were added to the site. By 1921, attendance had risen to 100 pupils, so the sloyd room was again in use as a classroom. The sloyd room served various uses as enrolment fluctuated and local needs changed.

In 1947, a new headmaster, unsatisfied with the standard of achievement, decided to hold the entire school back one year to improve academic outcomes. In 1965, enrolments decreased due to the destruction of a local timber mill in a bushfire.

In 1974, a new brick teacher's residence was built at the corner of Smith and Avon Streets, and later was sold to private interests. The original teachers’ residence with modifications remained on site until 1976 when it was demolished and the timber re-used in the construction of a private residential home.

In 1981, a small wooden portable classroom was brought in. At the time, one teacher was teaching in the red brick building, and two were sharing the large weatherboard room. The portable provided three separate teaching rooms. The small portable was replaced with a five-module relocatable building in 1994, along with the addition of an administration block. In 1996, the school had an enrolment of 132 and a mud brick arts and craft room was constructed.  

Over the years, student attendance at the school fluctuated due to various epidemics, often resulting in temporary closures. In 1875, a measles epidemic closed the school for two months. The same disease struck again in 1914, reducing attendance from 100 to just 10 students. In 1904, a diphtheria outbreak resulted in the death of a student. The school was closed again in 1937 due to polio and in 1965, the school was closed for two months due to scarlet fever. During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, the school was closed for 22 weeks, with remote learning conducted from home.
title: Briagolong Primary School (School No. 1117; previously known as Rural School No. 71, Top Plain 1871 - 1871; Briagolong Common School 1871 – 1873; Briagolong State School 1873 – 1970)

description:
Broadford Primary School (School No. 1125) (VA 5381) began as a non-vested Church of England School No. 48, which opened in 1857. The school operated out of a brick schoolhouse with a capacity for 70 students. It is located in Broadford, a town in central Victoria, eighty-seven kilometres north of Melbourne.

In August 1873, the church school closed and Broadford State School was established on the same site. The head teacher from the church school continued in the same role at the new, vested state school. In 1877, the brick building was extended to accommodate up to 104 students and in 1892, a portable timber classroom from the former Glenaroua School (School No. 1340) was added to the Broadford State School site after Glenaroua School closed.

In 1926, a play shelter was built and a concrete weir was constructed just north of the Sunday Creek bridge to create a children’s swimming pool. The school also established a vegetable garden, which generated profits for school funds. Additionally, an endowment plantation of 6,000 trees was planted as a fundraising scheme, with the intention of selling the mature pines for school profit.

In 1935, extensions were made to the infants' room. Later, in 1953, a building was relocated from the former Kurkurruc Creek State School (School No. 2212; also known as Kur Kurruc Creek State School) to serve as a classroom. In 1963, a new staff room, storeroom, and office were added to the site.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Broadford Primary School.

In 1995, the former Kurkurruc Creek school building was moved to the Broadford Historical Society on High Street. As of 2024, Broadford Primary School is still in operation with approximately 370 students enrolled and the school is planning for upgrade and modernisation works.
title: Broadford Primary School (School No. 1125; previously known as Church of England School No. 48 1857 - 1873; Broadford State School 1873 – 1970)

description:
Corio South Primary School (School No. 4927) (VA 5382) was a co-educational primary school located on Vermont Avenue in the northern suburbs of Geelong. The school opened in February 1965, driven by the rapid expansion of a housing commission project in the area during the early 1960s. Strategically positioned between Norlane Primary School (School No. 4734) and Corio Primary School (School No. 124), it originally operated under the name Norlane North Primary School, but this was changed to Corio South Primary School by the end of November of its opening year.

The school initially functioned out of a twelve-room pebble-tile and timber building with an enrolment of 330 students. In 1968, a six-room infant school was added. By 1970, enrolment had surged to 1,070 students, necessitating the use of thirteen portable classrooms.

Enrolments fluctuated over the years, dropping to 300 students by 1991 but rising again to approximately 680 by 2004 with the addition of an on-site kindergarten accommodating 66 children. Around 2004, Corio South was also selected as a Technology Specialist School, providing every grade 6 student with access to an Apple Computer. The school's computer area was utilized as an after-hours public computer centre, staffed and operated four nights per week.

In 2011, Corio South Primary School merged with several other schools to become the Vermont Avenue campus of Northern Bay P-12 College (School No. 8901) (VA 5358). This restructuring consolidated eight schools into a multi-campus institution, including:
  • Corio Bay Senior College (No. 7105)
  • Norlane West Primary School (No. 4880)
  • Corio Primary School (No. 124)
  • North Shore Primary School (No. 4301)
  • Norlane High School (No. 8175)
  • Corio South Primary School (No. 4927)

The Vermont Avenue Campus of Northern bay P-12 College operated until the end of 2013, when it was closed. Following multiple arson attacks, the buildings were demolished in 2014 and in November 2021, the site was sold to developers.
title: Corio South Primary School (School No. 4927; previously known as Norlane North Primary School 1965 – 1965)

description:
Garlick’s Lead State School (School No. 1287) was a co-educational primary school located at Newbury, about 6 kilometres from Trentham in Central Victoria. 

A committee was first formed in 1870 with the aim to establish a Common School at Garlick’s Lead, the small township that was a part of Newbury. By the time a one-acre site was reserved for a school at Garlick’s Lead in 1873, the Education Act of 1872 had established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and introduced free, compulsory and secular schooling for Victorian children. Accordingly, when the school at Garlick’s Lead eventually opened in a newly-constructed wooden building in February 1874, it opened as Garlick’s Lead State School. A teacher’s residence was added to the site in 1875.

On 25 February 1900, both the school and residence were completely destroyed by fire. Schooling continued in rooms leased from the Garlick’s Lead Wesleyan Church, though it was reported that it was bitterly cold and unsuitable. Eventually, the building from Jackson’s Creek State School (School No. 1633) was moved and re-erected at Garlick’s Lead.

The school burned down for a second time on 16 September 1914, with all buildings once again destroyed. This time the local Methodist Church was leased for classes, until the building from Upper Campaspe State School (School No. 1333) could be moved and re-erected at Garlick’s Lead.

Enrolments declined significantly over the years and in March 1952, the teacher at Garlick’s Lead State School was transferred away to Warragul State School (School No. 2104). As there were only 6 students then enrolled, the decision was made to close the school instead of appointing a new teacher and it officially closed on 2 April 1952. Remaining furniture and supplies were transferred to the neighbouring Trentham State School (School No. 1588) (VA 3936).
title: Garlick's Lead State School (School No. 1287)

description:
Greenvale opened as a Common School in 1868, in a newly built brick building on Somerton Road in Greenvale, an outer suburb north-west of Melbourne. Enrolment upon opening was 60, which increased to 80 by 1874.

In 1869 the school site was expanded by three acres, and in 1870 two classrooms and a wrap-around veranda were added to the building. The school became a State School sometime between 1873 – 1878.

In 1926, the school and teacher’s residence underwent renovation, however in December 1932 a deliberately lit fire destroyed the school, including all furniture and records. Classes were held in the local Methodist church until a building was relocated from Sunshine State School (No. 3113) and a new timber building was built.

The school changed its name to Greenvale Primary School around 1970. With the development of a new housing estate to the east of Mickleham Road in the early 1980s, the Education Department decided to build a modern school on the present Bradford Avenue site. On 10 April 1988 Greenvale Primary School officially relocated to the new site, retaining the original school number of 890. Enrolment at the time was 178.

A substantial building upgrade was completed in 2001, providing five additional classrooms, a vastly expanded library and a suite of administrative and staff facilities. In 2010 six new modern classrooms were built through the “Building the Education Revolution” program.

In 2020, development in the area resulted in enrolment reaching a peak of 823. By 2023, an additional public school opening nearby decreased this number to 652.

As of 2025, this school is still in operation.
title: Greenvale Primary School (School No. 890; previously known as Greenvale Common School 1868 – c.1873; Greenvale State School c.1873 – 1970)

description:
Johnstone’s Hill State School (School No. 5386) (VA 5386) was opened in May 1908 and operated from a leased hall, known as Victoria Hall, located in Boolarra in the Latrobe Valley. The first official Committee was held in 1911.

Johnstone’s Hill State School was subject to periods of temporary closure. The school first closed in September 1915, and re-opened as Victoria Hall State School in November 1921, on a part-time basis with Upper Tarra Valley State School (No. 4053; subsequently named Valley View School) and then opening full-time in October 1922.

The school closed temporarily in July 1923, with students attending Budgeree South East State School (No. 3504) (VA 4438) during the closed period. The school was reopened again as Johnstone’s Hill in June 1933.

In June 1938, the school building was destroyed by fire and classes were held in a leased room until the hall was rebuilt. In 1941, the Education Department (VA 714) erected a building on a donated site, however bushfires destroyed the building in March 1942. The school operated out of a house until the removal and re-erection of the school building from the former Gunyah Central State School (No. 3553) was completed in September 1942.

In 1951, student attendance dropped to 4 students and the school was left unstaffed, later closing temporarily between 1955 and February 1958, only to be left unstaffed again in June 1959. Johnstone’s Hill State School was permanently closed in November 1969.
title: Johnstone’s Hill State School (School No. 3580; also known as Johnson’s Hill State School; Johnston’s Hill State School; previously known as Victoria Hall State School 1921 – 1933)

description:
Macarthur Street Primary School (School No. 2022) (VA 5387) is a co-educational primary school in the Soldier’s Hill suburb of Ballarat, located on Macarthur Street between Armstrong and Doveton Streets. The school has operated in its original building since opening in 1878 as Ballarat (Macarthur Street) State School. It replaced the former Soldiers Hill School (School No. 587), a Presbyterian denominational school established in October 1857, which seems to have operated out of three leased buildings. Soldiers Hill School was struck off the roll in May 1878, shortly before Macarthur Street State School opened in June with an enrolment of around 650 students.

Construction of the Macarthur Street school building was tendered in October 1877, with furniture installed in 1878 once the building was complete. Around 1892, Macarthur Street State School absorbed Black Hill State School (School No. 2043; subsequently known as Black Hill Primary School) as a junior annex for grades one and two, while all higher grades from both schools were relocated to the Macarthur Street site. Despite this change, overcrowding continued, with enrolment across the amalgamated schools rising to approximately 1,159 students by May 1893. It is unclear how long Black Hill functioned as an annex, as Black Hill Primary School continues to operate independently as of 2024.

In early 1915, three additional buildings were leased to accommodate the growing enrolment: St. John’s Church of England School hall, Scots Hall, and Mingst’s Hall on Macarthur Street. A new wing with five classrooms was officially opened in February 1916, followed by a shelter pavilion for infant classes in February 1927. At this time, net enrolment was 687, with facilities to accommodate up to 780 students.

A pine plantation was established on the northwest corner of the junction of Havelock and Norman Streets in 1924. Proceeds from sales of trees to 1944 amounted to £485 for school profit as part of the School Endowment Pine Plantation. In 1948, approximately 8.5 acres of the plantation land was transferred to Urquhart Street (School No. 2103) for use as a plantation. 

By 1940, net enrolment at Macarthur Street Primary School had dropped to 518, with an average attendance of 469. In 1946, an opportunity grade was established to support students needing special instruction, a specialised provision in state schools from the late 1920s to early 1960s. That year, the school also became a Rural Training School, giving trainee teachers experience in a small rural school environment.

In 1950, a garage and residence were built at 13 Lilley Street. Throughout the 1950s to the 1970s, several small adjoining properties were purchased, expanding the school’s playing area. By 1963, enrolment had decreased to 214 students.

The name changed from state to primary likely around 1970, as there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the ‘Macarthur Street State School’ name was changed to ‘Macarthur Street Primary School’. 

In 1976 the library was built. By 2015, enrolment had dropped to 95 students. As of 2024, the school is still in operation and the facilities include four classrooms, a library, kitchen spaces, and two large playgrounds featuring a synthetic basketball court.

Note: Several schools in the region share similar names, though not all of the schools operated simultaneously. A non-exhaustive list includes:
  • Ballarat (Dana Street) (School No. 33) (VA 3548)
  • Ballarat (Erard Street) (School No. 227)
  • Ballarat (Eureka Street) (School No. 1071) (VA 3834)
  • Ballarat (Forest Street) (School No. 4936)
  • Ballarat (Humffray Street) (School No. 34) (VA 3549)
  • Ballarat (Lydiard Street) (School No. 82) (VA 5420)
  • Ballarat (Macarthur Street) (School No. 2022) (VA 5387)
  • Ballarat (Pleasant Street; also known as St Peter’s) (School No. 695)
  • Ballarat (Richards Street) (School No. 4981) (VA 3811)
  • Ballarat (Sturt Street) (School No. 603)
  • Ballarat (Urquhart Street) (School No. 2103)
  • Ballarat and Smythesdale Road (School No. 1306)
title: Macarthur Street Primary School (School No. 2022; previously known as Ballarat (Macarthur Street) State School 1878 – c.1970; also known as Macarthur Street, Ballarat 1878 – c.1970)

description:
Mallacoota P-12 College (School No. 3515) (VA 5388) is a co-educational combined school serving students years prep through to year 12. Located in the small town of Mallacoota in East Gippsland, Mallacoota P-12 College originally served a remote far-east community when it opened in April 1906. At that time, the closest neighbouring school was 24km up-river at Genoa River State School (School No. 3112). The area was isolated, largely functioning as a remote farming outpost. However, the opening of the Princess Highway in 1921 transformed Mallacoota into a more accessible and viable rural community, marking the beginning of its development into a township.

The names Mallacoota School and Mallacoota Inlet School were used interchangeably. The school first operated from a slab-bark building on the western side of Bottom Lake. After the first head teacher left within a year, Clement Baker took over around 1907, managing Mallacoota along with Wangrabelle (No. 3490) and Genoa State School part-time. Part-time schools were common in isolated areas but were costly for the Education Department (VA 714) and challenging to staff. Baker spent two and a half days at each school every fortnight, leaving lessons for the children to complete under parental supervision.

In 1917, the Department approved a new school building which was then transported by barge from Paynesville State School (No. 2343) to a site on land loaned by Karl Rasmus. This building became the new site for the school around 1919, with Baker appointed as the full-time teacher.

In 1936, after campaigning from parents, the school was relocated into the township, aligning with Mallacoota’s development into a viable rural community after the Princess Highway opened in 1921.

The 1950s and 1960s saw significant growth. In 1954, a timber residence and out-buildings were erected, followed by the addition of a primary classroom in 1957 and another in 1961. In 1964, the school expanded with the construction of a secondary classroom equipped with science facilities, along with a staffroom and office. 

By 1965, Mallacoota State School had expanded to offer post-primary education and was renamed Mallacoota Central School (or sometimes referred to as Mallacoota Central Classes), officially catering to students in Years 7 and 8 (formerly known as Forms I and II).  

By 1968, another room and storeroom were built for secondary use, but by 1975, these spaces were repurposed for primary education.  In 1970, enrolment stood at 54 primary and 18 secondary students.  

In 1978, the school expanded again to offer post-primary classes up to Year 10 (formerly known as From IV) and became Mallacoota Higher Elementary School.  At this point, the school had four permanent rooms, four portables, and a shed, with likely two additional portables arriving later that year. In 1979, the school relocated into 11 portables and a shed while a new building was constructed.  The new school building was officially opened in November 1980 by Hon. Norman Lacy M.P. Minister for the Arts and Assistant Minister of Education.  In 1981, enrolment had risen to 80 primary and 60 secondary students.  An adjoining block formerly owned by Mr. Hunter was purchased for the school, and additional Crown land and part of Hunter Street was added to increase the site by about 1 hectare. The new facilities included an open-plan complex with four primary classrooms, a library, a portable, and two sheds for pottery and metalwork.

As of 2024, Mallacoota P-12 College remains open and operational.
title: Mallacoota P-12 College (School No. 3515; previously known as Mallacoota State School 1906 – 1965; Mallacoota Central School 1965 - 1978; Mallacoota Higher Elementary School 1978 – 1989; also known as Mallacoota Inlet State School 1906 – 1965?)

description:
Norris Bank Primary School (School No. 3618) is a Prep to Year 6 co-educational public school situated in Bundoora, in Melbourne’s Northern Suburbs.

The school’s origins date back to 1839, when Horatio Cooper built a homestead named ‘Norris Bank’ on land purchased west of Plenty Road, in what was at the time a farming community. By the turn of the century, large properties in the region were being subdivided into smaller farms to encourage further settlement in the area then known as Thomastown Small Holdings, and Norris Bank was purchased by the Closer Settlement Board (VA 2266).

School No. 3618 (initially named ‘Thomastown Small Holdings’) was established on 25 May 1909 with Wilhelmina P. Sleeman as Head Teacher. It first operated in the old Norris Bank homestead, which had been ‘tidied up’ by the local settlers. Approximately three months later, the name of the school was changed to ‘Darebin’ at the suggestion of District Inspector Jackson, as the school building stood on a bank overlooking the Darebin Creek.

A site adjoining the old homestead near the junction of Darebin Creek and Settlement Road was bought in 1909-10 and a four room 24ft x 24 ft. house purchased for £80 was relocated there to serve as a schoolhouse. School began at the new site on the 24th of October 1910.

In May 1913 only 13 pupils attended the school, as many settlers were leaving the area. By April 1924, attendance had shrunk to 5. Despite this, the school remained open. This may be due in part to the voluntary maintenance work carried out by locals, which eased the running costs.
On 23 September 1925 the name of the school changed to Norris Bank. The name change was prompted by some confusion caused by the opening of Darebin Railway Station between Ivanhoe and Alphington in around 1923; mail for Darebin State School (No. 3618) was mistakenly delivered to Ivanhoe State School (No. 2436), and the Head Teacher of the latter had sent a complaint to the Department.

In connection with the deviation of Settlement Road in 1951, the Shire of Whittlesea approached the Public Works Department to acquire a portion of school grounds, upon which was the school building. A new school site of just under 5 acres in Bundoora was purchased from Mr. James Eldrige Rowe for approximately £695, and there was some consideration made to relocating the schoolhouse to this site. Ultimately this plan did not go ahead, as the poor condition of the building meant that it would soon need to be replaced. In June 1953 A.V. Jenkings began work on a new school building, a light prefabricated timber 24 ft x 24 ft classroom.

The old schoolhouse was demolished in 1953, with the best of the materials reused to build the shelter pavilion and a store shed at the new site. The shed was converted into a school canteen in 1971. The old school site became a pine plantation after the Settlement Road works were completed in 1954.

In 1958 an increase in enrolments lead to the addition of a further classroom and store. A dramatic increase in population over the following 10-15 years led in turn to increased enrolments; from 36 in 1960 to 292 in 1975.

In 1973 the Education Department purchased lots 82-90 in Greenhills Road for the school, and by 1975 six additional classrooms were promised. Buildings were removed from Brunswick North (School No. 3585) and re-erected at Norris Bank, becoming permanent after brick veneering. In 1976 a new library was erected. By 1977 the school had 389 students enrolled, which increased to 441 in 1978, and 483 in 1979. During this time extensive excavation works were carried out on the eastern side of the school, levelling the play area and adding football and cricket grounds. In 1984 a hall was opened by premier John Cain, the funds for it provided by the Mothers’ Club.

At some stage, the school’s name changed from ‘state’ to ‘primary’. This likely occurred in 1970, when there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools.

In the early 1990s enrolments began to decline, with 308 in 1992 and 287 in 1994, however they remained reasonably steady afterwards. In 1995 a Reading Recovery Centre and amphitheatre were established, followed by a computer room in 1997.

The library underwent renovations and reopened in 2008. In 2009-2010 building works commenced that demolished most of the oldest part of the school; 5 classrooms and adjacent office spaces were replaced with a new purpose-built facility.

As of 2024 the school is still in operation.
title: Norris Bank Primary School (School No. 3618; previously known as Thomastown Small Holdings 1909 - 1909; Darebin State School 1909 - 1925)

description:
Arthurs Creek Primary School (School No. 1666) (VA 5390) opened in January 1876 as Arthurs Creek State School. The government coeducational school is located in the small township of Arthurs Creek, approximately 33 kilometres north east of Melbourne, within the Shire of Nillumbik.

The Education Department (VA 714) purchased a two acre site for the school in 1875, and the school opened the following year.

By 1888, student attendance ranged between 30 and 50 students.

Additional classrooms were added in 1908, followed by a shelter shed in 1910 and a washhouse and bathroom in 1921.

In 1939, the school had an enrolment of 34 students.

A school plantation was established in 1952 on the site of the former Streamville School (School No. 3690). While the plantation's later history is unclear, it may have been incorporated into the School Endowment Pine Plantation scheme, under which timber was harvested and sold to generate funds for participating schools.

In 1959, the school's shed and fence were damaged by a tornado, and in 1962 the original school building was destroyed by fire. A replacement building was completed and occupied in February 1963.

In 1970, a statewide decision broadened the use of the term "State School" to include all government schools rather than referring exclusively to primary level schools. As a result, primary schools across Victoria adopted the term "Primary School" in their names, and Arthurs Creek State School became Arthurs Creek Primary School around this time.

As of 2024, the school had an enrolment of 32 students. As of 2026, Arthurs Creek Primary School remains in operation, with five major classroom learning spaces and a studio multipurpose room.
title: Arthurs Creek Primary School (School No. 1666; previously known as Arthurs Creek State School 1876 – circa 1970; also known as Arthur’s Creek State School)

description:
Rowville Primary School (School No. 5000) (VA 5392) opened in 1973, becoming the first primary school in Melbourne’s southeastern suburb of Rowville. Set on 23 acres, the school opened with 8 new classrooms and had an initial enrolment of approximately 250 students.

In March 1974, two additional classrooms, along with an office, library, and canteen, were added to the site. By 1976, a portable classroom was added, bringing the total number of classrooms to 11.

By the late 1980s, Rowville Primary School had grown to be one of the largest in the state. Pressure on the school's enrolment was eased by the opening of nearby schools, including Park Ridge Primary School (School No. 5281), Karoo Primary School (School No. 5295) and Heany Park Primary School (School No. 5345).

In 1990, the Western Campus of Rowville Secondary College (School No. 8734) opened on the shared site with Rowville Primary School. A small drop in enrolments occurred in 1995 due to new housing developments in the Dandelion Drive area and the relocation of Lysterfield Primary School (School No. 1866). Despite this, the predicted enrolment for 1996 was around 770 students.

In 2006, two new blocks of permanent buildings were added to the school. By 2012, an outdoor synthetic sporting facility, including a running track, long jump pit, and soccer and hockey fields, was also completed. In 2018, a Landcare Biodiversity Grant enabled the creation of a "frog bog" to enhance the biodiversity of the school’s gardens, which include a variety of natural play and learning spaces.

Rowville Primary School was still in operation as at 2024.
title: Rowville Primary School (School No. 5000)

description:
Toora North State School (School No. 3547) was a co-educational State school located 187 kilometres south-east of Melbourne, in the South Gippsland farming town of Toora. The area has been described as nestled between the hills of the Strzelecki Ranges and the waters of Corner Inlet. 

The school opened in October 1907 as Toora Tin Mines State School, also known as Tin Mine School, operating out of a newly built but leased wooden hall. In 1927, despite a petition from parents for a permanent building, the Education Department (VA 714) provided funds in lieu of three years' rent for renovations of the leased hall.

The school temporarily closed in 1937 due to low attendance but reopened in 1941 in the same leased hall.

In January 1951, the school’s name was changed to Toora North State School to reflect the name recognized by the local community and postal authorities. This change followed the closure of the area's tin mines around 1942 and the region's transition to dairy farming.

The school was unstaffed between 1953 and May 1955 when net enrolments reached 17. Toora North State School was permanently closed in November 1967.
title: Toora North State School (School No. 3547; previously known as Toora Tin Mines State School 1907 – 1950; also known as Tin Mine State School 1907 - 1950)

description:
Dinjerra Primary School (School No. 5450) (VA 5394) was established at the end of the 1996 school year as the result of a merger between Maidstone Primary School (School No. 4658) (VA 4650) and Tottenham Crossing Primary School (School No. 5415) (VA 5594).  The name Dinjerra is an Aboriginal word meaning “west” and also refers to the fish species, Pseudocaranx Dinjerra, found in northern Western Australia. 

The co-educational primary school is situated on the former Tottenham Crossing site on South Road, Braybrook and operates as single campus school.  The former Maidstone site was closed and later sold for development of the Wirilda Way housing estate.  Initially operating out of two light timber construction (LTC) buildings, Dinjerra Primary School had an enrolment of 160 students in 1998. 

In 2019, Dinjerra Primary School underwent a $7.4 million upgrade funded by the Victorian School Building Authority. The project included the demolition of the original LTC buildings and sheds, refurbishment of the library, and the construction of new administration, junior, middle, and specialist buildings. As of 2024, the school comprises four main buildings and has a total enrolment of 212 students. Dinjerra Primary School remains in operation as of 2025.
title: Dinjerra Primary School (School No. 5450)

description:
Woorarra Primary School (School No. 3410) opened as Wonyip State School in January 1902.  Located in Gippsland, the area was known for dairying and tin mining at the time. When the school first opened, it operated out of a 30ft x 16ft wooden building which was erected by local residents.

In 1924, a permanent school building was built, measuring 154 square meters built with weatherboard walls, corrugated iron roof and timber flooring. This building included a main hall and a kitchen area.

In June 1935, with student attendance dropping to nine, Woorarra State School began operating part-time, sharing its only teacher with Woorarra West (School No. 3434), who split their time between both schools. This arrangement lasted one month before Woorarra returned to full-time operation. By 1944, attendance was 12, rising to 21 in 1956 and 32 in 1960.

In 1967, a small portion of school land was transferred to the Country Roads Board (VA 722) for road purposes.
 
At some stage, the name changed from 'State School' to 'Primary School'. This likely occurred in 1970, as there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Woorarra Primary School. Whilst there was no formal announcement regarding the name change, VPRS 11392 School Council Files from around this time reflect the change. 

The school was unstaffed from December 1977 as school councils may vote to close or destaff schools with low or no enrolments for the coming year. Destaffing allows for reopening if enrolments rise. Woorarra Primary School permanently closed in June 1980, and the land was sold to private interests in 1986.
title: Woorarra Primary School (School No. 3410; previously known as Wonyip State School 1902 – 1908; Woorarra State School 1908 – c.1970)

description:
A Court of Petty Sessions was first appointed in Mildura in October 1855. In 1889 the court of the nearby town Yelta was revoked, and Mildura was appointed in its stead. A County Court and Court of General Sessions were both appointed in August 1891, followed by a Court of Insolvency for the Midland Insolvency District in January 1892. A courthouse was constructed for the town around 1892 to accommodate the increase in court activities. Mildra Licensing Court assumed responsibility for the Swan Hill Licensing District from the Swan Hill Licensing Court (VA 562) in 1923 and continued to hear liquor licensing proceedings until the Victorian Licensing Court (VA 2905) was abolished in 1968. The Court of Insolvency and Court of General Sessions also continued to sit in Mildura until those courts were abolished in 1928 and 1968 respectively. In 1950 Mildura was added to the Supreme Court circuit and the courthouse was extensively renovated and extended to accommodate Supreme Court hearings. 

In November 2004 a new legal complex, including new Courthouse and Police Station, was officially opened. The former courthouse was demolished as part of this redevelopment. A Koori Court was appointed in June 2005 followed by a Children’s Koori Court in August 2007. Although Mildura was appointed to hold County Koori Court proceedings in 2012, the County Koori Court program wasn’t implemented there until August 2016. Mildura remains on the County Court and Supreme Court Circuit as well as the Federal Court Circuit. Mildura sits within the Magistrates’ and Children’s Court Loddon-Mallee Court Regions. 

Mildura Courts includes:
  • Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1855 – Present)
  • Koori Court (2005 – Present)
  • Children’s Court (1907 – Present)
  • Children’s Koori Court (2007 – Present)
  • Licensing Court (1923 – 1968)
  • County Court (1891 – Present)
  • County Koori Court (2016 – Present)
  • Court of Insolvency (1892 – 1928)
  • Court of General Sessions (1891 – 1968)
  • Supreme Court (1950 – Present)

District and Circuit Court Systems

In the mid-19th to early 20th century, courts and court districts were established across Victoria of various levels. This practice remained until either the court was abolished, or a state-wide court entity was established. Once a statewide court was established, hearings continued in regional centres using a circuit court system.

Under the district system, courts largely administered themselves, with major decisions such as the appointment of judicial officers and court locations, as well the development of court rules, procedures and jury lists passed down by Governor in Council. Additionally, judicial officers, registrars and clerks were appointed to specific court locations. These functions were largely taken over by the primary court and their respective chief judicial officer once the primary court was established. Likewise, judicial officers were no longer appointed to specific court locations, but rather to the primary court then assigned to hearings according to the scheduled circuit.

Both district courts and circuit courts commonly used their own recordkeeping systems to manage cases until centralised recordkeeping systems were gradually introduced from the late 20th century. Administrative resources were often shared between the different levels of court when operating from the same location.

Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1838 – Present)

Courts of Petty Sessions were established to hear criminal and civil cases of minor offences and disputes. Courts of Petty Sessions were appointed to be held in population centres. These courts were renamed Magistrates’ Courts in 1971. Under the Magistrates’ Court Act 1989 (Vic), the Magistrates’ Court of Victoria (VA 5113) was constituted as the primary body, while the various courts were grouped into regions with the largest in each appointed as a headquarter venue. Magistrates and other Judicial Officers were assigned to regions to hear cases in each location according to the scheduled circuit. Individual Magistrates’ Courts continue to maintain their own case registries. As of 2023, there are 51 courts in 13 regions. The Court has several divisions including Koori Court, Drug Court, Assessment and Referral Court as well as several specialist family courts. These divisions are appointed to specific locations within regions, usually the headquarters court.

Children’s Court (1907 – Present)

Children’s Courts were established to hear and to inquire into charges against children. During the 1930s, these courts also began hearing other cases involving children such as child neglect. Children’s Courts were appointed to be held at locations that already held Courts of Petty Sessions or Magistrates’ Courts and operated as a division of the Magistrates’ Court until 2000. As such, Children’s Courts operated under the Magistrates’ Court district system until 1989 and continue to mirror the Magistrates’ Court’s regional system. Like the Magistrates’ Court, when the Children’s Court of Victoria (VA 4190) was constituted as the primary and independent body, courts were grouped into regions, and Judicial Officers and Support Services staff were assigned to these regions. Judicial officers were assigned to hearings according to each region’s circuit schedule. Individual courts continue to maintain their own case registries and often share administrative resources with the Magistrates’ Court registries. As of 2025, there are 33 courts in 6 regions. The Court has a Family division, and Criminal division, as well as a Children’s Koori Court for criminal matters. Like Magistrates' Koori Courts, Children's Koori Courts are appointed to specific locations.

Licensing Court (1885 – 1968)

Licensing Courts were first established to grant and transfer liquor licences. From 1865 to 1885, this function was administered by Licensing Benches of the Court of Petty Sessions. Licensing Courts were established in licensing districts under The Licensing Act 1885 at courts appointed to hold Court of Petty Sessions hearings. Other kinds of licences, such as Auctioneer and Hawkers licences, were granted at annual Licence meetings at Courts of Petty Sessions. This practice continued until 1916 when the Licensing Court of Victoria (VA 2955) was constituted, and a circuit system was introduced. Under the circuit system, 3 magistrates were appointed to the primary court who then held annual hearings at each appointed Licensing Court location according to the circuit schedule. When the court was replaced with the Victorian Licensing Court (VA 2905) in 1954, this was changed to one Judge of the County Court as Chair, and 2 magistrates. The court was abolished in 1968 and liquor licensing functions were transferred to the Liquor Control Commission (VA 1110). See also Licensing Courts (VA 2870).

County Court (1852 – Present)

County Courts were established to hear civil matters and assumed the functions of the Courts of Request, which had operated prior to Victoria’s separation from New South Wales. Regional County Courts operated under the district court system until 1957, when the County Court of Victoria (VA 686) was constituted under the County Court Act 1958 (Vic). Under the circuit court system, County Courts continued to maintain their own case registries until centralised recordkeeping systems were gradually introduced from the late 20th Century. As of 2023, the court is made up of a criminal division, criminal appeals division, commercial division, common law division, adoption division and a County Koori Court. There are 11 circuit locations outside of Melbourne, 6 of which also hold County Koori Court hearings. 

Court of Insolvency (1871 – 1928)

Courts of Insolvency were established in each proclaimed Insolvency District across Victoria according to the Insolvency Statute 1871. Courts of Insolvency were appointed at places that held County Courts hearings, and Insolvency Districts generally mirrored County Court Districts. All County Court judges outside of Melbourne were also appointed judges of the Court of Insolvency. Although the clerks of the District Courts of Insolvency were required to send a copy of the Order of Sequestration (Bankruptcy/Insolvency Order) to the Chief Clerk at Melbourne, these orders were not incorporated into the Register of Insolvencies (VPRS 757) created by the Court of Insolvency at Melbourne (VA 2304). Courts of Insolvency continued to operate under the County Court District system until the function of Bankruptcy and Insolvency hearings was transferred to the Commonwealth in 1928.

Court of General Sessions (1853 – 1968)

Courts of General Sessions were established to hear criminal cases of a more serious nature than the Court of Petty Sessions, excluding the most serious crimes such as murder and treason. The Court of General Sessions continued to operate under the district court system until 1968, when the County Court of Victoria (VA 686) assumed responsibility for Criminal Cases and the Court of General Sessions was abolished under the County Court (Jurisdiction) Act 1968 (Vic).

Supreme Court Circuit (1852 – Present)

Supreme Courts were first appointed in high-population centres under a circuit court system when the Supreme Court of N.S.W (VA 914) was established for the Port Phillip District in 1841. This system continued when the Supreme Court of Victoria (VA 2549) was established in 1852. These courts were first known as Circuit Courts, while Criminal Sessions were often referred to as Courts of Assizes until the turn of the century. From the 1890s, these courts were officially known as the Supreme Court of the designated location. As the need for criminal sessions decreased, many locations were revoked in the early 20th century, and some courts were only appointed to hear civil cases. Courts typically maintained their own case registries and shared resources with County Courts until centralised recordkeeping systems were gradually introduced from the late 20th Century. As of 2023, the Supreme Court Trial Division is made up of Criminal Division, Common Law Division and Commercial Court and sits at 12 circuit locations outside of Melbourne.

description:
Lower Murray Urban and Rural Water Corporation, trading as Lower Murray Water (LMW) is a Regional Water Authority and a Rural Water Authority as defined by the Water Industry Act 1994. It was constituted as the Lower Murray Urban and Rural Water Authority by an Order-in-Council in accordance with the provisions of the Water Act 1989 to take effect from the 1 of July 2004. The Lower Murray Region Water Authority (VA 4246) and Sunraysia Rural Water Authority (VA 3577) were abolished and their geographical areas, functions, land, liabilities, obligations, powers, property, rights and employees became the responsibility of LMW. LMW took responsibility of the following districts:
  • Carwarp/Yelta Waterworks District
  • Kerang Urban and Sewerage Districts
  • Koondrook Urban and Sewerage Districts
  • Lake Boga Urban and Sewerage Districts
  • Merbein Irrigation District
  • Millewa Rural District
  • Murrabit Urban District
  • Nangiloc-Colignan Water Management District
  • Nyah Urban District
  • Nyah West Urban and Sewerage Districts
  • Piangil Urban District
  • Red Cliffs Urban and Irrigation Districts
  • Robinvale Urban, Sewerage and Irrigation Districts
  • Swan Hill Urban and Sewerage Districts
  • Sunraysia Urban and Sewerage Districts
  • Woorinen Urban District

In 2008 the First Mildura Irrigation Trust (VA 1429) was abolished and LMW was appointed to take over the whole of the functions, powers and duties of the trust as specified under the Water Act as well as all its rights, property and assets.

Water Corporations

There was further water industry reform in 2006. According to amendments to the Water Act by the Water (Governance) Act 2006, all regional urban water authorities and rural water authorities became corporations to be in line with changes to governance already made to the Melbourne Water Corporation (VA 1007). Authority Members were replaced with Boards of Management and the governing functions, powers, duties, and objectives of water corporations were redefined. In 2012, former licensees of metropolitan water services also became corporations, allowing for uniform governance of water services across the state.

All water corporations are required to follow the Statement of Obligations, as issued by the responsible minister under the Water Industry Act. Statements of Obligations inform strategic goals and policy development, outline pricing submissions and procedures, responsibilities of the Board, customer communications and access to information, community engagement and education, risk management, dam safety, Blue Green Algae management and responses, water services standards and operations, and compliance management. As of 2024, the most recent statement was issued 20 December 2015. An additional Statement of Obligations for Emissions Reduction was issued 23 May 2022 giving corporations a target of net-zero reportable emissions by 2035.

In addition to the functions and activities outlined in a Statement of Obligations, responsibilities of water corporations are outlined in Part 6, Division 2 of the Water Act. All corporations are responsible for:
  • investigating, promoting and conduction research into any matter relating to their functions, powers and duties as well as educating the community about those functions
  • considering Aboriginal cultural values and uses of waterways as well as general social and recreational uses
  • ensure water resources are conserved and properly managed for sustainable use
  • facilitating and encouraging community involvement in conservation
  • integrating short and long term economic, environmental, Aboriginal cultural, social, and recreational considerations during policy development and decision making
  • conserving biological diversity and ecological integrity of waterways
  • immediately responding to threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage
  • exercising business efficiently as possible and consistently with commercial practice.

As both a Rural Authority and Urban Regional Authority, LMW is responsible for managing bulk water entitlements and irrigation services as well as domestic water supply and sewerage services.

As of 2024, the regulated entities as defined by the Water Industry Act are:
