description:
Kerriwichip State school first opened in 1894 as Beulah East State School, operating out of a building provided by local residents and leased by the Education Department (VA 714). The school was located approximately nine miles from the township of Beulah in Victoria’s southern Mallee region. 

Between 1898 and 1900, Beulah East State School was temporarily closed and a new lease was signed upon re-opening. For a brief period in 1909, the school operated part time with Beulah Central State School (School No. 3619) (VA 3188). It shared its only teacher with Beulah Central and the teacher split their time between both schools. When Beulah East State School reopened full time, it underwent a name change to Kerriwichip State School, retaining the school number 3212. Beulah Central took the name Beulah East and retained the school number 3619.

Kerriwichip State School went on to operate part-time with Reedy Dam State School (School No. 3197) (VA 3440) between 1912 and 1913 before closing again in 1920. The lease on the school building was terminated by the Department.

The school re-opened in May 1938 from a leased building until February 1942 when a weatherboard building had been removed and re-erected from Maida Vale State School (School No. 3445). It seems the new site was approximately another two miles north of the original leased site. If and when the site was reserved by the Department or when the school was moved to the new site is subject to further research. 

Kerriwichip State School was permanently closed in August 1948. In 1953, the building was removed and re-erected to Kellalac South State School (School No. 2358) (VA 3326) and the site was sold in 1957.

Kerriwichip State School (formerly Beulah East State School) should not be confused with the following similarly named schools:
•    Beulah East State School (School No. 3619) (VA 3188)
•    Beulah State School (subsequently named Golf Hill State School) (School No. 4521) (VA 5435)
•    Beulah Primary School (School No. 3109) (VA 5455)
•    Beulah West State School (School No. 3245) (VA 5422)
title: Kerriwichip State School (School No. 3212; previously known as Beulah East State School 1894 – 1909; also known as Kurdewerchup School)

description:
Kinkora State School opened in January 1919 in the township of Hopetoun, located in northwestern Victoria. The co-educational primary school operated out of a weatherboard building which had been removed from Goyura State School (School No. 2800) and re-erected on the Kinkora school site. 

Land was donated by local residents in 1924, though if and when the school was moved to that site is subject to further research.

The school was temporarily closed between March and August of 1926.

Kinkora Primary School permanently closed in April 1939. In November 1946, the school building, out-offices, two tanks and shelter pavilion were sold and removed from the site.  

The reserve was revoked by Order-in-Council of 23 May 1965 and gazetted on 31 March 1965.
title: Kinkora State School (School No. 3984; also known as Kinkora Primary School; Kiakora State School)

description:
Kolor South State School (School No. 3701) was a co-educational school near the town of Penshurst in the Southern Grampians region of Victoria. 

The first application for the establishment of a school was received by the Education Department (VA 714) in 1907 but due to a lack of suitable land in the area for purchase, the Department chose to delay opening a school. Following more petitions in 1910, the Department leased two acres of land on the corner of Kolor Lane and Penshurst-Warrnambool Road for 10 years at a price of £2 per year in January 1911. A 24ft x 16ft wooden building was removed from the Bootapool State School (School No. 1545) to the site in July 1911. Accordingly, Kolor South State School was opened on 26th of October 1911. 

The Public Works Department (VA 669) informed the Department that the site was waterlogged and will later “become a veritable quagmire”, and noted by the District Inspector and the Department of Public Health (VA 2904) as an urgent issue. Works were competed to grade and drain the site in April 1912.

Due to low enrolments, the school was ordered to be closed under a system of conveyance in December 1912. However, the school correspondent wrote to the Department explaining that the low enrolments were due to flooding in the area, leaving students unable to travel to school. In light of this, it was decided that Purdeet State School (School No. 1223) and Kolor South were to be worked part-time from 19th February, 1916.

Nevertheless, with only 8 pupils attending, the school closed at the end of April 1917 and Purdeet State School was made full-time.

In 1920, Australian Farms Co. purchased land surrounding the school, intended to be divided for the Soldiers Settlement Scheme. In July 1921, the Department purchased the 2 acres of land where the school had been situated from Australian Farms for £32.

The influx of new settlers led to the school re-opening in January of 1922 with an enrolment of 13 pupils. However, by the end of 1926 enrolments had decreased to 9 students and the Department decided to close the school once again.

In July 1928, the house of a local resident, Edgar Huf, burned down and he and his family were given permission to live in the two rooms in the school building until the end of October that year.

The school officially closed by Minister’s Order, dated 1st June 1929.

In 1931, the school building was removed from the site and relocated to Ardonachie State School (School No. 1169). 

The site was leased at 1 pound per annum starting September 1932 to local Reinhold Linke, whose property was adjoining the site. This continued until his death in October 1942, when his son, Antonius Linke continued leasing the site. In March 1953, the Education Department sold the land to Antonius Linke.
title: Kolor South State School (School No. 3701)

description:
Mount Eckersley State School (School No. 1720) (VA 5402) was a co-educational primary school in the Glenelg region of south-west Victoria. It first opened on 1st April 1876 under the Head Teacher Alexander McLeod. It operated until its closure in 1951 as part of the government's consolidation policy for rural schools which saw the closure and consolidation of a number of primary schools in the region.

In 1875, a petition and subsequent official application was raised for a new school in the Parish of Drumborg. It stated that there were about 31 potential students in the area, with an anticipated average attendance of 20. As there was already a school called Drumborg, and an application already raised for another new school to be called Myamyn, the name Mount Eckersley was proposed to be distinctive. When the school opened, it operated out of a leased building until a portable classroom could be provided.

In the 1880s, suggestions were made to work Mount Eckersley State School half-time with another school in the district, such as Homerton State School (School No. 1400) (VA 5438) or Myamyn State School (School No. 1692) (VA 5403). It is unclear if that occurred, but it does seem likely that it was at one point worked part-time with Condah South State School (School No. 3055), upon its opening in 1890. 

On 4th May 1926, the school building at Mount Eckersley burnt down, with lessons held temporarily in the church buildings, and then a private leased building nearby. Later that year a new building was built, and teaching commenced there from December. 

Discussions about merging state schools in the area began from 1944, when it was represented by parents to the Minister of Public Instruction that students would benefit from communal facilities such as libraries, art rooms, cafeterias, and sports facilities, that would otherwise not be available at small, often single-teacher, rural schools. This discussion included existing schools at Heywood, Heathmere, Myamyn, Drumborg and Homerton.

In 1951, the official process of consolidation began, with schools progressively closing and students moving to the Heywood State School (School No. 297) site to join the newly established Heywood Consolidated School (School No. 5226) (VA 5369). As well as Mount Eckersley, these schools included Condah State School (School No. 1019), Drumborg State School (School No. 1240), Hotspur State School (School No. 1260) (VA 5440) and Myamyn State School (School No. 1692) (VA 5403). 

Mount Eckersley State School was officially closed on 19th February 1951 and the Mount Eckersley school building was moved to form part of the new school site.
title: Mount Eckersley State School (School No. 1720)

description:
Myamyn State School (School No. 1692) (VA 5403) was a co-educational primary school in the town of Myamyn, in the Glenelg region of south-west Victoria. It first opened on 13th March 1876 under the Head Teacher George McHardy. It operated until its closure in 1951 as part of the government's consolidation policy for rural schools which saw the closure and consolidation of a number of primary schools in the region.

Parents petitioned the Education Department (VA 714) from 1875 for a school to service the local children, and a formal application was accordingly raised that same year. It was estimated that there would be an estimated average of 25 children to attend, more than were able to attend the closest school, Condah State School (School No. 1019) (VA 5446), at that time. Tenders for the erection of a school building and master’s residence were received in February 1879 and were subsequently built.

In 1891, the school building and master’s residence were burnt down in an accidental fire, completely destroying everything on the site. New buildings were provisioned in 1892 but were not deemed sufficient for the number of students attending. A new wooden building was eventually erected for the school in 1909. Despite this, it seems as though there were issues with the school building for a number of years and in 1924 it was reported that the school was being conducted in the local hall until the building could be removed from its present isolated position to a site closer to the township. 

Discussions about merging state schools in the area began from 1944, when it was represented by parents to the Minister of Public Instruction that students would benefit from communal facilities such as libraries, art rooms, cafeterias, and sports facilities, that would otherwise not be available at small, often single-teacher, rural schools. This discussion included existing schools at Heywood, Heathmere, Myamyn, Drumborg and Homerton.

In 1951, the official process of consolidation began, with schools progressively closing and students moving to the Heywood State School (School No. 297) site to join the newly established Heywood Consolidated School (School No. 5226) (VA 5369). As well as Myamyn, these schools included Condah State School (School No. 1019), Drumborg State School (School No. 1240), Hotspur State School (School No. 1260) (VA 5440) and Mount Eckersley State School (School No. 1720) (VA 5402). 

Myamyn State School was officially closed on 18th May 1951 and the Myamyn school building was moved to Heywood to form part of the new school site.
title: Myamyn State School (School No. 1692)

description:
Northern Timber Mill School (School No. 4485) (VA 5404) was a coeducational primary school located near Erica, in Western Victoria. It existed along the Moe to Walhalla railway, which was built to support a then-booming timber industry. 

The school first opened in 1931, at which time there were 13 sawmills operating around Erica. It closed just 12 years later, in 1943, likely due to population decline in the area, which had been significantly affected by bushfires. The railway was closed the following year in 1944. 

Northern Timber Mill School has been variously recorded as both the Northern Timber Mill School and Northern Mills State School.
title: Northern Timber Mill School (School No. 4485; also known as Northen Mills State School)

description:
Parwan South State School (School No. 4175) (VA 5405) was a co-educational primary school located on the Nerowie Estate, a large rural property near the locality of Parwan, east of Bacchus Marsh.

An application for a school at Nerowie was first lodged in March 1923, dependent on a suitable location being provided. A community hall was funded and erected by the residents of Parwan South and subsequently leased to the Education Department (VA 714) for this purpose. Parwan South State School opened accordingly on 23rd September 1923. 

From 1927 Parwan South State School was worked part-time with Mount Cotterell State School (School No. 804), before returning to full-time operation in 1929. 

Due to low enrolments and the range of other schools in the region for local children, Parwan South State School was officially closed on 25th August 1949. The hall was later utilised as the Parwan South Mechanics’ Institute and has remained a significant community facility. 

Parwan South State School should not be confused with Parwan State School (School No. 916) (VA 5406), which operated nearby from 1868 to 1951.
title: Parwan South State School (School No. 4175)

description:
Parwan State School (School No. 916) (VA 5406) first opened in June 1867, following a community meeting the previous year to establish a common school. Although a site had been reserved, no formal action had been taken. The school initially operated informally from a vacant house, furnished with improvised materials, and had approximately 40 students in attendance. It was located approximately two and a half miles outside the township of Bacchus Marsh, northwest of Melbourne.

Aid was subsequently granted from the Board of Education (VA 713) for both a teacher’s salary and the construction of a school building. A brick schoolhouse with an attached teacher’s residence was completed, and in July 1868 the school officially opened as Parwan Common School, with the same teacher continuing in charge.

Around 1875 the school changed its name to Parwan State School. This was due to the Education Act (Vic) 1872, which established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and a subsequent change to school naming conventions.

Parwan State School was permanently closed in 1951.
title: Parwan State School (School No. 916)

description:
Stone Church State School (School No. 4499) (VA 5407) was established in April 1932. The co-educational primary school was located approximately five miles from the township of Beulah, in the southern Mallee region of Victoria.

The school initially operated from a leased limestone church constructed in 1890. In August 1934, it moved into a relocated building that had previously been used by Beulah Primary School (School No. 3109) (VA 5455). The original limestone church building was likely demolished around this time.

Stone Church State School permanently closed in 1952, and in 1955 the school building was removed to Warracknabeal High School (School No. 8430) for use as a canteen.
title: Stone Church State School (School No. 4499)

description:
Sunday Creek State School (School No. 3293; also known as Lower Sunday Creek State School) (VA 5408) was a co-educational school located in the Hume region of Victoria, south of Broadford.

In September 1890, the District Inspector reported on the viability of a local school at Sunday Creek, estimating an enrollment of 11 children and suggesting that the school would likely become permanent. Parents had petitioned the Education Department (VA 714) to close the nearby Glenburnie State School (School No. 1200) and move it to a more central location in the district. By October 1891, the idea of conveying students to Glenburnie State School was also put forward to meet the educational needs of the area.

On July 29 1895, local parents petitioned the Education Department (VA 714), offering to erect a room for schooling. In September of that year, the department confirmed that Glenburnie State School would not be moved, and students would not be conveyed and therefore they supported the parents' petition. Land for the new school site was reserved on October 11, 1895. The school opened in a building constructed by residents in 1896, operating part-time with Upper Sunday Creek State School (School No. 1653; also known as Clonbinane State School) with an enrolment of 25 pupils. 

By October 1897, due to growing population in the area, parents had petitioned the Department over six times asking for the school to operate full-time, which the Education Department agreed to in May 1898.

Over the years various improvements were made, but overcrowding remained an issue. In 1906, due to the high enrolment rate of 42 students, seating for the school became rostered and students took turns standing up.

In 1907, there were plans to relocate the school building from Glenburnie State School to Sunday Creek, but they were eventually cancelled. In September 1907, local residents accepted the Department's offer to purchase the school building for £51.

In 1909, once again the possibility of the removal of Glenburnie State School building was requested after the Sunday Creek school was condemned by a health officer. However, this plan was abandoned, and the Glenburnie State School building was removed to Broadford State School (School No. 1125) instead.

The school was closed at the start of 1917 under a system of conveyance to the nearby Broadford State School. 

After protests from the residents, the school was re-opened on a trial basis in June 1917. Dwindling populations in the area led to the school once again being taught part-time with Upper Sunday Creek State School from 1928 until its permanent closure in 1930. The 3 students still enrolled at the school finished their education at Broadford State School (School No. 1125).

In 1942, the building was sold by the Education Department and bought by a local resident. The permissive occupancy for the site was cancelled in 1950. 

Note that the school was also referred to as the Lower Sunday Creek State School, to differentiate from the Upper Sunday Creek State School (School No. 1653).
title: Sunday Creek State School (School No. 3293; also known as Lower Sunday Creek State School)

description:
Tarrington State School (School No. 1908) (VA 5409) was established in July 1877 as Hochkirch State School. It was located in what is now the township of Tarrington, within the Southern Grampians Shire in south-west Victoria. At the time, the township was known as Hochkirch and had a strong German community. In 1918, both the township and the school were renamed Tarrington and Tarrington State School respectively.

The school operated from a new timber building that included a teacher’s residence, with an initial enrolment of 45 students and an average attendance of 27. The Head Teacher also conducted evening classes until around 1880, as the township did not have a Mechanics’ Institute.

By 1884, there were 64 students enrolled and an average attendance of 29. During the First World War, enrolments declined to 17 students. 

Tarrington State School permanently closed in 1929, and the school building was destroyed by fire in 1944.
title: Tarrington State School (School No. 1908; previously known as Hochkirch State School 1877 – 1918)

description:
Timboon State School was opened in 1883 as a co-educational public school in the Heytesbury Forest district of western Victoria.  The timber for the school building was sent from Melbourne to Warrnambool by sea and transported the remainder of the way by bullock wagon.  The school was built in dense scrub, about half a mile west of the modern township, north of the Timboon-Warrnambool Road, and opened with an enrolment of 25 students.

Bushfires were a constant threat, and in 1886, the school was destroyed and had to be rebuilt. As the township expanded following the arrival of the railway in 1892, parents petitioned to relocate the school to a safer, more central site.

In 1905, the Education Department (VA 714) acquired land and moved the school half a mile into the township. A shelter shed was added in 1915, and in 1920, an adjoining block was purchased to extend the grounds, providing space for a playhouse and stable. By 1930, the school had been expanded and remodelled, with an older building repurposed as a woodwork workshop. However, as the local population continued to grow, the school was no longer centrally located.

In October 1934, a new, larger school was built on a two-acre site donated by a local resident, near the town hall on Warrnambool Road. The former school residence remained in use at the original site.

Timboon State School closed in July 1948, with approximately 70 students transferring to the newly established Timboon Consolidated School (School No. 6253). The consolidation brought together around 19 rural schools from within a 10-mile radius, serving a total of 370 students.
title: Timboon State School (School No. 2517)

description:
Torrumbarry North State School (School No. 1738) (VA 5411) was a primary school located in the rural village of Torrumbarry in northern Victoria, north-west of Echuca on the Victorian border with New South Wales. It opened as a State school in 1876 under the Education Department (VA 714) with an enrolment of 67 pupils.

Torrumbarry North State School closed in 1949.
title: Torrumbarry North State School (School No. 1738)

description:
Tragowel Plains Primary School (School No. 2227) (VA 5412) was a co-educational primary school located in north-western Victoria. 

Petitions for a school at Tragowel Plains were first raised in 1877 by local families, and in 1878 a further request was made by the School District of Kerang, who noted that there was no State school between Kerang Durham Ox. In 1879, a 5-acre site in the Parish of Tragowel was acquired by the Education Department (VA 714), on which a two-room wooden portable school building was erected. The school, known then as Tragowel Plains State School, was opened accordingly in 1880, with approximately 50 students enrolled.  

In 1914, after several years of requests, the Education Department authorised a new site on Tragowel Road for the school and a new building was erected, in use from September 2015. A site for a teacher’s residence was also acquired for use in 1916, though it is not certain if a residence was ever built there. In 1935, a fire destroyed the school building, with instruction occurring in the Public Hall until the school was rebuilt the following year. 

In 1936, the decision was made to officially change the school name from Tragowel Plains to Tragowel State School.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Tragowel Primary School.

From 1990, calls were made to merge the two nearby schools of Macorna Primary School (School No. 2909) and Mincha West Primary School (School No. 1931) at Tragowel. This was finalised for the 1991 school year, with Macorna and Mincha West closing and merging with Tragowel Primary School on the Tragowel school site. In 1992, the name of the school was officially returned to Tragowel Plains Primary School. 

Due to declining enrolments, Tragowel Plains Primary School closed in 1997.
title: Tragowel Plains Primary School (School No. 2227; previously known as Tragowel Plains State School 1880 – 1936; Tragowel State School 1936 – c.1970; Tragowel Primary School c.1970 - 1992)

description:
West Sale State School (School No. 4648) (VA 5413) opened in January 1950 as a co-educational primary school. The school operated within a Commonwealth Migrant Centre, also known as the Immigration Holding Centre at West Sale, which was established after World War II on the site of the West Sale aerodrome to accommodate post-war migrants and displaced persons.

The school was conducted in repurposed army huts and a large tent, providing education for between 70 and 100 students over its two and a half years of operation. Evening classes were also held for adults, which ceased after approximately two years as many participants transitioned into employment.

In 1951, three rooms were destroyed by fire. These may have been rebuilt by the Commonwealth Government; however, further details about the buildings are subject to additional research.

The Commonwealth closed the West Sale Migrant Centre in July 1953, and West Sale State School was permanently closed at the same time.
title: West Sale State School (School No. 4648; also known as Migrant School West Sale)

description:
The Wodonga West State School (School No. 1058) (VA 5415) opened in January 1870 as Green Hills, initially operating as a non-vested school with an enrolment of 32 students in a wooden, unlined building. Located within the Wodonga local government area, approximately three hours north east of Melbourne, Green Hills became vested when aid was granted by the Board of Education (VA 713) in 1871, and a 2-acre site was reserved in April 1871.

The school was closed between September 1871 and February 1872 due to the resignation of the Head Teacher. In 1873 the District Inspector recommended relocating the school to the eastern side of the railway line. A new site was obtained at the corner of McKoy Street and the Hume Freeway.

Following the Education Act (Vic) 1872, which established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and changed school naming conventions, the school changed its name to Wodonga West State School, likely occurring in 1875. A new wooden school with four residential rooms attached was built and opened in March 1877. The old school building was sold, and the original site was revoked in 1891.

In October 1903, the school began to operate on a part time basis with Baranduda State School (School No. 2222) due to low attendance rates.  Wodonga West shared its only teacher with Baranduda and the teacher split their time between both schools.

The teachers' residence was condemned in approximately 1932, and despite extensive correspondence about its state of disrepair, it was likely never replaced. 

In 1935 a row of 15 ornamental trees were planted along the boundary fence, one for each pupil at the school.  

Wodonga West State School was vacant from 1945 to 1946, and the school permanently closed in May 1950 due to low attendance.   Bushfires swept through the property in February 1952, burning the fencing and outbuildings.  The site and what remained were sold to private interests in March 1954.

The new Wodonga West State School (School No. 4814; later known as Wodonga West Primary School) opened in Lawrence Street in 1959.

Wodonga West State School should not be confused with Wodonga West Secondary College (School No. 8477), a high school which operated from 1976 – 2005); or Wodonga West Primary School (School No. 4814), a primary school which opened in 1959 and is still in operation as of 2024.
title: Wodonga West State School (School No. 1058; previously known as Green Hills School 1870 - 1875?)

description:
Woodstock West State School (School No. 1236) (VA 5416) was opened in June 1873.  The co-educational primary school was located in Woodstock West, just north of Greater Melbourne within the City of Whittlesea (VA 3742) local government area. 

The school was established to serve farming families and rural communities in the district. It first operated from a leased building with an average attendance of 22 students. A permanent site was acquired in 1874, and a timber school with a two-room residence attached was constructed.

The school was closed between late 1916 and September 1917, and then operated part-time with Woodstock North State School (School No. 1245) from January 1935 to March 1939 due to low attendance rates. The two schools shared a single teacher, who divided their time between both sites.

Woodstock West State School permanently closed in January 1968.
title: Woodstock West Primary School (School No. 1236)

description:
Yabba Yabba State School opened in August 1882 located north of Dookie in the Goulburn Valley region of Victoria.  

The school was subject to periods of temporary closure due to the unsuitability of the area for intensive agriculture and therefore fluctuating school attendances. 

Yabba Yabba State School was first closed from September 1906 to February 1909.  In 1915, attendance and enrolment improved so that the Committee asked for enlargement of the school building which was completed in 1921.

Attendance declined, and the school was temporarily closed in May 1929. However, it reopened in August of the same year as a subsidised school.  Subsidised schools were introduced in areas where student numbers were too low to justify the operation of a full State School. Under this arrangement, the Education Department (VA 714) paid the teacher based on the number of enrolled students, while local parents were responsible for providing the teacher with free board and lodging. A minimum enrolment of four students was required for the school to operate under this model.

Yabba Yabba State School went on to re-open full time in July 1932 with the new name Yabba North State School and retained the school number 2483.

With an attendance of only 3 students, the school again closed from February 1943 to January 1949 when it began to operate part time with Waggarandall State School (School No. 4078).  The two schools shared a single teacher, who divided their time between both sites.

Yabba North State School was permanently closed in June 1951.  Students were transferred to Dookie State School (School No. 1432).
title: Yabba Yabba State School (School No. 2483; known as Yabba North State School 1932 – 1951)

description:
Yarraberb State School (School No. 2160) was a co-educational school in the Loddon Mallee region of Victoria, north of Bendigo. 

In April 1879, parents petitioned the Education Department (VA 714) to open a school in the area. 

The school opened 22 October, 1879 with 22 students in the local Wesleyan Church, furnished with desks and other items from the closed Three Mile Plain State School (School No. 1659). 

The Education Department (VA 714) purchased 2 acres of land in April 1880, opposite to the Wesleyan Church.

In January 1882, the 24ft x 16ft wooden school building from Three Mile Plain State School was erected on the site the Department had purchased. The building included the classroom and had two rooms attached for teacher’s quarters. 

The school re-opened October 1903, operating part-time with Leichardt East State School (School No. 2671) (VA 3612). However, due to insufficient number of students, by March 1904 the school had closed.

In 1915, the school building was sold for 25 pounds. 

In June 1919, local Richard Wright sold off two acres of his land to the Education Department in Allotment 46B2. After several petitions from parents, the Yarraberb school re-opened in September 1919, operating out of the local Methodist Church. This building was found suitable only for temporary schooling and the District Inspector recommended a permanent school building be built. 

In April 1921, the Department exchanged these two acres of land for another two acres in the north-east corner of Allotment 46B1, also owned by Richard Wright. In January 1922, a 21.6ft x 21ft wooden building to accommodate thirty students was erected on the new site and schooling out of this new building started 26th June, 1922.

The school became unstaffed in June 1951.

The school officially closed May 1953, and a school bus service was established to transport students to Bridgewater State School (School No. 1097). 

The school building was removed in 1954 to Wedderburn State School (School No. 794) (VA 794), and two years later, the shelter pavilion was removed to Bridgewater State School.

The site was sold in 1962 to Yarraberb Methodist Church.

Note that the school is sometimes spelt incorrectly as Yaraberb State School.
title: Yarraberb State School (School No. 2160)

description:
Otway Regional Water Authority was constituted by an Order-in-Council as the Colac Region Water Authority to take effect from the 1 July 1993. The Colac District Water Board (VA 2213), Lorne Water Board (VA 2236) and Lough Calvert Drainage Trust (VA 1929) were abolished and their geographical areas, functions, land, liabilities, obligations, powers, property, rights and employees  became the responsibility of the new authority. At the time of establishment, Colac Region Water took responsibility for the following districts:
  • Apollo Bay Sewerage District
  • Colac Rural, Sewerage, Urban and Waterworks Districts
  • Lorne Urban and Waterworks Districts
  • Lough Calvert Drainage District
  • Otway Coast Urban and Waterworks Districts

In 1995 the water authority was renamed the Otway Region Water Authority. Later that year the Aireys Inlet Water Board (VA 2560) was abolished and its property, rights, obligations and liabilities were transferred to Otway Regional Water Authority. The Aireys Inlet Sewerage, Urban and Waterworks districts were added to the water authority's purview.

Otway Regional Water Authority was abolished in 1997 and it's property, rights, obligations and liabilities were transferred to Barwon Regional Water Authority (VA 3756).

Regional Urban Water Authorities

Regional Urban Water Authorities are responsible for providing water supply and sewerage services to non-metropolitan urban areas. Regional authorities work with catchment management authorities and rural water authorities to supply water to regional areas and provide sewerage treatment services.

Until 2006, authorities were overseen by the membership of the authority, which consisted of qualified people to be appointed in writing by the Minister as specified by the Water Act. Collectively, membership of each water authority was to hold qualifications or experience in the business of the authority, public finance or economics, engineering, business management, commerce, banking, environmental and water resource management, and law.

Industry Reform

Water authorities underwent a program of amalgamation and structural reform throughout the 1990s under the auspices of the Office of Water Reform (later the Water Bureau, established as a division in Department of Conservation and Natural Resources VA 3097). Water Boards and Sewerage Boards were gradually replaced with regional water authorities. These authorities also took over the water management responsibilities from Local Government. 

Under Division 2 of Part 6 of the Water Act, the Minister had the power to restructure existing water authorities, to create new water authorities, unite existing water and sewerage districts, and to abolish existing water authorities. By publication of an Order-in-Council in the Victorian Government Gazette, the Minister was able to constitute a new authority to take over the property, rights, liabilities, obligations, powers, staff, and functions under the Water Act of one or more authorities, so long as the terms and conditions were agreed between the affected authorities, local councils, and the Minister. The Minister was required to provide in writing to the authorities and local councils affected by the restructuring the reasons behind the decision, ensure that a copy of the document was placed before both Houses of Parliament, and liaise with the Minister administering the Local Government Act 1989 if a local council was involved.

The membership of the new water authority as specified by the Order could not included more than three people to be appointed by the Minister unless the functions of the Authority were solely related to waterway management. Each new authority was to be a body corporate, with a common seal, be capable of being sued and of suing under its corporate name, be capable of acquiring, holding, managing, and disposing of property in accordance with the performance of its functions, and was to be capable of efficiently performing its functions and lawfully exercising its powers.

title: Otway Region Water Authority (previously Colac Region Water Authority 1993-1995)

description:
This school was a denominational school established by Wesleyan authorities on the 19th of February 1855 on the corner of Lydiard and Dana Streets, Ballarat. The schoolhouse was a small, low-walled building made of sandstone with basaltic boulders. Attendance in the first year was 73.

The Victorian Education Act of 1872 established a new government school system based on the principles of ‘free, compulsory and secular’ education, which resulted in the existing National Schools and Common Schools being either absorbed into the new system or closed. Most denominational schools ceased operating, with some exceptions. State aid was temporarily granted to some church schools; it is likely during this time that the Lydiard school was registered as State School No. 81.

State aid to church schools ceased in 1875 for those which had remained temporarily in the State system as capitation schools. Subsequently, this school was closed on the 31st of January 1876.
title: Ballarat State School (Lydiard Street) (School No. 81; previously known as Lydiard Street School, 1855 - c.1873)

description:
Ballendella Primary School (School No. 3732), initially named Bamawm East State School, opened in June 1912 as a co-educational primary school but was soon after renamed Ballendella State School. The school served the Bamawm Extension area, an irrigation settlement located between Rochester and Echuca. In its opening year, the head teacher reported an enrolment of 32 students.

The school operated out of a Federation/Interwar-style weatherboard building. Growing enrolments led to extensions to the building in 1919, and a shelter shed was erected on the school site in 1921.  

Further increase in enrolments prompted the construction of a new infant room, large entrance hall, and storeroom in 1961, with new septic toilets and a school residence added in 1962.

At some point, the name changed from “State School” to “Primary School,” likely in 1970, when a statewide policy change designated "State School" for all primary, secondary, and technical institutions, reserving "Primary School" for primary schools. Accordingly, the school’s name was updated to Ballendella Primary School.

By 2005, student numbers had declined to 21, with only eight expected to remain the following year. The local community chose to close the school at the end of 2005, and the Ballendella Primary School site was sold in June 2018.
title: Ballendella Primary School (School No. 3732; previously known as Bamawm East State School 1912 – 1912; Ballendella State School 1912 – c.1970)

description:
Beulah West State School (School No. 3245) was a co-educational school located in the southern Mallee region of Victoria, north of Warracknabeal. 

Parents petitioned the Education Department (VA 714) in July of 1893, with the request that they would erect a school building but the Department provide a teacher. Subsequently, a 24ft x 14ft wooden school building was erected by Johann Carl Ferdinand Jende on his property. The school opened 15th October 1895, operating part time with Rosebery West State School (also known as Byanga State School; School No. 3218). 

The Department leased the building for £3 annually, which increased to £5 in 1898 when the school began operating full-time. 

Dwindling attendance of 5 pupils led to the school’s closure in November 1906. 

Following a request from the Closer Settlement Board in 1919, the Department designated 3 acres on Liesfield’s Estate for a new school. The Soldiers Memorial Hall, built by the Settlement Board and completed in December 1921, was leased for £10 per year, allowing the school to reopen on June 15, 1922, with 14 students. 

In 1923, the Department purchased 3 acres adjacent to the hall site for continued school use. The Closer Settlement Board assumed control of the hall in June 1928. By 1936, with 21 students, the rent rose to £15 per year, and attendance remained stable until the mid-1940s.

By 1951, attendance had fallen to 4 and the school was permanently closed by ministerial order on 25th May 1953.

Arrangements were made to have the children conveyed to the newly consolidated Beulah Primary School (School No. 3109; previously known as Beulah State School) (VA 5455). It is believed that this consolidated school included the conveyance of students from Galaquil East State School (School No. 3318; previously known as Rosevale State School), Rosebery State School (School No. 3190), Beulah East State School (School No. 3619; previously known as Beulah Central State School 1910 - 1928) (VA 3188), and Galaquil State School (School No. 3083; previously known at Batchica North 1891 - 1902) (VA 5342), subject to further research.

The Education Department sold the land in 1985.
title: Beulah West State School (School No. 3245)

description:
Beyal North State School (School No. 4527) was a co-educational school located in the Mallee Region, in the north-west of Victoria.

Parents first petitioned the Education Department (VA 714) in June 1929 for a school. This petition was unsuccessful, and subsequently Mr. Anthony Clifford Everett modified a 22ft x 12ft building on his land into a classroom and privately hired a teacher to educate children in the area. As costs rose, Everett petitioned the Department for funding, and a subsidized school was approved, officially opening on 1st September 1932 with six students.

After the removal of the Galaquil East State School (School No. 3318; previously known as Rosevale State School) to another site in 1933 attendance at Beyal North school grew. On 5th June 1934, Beyal North State School officially opened on Everitts Road, still located on Mr. Anthony Everett’s land. The next year, enrolments reached 15 and the Head Teacher requested a permanent state building be erected.

In 1936, £60 was allocated towards a new building in lieu of five years’ rent, and classes began there on 24th April of that year. With enrolment dropping to five in 1942, the school briefly closed, then reopened with a new teacher in 1943. 

Finally, due to low enrolment of four students and no expected new students, the school was permanently closed by Minister’s Order on 14th February 1945. Remaining students were offered either conveyance allowances or correspondence education.
title: Beyal North State School (School No. 4527; previously known as Beyal North Subsidised School 1932 - 1934)

description:
Burn Brae State School (School No. 4396) was a co-educational school adjacent to the eponymous Burn Brae (also called Burnbrae) Homestead on the Hamilton Highway (then called Caramut Road), 7 kilometres east of Penshurst. 

The school officially opened 26th of May, 1928 in a leased 27ft x 11ft building on the land of Mr J. G. Kruger, with an enrolment of 13 students. Parents arranged for outhouses, a tank, and furniture from the closed Purdeet State School (School No. 1223) to be moved there in November. In July 1929, the shelter shed from the school was also removed. In lieu of purchasing the building, the rent was increased to £10 per annum in February 1930.

The school became unstaffed in late 1941. After the Head Teacher and District Inspector assessed a potential enrolment of 9 students, the Education Department (VA 714) reopened it in March 1943, although actual attendance was only six students.

On 6th September 1948, a storm damaged the school, which temporarily operated in a 16ft x 12ft wooden building on Mr. P. J. Fry's land until repairs were completed. Classes resumed in the original building on 12th October.

Due to low enrolment, Burn Brae became unstaffed on 1st June 1955. The Education Department suggested staffing it again in July, but it is unclear if it reopened. The school was permanently closed on 18th December 1959.
title: Burn Brae State School (School No. 4396)

description:
Carlton Teachers’ College Rural Practising School (School No. 3901) (VA 5425) opened in July 1915 and provided training facilities for Melbourne Teachers’ College student teachers, particularly for one-teacher rural schools. The practising school was located in the back paddock, on the northwest corner of the Melbourne Teachers’ College site and operated out of a newly constructed pavilion style classroom.

The need for a model rural training school near the Training College had been discussed since 1878. In 1880, ten small rural model schools were established at Carlton and Collingwood primary schools, allowing teacher trainees to observe one-teacher schools in operation. By 1900, a dedicated rural training school was opened on Queensberry Street, and in 1913, a six-month short course for rural teaching was introduced.  

A steady stream of student teachers visited the Carlton Practising Rural School, observing and teaching for a fortnight, while returning soldier-teachers from World War I undertook a six-week intensive course.  In 1920, the Head Teacher reported that up to 15 student teachers were present at any given time, with 170 passing through the school in the previous year. Grades 1–8 were taught until grades 7 and 8 were gradually phased out between 1944 and 1948. Enrolments remained steady, with approximately 40 students per year from 1915 to 1922, and between 60 and 70 students from 1931 to 1966.  

In 1923, approval was granted to replace the original pavilion building with a three-classroom wooden cottage school, relocated from Kew East (School No. 3161). The new classrooms opened in 1924, and the pavilion was subsequently demolished. Additional small rooms were constructed at either end of the school, serving as an office, staffroom, and cloakrooms for both pupils and student teachers. From 1948, one of these rooms was converted into a small library.

Despite a long waiting list for student admissions, the school was unstaffed by December 1966. The expansion of the Melbourne Teachers' College and the Secondary Teachers’ College, coupled with a reduced need for rural school teachers, led to its closure. Many students were transferred to North Melbourne, Errol Street State School (School No. 1402).

Carlton Teachers' College was officially closed by ministerial order on 30 September 1969 and gazetted in January 1970. The school building was demolished between 1968 and 1970.
title: Teachers’ College Rural Practising School, Carlton (School No. 3901; also known as Carlton Teachers’ College Practising School; Carlton Teachers’ College; Melbourne Teachers College Practising Rural School; Training College Practising School; Teachers’ College Practising; College Rural State School)

description:
Cokum Reserve Primary School (School No. 4296) (VA 5426) opened in 1926 as Cokum Reserve State School.  The school had an opening enrolment of 10 students and operated from a building relocated from the former Bungeluke State School (School No. 1973) in 1925. 

By 1961, the net enrolment had reached 21 students, and a new building was erected and occupied in July that year.  The original building was removed from the site in 1963.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Cokum Reserve Primary School around this time. 

The school became unstaffed in 1980 and was likely permanently closed shortly thereafter.   School councils can vote to close or destaff a school if there are low or no enrolments for the coming year. Destaffing a school allows it to reopen if enrolments emerge, although this is rare. After a school has been destaffed for a period, usually some years, it is officially closed.
title: Cokum Reserve Primary School (School No. 4296; Previously known as Cokum Reserve State School 1926 – c.1970)

description:
Coradjil State School (School No. 4786) (VA 5427) was a co-educational school located in the Western District of Victoria, 4km southwest of Bungador. 

In 1954, the Rural Finance and Settlement Commission (VA 2273) was given permission to develop 70,000 acres of the Heytesbury Forest into farming land. The growing number of farmers settling in the area led to the Education Department (VA 714) being petitioned by Coradjil Progress Association in 1955 to establish a school in the area. 

A five-acre site was reserved October 26th 1955 along Timboon-Colac Road, however, the school was not established until February 1957. The 31ft x 24ft single classroom school building made of light timber was constructed and the school was opened in October 1957 with 26 pupils. 

With just one pupil, the school became unstaffed in July 1964. The school closed by ministerial order on July 7th 1967. 

In 1968, the school building was transferred to Pirron Yallock State School (School No. 1242; also known as Pirron Yaloak) (VA 3639). The reservation for the land was revoked in April 1969 and it was incorporated into the Heytesbury Soldier Settlement, established by the Rural Finance and Settlement Commission in 1960.

The school history file (VPRS 14519) for Coradjil State School, created by the Education Department c.1970, notes that the records of the school were lost in a fire which destroyed the Colac State School (School No. 117) in 1964.
title: Coradjil State School (School No. 4786)

description:
Corio Bay Senior College (School No. 7105) (VA 5428) was a co-educational specialist school for senior students located on Goldsworthy Road, Corio.

The school began as Norlane Technical School, opening on February 2nd 1960 with an enrolment of 89 students as an annexe of the Gordon Institute of Technology. It had a temporary address in Spring Street, Geelong West, occupying the vacated East Geelong Technical School whilst a new school was being erected on 15 acres of undeveloped area of a Housing Commission (VA 508) estate in Corio.

At the request of the Principal, the name was officially changed to Corio Technical School on August 18th 1960, to better reflect the location of the school. By March 1961, the school had moved to its permanent location on Goldsworthy Road, Corio. At that time, only Stage 1 of construction had been completed, with a trades wing, science wing and social studies wing which included facilities for woodworking, metal fabrication, music, and science laboratories. At the beginning of 1962, enrolments reached 301 students and the existing buildings could not accommodate class sizes, and some students were transported to Geelong West Technical School for practical classes. 

Corio Technical School was officially opened Thursday 19th March, 1964 with an enrolment of 420 students. In 1965, the school became co-educational, with an enrolment of 113 girls and 583 boys. Over the following years, Stage 2 and 3 of the construction were being completed, with revisions to now include a so-called ‘Girls Section’ for an estimated cost of $517,000. A home economics wing, and commercial and art wing were constructed, which included facilities for home management, cooking, needlework, and art rooms.  There were also extensions to the science wing to provide for a physics laboratory, a dark room and more office space. 

By 1970, enrolments had grown to 1,055 students. In 1973, the Technical School received a Commonwealth Secondary Libraries Grant, which enabled them to construct a library complex on-site.
Through the Northern Education Complex (NEC), the school had a strong relationship with Norlane High School (School No. 8175), and Flinders Peak Secondary College (School No. 7744) (VA 5322), their 7-10 associate schools.

Corio Community College was officially established in 1995 as a dedicated secondary school with an enrolment of 476 students, though it was also operating in 1994. There was a focus on the completion of the Victorian Certificate of Education (VCE) and Vocational Education and Training (VET). It is unknown if there was a period of closure between the Technical School and the establishment of the Community College. 

On March 8th 2001, the school’s name changed from Corio Community College to Corio Bay Senior College. In 2003, an on-site childcare centre opened. The centre catered for a growing number of young mothers who were enrolled into the school’s Young Parents’ Access Program. The childcare centre (which was officially opened at the end of 2005) and the young parents’ access program (YPAP) enabled young parents to re-engage with education.

In 2007, the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development (DEECD) (VA 4840) commenced planning for the Corio-Norlane Education Regeneration Project under the Building Futures policy framework. This multi-staged project involved the re-configuration of 9 government schools in Corio and Norlane into one prep to year 12 college across five campuses, to be called Northern Bay College (VA 5358). 

Accordingly, Corio Bay Senior College was permanently closed in December 2010, along with Flinders Peak Secondary College (School No. 7744) (VA 5322), Norlane West Primary School (School No. 4880) (VA 5441), Corio Primary School (School No. 124), Corio West Primary School (School No. 5031), North Shore Primary School (School No. 4301), Norlane High School (School No. 8175), and Corio South Primary School (School No. 4927) (VA 5382) to form the new Northern Bay P-12 College (School No. 8901) (VA 5358).

The school became the senior campus and administration centre of the merged schools. In June 2012, the campus was renamed as Campus 1 – Goldsworthy Road 9-12 Campus (formerly called Goldsworthy Road 10-12 Campus).
title: Corio Bay Senior College (School No. 7105; also known as Corio Secondary College; previously known as Corio Community College 1995 – 2001; Corio Technical School 1960 – 1995; Norlane Technical School 1960)

description:
Dockers Plains State School (School No. 1962) (VA 5429) was a co-educational school located 7kms north of Wangaratta, in north-east Victoria. 

Dockers Plains State School (also frequently written as Docker’s Plains) replaced the Catholic Capitation School No. 832, which opened July 1st 1866. This school was struck off on 30th of September 1877 and closed 2 weeks later. 

The Board of Education (VA 713) purchased one acre of land on the corners of McDonald and Boorhaman Road in December of 1876. A tender was put out for construction of a 30x18ft wooden building, with an attached four-room teacher’s residence. The building was completed September 1877 and the school opened October 1st of the same year.

In August 1878, the average attendance was 57 pupils. In 1880, locals sank a 68ft well to provide clean drinking water for the school.

The school was closed June 1898 under a system of conveyance to Wangaratta North State School (School No. 2391). The school was re-opened in March 1902 after petition from parents and an average attendance of 20 students.

In 1902, the Head Teacher wrote to the Education Department (VA 714) about white ant (termite) damage to the school and residence. This would be a frequent complaint from both the Head Teachers and the District Inspectors across the decades of the school’s existence. The school was closed for a month in May 1918 whilst repairs to remedy the white ant damage at the school and residence were completed and many other repairs were completed throughout the years to address termite damage. 

In September 1932 the verandah of the residence and school was enclosed to create a sleepout.

In 1937, enrolments had reduced to 14 and by 1942, they had decreased further to only 5 students with no expected enrolments for the next year. Due to the lack of nearby schools for students to attend, it was agreed to be kept open. However, the school was closed by Ministerial Order on July 3rd 1944, due to low enrolments.

After the school was closed, the Head Teacher of Boorhaman State School (School No. 1996) occupied the teacher’s residence from 25 January 1945 until at least mid-1948, when a new residence was erected at the Boorhaman School.

The Minister approved the re-opening of the school 8th March 1949, after petitions from locals. The opening of the school was deferred until the teacher’s residence was vacated, providing time for necessary repairs to the building. The cost of the repairs was an estimated £543, largely due to the damage caused by termites. Deciding the cost was too high, in August 1949 students were instead conveyed to Wangaratta North State School and the school remained closed. 

In October 1949, the residence was occupied by the Head Teacher of Peechelba East State School (School No. 4424), who vacated in December 1950. The successive Head Teacher from the same school occupied the residence from September 1951 and vacated by February 1952.

In September 1951, the shelter pavilion was removed to Boorhaman State School. By 1952, the buildings were deemed unsuitable to remove to another site due to termite damage. The Education Department sold the land and buildings on May 1st 1953 for £770.
title: Dockers Plains State School (School No. 1962)

description:
Doogalook State School (School No. 2467) (VA 5430) was a coeducational primary school located near Homewood, in the Goulburn Valley region of Victoria. The name likely refers to the Doogalook Homestead in the same area, originally built around 1844, though the exact nature of the relationship between school and homestead remains subject to further research.

Doogalook State School first opened in 1882, operating out of a slab railing hut on Dairy Flat Rd. In 1903, a school building was brought to Doogalook State School from Murrindindi State School (School No. 2228), which had closed the previous year. 

From 1912, Doogalook State School was worked part-time with the nearby Homewood State School (School No. 1433; previously known as Yea State School 1874 – 1885; also known as Gill’s Gully State School) (VA 5439). During the 1915-1916 summer holidays, the Homewood and Doogalook schools merged onto a central site donated by a local resident. The building from Doogalook State School was removed and re-erected on this central site, one mile away from its original site. The merged school continued under the Homewood name and school number, and Doogalook was officially closed. 

The recorded spelling of the school and homestead has been variously recorded over the years as Doogalook, Doogallook and Doogolook.
title: Doogalook State School (School No. 2467)

description:
Ferntree Gully Primary School (School No. 1307) (VA 5431) began as Rural School 119 Ferntree Gully in 1871, serving Melbourne’s eastern suburb at the foothills of the Dandenong Ranges. The United Methodist Free Church purchased the original site for use as a church and school, and a two-room weatherboard hall, later named Dobson’s Hall, was built by public subscription. The school had 30 students in 1871 and received government aid from January 1872 to December 1873. In January 1874, the Minister of Public Instruction leased the building, formally establishing it as Ferntree Gully State School (School No. 1307).

In 1880, a one-acre site located just across the road was donated to the school and a new brick building with an attached four-room teachers’ residence was constructed. The original weatherboard hall was vacated in late 1883 and the school relocated to the new site. Space shortages led to lower classes being temporarily housed again in Dobson’s Hall from September 1898 to October 1901. The Education Department (VA 714) expanded the school in 1901 with an additional classroom and added another room to the residence in 1905. In 1912, three acres of adjacent land were purchased and provided access to the modern Dorset Road.  Further extensions, including a cloakroom, bathroom, pantry, and lobby, were completed in 1914.

During the 1920s, a sloyd woodworking and cookery centre opened for senior pupils from nearby schools who attended one day per week. Enrolments grew to 113 students by 1930, necessitating an additional classroom in 1934. By 1961, the school had 500 students across eleven classrooms and during this decade the school purchased the neighbouring Methodist churchyard.  A library was completed in 1973.  

The school likely changed its name from "State School" to "Primary School" around 1970, following a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools.   Whilst there was no formal announcement regarding the name change, Victoria Government Gazette notices from around this time reflect the change with both names being used interchangeably for some time.

By 2006, enrolments had declined to 106, leading to the merger of Ferntree Gully Primary School with Wattle View Primary School (School No. 5012). It is unclear whether classes continued at the Ferntree Gully site after the merger. However, the State Government retained ownership of it, and as part of the Nation Building and Economic Stimulus Project, a State and Federally funded social housing estate was constructed there. Completed in 2013, the development incorporated the heritage-listed school building into its design.
title: Ferntree Gully Primary School (School No. 1307; previously known as Rural School 119 Ferntree Gully 1871 – 1874; Ferntree Gully State School 1874 – c.1970?)

description:
French Island North Primary School (School No. 4769) (VA 5432) was a co-educational school situated in the Fairhaven locality of French Island, located in the middle of Western Port. 

Parents petitioned the Education Department (VA 714) in July 1954 for the erection of a new school on the north end of French Island. They described the difficulties students had in travelling over 6 miles on unpaved tracks to the closest school on the island, Perseverance State School (School No. 3261). The District Inspector reported that the tracks are often underwater and thus pupils attended the Perseverance school very irregularly. 

Mr. Easy offered a building on his property on the north of the island for use as a school. Ultimately the Inspector recommended that the building on Mr. Easy’s land would be suitable, if a water tank and toilets were added to the site. 

Those changes were made, and the school officially opened May 24th, 1955. Due to a decline in school-aged children, the school became unstaffed in 1962 and permanently closed in March 1965.
title: French Island North Primary School (School No. 4769)

description:
Glen Forbes State School (School No. 4008) was a co-educational school located on the Bass Coast, in the south-east of Victoria. 

The school began as Glen Forbes Railway Station State School on 20th September 1919 operating out of the leased 50ft x 30ft wooden town hall. The school was intended to replace Glen Forbes State School (School No. 3519), whose location on Watson Road, a steep road located 2 miles from the township of Glen Forbes, made it difficult for students to travel to. The school opened with an enrolment of 16 pupils, however enough students still chose to travel to Glen Forbes State School, and it stayed open until 1926. 

In February 1924, the removal of the building from Glen Forbes South State School (School No. 3749) for the school’s use was approved for £220. An additional £200 was approved to extend the 18ft x 14ft building to accommodate all the students. However, action on the requisition was paused as no land was yet secured in the area for a permanent school. 

In February 1925 the residents of Glen Forbes raised £70 for the purchase of 2 acres of land from Jane Shackleford. The previous requisition of removing the Glen Forbes South school building was cancelled, and instead a new building was erected on this land. The building had one 21.6ft x 21ft classroom, with an attached cloakroom and storeroom. The town hall was vacated and schooling began out of the new wooden building on December 1st 1925.

In 1929 a shelter pavilion was constructed, and a pony paddock within the school area was fenced in. The District Inspector, School Committee and Head Teacher recommended that the name of the school be changed to better reflect the name as its known in the community. Accordingly, the school was officially renamed to Glen Forbes State School on August 1st 1950. 

Enrolments remained steady in the high teens from its opening, reaching 23 in 1951. This high enrolment led to the school committee requesting a teacher’s residence. Expenditure of £2,778 was approved October 1951, however the school was not selected by the Residence Selection Committee for the provision of a new residence and the requisition was cancelled in 1954. 

The school became unstaffed at the end of 1972, and students were transferred to nearby schools. The school was closed by March 1974, though the exact date is unknown. 

The land was bought by Spensley Street Primary School (School No. 3146; previously known as Clifton Hill State School) in 1977 to be used as a school camp. As of 2025, it was still being used by the school for that purpose.
title: Glen Forbes State School (School No. 4008; previously known as Glen Forbes Railway Station State School 1919 – 1950)

description:
Glenore State School (School No. 3770) (VA 5434) was a co-educational school located in north-west Victoria, 17 kilometres west of Hopetoun. 

Parents first petitioned the Education Department (VA 714) in November 1911 for a school in the area. Locals erected a 40ft x 20ft galvanised iron hall to act as a school in August 1912 on the corner of Glenore Road and Glenore School Road. The Department provided out offices and a teacher and the school officially opened 20 November 1912, leased to the Department for £10, 7 shillings a year. 

In October 1928 the enrolment for the school was only 9 pupils and it was decided that the school would be worked part-time with Wirrbibial State School (School No. 3579) (VA 3579). By January 1930, 14 were enrolled and the school was once again made full-time. In February 1935, the school was again operated part-time with Wirrbibial State School due to lowered enrolments. After protests from the parents, the school was conducted full-time from May 1st 1935.

In July 1937, the school was made part-time with Wyperfeld State School (School No. 4264). After further protests, the school was opened full-time the following month and the Wyperfeld school was closed. The school committee requested that the building of the now-closed Wyperfeld school be removed for the school’s use, which was permitted by the Department on the condition that the residents arrange a site that would be owned by the state. A site was obtained and the 21.6ft x 21ft wooden building was removed and re-erected, and schooling began in this new building November 27th 1939. The Department officially bought the land, across the road from the original school, on March 18th 1940. 

The school did not re-open for the 1948 school year, and the pupils were conveyed to Hopetoun State School (School No. 3167). The school officially closed June 4th 1948. The school building and furniture was moved to the Hopetoun State School in 1952 and the land was later sold.
title: Glenore State School (School No. 3770)

description:
Golf Hill State School (School No. 4521) (VA 5435) was a co-educational, non-denominational primary school, that opened in October 1933.  It was located approximately 10 miles west of Beulah, in Victoria’s southern Mallee region. 

The school operated from a leased building, with the Minister agreeing to contribute an amount equivalent to five years' rent in advance to help provide a suitable building.

Due to low enrolment and staffing difficulties, the school appears to have been unstaffed from 1944. Golf Hill State School permanently closed in June 1946, with the building lease terminated in April of that year.
title: Golf Hill State School (School No. 4521; also known as Golf Hill, Beulah State School)

description:
Greens Creek State School (School No. 1381) (VA 5436) opened in January 1874. The co-educational primary school was located on the Stawell-Navarre Road, to the north of Stawell in the Grampians region of Victoria. Initially operating from a single wooden classroom, enrolment reached 25 students by 1877.  

At some stage between 1877 and 1902 the school operated part time with Glenwylln State School (School No. 3234). It shared its only teacher with Glenwylln and the teacher split their time between both schools, before it was closed in July 1902, likely due to low enrolments. When it reopened in November 1911, Greens Creek State School operated from a leased building.

A three-room weatherboard school was officially opened in August 1927. However, declining enrolments led to its closure in June 1945. Greens Creek State School reopened part-time with Joel Joel State School (School No. 1702) in November 1948 but reverted to full-time in June 1952 following Joel Joel’s closure. 

Greens Creek State School appears to have been unstaffed from February 1956 and was permanently closed in 1957 due to low enrolments.

A 1966 report described the site as having a single weatherboard classroom with attached cloakroom, outbuildings and a timber shed with two standard tanks and stands. A 1967 inspection noted a small school plantation of pine and sugar gum trees with little to no market value. It is unclear if this was ever forested.  

The school reservation site was officially revoked and gazetted on 27th June, 1984.
title: Greens Creek State School (School No. 1381)

description:
Heathmere State School (VA 5440) was a co-educational primary school in the small town of Heathmere, in the Glenelg region of south-west Victoria. It first opened on 17th June 1934 under the Head Teacher Beryl Gallacher and operated until its closure just over 20 years later, in 1955, as part of the government's consolidation policy for rural schools which saw the closure and consolidation of a number of primary schools in the region.

Petitions for a new school were raised from 1930 at which time it was estimated nine students would regularly attend. The proposal included working the school part-time with the neighbouring Gorae State School (School No. 2532) (VA 3299), though it is unclear whether this actually occurred. The official application for the new school at Heathmere was eventually raised in 1934, and a school building erected by the end of May.

Discussions about merging state schools in the area began from 1944, when it was represented by parents to the Minister of Public Instruction that students would benefit from communal facilities such as libraries, art rooms, cafeterias, and sports facilities, that would otherwise not be available at small, often single-teacher, rural schools. In the 1940s, this discussion included existing schools at Heywood, Heathmere, Myamyn, Drumborg and Homerton.

In 1951, the official process of consolidation began, with schools progressively closing and students moving to the Heywood State School (School No. 297) site to join the newly established Heywood Consolidated School (School No. 5226) (VA 5369). These schools included Condah State School (School No. 1019) (VA 5446), Drumborg State School (School No. 1240), Hotspur State School (School No. 1260) (VA 5440), Mount Eckersley State School (School No. 1720) (VA 5402) and Myamyn State School (School No. 1692) (VA 5403).

However, it wasn’t until 1955 that Heathmere State School was finally slated for consolidation, along with Homerton State School (School No. 1400) (VA 5438). Heathmere State School was officially closed on 29th April 1955 with all the students moving to Heywood Consolidated School. In 1956 suggestions were made to remove buildings from the closed Heathmere and Homerton schools to Heywood for conversion to a domestic arts wing, but new buildings for this purpose were erected instead.
title: Heathmere State School (School No. 4526)

description:
Homerton State School (VA 5438) was a co-educational primary school in the small town of Homerton, in the Glenelg region of south-west Victoria. It first opened in 1875 under the Head Teacher Sydney Underwood. It operated until its closure in 1955 as part of the government's consolidation policy for rural schools which saw the closure and consolidation of a number of primary schools in the region.

Parents petitioned the Education Department (VA 714) from 1873, leading to land being granted for a new school later that year. A school building was subsequently built in 1874 and the school officially opened 25th February 1875.

Due to small numbers of students in the area, Homerton State School was frequently worked part-time with other schools. From late 1875, the school was run part-time with Bessiebelle State School (School No. 1238), until a new school, Broadwater (Bessiebelle) State School (School No. 2147), opened in 1879. At a few different times during the 1880s, Homerton State School was worked part-time with Mount Clay State School (School No. 2384). In 1898, it was worked part-time with Condah South State School (School No. 3055) and at a later date was likely also worked part-time with Lake Condah State School (School No. 2747). 

In 1900, Homerton State School was closed for repairs, and after a new site was identified at Ettrick, in 1902 the school building was moved and re-opened.

Discussions about merging state schools in the area began from 1944, when it was represented by parents to the Minister of Public Instruction that students would benefit from communal facilities such as libraries, art rooms, cafeterias, and sports facilities, that would otherwise not be available at small, often single-teacher, rural schools. This discussion included existing schools at Heywood, Heathmere, Myamyn, Drumborg and Homerton.

In 1951, the official process of consolidation began, with schools progressively closing and students moving to the Heywood State School (School No. 297) site to join the newly established Heywood Consolidated School (School No. 5226) (VA 5369). These schools included Condah State School (School No. 1019) (VA 5446), Drumborg State School (School No. 1240), Hotspur State School (School No. 1260) (VA 5440), Mount Eckersley State School (School No. 1720) (VA 5402) and Myamyn State School (School No. 1692) (VA 5403).

However, it wasn’t until 1955 that Homerton State School was finally slated for consolidation, along with Heathmere State School (School No. 4526) (VA 5437). Homerton State School was officially closed on 22nd June 1955 with all the students moving to Heywood Consolidated School (School No. 5226) (VA 5369). While it was thought to move the Homerton school building to the Heywood site, it was eventually deemed too old and instead became used as a community hall.
title: Homerton State School (School No. 1400)

description:
Homewood State School began unofficially as Gill’s Gully School, operating from the home of a local resident and parent from January 1874. In July of that year, a barn on the same property was leased to the Education Department VA 714), and the school was officially opened as Yea State School (School No. 1433), serving Victoria’s Upper Goulburn region near the Yea and Seymour townships.

In August 1874, the school began operating part time with King Parrot Creek School (later to become School No. 1878) under the shared number 1433, with a combined average attendance of 27 students. Yea State School became full time in May 1877.   

In July 1878, a portable school with two-room teacher’s quarters was erected on a nearby site, selected by the Department in 1874, accommodating up to 30 students. 

In April 1885 the school was renamed Homewood State School, as it was located within one mile of the newly established Homewood railway station. 

Due to low enrolments, the school was closed from September 1908 to November 1912, reopening part-time with Doogalook State School (School No. 2467) (VA 5430). During the 1915-1916 summer holidays, Homewood and Doogalook schools merged onto a central site donated by a local resident. The building from Doogalook State School was removed and re-erected on this central site, while the building from the previous Homewood State School site was sold in 1918 to a local family for use on their property as a machinery shed.

Homewood State School became unstaffed in March 1971 and permanently closed in December 1971.

The site was sold in January 1975 to Saint’s Peter and Paul’s Primary School, East Doncaster for use as a school camp.
title: Homewood State School (School No. 1433; previously known as Yea State School 1874 – 1885; also known as Gill’s Gully State School)

description:
Hotspur State School (School No. 1260) (VA 5440) was a co-educational primary school in the small town of Hotspur, in the Glenelg region of south-west Victoria. It first opened on 1st September 1873 under the Head Teacher John Hendy. It operated until its closure in 1951, as part of the government's consolidation policy for rural schools which saw the closure and consolidation of a number of primary schools in the region.

Prior to the establishment of this school, there was a previous Hotspur Common School (School No. 310), which was in operation from as early as 1864 (subject to further research). From early 1873, petitions were raised to establish a new school at Hotspur, and a new site was accordingly acquired for a new state school.

At some point during 1921 to 1930, Hotspur State School worked part-time with the nearby Morven State School (School No. 3826). 

Discussions about merging state schools in the area began from 1944, when it was represented by parents to the Minister of Public Instruction that students would benefit from communal facilities such as libraries, art rooms, cafeterias, and sports facilities, that would otherwise not be available at small, often single-teacher, rural schools. This discussion included existing schools at Heywood, Heathmere, Myamyn, Drumborg and Homerton.

In 1951, the official process of consolidation began, with schools progressively closing and students moving to the Heywood State School (School No. 297) site to join the newly established Heywood Consolidated School (School No. 5226) (VA 5369). As well as Hotspur, these schools included Condah State School (School No. 1019) (VA 5446), Drumborg State School (School No. 1240), Myamyn State School (School No. 1692) (VA 5403) and Mount Eckersley State School (School No. 1720) (VA 5402). 

Hotspur State School was officially closed on 6th February 1951 and the Hotspur school building was moved to form part of the new school site.
title: Hotspur State School (School No. 1260)

description:
Norlane West Primary School (School No. 4880) (VA 5441) was a coeducational primary school located in the Geelong suburb of Norlane.

The school first opened in 1962, as a response to a rapid growth of Housing Commission in the area. During 1960-61, Norlane State School (School No. 4734) (VA 4629) had become overcrowded and so the Education Department (VA 714) purchased additional land on Peacock Avenue to form the new Norlane West State School. In 1963, four new rooms were added and by 1965, enrolment had reached 554 pupils.
