Located in Chewton on Djaara Country in central Victoria, this school first opened as a Common School in October 1870. The original schoolhouse was located opposite the Town Hall.

Initial enrolment in the school was 33 (74 boys and 59 girls). This included students from Common School No. 139 and Common School 153.

A new brick schoolhouse was built in 1871 at a site known as ‘the Park’; subsequently, the school was locally known as the ‘Park School’.

It became a State School at some stage between 1873 and 1878, following the Education Act (Vic) 1872, which established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and a subsequent change to school naming conventions.

In September 1892 Chewton East State School No. 1928 was made an adjunct of State School No. 1054 due to declining attendance. At the time there were 83 pupils attending Chewton East.

By 1900, the school was overcrowded, with the number of students attending the school having grown to 333. It wasn’t until 1911 that a new school building was constructed and opened on Hunter Street. The old school building was demolished in 1917.

In 1927 a pine tree plantation was created. The trees would be sold when grown to raise money for the school. The first trees were sold for £1,182 pounds, with the money invested and used to buy equipment for the school.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school’s name was changed to Chewton Primary School.

The school building and grounds have undergone numerous developments over the years, including upgrading and restoring the heritage-listed 1911 building, modernizing teaching spaces, and developing outdoor play areas and gardens.

Chewton Primary School is still in operation as of 2025.
title: Chewton Primary School (School No. 1054; previously known as Chewton Common School 1870 - c.1873, Chewton State School c.1873 - c.1970)

description:
Gisborne Secondary College (School No. 7857) (VA 5487) is a co-educational secondary school located in Gisborne, in the Macedon Ranges, about 57 km north-west of metropolitan Melbourne. 

The school first opened in 1981 as Gisborne High Technical School. The name was changed in 1990 to Gisborne Secondary School, in line with a broader move away from specialised technical schools, and a change in high school naming conventions, in the 1980s and 1990s.

As of 2025, Gisborne Secondary College continues to operate.  It continues to offer specialised trade learning facilities, with a dedicated trades hub due to be completed in 2026.
title: Gisborne Secondary College (School No. 7857; previously known as Gisborne High Technical School 1981 - 1990)

description:
Northcote Primary School (School No. 1401) (VA 5488) is a co-educational primary school in the suburb of Northcote, in the inner north of Melbourne.

The school was first established in May 1874. It was variously known as Helen Street State School (for the street on which it was located), and as Northcote State School. It was the first state school to open in the area after the passing of the Education Act in 1872 and replaced a number of existing denominational schools. The school was designed by the Education Department Architect, Henry Bastow, in the Gothic Revival style common to state schools of the time. 

Increasing population in the area meant that additional brick rooms and an office were added to Northcote State School in 1886, plus accommodation for infants and a caretaker’s cottage in 1888. In 1891, a new state school was established in the area, also called Northcote State School (School No. 3139; later called Wales Street State School), which was expected to ease some of the pressure of increasing enrolments. It operated as an adjunct to Northcote State School (Helen Street) from 1891 until 1903.

From 1926 until the end of 1957, Northcote State School also ran central, or post-primary classes. In 1958 Keon Park Technical School (School No. 7210) (VA 3777) occupied rooms at Northcote State School for its first year of operation, as did Preston East Technical School (School No. 7300) in 1960. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Northcote Primary School. 

As of 2025, Northcote Primary School continues to operate. The school has retained the original Victorian and later Edwardian heritage buildings, which received extensive upgrades and modernisation from 2018 to 2020. 

Northcote Primary School should not be confused with the following schools that also operated in the area:
  • Northcote Wesleyan School (School No. 460; previously known as Newmarket School), operating from 1854 – 1874
  • Northcote Church of England School (School No. 470), operating from 1860 – 1874
  • Wales St Primary School (School No. 3139; previously known as Northcote State School and Upper Northcote State School), operating from 1891 – present
  • Northcote High School (School No. 8180; previously Northcote Boys High School), operating from 1926 – present 
  • Northcote Technical School, operating from 1966 - 1991
title: Northcote Primary School (School No. 1401; also known as Helen Street School; previously known as Northcote State School 1874 – c.1970)

description:
Scotchmans Lead State School (School No. 589) (VA 5489) was a government primary school located at Scotchmans Lead, a mining settlement near Ballarat and approximately two miles from Buninyong. The area was also known as Yarrowee.

The school opened in January 1859 as a church school and likely operated from a schoolroom attached to St. Francis’ Church. In 1863, the average attendance was 53 students.

In 1869, a new school building was built and the school became recognised as a Common School by the Board of Education (VA 713).

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming known as Scotchmans Lead State School.

In 1874, the school building was extended to accommodate 220 students. No teacher’s residence was constructed at the site.

Due to declining enrolments, the school became unstaffed in 1958. Under departmental policy, schools with low or no enrolments could be destaffed, allowing for the possibility of reopening if enrolments increased. Following a period of destaffing, the school was permanently closed in February 1963.
title: Scotchmans Lead State School (School No. 589; previously known as Scotchmans Lead School 1859 – 1869; Scotchmans Lead Common School 1869 – 1873)

description:
Yuille Primary School (School No. 5198) (VA 5490) was a coeducational primary school, located in Gillies Street, Wendouree, in the northern suburbs of Ballarat. It first opened in 1980.

In 2006, Yuille Primary School closed and merged with Grevillea Park Primary School (School No. 4701) to form Yuille Park Community College (School No. 5520; previously known as Yuille/Grevillea Park Primary School 2007 – 2008; Yuille Park P-8 Community College 2008 - 2024) (VA 5467). The former primary school site continues to be used as the Yuille Campus.
title: Yuille Primary School (School No. 5198)

description:
Lalbert West State School (School No. 4541) (VA 5491) was a coeducational primary school located in the rural district of Lalbert, approximately 40km south of Swan Hill in north-western Victoria.

The school first opened in 1936, at the request of local parents. It operated out of a leased two-room building.

Just ten years later, in April 1946, a shortage of teachers led to the closure of Lalbert West State School, with the students conveyed instead to Lalbert State School (School No. 559).
title: Lalbert West State School (School No. 4541)

description:
Tittybong State School (School No. 2583) (VA 5492) was a small coeducational government school in the regional town of Tittybong, within the Gannawarra Shire in northwest Victoria.

A formal application for a school was first made by residents in 1880 but was denied by the Department of Education (VA 714) due to there being only 10 school age children within 3 miles of the proposed site. In 1883 the residents renewed their application and forwarded a petition through the Hon. M.P W. Madden, stating that the nearest school at the time was 14 miles away. The site proposed by the residents was only 3-4 miles north on the Swan Hill Road near Tittybong Home Station, which would suit the 15-20 children ready to attend. The District Inspector this time recommended the establishment of a half-time school, using the building materials taken from a site at Towanninie East. Erection of a portable building was completed in March 1884 and Tittybong State School (School No. 2583) opened on 18 August, running half-time with Towaninnie State School (School No. 2427). The combined average attendance of the two was 27 (13 boys and 14 girls). By 1886 this had fallen to 19 (12 boys and 7 girls).

In January 1889 the Towanninie school was burned down and Tittybong ran as a full-time school, with an average attendance of 7–the total number of children living in the town at the time. Many farmers and families had moved away due to bad crops and water scarcity, and there was believed to be no prospect of improved attendance. Because of this, the school was closed in May the same year, and the school building was moved to Quambatook (School No. 2443).

The school re-opened and ran half time with Lalbert Road State School (School No. 2990) on the 8th of October 1895 after several years of agitation from locals and a steady population increase in the district. A new 42’ x 20’ Mechanics Institute building was erected by the residents to the north of the old school site to serve as the school building. The average attendance in November of that year was 13.

In October 1901 Tittybong ceased operating half-time with Lalbert State School and ran as a full-time school until August 1903, when it once again moved to half-time, alongside Kalpienung State School (School No. 3387). On the 9th of March 1905 Tittybong was closed and replaced by a new school – Cannie State School (School No. 3498), which opened the following day. Parents petitioned for Tittybong to be reopened in 1917 and 1919, submitting lists of up to 25 prospective students. A building with attached living quarters was removed from Barraport State School (School No. 2952) and re-erected at Tittybong for £30, and the school was reopened on the 14th of May 1920, with Kathleen Coleman as Head Teacher.

By 1938 the average attendance was 15, and after no improvement the Department decided to no longer appoint a teacher to the school, unofficially closing it from February 1946. Parents were advised to have their children enrolled for Correspondence learning. The school was later officially closed on the 11th of August 1947 and the building was sold to the Swan Hill Boy Scouts for £110. The site, which had originally been donated to the Department by a Mr. King, was sold for £15 to Messrs. E.E. and L.H. Richmond in March 1952.


Much of the above information was produced by Research Officer Olga Marion of the Education Department, December 1982.
title: Tittybong State School (School No. 2583)

description:
Albion Primary School (School No. 427) (VA 5495) is a coeducational primary school located in the Western suburbs of Melbourne.

The school was first opened in 1926 as Albion State School. It was built on a 4-acre block of land owned by H.V. McKay and was intended to ease overcrowding at the existing Sunshine State School (School No. 3113) (VA 5715).  

In 1961, the new Ardeer State School (School No. 4848) opened nearby, which caused Albion State School’s enrolments to drop. Consequently, space was made available for the erection of a central library at Albion. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Albion Primary School.

As of 2025, Albion Primary School continues to operate and in 2026, it will celebrate its 100th anniversary.

Albion Primary School should not be confused with Albion School (School No. 6), a non-vested Church of England school then Common School, that existed in the same area from 1855 – 1872.
title: Albion Primary School (School No. 4265; previously known as Albion State School 1926 – c.1970)

description:
Athlone Primary School (School No. 3623) (VA 5494) was a coeducational primary school located in in Athlone, along the Drouin – Korumburra Road in the Shire of Baw Baw (VA 3672).

The school first opened in 1909, as Longwarry South State School (also known as Longwarry South-East State School). It was conducted semi-officially out of residential houses before a single classroom school building was built in September 1909. In 1965, the original building was demolished and replaced with a two-classroom building. 

It seems that the name of the school was changed to Athlone State School between 1910 and 1912, though the exact date remains subject to further research.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Athlone Primary School.

In 2013, Athlone Primary School was closed due to declining student numbers, and the land was declared surplus to educational needs by the Victorian government.
title: Athlone Primary School (School No. 3623; previously known as Longwarry South, or South-East, State School 1909 – c.1912; Athlone State School c.1912 – c.1970)

description:
Mount Clear Primary School (School No. 427) (VA 5495) is a coeducational primary school located in the outer suburbs of Ballarat, six kilometres south of the city centre.

The Mount Clear school was first opened in 1858. It was requested by local citizens to meet the needs of the gold mining community at the time and was responsible to the Independent Denomination, under the Denominational School Board of Education (VA 703). 

In 1862, through the Common Schools Act, the Victorian Parliament abolished the two existing centralised boards and created a single Board of Education (VA 713).  In 1863, the school was accordingly re-named Mount Clear Common School and was given the Victorian school number 427. 

The Education Act of 1872 later established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked a further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Mount Clear State School from 1 January 1873. For a few months in 1877-1878, Mount Clear State School accommodated a Night School. 

From 1950, year 7 and 8 classes were no longer run at the school, in line with a shift towards dedicated post-primary schooling. In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Mount Clear Primary School.

When it was first established, the Mount Clear school initially operated of the local Union Church building. In 1863, the school moved to a newly built schoolhouse, with the hectare of land officially reserved for a school in 1865. In 1867 the building was extended to meet increasing enrolments. In 1880, a new two-room school building was erected. In 1922, additional land was purchased by the Education Department, almost doubling the school’s footprint. In 1950, a wooden teacher’s residence was erected and in 1969, six brick-veneer classrooms were built. 

As of 2025, Mount Clear Primary School continues to operate.
title: Mount Clear Primary School (School No. 427; previously known as Mount Clear School 1858 - 1964; Mount Clear Common School 1864 – c.1872; Mount Clear State School c.1872 – c.1970)

description:
Bendigo East Primary School (School No. 3893) (VA 5496) was a coeducational primary school located in the outer suburbs of Ballarat, six kilometres south of the city centre.

The school was first opened in 1916 as Bendigo East State School, with a new brick building erected for it on a site close to the railway workshops. In 1924, part of the land was excised for railway purposes, with adjoining Crown land reserved for the school in exchange. 

From February 1959, the school was proclaimed a training school for the Bendigo Teachers College (VA 3090). Additional classrooms were built in 1959, 1963 and 1969.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Bendigo East Primary School.

At the end of 1998, Bendigo East Primary School merged with White Hills Secondary College (School No. 7405) to form White Hills P-10 College (School No. 7405). The Bendigo East Primary School site was closed at the end of Term 1 of 1999, with the school consolidating on the White Hills Secondary College site. In 2000, White Hills P-10 College was renamed Weerona College Bendigo.
title: Bendigo East Primary School (School No. 3893; previously known as Bendigo East State School 1916 – c.1970)

description:
Gruyere Primary School (School No. 2956) (VA 5497), originally known as Gruyere South State School, was a co-educational primary school that opened in August 1889. Located in the Yarra Valley, 43km northeast of Melbourne, the school initially operated out of a leased building. Around 1919, it moved to a new building on a permanent site, with the shelter shed being relocated to the new location as well.

Over the years, enrolments at Gruyere Primary fluctuated, with 19 students in 1935, 27 students in 1950, and just 11 students in 1971. In 2017, the school had an enrolment of 28 students.

A pine plantation was established on the school property in 1949, which was later milled in 1967 for school profit as part of the School Endowment Pine Plantation.

Between 1958 and 1979 the school name was changed and shortened from “Gruyere South State School” to “Gruyere Primary School”.  This change likely occurred in 1970, as there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Victoria Government Gazette notices from around this time reflect the change.

In 2021, the school was part of the Wollombi Cluster of Small Schools. The cluster also consisted of Chum Creek Primary School (School No. 3279), Dixons Creek Primary School (School No. 1585), Don Valley Primary School (School No. 3956), Hoddles Creek Primary School (School No. 2541), Silvan Primary School (School No. 1801), Toolangi Primary School (School No. 3237) and Yering Primary School (School No. 1034). The cluster encouraged small schools to join combined camps, events, and activities. Details on the Wollombi Cluster, including its active dates, are subject to further research.

Gruyere Primary School appears to have been destaffed around 2021, likely due to low enrolment.  The school has continued to receive annual maintenance funding for bushfire preparedness from 2018 to 2024.

School councils can vote to close or destaff a school if enrolments are low or absent for the upcoming year. Destaffing allows a school to reopen if enrolments increase. After a period of being destaffed, typically several years, a school is officially closed.

As of 2024, the school does not appear to have been permanently closed.

Gruyere Primary School (School No. 2956) (VA 5497) should not be confused with the former Gruyere State School (School No. 1695) (VA 5513), which operated from 1879 – 1892.
title: Gruyere Primary School (School No. 2956; previously known as Gruyere South State School 1889 – c.1970)

description:
The Docklands Authority was formed in accordance with the Docklands Authority Act 1991, which came into operation on 5 July 1991. Docklands Authority was a statutory body and held its property on behalf of the Crown. It was responsible to the Minister for Major Projects.

The role of the Docklands Authority was to redevelop the Docklands area which involved:
  • Promoting and assisting in the coordination of the area's economic, cultural and social development
  • Promoting and encouraging private sector involvement
  • Overseeing and coordinating the development by others
  • Preparing and implementing development strategies
  • Investigating infrastructure options
  • Preparing and implementing infrastructure coordination plans
  • Taking, supporting, or promoting measures to encourage people to live and work in the area
  • Developing the area as an attractive environment
  • Facilitating and supporting reorganisation of port facilities
  • Promoting tourism, recreational, social and cultural activities in or for the benefit of the area

Projects managed by the Docklands Authority included Stadium development, NewQuay, Victoria Harbour, Gasworks remediation, Collins Street Extension and Studio City.

In 2003 the Victorian Urban Development Authority Act 2003 amended and renamed the Docklands Act 1991. The Docklands Authority was abolished and its responsibilities transferred to the Victoria Urban Development Authority (VA 5004), essentially merging with the Urban and Regional Land Corporation (VA 5295).

description:
Grampians Health was established on 1 November 2021 when Ballarat Health Services (VA 5500), Edenhope and District Memorial Hospital (VA 1685), Stawell Regional Health (VA 1736) and Wimmera Health Care Group (VA 5501) were formally amalgamated to form one public health service according to the Health Services Act 1988.

Grampians Health is based in Ballarat and operates across five campus hospitals: Ballarat Base Hospital, Stawell Hospital, Wimmera Base Hospital (Horsham), Dimboola Hospital and Edenhope Hospital. The health service also operates the Queen Elizabeth Centre, Ballarat, and Edenhope Health and Wellness Hub, which provide a number of allied health services, community programs and outpatient services. In addition to these hospitals, Grampians Health delivers several specialised health services including dental, aged care, disability care and mental health.

Grampians Health was formed during the COVID-19 pandemic and was responsible for leading a number of pandemic responses in the Grampians area. Responsibilities included the rollout and training of wearing personal protective equipment and risk minimisation strategies; COVID testing, vaccination, infection control and minimisation and outbreak management of the region’s public and private Aged Care and Disability Services providers; and the management of several community testings sites. Grampians Health was also responsible for establishing and managing several community vaccination hubs, provided outreach vaccination services to high-risk industries and communities, and worked directly with Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisations to support COVID vaccination and testing within indigenous communities. Many of these initiatives were led by the Grampians Public Health Unit (GPHU), established January 2021 by the Department of Health (VA 5255) to be administered by Ballarat Health Services prior to amalgamation, who partnered with local leaders across the regions to lead these initiatives.

GPHU is one of nine public health units that were established to manage pandemic responses. Since then, the GPHU’s responsibilities shifted to more general public health activities including promoting healthy lifestyles, research disease and injury prevention, and detecting, preventing and responding to communicable diseases and other threats to the general health of the Grampians residents. The GPHU is managed by Grampians Health and works with health services and other agencies throughout the Grampians Region.

Grampians Health was nominated as the lead health service of the Grampians Region Health Service Partnership, one of many health service partnerships created by the Department of Health to foster greater collaboration between health services throughout Victoria. Key priorities include COVID-19 responses, reforming elective surgery, implementing at home health care reforms, addressing recommendations of the Royal Commission into Mental Health and developing gender equality action plans. Through this partnership, Grampians Health have led the rollout of the Health Department’s Better at Home strategy to provide health services such as at-home chemotherapy, chronic illness support, outpatient at home care services, telehealth, and district nursing.

Grampians Health is also a key member of the Western Alliance, an academic health science centre focused on regional health outcomes, which includes public and private health services, universities and other research centres. Grampians Health is also a member of the Victorian Collaborative Centre of Mental Health and Wellbeing, a partnership led by The University of Melbourne and Royal Melbourne Hospital designed to allow people with lived experience, researchers and health professionals lead improvements in the Victorian mental health system.

Aged Care
Grampians Health is one of the largest providers of public residential aged care in Australia. Aged Care services include residential care, dementia and cognitive impairment care, mental health services, respite care and in-home care. Facilities include:
  • Talbot Place, Ballarat Central
  • Eureka Village, Ballarat East
  • Geoffrey Cutter Centre, Ballarat East
  • Hailey House, Ballarat North
  • Jack Lonsdale Lodge, Sebastopol
  • James Thomas Court, Sebastopol
  • W.B. Messer, Wendouree
  • P.S. Hobson, Wendouree
  • Bill Crawford Lodge, Ballarat Central
  • Steel Haughton Aged Acute Unit, Ballarat Central
  • Barkuma Respite Centre, Horsham
  • Kurrajong Lodge, Horsham
  • Wimmera Nursing Home, Horsham
  • Dimboola Nursing Home, Dimboola
  • Macpherson Smith Residential Care, Stawell
  • Lakeside Living, Edenhope
  • Barkala Flats, Edenhope

Cancer Centres
The Ballarat Regional Integrated Cancer Centre provides cancer treatment and support including radiation therapy, Wellness Centre, day oncology, a symptom and urgent review clinic, and accommodation services. The centre also supports clinical trials of cancer treatments. Day oncology services are also available in Horsham and Stawell.

Radiation therapy in the region is provided by the Ballarat Austin Radiation Oncology Centre and the Stawell Austin Radiation Oncology Service, both of which are made possible by a partnership between Grampians Health and Austin Health.

Indigenous Health Services
Grampians Health provides Aboriginal Hospital Liaison officers at each hospital to provide a culturally safe environment for patients and families, facilitate access to preventative health programs and health services, assist patients during decision-making and treatment, advise clinical staff on patients’ cultural needs, liaise with staff regarding patient care issues, and provide appropriate support services upon discharge. These liaison teams also provide contracted services to East Grampians Health Services (VA 5617) and Beaufort Skipton Health Service (VA 5618).

At the time of constitution, the Grampians Health catchment area encompassed lands of the Wotjobaluk, Jaadwa, Jardwadjali, Wergaia, Jupagalk, Djab wurrung and Wadawurrung peoples.

Women and Children’s Health Services
Specialists Women and Children’s health services provided by Grampians Health are largely administered at the Ballarat campus, which includes a Maternity Unit, Parent & Infant Unit, Special Care Nursery, Paediatric and Adolescent Ward, Breastfeeding Services, Fertility Care Service, and an Early Parenting Centre as well as specialist mental health services. In December 2022, the Wimmera Base Hospital expanded its maternal care capability with the establishment of a new Maternal Outpatients Unit. The hospital also provides antenatal classes, breastfeeding support and domiciliary postnatal services

Mental Health Services
Grampians Health manages a number of mental health services in Ballarat, including inpatient care, community services, peer support and consumer/carer consultants, ranging from perinatal to aged care. Grampians Health also manages community mental health teams for adults Horsham and Ararat. Psychiatric services are also available in Horsham, as well as Drug and Alcohol coordinators.

Medical Centres and Oral Health
Grampians Health operates several medical clinics that provide access to General Physicians, Surgeons, and various specialists. These centres include:
  • Alan Wolff Medical Centre, Horsham
  • Read Street Medical Clinic, Horsham
  • John Pickering Medical Centre, Dimboola
  • Stawell Medical Centre, Stawell

Grampians Health also provides oral health programs and provides public dental health services at Yuille Park Dental Clinic Wendouree, Grampians Health Dental Clinic and School Sebastopol, as well as dental clinics in Horsham and Edenhope.

description:
Ballarat Health Services (BHS) was formed in December 1996 when the Ballarat Base Hospital (VA 1263) and The Queen Elizabeth Centre, Ballarat (VA 1284) merged, along with the Queen Elizabeth Centre subsidiary Ballarat and District Aged Persons’ Homes Association. When established, BHS was appointed as an approved mental health service known as Grampians Psychiatric Services (GPS) under the Mental Health Act 1986.

Integration of psychiatric health care into mainstream health services was a major focus of BHS throughout the 1990s. GPS was established to provide psychiatric services to the Grampians Region, including areas outside of BHS’s usual catchment area. The service built on the teleconferencing program established in 1995 to expand its psychiatric services to remote communities in the Grampians area, even reaching international patients by the late 1990s. The Steele Haughton Unit was opened in 1996, which provided acute and extended Geriatric Psychiatry care at the Queen Elizabeth Centre, and the Community and Inpatient Psychiatric unit for adult, child and adolescent psychiatric services was officially opened in July 1997. A Clinical Academic Unit was created in partnership with the University of Melbourne to establish research and education programs in 1999. This included the development of a Rural Psychiatry module for the Graduate Diploma of Community Mental Health.

Other new additions to BHS in 1997 include the Gandarra palliative care unit, Argyle Lodge at the Queen Elizabeth Village, which provided dementia-specific care in lieu of the closed Argyle nursing home, and an extension of the WB Messer Hostel. A Breastfeeding Support Unit was established at the hospital in 1998, a program developed by World Health Organization and UNICEF and one of the first established in Australia. Also in 1998, the Centre Against Sexual Assault was established as a 24-hour emergency service, significantly expanding on services established by its predecessor Crisis Centre. Talbot Place aged care home was officially opened in March of that year, and the Geoffrey Cutter Centre began taking aged care residents.

The Education Resource Centre containing a 120-seat lecture theatre was opened in October 1999 followed by the Peter Heinz Rehabilitation Centre, completed December 1999, which provided allied health services including hydrotherapy pool, gymnasium, as several consulting and treatment rooms. Hailey House was moved to a purpose-built aged care hostel in Ballarat North in 2000.

In 1999 BHS began implementing central information management systems beginning with patient administration. IT projects continued with the implementation of systems for staff management and rostering, clinical information, and theatre management.

BHS began working more closely with the neighbouring private hospital St. John of God throughout the 1990s. A connecting walkway over the road separating the two hospitals was completed in 2002, allowing the two hospitals to provide shared services and work more closely on collaborative projects. One such project was establishing the Ballarat-Austin Radiation Oncology Centre (BAROC), which was developed in partnership with the Austin and Repatriation Medical Centre of the Austin Hospital (VA 1243) and officially opened in September 2002.

Other major projects completed during 2000s include the Tattersall’s Emergency Centre and a new Dialysis Unit. In May 2008 BHS assumed responsibility for the Ballarat public dental health clinic from Dental Health Services Victoria. To improve access to dental services, BHS entered into a partnership with La Trobe University to establish the clinic as a teaching clinic for dental health students. Public dental services were extended in April 2009 when BHS opened a new dental health clinic at Yuille Park Community College. Also in April 2009, BHS launched a breast screening unit for early detection of breast cancer.

In 2006 BHS began an Aboriginal Health Taskforce to work with the Ballarat and District Aboriginal Collective to improve access to health programs for First Nations peoples as well as to improve and cultural awareness and sensitivity of clinical and support staff working at BHS. Outcomes from this Taskforce included in the Aboriginal Midwife program and appointment of Aboriginal Mental Health Liaison Officers.

In 2010 Grampians Psychiatric Services was revoked as a mental health service and the Ballarat Health Service Mental Health Service was appointed under the Mental Health Act 1986. This appointment was applied to any services provided by BHS excluding residential care services defined by the Aged Care Act 1997 (Commonwealth). The service continued to deliver mental health services to the Greater Grampians region.

Other major developments in the 2010s include the opening of the Ballarat Clinical School for students from the University of Melbourne and Deakin University in June 2010; Adult Acute Unit in August 2010; the Emergency Department Short Stay Unit in February 2011; Cardiovascular Suite in October 2011; Ballarat Regional Integrated Cancer Centre in July 2013; MRI facility in June 2014; new dental clinic at Phoenix College, Sebastopol, in April 2015; helipad in June 2015; Mother and Family Mental Health Clinic in November 2015; Midlands Child, Youth and Family Mental Health clinic in July 2016; the Gardiner-Pittard wing in February 2017; and Grampians Prevention and Recovery Centre in July 2020.

BHS was key to facilitating the COVID-19 response in the Grampians Region with the establishment of the Community Vaccination Hub in March 2021, establishing the Grampians Public Health Unit, creating and managing rapid response testing teams, and supporting outbreak management and vaccination education throughout the Grampians area.

In 2021 Ballarat Health Services merged with Stawell Regional Health (VA 1736), Edenhope and District Memorial Hospital (VA 1685) and Wimmera Health Care Group (VA 5501) to form Grampians Health (VA 5499). The Ballarat Base Hospital and Queen Elizabeth Centre continued to operate under the name Grampians Health Ballarat.

description:
Wimmera Health Care Group was formed in November 1995 when the Wimmera Base Hospital (VA 1271) (in Horsham) and Dimboola District Hospital (VA 1680) were merged. The merger coincided with the opening of a new acute care hospital in Horsham, which began taking patients in December 1995 and officially opened in April 1996. The original hospital building, constructed in 1942, was later demolished to make way for new allied health facilities, dental clinic, library, administration and support services facilities, which opened officially opened in November 2001.

There were also significant renovations to residential aged care facilities in Horsham in 1996 when the Sir Robert Menzies Nursing Home and Matron Arthur House were redeveloped and brought together under one roof, forming the Wimmera Nursing Home. This was followed by the opening of the Kurrajong Lodge residential hostel in April 1997.

The Dimboola Campus received significant redevelopment of its acute care hospital, allied health service facilities and residential aged care facilities, which were officially opened in 2002. The new facility expanded the hospital to a 30-bed capacity, including four acute care beds, 16 residential aged care beds, and 10 aged care hostel beds; as well as allied health services such as dental clinic, district nursing, and social work.

In June 2019, the Wimmera Cancer Centre was officially opened after receiving its first patients in February of that year. The new facility provided specialist palliative care, community support services, and dialysis services to people with cancer living in the region.

In 2021 Wimmera Health Care Group merged with Stawell Regional Health (VA 1736), Edenhope and District Memorial Hospital (VA 1685) and Ballarat Health Services (VA 5500) to form Grampians Health (VA 5499). The Horsham and Dimboola hospitals continued to operate under the names Grampians Health Horsham and Grampians Health Dimboola.

description:
Campaspe Regional Water Authority was constituted by an Order-in-Council to take effect on the 30 March 1992 under the provisions of the Water Act 1989. The Elmore Water Board (VA 2230), Rochester Water Board (VA 2250) and Echuca Water Board (VA 2557) were abolished and their geographical areas, functions, land, liabilities, obligations, powers, property, rights and employees  became the responsibility of the new authority. At the time of establishment, the new water authority took responsibility for the following districts:
  • Echuca Sewerage and Waterworks Districts
  • Elmore Urban and Waterworks Districts
  • Lockington Urban District
  • Rochester Sewerage, Uban and Waterworks Districts

The water authority was abolished in 1994 and it's property, rights, obligations and liabilities were transferred to Coliban Regional Water Authority (VA 3996)

Regional Urban Water Authorities

Regional Urban Water Authorities are responsible for providing water supply and sewerage services to non-metropolitan urban areas. Regional authorities work with catchment management authorities and rural water authorities to supply water to regional areas and provide sewerage treatment services.

Until 2006, authorities were overseen by the membership of the authority, which consisted of qualified people to be appointed in writing by the Minister as specified by the Water Act. Collectively, membership of each water authority was to hold qualifications or experience in the business of the authority, public finance or economics, engineering, business management, commerce, banking, environmental and water resource management, and law.

Industry Reform

Water authorities underwent a program of amalgamation and structural reform throughout the 1990s under the auspices of the Office of Water Reform (later the Water Bureau, established as a division in Department of Conservation and Natural Resources VA 3097). Water Boards and Sewerage Boards were gradually replaced with regional water authorities. These authorities also took over the water management responsibilities from Local Government. 

Under Division 2 of Part 6 of the Water Act, the Minister had the power to restructure existing water authorities, to create new water authorities, unite existing water and sewerage districts, and to abolish existing water authorities. By publication of an Order-in-Council in the Victorian Government Gazette, the Minister was able to constitute a new authority to take over the property, rights, liabilities, obligations, powers, staff, and functions under the Water Act of one or more authorities, so long as the terms and conditions were agreed between the affected authorities, local councils, and the Minister. The Minister was required to provide in writing to the authorities and local councils affected by the restructuring the reasons behind the decision, ensure that a copy of the document was placed before both Houses of Parliament, and liaise with the Minister administering the Local Government Act 1989 if a local council was involved.

The membership of the new water authority as specified by the Order could not included more than three people to be appointed by the Minister unless the functions of the Authority were solely related to waterway management. Each new authority was to be a body corporate, with a common seal, be capable of being sued and of suing under its corporate name, be capable of acquiring, holding, managing, and disposing of property in accordance with the performance of its functions, and was to be capable of efficiently performing its functions and lawfully exercising its powers.

description:
The Major Transport Infrastructure Authority (MTIA) was established by an Order-in-Council on the 1 January 2019 as an administrative office in relation to the Department of Transport (VA 5250) (Victorian Government Gazette, No. S 580 Friday 21 December 2018).

With the establishment of MTIA, multiple administrative offices were abolished and responsibility for major road and rail projects was passed to MTIA. This included the following authorities: 
  • The Level Crossing Removal Authority,
  • The Major Roads Projects Authority,
  • The North East Link Authority,
  • The Rail Projects Victoria (VA 5522), and 
  • The West Gate Tunnel Authority.

MTIA worked closely with the Suburban Rail Loop Authority (SRLA) to deliver the major transport projects that make up Victoria’s Big Build initiative. 

As of 2 April 2024, by Order-in-Council, MTIA’s name changed to the Victorian Infrastructure Delivery Authority (VIDA) (Victorian Government Gazette, No. S 144 Tuesday 26 March 2024) remaining with the Department of Transport and Planning (VA 5286).

At the same time the Victorian Health Building Authority (VHBA), previously a branch of the Department of Health (VA 5255), was absorbed as a Project Office into VIDA to bring major transport and health infrastructure programs under one administrative office. The Minister for Health Infrastructure and the Minister for Transport Infrastructure retained their respective portfolios. 

As of 2024, VIDA is made up of 4 Project Offices:
  • Level Crossing Removal Project (also delivering Regional Rail Revival and Melbourne Airport Rail)
  • Major Road Projects Victoria (incorporating Big Build Roads, West Gate Tunnel Project and North East Link)
  • Metro Tunnel Project
  • Victorian Health Building Authority.

description:
On 1 January 2022, following recommendations from the Finkelstein Royal Commission into the Casino Operator and Licence, Stephen O’Bryan KC commenced as the Special Manager for the Melbourne Casino Operator, pursuant to section 36B of the Casino Control Act 1991 (Vic).

The Special Manager provided biannual reports to the Victorian Gambling and Casino Control Commission and the Minister for Casino, Gaming and Liquor Regulation assessing Crown’s reforms and associated matters relevant to whether Crown was suitable to hold the Melbourne casino operator licence.

The Special Manager’s statutory term concluded on 30 June 2024.

description:
Somers School Camp (VA 4647) is a co-educational primary school located in Somers on the Mornington Peninsula in Victoria.

The Children’s School Health and Recreation Camp (School No. 4647) first opened in February 1947 at Crow’s Nest, Queenscliff. It operated out of a training camp leased from the Commonwealth Department of the Army, who continued to occupy the site every January to train senior cadets. It was also informally referred to as Crow’s Nest Camp, and Physical Education Camp.

The Education Department (VA 714) agreed to a five-year lease and made slight changes in the site to facilitate a school camp. Part of the cost of upgrading the facilities were paid by the Department for National Fitness, whilst overall exterior maintenance was funded by the Department of the Army. The school consisted of a Head Teacher and a permanent staff of four physical educators, who lived onsite, and one transport officer. Two cooks and three assistants were also hired to provide meals throughout the 10-day camps. The camp could accommodate 100 students at one time, in addition to visiting teachers, who helped supervise students. 

The school was forced to vacate Crow’s Nest in July 1952 when the lease ended, and the Army resumed occupancy of the area. In its 5 years, 6,670 students attended over 99 camps, as well as several teachers during Secondary Seminar and Teachers’ College Training camps. The camp officially closed 9th September 1952.

Both the Director and Minister of Education were eager to re-establish a State-run school camp, as every other state in Australia had one or more.  In 1958, land in Somers, formerly a Commonwealth Migrant Holding Centre, was selected to reopen the camp.  Somers Migrant Centre State School (School No. 4653) had also operated on the site from 1949 to 1957 with 9 children in attendance.  In 1958, when no longer needed as a Migrant Centre and school, the camp was purchased by the Education Department.

The purchase of the camp included the entirety of the buildings and assets already onsite, including but not limited to: 
•    An administrative block
•    22 huts to provide schoolrooms and living quarters
•    Shower buildings and toilet blocks
•    Hall and cinema
•    Playground
•    Library
•    Sewerage, electric light and water supply

Anything not purchased by the Education Department was purchased by the Department of the Interior. In June 1959, the name officially changed from Health and Recreation Camp to Children’s School Camp (more commonly referred to as Children’s School Camp, Somers).

In September 1959 the first camp was held with 100 boys from the St Kilda Inspectorate. The official opening being held on the 27th of November 1959.

Initially, bookings for the 10-day Grade 5 and 6 camps were taken but soon afterwards it was necessary to operate on a rotation basis throughout all districts in the state due to popularity and support. Inspectorial districts were allotted camps by the Assistant Chief Inspector of Primary Schools on application from District Inspectors. If selected, a District Inspector appointed a secretary who organised the selection of 160 boys or girls between the ages of 10 and 14 to attend. However, selection of children within schools was the responsibility of the Head Teacher. Eight visiting teachers were selected by the District Inspector. 

At the conclusion of each camp, the District Secretary was required to forward to the Education Department, through the District Inspector, a brief report of the camp. As of 1994, a similar system of compiled evaluation from the District Secretary and visiting teachers was still in place, though camps were 9-days only. 

The camps alternated boys’ camps and girls’ camps until August of 1976 when four new purpose-built dormitory blocks were erected, which replaced all the sleeping huts. This enabled the camps to become co-educational with 192 pupils attending at the same time. It is not known when the rotation of inspectorial districts ceased, and school camps instead were conducted with students from only one school at a time.

The focus of these camps is environmental, outdoor recreational and adventure activities. Students can participate in art and drama, boating, bushcraft, orienteering, ropes courses, archery, and more. 
The site adjoins the historical Coolart Wetlands and Homestead, of which its bird and wildlife are used extensively in the camp’s environmental studies programs. 

In 1994, the camp was inducted into the Schools of the Future program, with the goal to become self-managing. Reflecting its unique position in the Victorian Education System, although it had a school number, it was not until then that a school council was formed, despite school councils becoming legislated with the Education Act 1958 (Vic). Additionally, they had no formal school principal until this date, instead having a camp director. 

In 2000, the name changed from Children’s School Camp to Somers School Camp.

In 2007, the school type changed from Camp to Primary, after representations from the Residential Outdoor Schools Association.

In February 2010, Somers School Camp expanded with the addition of Woorabinda School Camp as an annexed campus and assigned the school number 4647-02. Located on the north shore of Lake Narracan, Woorabinda School Camp was originally an inspectorate camp for the children of the Warragul inspectorate. The buildings were once the nurses’ quarters from the Yallourn Hospital, and includes a combined kitchen and dining building, girls dormitory, boys dormitory, a recreation building, an equipment storage shed and two staff residences. The Department paid for the necessary capital improvements to make the camp compliant with building code and safety standards, and for bushfire readiness. 

Woorabinda School Camp takes a younger cohort, Grades 3 to 5, for shorter, three- and five-day programs. The two sites have the capacity to cater for 6,080 students across both campuses each year.

The Somers School Camp and Woorabinda School Camp are operational as of 2024. 

Researchers should note that Somers School Camp is not to be confused with Lord Somers Camp, a privately-owned recreation camp located on adjoining sites, or with Somers Primary School (School No. 4458; previously known as Somers State School; Palm Beach State School) located in the town of Somers. For further correspondence regarding the sites when under occupation of the Commonwealth Government, see the National Archives of Australia.
title: Somers School Camp (School No. 4647; previously known as Children’s School Health and Recreation Camp 1947 – c. 1958; Health and Recreation Camp 1959; Children’s School Camp 1959 – 2000)

description:
Hesket Primary School is a small government school located in Hesket, within the Macedon Ranges Shire of Central Victoria.

The school was first established following an application sent to the Board of Education (VA 713) by residents of Newham and Rochford in June 1869, accompanied by a list of 71 children in the district. In November the same year, a grant of £50 and teacher’s salary was provided by the Board, with the community expected to match this amount. Half an acre was donated by Richard Bowen for use by the school, upon which residents built a 10m x 5m wooden building with a brick chimney and shingle roof. A detached teacher’s residence consisting of two rooms was rented by the Head Teacher. This residence was later sold and removed from the site in 1883.

The school, then known as The American Steam Sawmill School, was opened on the 30th of May 1870. The name of the school was changed to Hesket State School, No. 1004, in 1879.

By 1884, net enrolment was 87 and the average attendance was between 30-40. By 1886 the school was overcrowded, and a new wooden schoolroom with attached 4-roomed quarters was built. The old building was sold for approximately £13.

Overcrowding again became an issue in early 1890, causing children to be excluded from the school. In 1908 a new timber classroom was added.

From 1911 to 1926 enrolment rose from 43 to 53. In 1928 a School Plantation was acquired; such plantations were seen as a good way to reforest land that had previously been logged. They also provided schools with another income stream as timber would eventually be logged and sold with proceeds going to the school.

During the 1930s enrolment fluctuated between 25-30. A series of buildings and ground works were completed, including the construction of a sports oval, a cricket pitch, a basketball court and a small pavilion.

From 1960 – 1970, enrolment averaged around 20 pupils per year. In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term “State school” to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use “primary school” in the name. Accordingly, the school’s name was changed to Hesket Primary School.

During the early 1980s, the School Council sought additional land, and the Education Department (VA 714) confirmed the leasing of .4 of a hectare from local farmer, Mr. Bert Bowen. The school also joined the Mobile Area Resource Committee (MARC Van). This service provided a mobile library and library trained teacher for the school.

An all-time low enrolment of 7 placed the school under threat of closure in 1987, however within the next three years it had risen to 42, and the school was able to continue operating. Internal works were carried out on the old school building in 1990, adding a computer space and storage area to the southern wall. A third classroom was added the same year.

Until this time the school’s playground was across the road from the school building. This meant that children had to be escorted over the road to use it, creating concern for the safety of staff and students. Subsequently, just over 6,000 square metres of land was purchased by the Ministry of Education and Training (VA 1112), again from Mr Bert Bowen, and added to the school site. The old playground was sold.

During 1992 – 2009 enrolment grew to 81 before settling between 55 and 65. During this time there were numerous improvements made to the school facilities. This included the remodelling of the teacher’s residence to provide an art room, an art store and a small canteen/food preparation area; various groundwork to provide storage and sporting areas; a new block of toilets constructed in 2003, and in 2006 an extra classroom was added, and two portable rooms were replaced by a new Mod 5 double room.

From 2019 – 2025 the school’s enrolment grew from 18 students to 78.

As of 2025 this school is still in operation.
title: Hesket Primary School (School No. 1004; previously The American Steam Sawmill School 1870-1879; Hesket State School 1879-1970)

description:
Clayton Primary School (School No. 4747) (VA 5509) was a government primary school located on Browns Road, Clayton, in Melbourne’s south-eastern suburbs.

The school opened in February 1956 during a period of residential growth in the Clayton area after World War 2. Opening enrolment was 316 students, increasing to almost 600 students by the following year.

The school initially comprised eight classrooms. Five additional classrooms were added in 1957, increasing the total to thirteen. A further two classrooms were added in 1965.

Enrolment declined to 169 students by 1996 and to 61 students by 2010.

Clayton Primary School permanently closed in December 2010.

Clayton Primary School should not be confused with Clayton North Primary School (School No. 734), which operated nearby from 1865 and was previously named Clayton’s Road State School and Clayton State School.
title: Clayton Primary School (School No. 4747; also known as Brown’s Road State School)

description:
Newlyn Primary School (School No. 453) (VA 5510) was established in 1858, originally operating out of the local Wesleyan Church. In June 1861, the National School Board (VA 919) subsidised a two-acre site, and local residents erected a new wooden building for the school, creating a National School in the rural community of Newlyn, north of Ballarat.

Following the passing of the Common Schools Act in 1862, the two existing centralised boards were abolished and replaced with a single Board of Education (VA 713). The school was renamed Newlyn Common School and was allocated the number 453. 

An infant room for younger students was added to the site in 1870 and an additional brick building was built on the site in 1887.

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Newlyn State School around this time.  

A four-room teacher’s residence had been constructed nearby in 1865, however this was replaced by a new on site five-room residence in 1913.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Newlyn Primary School around this time. 

Enrolments increased from six students in 2018 to 28 students in 2023. As of 2025, Newlyn Primary School remains in operation, with the brick building built in 1887 still in use.
title: Newlyn Primary School (School No. 453; previously known as Newlyn National School 1861 – 1862; Newlyn Common School 1862 – c.1875; Newlyn State School c. 1875 – c. 1970)

description:
Beaconsfield Primary School (School No. 3033) (VA 5511) opened in June 1890 as Beaconsfield Railway Station School.  The co-educational primary school is located in Melbourne’s South Eastern suburb of Beaconsfield and initially operated from a leased private residence.  Within a few months, the school moved into a new brick building on land purchased by the Education Department (VA 714) at the corner of Lyall Avenue and Old Princes Highway. A teachers’ residence was completed on the site in 1892.

From March 1895 to March 1902 the school operated part-time with Berwick State School (School No. 40) due to low enrolments. During this period, Beaconsfield offered classes up to Grade 3, while older students attended Berwick for Grades 4 to 6. 

Beaconsfield Railway Station School reopened full time in March 1902 and enrolments grew steadily from 28 students in August 1902 to over 50 students by March 1903.  Between 1902 and 1911, the school’s name was changed to Beaconsfield State School. A shelter shed was added in 1905, and in 1907, an extra room was built onto the teacher’s residence, expanding it to five rooms. That same year, a measles epidemic affected three-quarters of the student population, prompting the Health Inspector to close the school for three weeks. 

In 1910, neighbouring land was leased as a student play area and was later purchased by the Department in July 1915. During repairs that same year, the school temporarily operated from the local Mechanics’ Hall for six weeks. 

In 1944, the front section of the school grounds was sold to the Country Roads Board (VA 722). By 1954, enrolments had exceeded 80 students, prompting the addition of a third classroom in March 1955 and the construction of an office. In 1956, five acres of neighbouring land were purchased, likely forming what became known as the ‘Cardinia Dam Site’.

The teachers’ residence was condemned in 1962 after a fire damaged the laundry and the building was found to be sinking into the ground. The head teacher was permitted to remain in the building until 1965, when the old residence was sold and removed.  A new residence was built on the Cardinia Dam Site. 

In 1970, the shelter shed was removed, and a fourth classroom and a staffroom were added south of the main building.  A weatherboard building was relocated from Narre Warren Primary School (School No. 2924) and attached to the original brick building at Beaconsfield State School. 

Around this time, the name changed from Beaconsfield State School to Beaconsfield Primary School, following a statewide policy shift in 1970. The term "State School" was broadened to refer to all government schools, and all primary schools were encouraged to adopt "Primary School" in their name.

By approximately 1975, enrolment had reached 101 students. In 1976, a new school hall was constructed on the Cardinia Dam Site. In 1978, enrolments had grown to 166 students. A library was established in the multi-purpose room, and two portable classrooms were added to the site. From 1979, the Pakenham Teachers’
Centre operated from this hall two days per week. Enrolment rose to 203 students in 1980, before declining to 168 in 1981, coinciding with the expansion of St. Michael’s School in nearby Berwick.  

Between 1982 and 1986–87, Beaconsfield Primary School underwent a major upgrade. This included modifications to existing buildings and a large-scale landscaping project that developed the school’s oval and playground. During this time, the school hall on the Cardinia Dam Site was placed under a community-use agreement with the Shire of Pakenham (VA 2418).

In 2007, a new administration block was completed, incorporating a library, computer room, and seven classrooms. By 2025, further upgrades had delivered nine learning hubs, meeting rooms, a gallery, gymnasium, multi-purpose room, art room, and music centre.

As of 2022, the school had an enrolment of 655 students and remains operational in 2025.

Beaconsfield Primary School (School No. 3033) should not be confused with the former Beaconsfield State School (School No. 2998), which operated nearby from 1889 – 1891.
title: Beaconsfield Primary School (School No. 3033; previously known as Beaconsfield Railway Station State School 1890 – c.1902; Beaconsfield State School c.1902 - c.1970s; also known as Lower Beaconsfield School)

description:
St Kilda Primary School (School No. 1479) (VA 5512) is a coeducational primary school located in the inner Melbourne suburb of St Kilda, south of the city centre. 

The school, originally known as Brighton Road State School, first opened on 11th January 1875, in a purpose-built building designed by Education Department (VA 714) architect Henry Bastow. Under Head Teacher John Hadfield, a Scholars’ Lending Library was opened in August 1875, free night classes were offered, and a State School Cadet Corps was formed. 

By the 1880s, the school had become overcrowded, and the new St Kilda Park State School (School No. 2460) was built nearby in 1882, to try and ease the pressure of increasing enrolments. It is thought that the two schools were amalgamated for a time before separating in 1907, however this remains subject to further research. 

During the influenza epidemic of 1919, the school served as a temporary hospital, with the shelter shed utilised as a morgue.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term “State school” to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use “primary school” in the name. The school name was officially changed to St Kilda Primary School at this time. 

In 2019, an accessible outdoor sensory play area was built, and in 2022, major upgrades were completed including the erection of a multi-storey education building on the Brighton Road side of the campus. 

As of 2025, St Kilda Primary School continues to operate. The original 1875 building is still used, having been added to the Victorian Heritage Register in 1982.

St Kilda Primary School should not be confused with the following primary schools that have also operated in the St Kilda area over the years:
  • St Kilda Park (School No. 2460), existing 1882 - Present 
  • St Kilda (Inkerman St) (School No. 584), existing 1856 - 1874 
  • St Kilda (Neptune St & Evelyn Street) (School No. 543), existing 1855 – 1874
  • St Kilda (Acland St) (School No. 565), existing 1851 - 1882
title: St Kilda Primary School (School No. 1479; previously known as Brighton Road State School 1875 – c.1970)

description:
Gruyere State School (School No. 1695) (VA 5513) was a co-educational primary school that opened in January 1876 in the Yarra Valley, 43km northeast of Melbourne. The school operated out of a state-owned wooden building with a two-room teacher’s residence attached and could accommodate up to 40 students, though the first year saw an average attendance of 20 students.

In February 1886, the District Inspector recommended part-time operation with Tarrawarra State School (School No. 1505), but it is unclear if this was implemented. Despite protests and petitions from parents, Gruyere State School closed in September 1892, and the site was sold in May 1919.

Gruyere State School (School No. 1695) (VA 5513) should not be confused with Gruyere Primary School (School No. 2956) which operated nearby from 1889 – 2024? (See VA 5497 for more information about its closure).
title: Gruyere State School (School No. 1695)

description:
Bungaree Primary School (School No. 1960) (VA 5514) is a co-educational primary school located in the township of Bungaree, in the Central Highlands of Victoria. It began in 1867 as St John’s Common School No. 944, a Church of England school in Warrenheip, operating from a single-room building with 35 students.

In 1875, the Education Department (VA 714) purchased land in Bungaree and built a new bluestone building for 100 students. It opened in September 1877 as Bungaree Junction State School and assigned the number 1960, replacing the original school, which was then closed.

In 1880, a four-roomed teacher’s residence was relocated from the former Ormond State School (School No. 2004) to the Bungaree site.  Parts of the school land were excised in 1876 and 1900 for proposed railway use.

In 1909, the school’s name was changed from Bungaree Junction State School to Bungaree State School. 

The original bluestone building was condemned in 1924, and a new red-brick school opened in July that year, 200 yards east of the railway on land donated by a local resident. A teacher’s residence was built soon after.

The wooden residence was fully renovated in 1968. At the time, enrolment was nine students.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Bungaree Primary School.  Whilst there was no formal announcement regarding the name change, Victoria Government Gazette notices from around this time reflect the change with both names being used interchangeably for some time. 

In 1982, the school residence was vacated and repurposed as a classroom and office. A portable classroom was removed from the former Lakeside Hospital and was relocated to the eastern side of the red brick building in 1989. 

The residence was removed in 1994. Following the closure of nearby schools, enrolments increased to 39 by 1999. In 2000, a portable building that had previously been used as accommodation during the Sydney Olympic Games was relocated to the site to support the growing student population.   In 2007, two of the three portable classrooms were removed and replaced with two new classrooms, a toilet block and multipurpose gym. 

As of 2024, Bungaree Primary School remains in operation with an enrolment is 20 students. The school comprises an office, one classroom, a staff room, a two-classroom portable, a large gymnasium, and a portable housing an art room and kitchen.
title: Bungaree Primary School (School No. 1960; previously known as St John’s Common School No. 944 Warrenheip 1867 – 1877; Bungaree Junction State School 1877 – 1909; Bungaree State School 1909 – c.1970; also known as Junction School; Junction Bungaree School)

description:
A Court of Petty Sessions was appointed in Merbein in April 1950. It was authorised to hear Children’s Court and Court of Petty Session/Magistrates’ Court proceedings until it was closed as of the 11 November 1981. At the time of closure, the court’s records were directed to be sent to the clerk of the Mildura Magistrates’ Court (VA 5396). 

Merbein Courts includes:
  • Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1950 – 1981)
  • Children’s Court (1950 – 1981)

District and Circuit Court Systems

In the mid-19th to early 20th century, courts and court districts were established across Victoria of various levels. This practice remained until either the court was abolished, or a state-wide court entity was established. Once a statewide court was established, hearings continued in regional centres using a circuit court system.

Under the district system, courts largely administered themselves, with major decisions such as the appointment of judicial officers and court locations, as well the development of court rules, procedures and jury lists passed down by Governor in Council. Additionally, judicial officers, registrars and clerks were appointed to specific court locations. These functions were largely taken over by the primary court and their respective chief judicial officer once the primary court was established. Likewise, judicial officers were no longer appointed to specific court locations, but rather to the primary court then assigned to hearings according to the scheduled circuit.

Both district courts and circuit courts commonly used their own recordkeeping systems to manage cases until centralised recordkeeping systems were gradually introduced from the late 20th century. Administrative resources were often shared between the different levels of court when operating from the same location.

Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1838 – Present)

Courts of Petty Sessions were established to hear criminal and civil cases of minor offences and disputes. Courts of Petty Sessions were appointed to be held in population centres. These courts were renamed Magistrates’ Courts in 1971. Under the Magistrates’ Court Act 1989 (Vic), the Magistrates’ Court of Victoria (VA 5113) was constituted as the primary body, while the various courts were grouped into regions with the largest in each appointed as a headquarter venue. Magistrates and other Judicial Officers were assigned to regions to hear cases in each location according to the scheduled circuit. Individual Magistrates’ Courts continue to maintain their own case registries. As of 2023, there are 51 courts in 13 regions. The Court has several divisions including Koori Court, Drug Court, Assessment and Referral Court as well as several specialist family courts. These divisions are appointed to specific locations within regions, usually the headquarters court.

Children’s Court (1907 – Present)

Children’s Courts were established to hear and to inquire into charges against children. During the 1930s, these courts also began hearing other cases involving children such as child neglect. Children’s Courts were appointed to be held at locations that already held Courts of Petty Sessions or Magistrates’ Courts and operated as a division of the Magistrates’ Court until 2000. As such, Children’s Courts operated under the Magistrates’ Court district system until 1989 and continue to mirror the Magistrates’ Court’s regional system. Like the Magistrates’ Court, when the Children’s Court of Victoria (VA 4190) was constituted as the primary and independent body, courts were grouped into regions, and Judicial Officers and Support Services staff were assigned to these regions. Judicial officers were assigned to hearings according to each region’s circuit schedule. Individual courts continue to maintain their own case registries and often share administrative resources with the Magistrates’ Court registries. As of 2025, there are 33 courts in 6 regions. The Court has a Family division, and Criminal division, as well as a Children’s Koori Court for criminal matters. Like Magistrates' Koori Courts, Children's Koori Courts are appointed to specific locations.

description:
A Court of Petty Sessions was appointed in Ouyen in January 1912. A County Court and an Insolvency Court for the Midland Insolvency District were both pointed in December 1913. A courthouse was constructed for the town around 1914 and remained in use until 1984. The Court of Insolvency sat in Ouyen until this court was abolished in 1928, and the Ouyen County Court sat until its appointment was discontinued in May 1942 and its records were ordered to be delivered to the Mildura County Court (VA 5396). In 1984, court operations were moved to the neighbouring Shire Office, and the former courthouse was handed over to the local historical society. The court was authorised to hear Children’s Court cases however it is unclear if there were any hearings. The dates below reflect when the Children’s Court was a branch of the Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court. The court continues to hear Magistrates’ Court criminal matters and sits within the Loddon-Mallee Court Region. It is administered by the Mildura Magistrates’ Court (VA 5396).

Ouyen Courts include:
  • Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1912 – present)
  • Children’s Court (1912? – 1999?)
  • County Court (1914 – 1942)
  • Court of Insolvency (1914 – 1928)

The Court has a Family division, and Criminal division, as well as a Children’s Koori Court for criminal matters. Like Magistrates' Koori Courts, Children's Koori Courts are appointed to specific locations.).

County Court (1852 – Present)

County Courts were established to hear civil matters and assumed the functions of the Courts of Request, which had operated prior to Victoria’s separation from New South Wales. Regional County Courts operated under the district court system until 1957, when the County Court of Victoria (VA 686) was constituted under the County Court Act 1958 (Vic). Under the circuit court system, County Courts continued to maintain their own case registries until centralised recordkeeping systems were gradually introduced from the late 20th Century. As of 2023, the court is made up of a criminal division, criminal appeals division, commercial division, common law division, adoption division and a County Koori Court. There are 11 circuit locations outside of Melbourne, 6 of which also hold County Koori Court hearings. 

Court of Insolvency (1871 – 1928)

Courts of Insolvency were established in each proclaimed Insolvency District across Victoria according to the Insolvency Statute 1871. Courts of Insolvency were appointed at places that held County Courts hearings, and Insolvency Districts generally mirrored County Court Districts. All County Court judges outside of Melbourne were also appointed judges of the Court of Insolvency. Although the clerks of the District Courts of Insolvency were required to send a copy of the Order of Sequestration (Bankruptcy/Insolvency Order) to the Chief Clerk at Melbourne, these orders were not incorporated into the Register of Insolvencies (VPRS 757) created by the Court of Insolvency at Melbourne (VA 2304). Courts of Insolvency continued to operate under the County Court District system until the function of Bankruptcy and Insolvency hearings was transferred to the Commonwealth in 1928.

description:
A Court of Petty Sessions was appointed in Red Cliffs (occasionally spelled Redcliffs) in July 1936. A courthouse was designed in for the town around 1937, however construction was not completed until 1940. Until the courthouse’s opening, hearings were held in the local Methodist Hall. After the Red Cliffs Riot of March 1939, the resulting hearings had to be moved to the Diggerland Theatre to accommodate the number of spectators. The court was authorised to hear Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court and Children’s Court hearings until it was closed as part of the 1985 Courts Management Rationalisation Program. The court was closed as of 1 January 1990, and its records were directed to go to the clerk of the Mildura Magistrates’ Court (VA 5396).

Red Cliffs Courts includes:
  • Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1936 – 1989)
  • Children’s Court (1936 – 1989)

Individual Magistrates’ Courts continue to maintain their own case registries. As of 2023, there are 51 courts in 13 regions. The Court has several divisions including Koori Court, Drug Court, Assessment and Referral Court as well as several specialist family courts. These divisions are appointed to specific locations within regions, usually the headquarters court.

Children’s Courts were established to hear and to inquire into charges against children. During the 1930s, these courts also began hearing other cases involving children such as child neglect. The Court has a Family division, and Criminal division, as well as a Children’s Koori Court for criminal matters. Like Magistrates' Koori Courts, Children's Koori Courts are appointed to specific locations.

description:
A Court of Petty Sessions was appointed in Robinvale in November 1935. A courthouse was proposed for the town in 1958 and constructed from a standardised plan the following year. The court was authorised to hear Children’s Court cases however it is unclear when hearings ceased. The dates below reflect when the Children’s Court was a branch of the Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court. The court continues to hear Magistrates’ Court criminal matters and sits within the Loddon-Mallee Court Region. It is administered by the Mildura Magistrates’ Court (VA 5396).

Robinvale Courts include:
  • Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1936 – present)
  • Children’s Court (1935 – 1999?)

description:
A Court of Petty Sessions was appointed in Woomelang in October 1911. A weatherboard courthouse was constructed for the town around 1913. The court was last visited by a magistrate in 1971 and was recommend for closure in 1970 and 1977. It was authorised to hear Children’s Court and Court of Petty Session/Magistrates’ Court proceedings until it was closed as of the 1 May 1981. At the time of closure, the court’s records were directed to be sent to the clerk of the Ouyen Magistrates’ Court (VA 5517).

Woomelang Courts includes:
  • Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1911 – 1981)
  • Children’s Court (1911 – 1981)
