description:
The Moving Victoria – Rail Office was established by an Order-in-Council on the 1 July 2014 as an administrative office in relation to the Department of Transport, Planning and Local Infrastructure (VA 5003) (Victorian Government Gazette, No. S 231 Tuesday 1 July 2014). 

The Andrews Government announced commencement of the Melbourne Metro Tunnel Project in early 2015, with planning and environmental assessments to take place from 2015 prior to major construction slated for 2018. As such, the Rail Office was renamed to the Melbourne Metro Rail Authority (MMRA) on the 5 May 2015 (Victorian Government Gazette, No. G 18 7 May 2015). The Melbourne Metro Rail Authority was responsible for overseeing the delivery of the Melbourne Metro Tunnel Project.

In June 2018, MMRA was renamed to Rail Projects Victoria (RPV) to reflect the expanded responsibility for major rail infrastructure projects including the Metro Tunnel, Regional Rail Revival and Melbourne Airport Rail projects (Victorian Government Gazette, No. G 24 14 June 2018). 

As of the 1 January 2019, RPV was abolished as an Administrative Office and absorbed as a Project Office in the newly established Major Transport Infrastructure Authority (VA 5503) (Victorian Government Gazette, No. S 580 Friday 21 December 2018). As a Project Office, RPV continued to be responsible for the delivery of major rail projects. 

RPV became the Metro Tunnel Project in April 2024 to focus on testing and commissioning ahead of the tunnel’s planned opening in 2025. The Regional Rail Revival and Melbourne Airport Tunnel was transferred to the Level Crossing Removal Project.
name.official_title.title: Rail Projects Victoria (Previously known as Moving Victoria - Rail Office 2014-2015; Melbourne Metro Rail Authority 2015-2018)
title: Rail Projects Victoria (Previously known as Moving Victoria - Rail Office 2014-2015; Melbourne Metro Rail Authority 2015-2018)

description: Agency created for PROV system testing purposes only.
title: Test Agency I

description:
Fryerstown State School (School No. 252) (VA 5569) was a coeducational primary school located in Victoria’s Central Goldfields. 

The school first opened in 1853 as Fryerstown National School under the Nationals School Board (VA 919), operating out of a tent across several different sites in its initial years of operation. In 1855 a permanent school building was erected next to the Wesleyan Chapel in Heron Street.

In 1862, through the Common Schools Act, the Victorian Parliament abolished the two existing centralised boards and created a single Board of Education (VA 713). With the passing of this act, the school was re-named Fryerstown Common School and was given the number 252.

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Fryerstown State School.  

In 1915, the school moved to a new weatherboard school building on a site adjacent to the local Mechanics Institute. 

Fryerstown State School closed in 1967 due to low enrolments. From 1973 to 2003, the site was used as a school camp facility. In 2010, the former school building was taken over by a management committee and restored for use by the local community.
title: Fryerstown State School (School No. 252; previously known as Fryerstown National School 1853 – 1862; Fryerstown Common School 1862 - 1872)

description:
Nelson Park School (School No. 4768) (VA 5570) opened in September 1968 as Geelong Special School on Libau Avenue, Geelong, Victoria. The school is a Prep to Year 12 Special School for students diagnosed with mild intellectual disability. It initially opened in a fourteen-room brick veneer building with an attendance of 50 students within the first two weeks.

The school name was changed to Nelson Park School in December 1989. 

At the end of 2010, Flinders Peak Secondary College (School No. 7744) (VA 5322) closed and the site became the Hendy Street Campus of Nelson Park School from early 2011. Around 2012, the Hendy Street Campus was relocated to Illinois
Avenue, Corio, co-located with Northern Bay P–12 College (School No. 8901) (VA 5358), where it became known as the Illinois Annexe (also known as the Illinois Avenue Campus). The original school site likely became known as the Libau Avenue Campus as this time.

Funding was allocated through various State Budgets between 2016 and 2023 for upgrade and modernisation works, including the creation of a learning and community hub in Building B at the Libau Avenue Campus and several smaller projects. A new six-room learning centre at the Illinois Annexe, comprising four general purpose classrooms and two specialist areas, together with a separate administration building, decking and landscaping, is scheduled for completion in 2026.

In 2022, the school recorded an enrolment of 301 students. As of 2025, Nelson Park School operates across two sites: Foundation to Year 9 students are located at the Libau Avenue Campus, Bell Park, while Year 10 to 12 students attend the Illinois Annexe. A satellite unit is also based within the Geelong Industry Trade Training Centre (GITTC).
title: Nelson Park School (School No. 4768; previously known as Geelong Special School 1968 – 1989)

description:
Regency Park Primary School opened in 1977 as a co-educational primary school in a popular residential estate in Wantirna, at the foothills of the Dandenong Ranges, 30 km east of Melbourne.

By 2000, the school comprised eight permanent classrooms, six portable classrooms, an art and craft facility, a multi-purpose room, a library, and a computer laboratory.

By 2023, enrolments had grown to approximately 550 students, and the school’s facilities had expanded to include an artificial turf sports ground, multiple basketball courts, upgraded play equipment, a carpeted hall with a stage, a library, an art room, a music room, a STEM room, and breakout learning areas.

As of 2025, Regency Park Primary School remains in operation.
title: Regency Park Primary School (School No. 5131)

description:
In 1879, the Department of Education (VA 714) established the Rowsley State School (School No. 2183) (VA 5572) on two acres of Crown Land then known as ‘Goat Hill’ in Rowsley, just outside Bacchus Marsh.

The school was later moved to a site near Collie’s Bridge, where the railway crossed the Bacchus Marsh–Geelong Road. A multi-award-winning garden was maintained at the school until 1930. The same year a plantation was established and likely later milled for school profit as part of the ‘School Endowment Pine Plantation Scheme’. Attendance during this time was approximately 18, and rose to 34 the following year.

Rowsley State School permanently closed in December 1948. The school plantation was transferred to Bacchus Marsh Primary School (School No. 28), while the school building and attached residence was sold for removal in 1968.
title: Rowsley State School (School No. 2183)

description:
Wantirna College (School No. 8428) (VA 5573) is a coeducational high school, located in the City of Knox, in Melbourne’s eastern suburbs.

The school first opened in 1980 as Wantirna High School, to meet the increased demands for schooling as the surrounding area was developed from fruit orchards into housing estates.

In 1990, the school name was changed to Wantirna Secondary College, in line with a broader change in high school naming conventions. In 1999, the name was changed once more to Wantirna College.

As of 2025, Wantirna College continues to operate. In the 2022-23 State Budget, the school received significant funding for upgrades and modernisation, including the construction of a competition-grade gym and new music and drama classrooms.
title: Wantirna College (School No. 8428; previously known as Wantirna High School 1980 – 1990; Wantirna Secondary College 1990 - 1999)

description:
Alfredton Primary School (School No. 1091) (VA 5574) opened in January 1868 as Western Public School Ballarat, a co-educational primary school operating out of a leased building.  The school became Alfredton Common School in 1871 with an average attendance of 85 students and served the western fringe of Ballarat. By 1877, enrolment had risen to 111 students.

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Alfredton State School around this time.  

By 1879, the Department had purchased a new site and erected a two-room brick building that could accommodate 150 students.  Enrolments declined in the 1880s due toa downturn in mining in the area, and in 1893 Alfredton State School became an adjunct of Pleasant Street State School (School No. 695), requiring students to travel there for their daily classes.  The Alfredton site resumed full-time operation in 1907 as numbers increased again.

Growth in the surrounding area during the 1960s led to the addition of a classroom and staffroom, followed by two more classrooms in 1963.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Alfredton Primary School around this time. 

A new library and 8 classroom complex opened in 2011, and in 2025, Alfredton Primary School is still in operation.
title: Alfredton Primary School (School No. 1091; previously known as Western Public School Ballarat 1868 – 1871; Alfredton Common School 1871 – c. 1872; Alfredton State School c. 1872 – c.1970)

description:
Greensborough Secondary College (School No. 8750) (VA 5575) is a coeducational secondary school located in the City of Banyule, in the north-east suburbs of Melbourne. 

The school was established in 1990, as the result of a merger between Watsonia Technical School (School No. 7400) and Watsonia High School (School No. 8445). Initially Greensborough Secondary College ran as a dual-campus school, however in 1992 the Nepean Street campus (formerly the high school) was closed, and Greensborough consolidated on the former technical school site on Nell Street. 

The school has been significantly upgraded over the years. In 2018, a new sports hall and senior school building were completed, and an old gymnasium building was converted into a specialist centre. In 2022, additional works were completed including construction of a new administration block, science block, and learning areas. The school has also received funding through the North East Link Project for major upgrades to its sporting facilities, including new playing fields and a new pavilion, which were completed in 2021. The sporting grounds are used by the school during school hours but are also available for the community, casual users and local clubs. 

As of 2025, Greensborough Secondary College continues to operate.
title: Greensborough Secondary College (School No. 8750; also known as Greensborough College)

description:
Heathmont East Primary School (School No. 4819) (VA 5576) opened in June 1962 in Melbourne’s eastern suburbs with an initial enrolment of 113 students.  The co-educational primary school operated from a new six-classroom building constructed that year.

Enrolment steadily increased with local development, reaching 400 students by May 1969. Six additional classrooms, a central library, and a storeroom were completed in 1970, bringing the total number of classrooms to 12, with enrolment rising to 450 students.

In 2014, the school had 463 students enrolled, increasing to 589 by 2024. Funding for an upgrade and modernisation project was allocated in the 2023–24 State Budget.

Heathmont East Primary School remains in operation in 2025.
title: Heathmont East Primary School (School No. 4819)

description:
Hurstbridge Primary School (School No. 3939) (VA 5577) is a coeducational primary school located in the town of Hurstbridge, north-east of Melbourne.

The school first opened in 1916, as Hurstbridge State School, initially out of the rented Church of England Sunday School Hall on Main Road, Hurstbridge. In 1919, the Education Department (VA 714) agreed to build a dedicated school building, and in 1922 students were moved into the new single-room school building on Anzac Avenue. 

To match increasing enrolments, various additions were made to the school facilities throughout the 1940s to 1960s. This included receipt of a classroom and teacher’s residence from Gobur State School (School No. 1047) upon its closure in 1947.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Hurstbridge Primary School. 

In 1982, the school was moved to its current site on Heidelberg-Kinglake Road. In 2003, the buildings were completely destroyed by fire, however the school was re-built on the same site in 2005. 

As of 2025, Hurstbridge Primary School continues to operate.
title: Hurstbridge Primary School (School No. 3939; previously known as Hurstbridge State School 1916 - 1970)

description:
Taylors Lakes Secondary College (School No. 8787) (VA 5578) is a coeducational year 7-12 school located in the north-west Melbourne suburb of Taylors Lakes, approximately 22 km from the CBD.

The school was first established in 1992, in line with the residential development of Taylors Lakes in the 1980s and 1990s.

In 2020, a new multi-purpose space was built to better support working with students with special needs. In 2022, the gymnasium was upgraded to be a multipurpose hall. 

As of 2025, Taylors Lakes Secondary College continues to operate, with over 1400 students enrolled.
title: Taylors Lakes Secondary College (School No. 8787)

description:
Winters Flat Primary School (School No. 652) (VA 5579) is a coeducational primary school located in the town of Castlemaine, north-west of Melbourne. It was first established in 1860 as a National School, under the National School Board (VA 919), operating out of a rented room. 

In 1862, through the Common Schools Act, the Victorian Parliament abolished the two existing centralised boards and created a single Board of Education (VA 713).  With the passing of this act, the school was re-named Winters Flat Common School and was given the school number 652. At the same time, a new brick school building was built on Monaghan Street, completed in 1862. 

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Winters Flat State School.  In 1878, a recommendation was made to close the school due to its proximity to other schools, however parents objected and the school remained opened. 

From 1893, it is thought that the school became a part of Campbell’s Creek State School (School No. 120), with students in grades 1 and 2 continuing to attend Winters Flat and the rest of the students travelling to Campbell’s Creek for classes. This arrangement remains subject to further research. 

Several times throughout the 1940s, Winters Flat State School was considered for closure again without action being taken. Eventually, in 1948, the decision was made to continue classes for all grades at Winters Flat. In 1964, a new six classroom school was opened on Roberts Avenue, to meet the demands of increasing enrolments. The old building was demolished and the site became the school’s timber plantation. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Winters Flat Primary School. 

In 1985, the school celebrated its 125th anniversary with the publication of a school history. In 2010, Winters Flat marked its 150th anniversary with the opening of a new building, known as the Creekview building.

During the period 2018 to 2020, older buildings containing asbestos were replaced with the construction of new permanent modular buildings, including a multipurpose hall, an art room and external learning spaces. 

As of 2025, Winters Flat Primary School continues to operate.
title: Winters Flat Primary School (School No. 652; Winters Flat National School 1860 – 1862; Winters Flat Common School 1862 – 1872; Winters Flat State School 1872 – c.1970)

description:
Yarra Ranges Special Developmental School (School No. 5246) (VA 5580) opened in January 1985 as Mount Evelyn Special Developmental School.  It is a co-educational government school for students who have a moderate to profound intellectual disability, with many students experiencing additional impairments, including sensory, physical, and/or autism spectrum disorder. 

In 1991, the school relocated to Morrison Reserve, Mount Evelyn, where it shares the site with Yarra Hills Secondary College (School No. 8815) and Fernhill Preschool and is set in a semi-rural environment at the foothills of the Dandenong Ranges.   The original location remains subject to further research. 

The school caters for children aged 2 years and 8 months to 18 years. Class groups are organised around friendships, strengths, interests, and age, with an average of 5 to 8 students per group. Enrolment was 123 students in 2003. In 2022, there were 85 school-aged students enrolled. A Satellite Unit, located at Healesville
Primary School (School No. 849), catered for students from Foundation to Grade 6, who were diagnosed with a mild to moderate intellectual disability and included in the primary school educational program as appropriate.

In 2014, the school name was changed to Yarra Ranges Special Developmental School.

As part of a series of projects delivered through State Budget allocations and the school’s master planning process, significant upgrades have taken place from 2017 to 2025. In 2019, the relocatable administration building was replaced with a new administration building. In 2021, a new junior learning building with four classrooms was completed and an old relocatable building was removed. 

In 2024, a major redevelopment delivered a middle school building and specialist learning spaces, including five classrooms, a library, TV production studio, digital media and food technology facilities, fitness centre, performance and multipurpose spaces, art room, and associated amenities. The following year, in 2025, the construction of the senior years learning building and additional administration space was completed,

As of 2025, Yarra Ranges Special Developmental School remains in operation.
title: Yarra Ranges Special Developmental School (School No. 5246; previously known as Mount Evelyn Special Developmental School 1985 – 2014; also known as Mt Evelyn SDS; Yarra Ranges SDS)

description:
Dunrobin Primary School (School No. 3777) (VA 5581) opened in February 1913 as Dunrobin State School, although it may also have been referred to as Dunrobin Estate State School. The co-educational primary school was located in western Victoria along the Glenelg River, with classes initially held in the woolshed at Dunrobin Railway Station.

A new wooden school building was completed in March 1914.

A teachers’ residence was added to the site in 1956, followed by a shelter pavilion in 1957.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Dunrobin Primary School around this time. 

Dunrobin Primary School was permanently closed in 1976.
title: Dunrobin Primary School (School No. 3777; previously known as Dunrobin State School 1913 – c.1970)

description:
Sandhill Lake State School (School No. 4797) (VA 5582) was a primary school located near Kerang in north-western Victoria.

The school opened in 1957, operating out of a public with 8 pupils in attendance. 

Sandhill Lake State School closed in 1970, likely due to low enrolments.
title: Sandhill Lake State School (School No. 4797)

description:
Carapook Primary School (School No. 1969) (VA 5584) opened in October 1877 as Carapook State School following the consolidation of Carrapook School (School No. 1624) and Bruk Bruk School (School No. 915). The co-educational primary school was located in the Shire of Glenelg, in south-west Victoria.

The school operated from a stone school building with an adjoining teacher’s residence. It appears likely that the teacher’s residence was removed in 1940.

In 1970 a statewide decision was made to extend the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all primary, secondary and technical schools, and to rename all primary schools as ‘Primary Schools’. Accordingly, the school was renamed Carapook Primary School around this time.

Carapook Primary School was permanently closed in January 1977 and the buildings were removed. The school site was revoked and gazetted on 28 April 1982.
title: Carapook Primary School (School No. 1969; previously known as Carapook State School 1877 – c.1970)

description:
Morgiana Primary School (School No. 4749) (VA 5586) was a coeducational primary school located in south-western Victoria, west of Hamilton. 

In 1951, a large station called Morgiana was subdivided into ten blocks. The children of families who settled in the developed housing initially studied by correspondence, before travelling 8 miles to Yulecart State School (School No. 1587). A school for these children was then formally established in 1955, as Morgiana State School. A single classroom school building was brought from Muntham State School (School No. 2112) and situated on Morgiana Road ten miles from Hamilton. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Moragiana Primary School. 

Morgiana Primary School closed shortly after the name change, in 1971, likely due to low enrolments.
title: Morgiana Primary School (School No. 4749; previously known as Morgiana State School 1955 – 1970)

description:
Nareen Primary School (School No. 2303) (VA 5587) was a coeducational primary school located in the Nareen area in western Victoria.

The first school in Nareen was opened in 1969, as a privately run school organised by local residents who erected a bluestone building to be used as both school and public hall. In June 1870, this school became Nareen Common School No. 1377, under the Board of Education (VA 713). 

Nareen Common School eventually became Nareen State School, with the new registered state school number 2303, however the exact year of this change remains subject to further research. While some records suggest it changed in 1880, it appears that it was definitively Nareen State School by 1898. In 1898, the building from nearby Koolomert State School (School No. 1893) was transported to become the new Nareen State School. 

In 1948, a new school building was required, and the building from Wando Bridge State School (School No. 3842) was moved to the Nareen school site to replace the old Koolomert school building, 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Nareen Primary School. 
In 1978, Nareen Primary School became de-staffed due to low enrolments, and the remaining students were conveyed to Wando Vale Primary School (School No. 3397). Nareen Primary School officially closed in 1985.
title: Nareen Primary School (School No. 2303; previously known as Nareen Common School No. 1377 1870 – 1898?; Nareen State School 1898? - 1970)

description: The Electric Supply Company of Victoria (ESCV) was a British company that had its headquarters in Liverpool. Established in 1903 as a subsidiary of the British Insulated Wire Company, ESCV operated power stations and electric tramways in the regional cities of Bendigo and Ballarat in Victoria. Following the expiry of its 30-year franchise of the electricity business, the ESCV was acquired by the State Electricity Commission of Victoria in 1934, which thereafter took over both the electricity supply business and tramway operations in Bendigo and Ballarat.
title: Electric Supply Company of Victoria

description:
Ferguson State School (School No. 4579) (VA 5590) was a coeducational primary school located in the Otway Ranges, that existed for less than a decade.

It opened in January 1940, operating out of a building that had been moved there from the closed Moorbanool State School (School No. 3247) in 1939. 

Ferguson State School closed just eight years later in 1948. It was one of several small schools in the region that were consolidated over several years to form what would eventually become known as Lavers Hill Consolidated School (School No. 6231). The Ferguson State School building was moved to Lavers Hill as part of the consolidation and the site became an endowment plantation.
title: Ferguson State School (School No. 4579)

description:
Gellibrand Primary School (School No. 2740) (VA 5591) opened in June 1891 as Gellibrand River East State School. The government coeducational school was located in the township of Gellibrand in the Otway Ranges of south western Victoria. The school was situated on the eastern side of the Gellibrand River, from which its original name was derived.

The school initially operated from a portable building designed to accommodate 30 students. In 1892, there were 22 students in attendance.

In 1904, Gellibrand River East and Moorbanool State School (School No. 3247) entered into a half time arrangement, sharing a single teacher who divided their time between the two schools. It is unclear how long this arrangement remained in place.

The school was renamed Gellibrand State School in June 1912. At the time, the school was experiencing overcrowding, with average attendance ranging between 39 and 45 students. Around this period, an additional half acre was added to the school site and a five room detached teacher's residence was constructed, being completed in February 1913. Extensions to the school building were completed in March 1914.

By the 1950s, attendance had increased to more than 60 students. The Education Department (VA 714) approved the construction of a larger school on a more central site within the township. The new school buildings were occupied in 1957, and a new teacher's residence was also constructed.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Gellibrand Primary School around this time.

In April 1994, Gellibrand Primary School merged with Lavers Hill Consolidated School (School No. 6231), Kawarren Primary School (School No. 3894) (VA 5635) and Barongarook Primary School (School No. 2210) (VA 5634) to form Lavers Hill P-12 College. The newly merged school retained the entity number 6231 and operated as a four site school under a single principal and school council.  The Gellibrand campus closed in 2008, and the school buildings were demolished in June 2017.
title: Gellibrand Primary School (School No. 2740; previously known as Gellibrand River East State School 1881 – 1912; Gellibrand State School 1912 – circa 1970)

description:
Glengala Primary School opened in 1972 in Melbourne’s western suburb of Sunshine West, near Kororoit Creek, and central to the Glengala Housing Estate. The traditional custodians of the land are the Wurundjeri people.

In 1977, a survey reported the school consisted of 25 classrooms in total - 18 permanent and 7 portable classrooms, plus a library. 

The 1990s saw widespread changes in Victoria’s education system, as the Jeff Kennett government implemented numerous school closures and mergers across the state. In 2000, Sunshine West Primary School (School No. 5077; formerly Glengala Park Primary School) merged with Glengala Primary School, retaining the school number 5050. It seems likely around this time the school was also known as Glengala / Sunshine West Primary School.  This merger allowed Sunshine Special Developmental School (School No. 5267) to expand into the former Sunshine West Primary School site.  

As part of the Victorian School Building Authority’s Permanent Modular Building Replacement Program (2017–2018), a new building opened in late 2018, replacing the North Wing. It included four general-purpose learning areas and a multipurpose room, connected by external learning spaces.

In late 2019, additional learning spaces, an arts learning area, and upgraded office and staff facilities were completed.
In March 2019, the school was officially renamed Glengala Primary School.

As of 2023, Glengala Primary School had an enrolment of approximately 150 students and is still in operation. 

Glengala Primary School should not be confused with the former Glengala Park Primary School (School No. 5077; later known as Sunshine West Primary School), which operated nearby from 1976 and merged into Glengala Primary School in 2000.
title: Glengala Primary School (School No. 5050; also known as Glengala / Sunshine West Primary School c.2000 - 2019)

description:
Hordern Vale State School (School No. 3858) (VA 5593) was a coeducational primary school in Hordern Vale, a rural locality adjacent to Cape Otway. 

The school first opened in 1914 with 12 children present, out of a building erected by the local community and leased to the Department of Education (VA 714). 

It seems likely that for some years, Hordern Vale State School was worked half-time with the nearby Cape Otway Lighthouse School (School No. 2352), however this remains subject to further research.

In 1939, enrolments at Hordern Vale State School dropped when Glen Aire State School (School No. 4578) (VA 4578) was opened nearby. In 1942 the school was briefly closed before reopening again temporarily; it officially closed for the last time in 1944.
title: Hordern Vale State School (School No. 3858)

description:
Tottenham Crossing Primary School (School No. 5415) (VA 5594) was established in 1994 through the merger of Tottenham Primary School (School No. 4707) (VA 3884) and Tottenham North Primary School (School No. 4703) (VA 5595). Following the merger, the Tottenham Primary School site was closed, and the newly formed school was consolidated at the former Tottenham North site on South Road, Braybrook. The school likely operated from two Light Timber Construction (LTC) buildings.

Tottenham Crossing Primary School permanently closed at the end of the 1996 school year.  The school merged with Maidstone Primary School (School No. 4658) (VA 4650) to form Dinjerra Primary School (School No. 5450) (VA 5394), which continued to operate from the former Tottenham Crossing site.

The 1990s marked a significant era of transformation in education throughout Victoria, as the Jeff Kennett government initiated numerous school closures and mergers across the state.
title: Tottenham Crossing Primary School (School No. 5415)

description:
Tottenham North Primary School (School No. 4703) (VA 5595) opened in May 1953 as Tottenham North State School. Located on South Road, Braybrook, in Melbourne’s western suburbs, the school commenced with an initial enrolment of 495 students, and a waiting list of 50 additional students.

The site was originally purchased in January 1929, on South Road west of Melon Street. In 1951, following ongoing negotiations with the Housing Commission (VA 508) regarding the use of the land, a District Inspector recommended the establishment of a school for 500 students to accommodate the area's growing population. Tottenham North Primary School officially opened in May 1953, operating from a new building comprising 10 prefabricated classrooms. Additional classes were temporarily held at the leased Tottenham Migrant Hostel until October 1953, when two more classrooms were added to the school site. Further expansions included a staffroom and two additional classrooms in 1955, followed by three more classrooms in 1957.

In February 1961, the school was destroyed by fire and students were temporarily accommodated at schools nearby, including Yarraville West Primary School (School No. 2832), Maidstone Primary School (School No. 4658) (VA 4650), and Sunshine East Primary School (School No. 4645), whilst Tottenham North State School was being rebuilt. A new school building, consisting of 16 classrooms, an arts and crafts room and an assembly hall, was officially opened by the Director of Education in August 1962. 

The school name was changed from Tottenham North State School, to Tottenham North Primary School.  This likely occurred around 1970, as there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Tottenham North Primary School. 

Tottenham North Primary School permanently closed at the end of the 1993 school year when it merged with Tottenham Primary School (School No. 4707) (VA 3884) to form Tottenham Crossing Primary School (School No. 5415) (VA 5594).  The new school continued operations from the former Tottenham North site on South Road in Braybrook.
title: Tottenham North Primary School (School No. 4703; previously known as Tottenham North State School 1953 – c.1970)

description:
Lower Gellibrand State School (School No. 3065) (VA 5596) was a primary school located in the Otway Ranges.

It first opened in 1890 as Gellibrand River Lower State School, operating out of the Lower Gellibrand Public Hall. The school moved to a private house in Burrupa in early 1894, with the school name changing to Burrupa State School accordingly. 

In 1919, the school was moved to the other side of the Gellibrand River and renamed Wattle Hill State School. It was moved once again in 1942 and renamed Lower Gellibrand State School.

Lower Gellibrand State School closed in 1948. It was one of several small schools in the region that were consolidated over several years to form what would eventually become known as Lavers Hill Consolidated School (School No. 6231). The Lower Gellibrand State School building was moved to Lavers Hill as part of the consolidation.
title: Lower Gellibrand State School (School No. 3065; previously known as Gellibrand River Lower State School 1890 - 1894; Burrupa State School 1894 - 1919; Wattle Hill State School 1919 - 1942)

description:
A Court of Petty Sessions was appointed in Cohuna in May 1901 only for the purposes of hearing applications for Voters’ Certificates under The Constitution Act Amendment Act 1898 (No. 1601). Cohuna was later appointed a Court of Petty Sessions proper in September 1911, and a courthouse was constructed for the town in 1912, which also housed the local office of the State Rivers and Water Supply Commission (VA 723). The Court’s jurisdiction was extended to the issue of Auctioneer Licences in 1917. The court heard Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court and Children’s Court hearings until the court was closed as part of the 1985 Courts Management Rationalisation Program. The court was closed as of 1 January 1990 and its records were directed to go to the clerk of the Kerang Magistrates’ Court (VA 5610).

Cohuna Courts includes:
  • Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1901, 1911 – 1989)
  • Children’s Court (1911 – 1989)

District and Circuit Court Systems

In the mid-19th to early 20th century, courts and court districts were established across Victoria of various levels. This practice remained until either the court was abolished, or a state-wide court entity was established. Once a statewide court was established, hearings continued in regional centres using a circuit court system.

Under the district system, courts largely administered themselves, with major decisions such as the appointment of judicial officers and court locations, as well the development of court rules, procedures and jury lists passed down by Governor in Council. Additionally, judicial officers, registrars and clerks were appointed to specific court locations. These functions were largely taken over by the primary court and their respective chief judicial officer once the primary court was established. Likewise, judicial officers were no longer appointed to specific court locations, but rather to the primary court then assigned to hearings according to the scheduled circuit.

Both district courts and circuit courts commonly used their own recordkeeping systems to manage cases until centralised recordkeeping systems were gradually introduced from the late 20th century. Administrative resources were often shared between the different levels of court when operating from the same location.

Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1838 – Present)

Courts of Petty Sessions were established to hear criminal and civil cases of minor offences and disputes. Courts of Petty Sessions were appointed to be held in population centres. These courts were renamed Magistrates’ Courts in 1971. Under the Magistrates’ Court Act 1989 (Vic), the Magistrates’ Court of Victoria (VA 5113) was constituted as the primary body, while the various courts were grouped into regions with the largest in each appointed as a headquarter venue. Magistrates and other Judicial Officers were assigned to regions to hear cases in each location according to the scheduled circuit. Individual Magistrates’ Courts continue to maintain their own case registries. As of 2023, there are 51 courts in 13 regions. The Court has several divisions including Koori Court, Drug Court, Assessment and Referral Court as well as several specialist family courts. These divisions are appointed to specific locations within regions, usually the headquarters court.

Children’s Court (1907 – Present)

Children’s Courts were established to hear and to inquire into charges against children. During the 1930s, these courts also began hearing other cases involving children such as child neglect. Children’s Courts were appointed to be held at locations that already held Courts of Petty Sessions or Magistrates’ Courts and operated as a division of the Magistrates’ Court until 2000. As such, Children’s Courts operated under the Magistrates’ Court district system until 1989 and continue to mirror the Magistrates’ Court’s regional system. Like the Magistrates’ Court, when the Children’s Court of Victoria (VA 4190) was constituted as the primary and independent body, courts were grouped into regions, and Judicial Officers and Support Services staff were assigned to these regions. Judicial officers were assigned to hearings according to each region’s circuit schedule. Individual courts continue to maintain their own case registries and often share administrative resources with the Magistrates’ Court registries. As of 2023, there are 47 courts in 6 regions. The Court has a Family division, and Criminal division, as well as a Children’s Koori Court for criminal matters. Like Magistrates' Koori Courts, Children's Koori Courts are appointed to specific locations.
name.official_title.title: Cohuna Courts
title: Cohuna Courts

description:
A Court of Petty Sessions was appointed in Koondrook in May 1901 only for the purposes of hearing applications for Voters’ Certificates under The Constitution Act Amendment Act 1898 (No. 1601). Koondrook was later appointed a Court of Petty Sessions proper in October 1911. The appointment was revoked in May 1916 and the court’s records were directed to go to the clerk of the Kerang Court of Petty Sessions (VA 5610), however Koondrook was reappointed again October 1920. The court continued to hear Court of Petty Sessions and Children’s Court hearings until the appointment was revoked in November 1967. The court was closed as of 1 January 1968 and its records were again directed to go to the clerk of the Kerang Court of Petty Sessions.

Koondrook Courts includes:
  • Court of Petty Sessions (1901, 1911 – 1916, 1920 – 1967)
  • Children’s Court (1911 – 1916, 1920 – 1967)

description:
Nunawading Migrant Centre School (School No. 4706) (VA 5522), also known as Migrant Hostel Nunawading or Nunawading Immigration Hostel School, was established in September 1952. Located on Rooks Road, Nunawading, in Melbourne’s eastern suburbs, the school operated from a leased Commonwealth-owned site that was shared with a Commonwealth residential migrant hostel of the same name (and later renamed to Eastbridge Migrant Centre).

The hostel was purchased by the Commonwealth Government in 1949 as emergency accommodation for migrants following World War II. Both the hostel and the school began operations in 1952. The school comprised four classrooms, created by converting three Nissen huts originally intended as staff quarters, along with an office and a storeroom.

Nunawading Migrant Centre School closed permanently in September 1958, with many students transferring to nearby Nunawading South Primary School (later Mount Pleasant Road Nunawading Primary School) (School No. 4808), which opened that same month. Two classes continued to operate at the Migrant Centre as an adjunct of Nunawading South Primary School, although it is unclear how long this arrangement lasted.

Following the school’s closure, the residential migrant centre remained in operation until 1983. The Commonwealth Government sold the site in 1985.
title: Nunawading Migrant Centre (School No. 4706; also known as Migrant Hostel Nunawading, Nunawading Immigration Hostel School)

description:
Penshurst North State School (School No. 4576) (VA 5600) was a small rural primary school located in the former Shire of Mount Rouse (VA 2476), in south-western Victoria.

The school was established in 1939 at the request of a local station owner, who wished to have a school for the benefit of the employees’ children. The school was held in a room at the station for 10 years until it became unstaffed, likely due to insufficient enrolments. 

Penshurst North State School officially closed in November 1951. 

Penshurst North State School (School No. 4576) should not be confused with Penshurst State School (School No. 486), which opened as a National School in 1858 and as of 2025, continues to operate.
title: Penshurst North State School (School No. 4576)

description:
Watchbox Gully State School (School No. 2375) (VA 5601) was a coeducational primary school located in the Watchbox Gully adjacent to Barfold, in Central Victoria. 

It first opened in 1881 on 2 acres of land, with 19 students enrolled.

In 1904 the school was transferred to a site closer to the main Kyneton-Heathcote Road, in the process closing and becoming part of the recently established Barfold State School (School No. 3424) (VA 3176).
title: Watchbox Gully State School (School No. 2375)

description:
Wattle Flat Primary School (School No. 730) (VA 5602) opened in May 1864 as Wombat Hill Common School. The government coeducational school was located at Wattle Flat, northeast of Ballarat in central Victoria. The school initially operated from a timber schoolhouse with a shingle roof that could accommodate 74 students and included a four room timber teacher's residence.

Between 1873 and 1878, the school became known as Wombat Hill State School following the introduction of the Education Act (Vic) 1872, which established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and led to changes in school naming conventions.

In 1877, the average student attendance was 70.

In 1888, the school relocated to a new one acre site, where a new timber schoolhouse and four room teacher's residence were constructed.

The school was renamed Wattle Flat State School in 1890. By 1892, enrolment had declined to 14 students.

In 1946, there were 27 students enrolled.

Wattle Flat State School became unstaffed in May 1956 and was permanently closed in October 1959 due to low enrolments.
title: Wattle Flat State School (School No. 730; previously known as Wombat Hill Common School 1864 – circa 1875; Wombat Hill State School circa 1875 – 1890)

description:
Ashbourne State School (School No. 1333) (VA 5603) was a coeducational primary school located in the Macedon Ranges, north-west of Melbourne.

The school first opened in 1871 as Upper Campaspe State School, and was closely tied to Lower Campaspe State School, which opened at the same time. The two schools were worked part-time together from the beginning and were registered under the one number with the Board of Education (VA 713), School No. 1333. In 188,1 Lower Campaspe was registered under the separate number of 2539, while Upper Campaspe continued under the number of 1333. Due to fluctuating enrolments, it seems likely that the two schools were worked together off and on until Lower Campaspe State School was permanently closed at the end of 1897. 

Following the closure of Lower Campaspe State School, Upper Campaspe State School was worked full-time. In 1900, the Department of Education (VA 714) purchased five acres on Red Hill Rd on which a new school was erected. Further increases in enrolment led to an additional new weatherboard building being built in 1908, however in 1915 the new building was removed to Garlick’s Lead State School (School No. 1287) (VA 5383) and the old building was renovated for ongoing use by Upper Campaspe State School. 

From 1918, Upper Campaspe State School was worked part-time with Ashbourne State School (School No. 3751). Sometime following the closure of Ashbourne State School (School No. 3751) in 1923, Upper Campaspe State School changed its name to Ashbourne State School, retaining the number 1333. The newly named Ashbourne State School continued to be worked part-time intermittently with other local schools including Trentham East State School (School No. 923), Tantaraboo State School (School No. 1475) and Fentona State School (School No. 4163). It resumed full-time schooling in 1942.

Ashbourne State School closed in 1967. In 1971, several schools joined together to establish camping facilities at the former Ashbourne State School site and it operated as Ashbourne Camp for several years, though for how long remains subject to further research.

Ashbourne State School (School No. 1333) should not be confused with Ashbourne State School (School No. 3751), which operated from 1912 to 1923.
title: Ashbourne State School (School No. 1333; previously known as Upper Campaspe State School 1871 – c.1926)

description:
This school was initially founded in 1918 as a Domestic Arts School (also known as a Domestic Arts Centre or School of Domestic Economy). It opened in Hopetoun Street in the old weatherboard buildings of Ballarat East State School (School No. 1919) (VA 3810), which had closed in 1914. The site had undergone extensive remodelling prior to being repurposed by the new school, which aimed to provide girls over the age of 12 education and training in ‘domestic economy’ in combination with ‘scholastic and literary subjects’.

General subjects such as English and arithmetic were taught up to an 8th Grade standard. For three days of the week, additional subjects such as needlework, mending, laundering, personal and domestic hygiene, cooking, serving tables, and home management were taught.

Facilities included several general classrooms, a cookery room, a laundry room, and a cottage attached to the school and occupied by the Headmistress, also used to teach household management. An additional feature of the school was a public dining room, where members of the public could be served meals prepared by students.

Upon opening, 217 students were enrolled at the school, including 101 transfers from State Schools in the surrounding district.

Between 1918 and 1930, the school was known interchangeably as the ‘Domestic Arts School Ballarat’, or the ‘Domestic Arts Centre Ballarat East’. Around 1930 it started being referred to as the ‘Ballarat Girls’ School’, or the ‘Girls’ School Ballarat East’.

Increased enrolments in the early 1930s caused overcrowding problems, resulting in the school holding classes in various locations. The ‘old school’ at Dana Street (School No. 33) was partially used, as was the old Ballarat East Town Hall on Barkley Street. In 1947 the site including the town hall was purchased, and in 1951 building began on a new secondary school. The old Town Hall and adjacent police station were knocked down during the process.

On the 10th of December 1954 the new double-storied redbrick school building opened on Barkley Street. The old weatherboard school on Hopetoun Street was vacated and in 1955 repurposed by Ballarat East High School (School No. 7545).

By approximately 1940 the school had begun to be referred to as both Ballarat Girls’ Secondary College and Ballarat Girls’ High School, however the name was not officially changed to Ballarat Girls’ High School until approximately 1968.

In 1977 Ballarat Girls’ High School merged with Ballarat Technical School (School No. 7020) and moved to Mount Clear to become Ballarat Technical High School (School No. 7267). This in turn became Mount Clear Secondary College in 1990, then Mount Clear College in 2001. The Barkley Street campus was used by the College and later by the Ballarat School of Mines as a satellite site until approximately 2000, when it became the senior campus for Ballarat Secondary College (School No. 8828). The Barkley Street campus closed in 2016.
title: Ballarat Girls High School (School No. 7541; previously known as The Ballarat School of Domestic Arts 1918 – c.1930; Ballarat Girls’ School c.1930 – c.1968; Ballarat Girls’ High School c.1968 – 1977; also known as the Domestic Arts School Ballarat 1918 – c.1930; Girls’ School Ballarat East c.1930 – c.1968 and Ballarat Secondary College c.1940 – 1968)

description:
Coburg Preston Secondary College (School No. 8822) (VA 5605) was a coeducational secondary school located in Melbourne’s northern suburbs, that operated for a short time between 1994 and 1996.

Coburg Preston Secondary College was established as a new school in 1994, when Coburg High School (School No. 7730) merged with Preston Secondary College (School No. 7297; previously known as Preston Technical School), on the former Coburg High School site on Bell Street.

At the end of 1996, Coburg Preston Secondary College was closed and merged with Coburg East Primary School (School No. 4260) to form a new P-12 school, called Moreland City College (School No. 6244), which opened in 1997 on a site on Alma Grove.
title: Coburg Preston Secondary College (School No. 8822)

description:
Wangie State School (School No. 3530) (VA 5606) was a co-educational primary school located in northwestern Victoria. The school operated from an unlined softwood timber building with an iron roof, built by local residents and leased to the Education Department (VA 714).

The school first opened in November 1906, with an average attendance of 11 to 12 students the following year. Wangie State School was subject to periods of part-time operation and temporary closure. From 1908 to 1910, it operated part-time with Sutton State School (School No. 3257) due to low attendance, with a single teacher shared between both schools.

After an early closure, the school reopened in September 1919. It appears likely that Wangie again operated on a part-time basis with Pine Plain State School (School No. 3891) from around September 1921. The school closed in February 1924, and the lease for the building was terminated.

Wangie reopened in April 1931 in a newly leased building and remained in operation until May 1943, when the lease was again terminated and the school closed. The school reopened once more in February 1945 in leased premises, but by about February 1948 it had become unstaffed. Around this time, a bus route was established to convey children to Berriwillock State School (School No. 3250) (VA 3555).

Wangie State School was permanently closed in early 1952.
title: Wangie Primary School (School No. 3530)

description:
Bena Primary School (School No. 3062) (VA 5607) was a coeducational primary school located in South Gippsland Shire.

The school first opened in 1890 as Bena State School, operating out of a former coffee palace. In 1895, a dedicated building was provided on a new site on Greens Road. In 1921, a new weatherboard building was erected, with numerous additions made it during the following years. In 1933 a new teacher’s residence was erected. Enrolments peaked in the 1930s with around 85 students attending.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Bena Primary School. 

Bena Primary School was officially closed at the end of 2006, likely due to low enrolments. In 2011 the school site was sold to private interests.
title: Bena Primary School (School No. 3062; previously known as Bena State School 1890 - 1970)

description:
Croydon South Primary School (School No. 4890) (VA 5608) opened in March 1967 on the corner of Belmont Road and Bacchus Drive, Croydon, in Melbourne’s eastern suburbs. The co-educational primary school was established on a bushland site of approximately five acres and initially operated from a single main building comprising ten classrooms. The opening enrolment was 337 students, increasing to 373 by the end of 1967.

Rapid residential development in the surrounding area led to significant fluctuations and overall growth in enrolments during the late 1960s and 1970s. By 1969, enrolment had reached 515 students and three portable classrooms had been installed, bringing the total number of classrooms to fourteen. In 1970, enrolment rose to 620 students. Four additional classrooms were constructed on the front wing, while four portables remained in use until a second wing and toilet block were completed.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Croydon South Primary School. 

By 1972, enrolment had grown to approximately 760 students and the school site was expanded from five to seven acres. Enrolment peaked at 951 students in 1976. At the beginning of 1977, there were 20 permanent classrooms and four portables; however, the opening of Tinternvale Primary School (School No. 5075) (VA 5316) that year saw a number of students transfer, reducing enrolment to 899.

Further declines followed with the opening of Dorset Primary School (School No. 5132) in 1978. By that year, enrolment had fallen to 530 students, with 15 classrooms and one portable in use. In 1981, enrolment stood at 425 students across 15 classes. In September 1981, additional land on Belmont Road was acquired by the Education Department (VA 714). An art and craft room and a multipurpose room were officially opened in 1983.

By 1999, enrolment had declined to 257 students. Despite upgrades to school buildings and facilities in later years, declining enrolments led to the school’s permanent closure in December 2008. In January 2009, the school was merged into Tinternvale Primary School (School No. 5075) (VA 5316). The buildings were demolished soon after. In 2016, approximately two-thirds of the former school site was transferred to Maroondah City Council (VA 3668) by the Department and incorporated into Woodland Park.
title: Croydon South Primary School (School No. 4890; previously known as Croydon South State School 1967 – 1970)

description:
Culgoa Primary School (School No. 3246) (VA 5609) opened in October 1895 as Kaneira State School. The co-educational primary school operated from a leased building constructed by local residents and was located in the rural village of Kaneira in northwestern Victoria, near where Tyrrell Creek crosses the Calder Highway. In the 1920s, the township name was changed to Culgoa to avoid confusion with Kaniva. It is thought that the name Culgoa is derived from an Aboriginal expression describing a flowing river (Tyrrell Creek).

In 1902, the original school building was sold for use at Meatian State School (School No. 3761) (VA 819), and Kaneira thereafter operated from the leased local hall or Mechanics’ Institute from June 1902. By June 1910, the Education Department (VA 714) had purchased a permanent site and a new school building was ready for occupation.

In September 1911, a five-roomed wooden teachers’ residence, funded through land donated by the Head Teacher, was occupied opposite the school. By 1913, the timber school building provided accommodation for 63 students. Due to overcrowding, the building was extended and reopened in February 1924. By 1928, average attendance had risen to 79 students.

In 1929, the school was renamed Culgoa State School to align with the railway station and post office. An additional classroom was erected and occupied in February 1931. By 1946, attendance had declined to around 30 students.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Culgoa Primary School around this time.

By 1998, the school operated with a single composite class of 21 students. Culgoa Primary School was permanently closed in December 2008 due to low enrolments. The school land was formally gazetted as revoked in March 2016.
title: Culgoa Primary School (School No. 3246; previously known as Kaneira State School 1895 – 1929; Culgoa State School 1929 – c.1970)

description:
A Court of Petty Sessions was appointed at Kerang in February 1858 and a permanent courthouse was constructed in 1860. Extensive building extensions alterations were completed in 1864, indicating that court operations had already exceeded the building’s capacity. A County Court was appointed to Kerang in July 1879, and the courthouse was extended again in 1880-81, then again in 1884-5. A Court of Insolvency was appointed in Kerang for the Midland Insolvency District in August 1890. After the Court of General Sessions was appointed in November 1911, it became clear that court operations had again exceeded the building’s capacity, and the courthouse was demolished and replaced the existing courthouse building in 1912.

The Court heard liquor licensing proceedings for Kerang and the surrounding districts until 1954, when responsibility for the area was transferred to the Bendigo Licensing Court (VA 3008). The court was authorised to hear Court of Insolvency and Court of General Sessions proceedings until those courts were abolished in 1928 and 1968 respectively. The County Court continued to sit in Kerang until 1999, although it's appointment was never officially revoked. The court was authorised to hear Children’s Court cases however it is unclear when hearings ceased. The dates below reflect when the Children’s Court was a branch of the Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court. The court continues to hear Magistrates’ Court criminal matters and sits within the Loddon Mallee Court Region.

Kerang Courts include:
  • Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1858 – present)
  • Children’s Court (1907 – 1999?)
  • Licensing Bench/Licensing Court (1865 – 1954)
  • County Court (1879 – 1999)
  • Court of Insolvency (1890 – 1928)
  • Court of General Sessions (1912 – 1968)

District and Circuit Court Systems

In the mid-19th to early 20th century, courts and court districts were established across Victoria of various levels. This practice remained until either the court was abolished, or a state-wide court entity was established. Once a statewide court was established, hearings continued in regional centres using a circuit court system.

Under the district system, courts largely administered themselves, with major decisions such as the appointment of judicial officers and court locations, as well the development of court rules, procedures and jury lists passed down by Governor in Council. Additionally, judicial officers, registrars and clerks were appointed to specific court locations. These functions were largely taken over by the primary court and their respective chief judicial officer once the primary court was established. Likewise, judicial officers were no longer appointed to specific court locations, but rather to the primary court then assigned to hearings according to the scheduled circuit.

Both district courts and circuit courts commonly used their own recordkeeping systems to manage cases until centralised recordkeeping systems were gradually introduced from the late 20th century. Administrative resources were often shared between the different levels of court when operating from the same location.

Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1838 – Present)

Courts of Petty Sessions were established to hear criminal and civil cases of minor offences and disputes. Courts of Petty Sessions were appointed to be held in population centres. These courts were renamed Magistrates’ Courts in 1971. Under the Magistrates’ Court Act 1989 (Vic), the Magistrates’ Court of Victoria (VA 5113) was constituted as the primary body, while the various courts were grouped into regions with the largest in each appointed as a headquarter venue. Magistrates and other Judicial Officers were assigned to regions to hear cases in each location according to the scheduled circuit. Individual Magistrates’ Courts continue to maintain their own case registries. As of 2023, there are 51 courts in 13 regions. The Court has several divisions including Koori Court, Drug Court, Assessment and Referral Court as well as several specialist family courts. These divisions are appointed to specific locations within regions, usually the headquarters court.

Children’s Court (1907 – Present)

Children’s Courts were established to hear and to inquire into charges against children. During the 1930s, these courts also began hearing other cases involving children such as child neglect. Children’s Courts were appointed to be held at locations that already held Courts of Petty Sessions or Magistrates’ Courts and operated as a division of the Magistrates’ Court until 2000. As such, Children’s Courts operated under the Magistrates’ Court district system until 1989 and continue to mirror the Magistrates’ Court’s regional system. Like the Magistrates’ Court, when the Children’s Court of Victoria (VA 4190) was constituted as the primary and independent body, courts were grouped into regions, and Judicial Officers and Support Services staff were assigned to these regions. Judicial officers were assigned to hearings according to each region’s circuit schedule. Individual courts continue to maintain their own case registries and often share administrative resources with the Magistrates’ Court registries. As of 2023, there are 47 courts in 6 regions. The Court has a Family division, and Criminal division, as well as a Children’s Koori Court for criminal matters. Like Magistrates' Koori Courts, Children's Koori Courts are appointed to specific locations.

Licensing Court (1885 – 1968)

Licensing Courts were first established to grant and transfer liquor licences. From 1865 to 1885, this function was administered by Licensing Benches of the Court of Petty Sessions. Licensing Courts were established in licensing districts under The Licensing Act 1885 at courts appointed to hold Court of Petty Sessions hearings. Other kinds of licences, such as Auctioneer and Hawkers licences, were granted at annual Licence meetings at Courts of Petty Sessions. This practice continued until 1916 when the Licensing Court of Victoria (VA 2955) was constituted, and a circuit system was introduced. Under the circuit system, 3 magistrates were appointed to the primary court who then held annual hearings at each appointed Licensing Court location according to the circuit schedule. When the court was replaced with the Victorian Licensing Court (VA 2905) in 1954, this was changed to one Judge of the County Court as Chair, and 2 magistrates. The court was abolished in 1968 and liquor licensing functions were transferred to the Liquor Control Commission (VA 1110). See also Licensing Courts (VA 2870).

County Court (1852 – Present)

County Courts were established to hear civil matters and assumed the functions of the Courts of Request, which had operated prior to Victoria’s separation from New South Wales. Regional County Courts operated under the district court system until 1957, when the County Court of Victoria (VA 686) was constituted under the County Court Act 1958 (Vic). Under the circuit court system, County Courts continued to maintain their own case registries until centralised recordkeeping systems were gradually introduced from the late 20th Century. As of 2023, the court is made up of a criminal division, criminal appeals division, commercial division, common law division, adoption division and a County Koori Court. There are 11 circuit locations outside of Melbourne, 6 of which also hold County Koori Court hearings. 

Court of Insolvency (1871 – 1928)

Courts of Insolvency were established in each proclaimed Insolvency District across Victoria according to the Insolvency Statute 1871. Courts of Insolvency were appointed at places that held County Courts hearings, and Insolvency Districts generally mirrored County Court Districts. All County Court judges outside of Melbourne were also appointed judges of the Court of Insolvency. Although the clerks of the District Courts of Insolvency were required to send a copy of the Order of Sequestration (Bankruptcy/Insolvency Order) to the Chief Clerk at Melbourne, these orders were not incorporated into the Register of Insolvencies (VPRS 757) created by the Court of Insolvency at Melbourne (VA 2304). Courts of Insolvency continued to operate under the County Court District system until the function of Bankruptcy and Insolvency hearings was transferred to the Commonwealth in 1928.

Court of General Sessions (1853 – 1968)

Courts of General Sessions were established to hear criminal cases of a more serious nature than the Court of Petty Sessions, excluding the most serious crimes such as murder and treason. The Court of General Sessions continued to operate under the district court system until 1968, when the County Court of Victoria (VA 686) assumed responsibility for Criminal Cases and the Court of General Sessions was abolished under the County Court (Jurisdiction) Act 1968 (Vic).

description:
A Court of Petty Sessions was appointed in Quambatook in July 1909. The court was authorised to hear Children’s Court and Court of Petty Session proceedings until it was closed as of the 31 December 1964. At the time of closure, the court’s records were directed to be sent to the clerk of Kerang Court of Petty Sessions (VA 5610).

Quambatook Courts includes:
  • Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1909 – 1964)
  • Children’s Court (1909 – 1964)

description:
Beechworth Primary School (School No. 1560) (VA 5612) is a coeducational primary school located in the town of Beechworth, in Victoria’s north-east.

The school was first opened in 1875, as a response to increasing enrolment demands on a number of existing schools in the area. The new Beechworth State School was established on a site that had been part of an old botanical reserve. A brick building with sixteen rooms was erected and officially opened on 2nd July 1875 by the Hon. G.B. Kerferd, then Premier of Victoria. There were more than 1000 students enrolled at the time of opening. 

From 1912, the school became a Higher Education School (HES), continuing as such until 1959 when the higher elementary part of the school was proclaimed a high school. The new Beechworth High School (School No. 7575; subsequently known as Beechworth Secondary College) continued to share premises with Beechworth State School until it could occupy its newly built premises on Sydney Road in 1962. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Beechworth Primary School. 

In 2025, Beechworth Primary School celebrated 150 years of education, and as of 2026 continues to operate. The original red brick building was listed on the Victorian Heritage Register in 1982 and continues to be used by the school, having received State Government funding for upgrades and modernisation in 2020. 

Beechworth Primary School (School No. 1560) should not be confused with the following schools:
  • Beechworth Common School (School No. 36; previously known as Beechworth National School), operating 1858 – 1875
  • Beechworth Church of England School (School No. 61), operating 1856 – 1875
  • Beechworth West Wesleyan School (School No. 82), operating 1855 – 1863
  • Beechworth Catholic School (School No. 94), operating 1857 - 1875 
  • Beechworth Road State School (School No. 1984; previously known as Upper Black Dog Creek State School), operating 1877 – c.1946
  • Beechworth Technical School, operating 1912 - 1930
title: Beechworth Primary School (School No. 1560; previously known as Beechworth State School 1875 – 1970; also known as Beechworth Higher Elementary School 1912 – 1959)

description:
Broadmeadows Valley Primary School (School No. 5098) (VA 5613) was established in 2009 through the merger of Broadmeadows West Primary School (School No. 5029), Jacana Primary School (School No. 4839) and Meadowfair North Primary School (School No. 5098).

The government coeducational school is located in Melbourne's northern suburbs. Following the merger, the school initially operated as a temporary multi campus school across the three former school sites.

In December 2009, the campuses were consolidated, and in 2010 the school relocated to a new purpose built site on Dimboola Road, Broadmeadows.

As of 2026, Broadmeadows Valley Primary School remains in operation. School facilities include a large flexible learning space and a multipurpose hall.
title: Broadmeadows Valley Primary School (School No. 5098)

description:
This school first opened as Daylesford Road Common School (School No. 1000) (VA 5614) in 1871. Located approximately 6.5 kilometres from Ballan, the schoolhouse was a timber construction that included a teacher’s residence with five rooms. Although the school could accommodate 60 pupils, the average enrolment for the first year was 20.

In 1873 the school changed its name to Daylesford Road State School. This was due to the Education Act (Vic) 1872, which established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and a subsequent change to school naming conventions. The school number was retained.

By 1890 enrolment had dropped to 12, and in 1893 the school closed.
title: Daylesford Road State School (School No. 1000; previously known as Daylesford Road Common School (1881 - 1873)

description:
Gladstone Park Secondary College (School No. 7858) (VA 5615) is a coeducational year 7 - 12 school located in the suburb of Gladstone Park, approximately 20 km north-west of central Melbourne. 
 
The school was first established as Gladstone Park High School in 1974, following the significant development of the suburb from agricultural grazing to residential in the 1960s.  

In 1990, the school name was changed to Gladstone Park Secondary College as part of a broader change in secondary school naming conventions. 

As of 2025, Gladstone Park Secondary College continues to operate. The school received State government funding for works that are expected to be completed in 2026, including industry-standard digital arts and technology facilities, and upgraded learning spaces and facilities throughout the school.
title: Gladstone Park Secondary College (School No. 7858; previously known as Gladstone Park High School 1974 - 1990)

description:
Monbulk Primary School (School No. 3265) (VA 5616) is a coeducational primary school located in the Yarra Ranges, east of Melbourne. 

The school was first opened in 1897 and was known at this time as Dandenong Forest Village Settlement State School. The school building was one that had been removed from Wellington Road State School (School No. 2172) and re-erected. The school name was changed to Monbulk in 1898, when the first official Monbulk post office was established. 

In February 1913, the school was among several buildings destroyed by a fire that burned through Mt Dandenong. Staff and students worked out of the Methodist Church until the new school was constructed in November. Additions were made to this new school throughout the next decades 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Monbulk Primary School. 

As of 2025, Monbulk Primary School continues to operate. The school received significant State funding in 2020 for new facilities, including a dedicated senior years’ building, administration building, library and two outdoor competition-grade netball courts. The netball courts and cricket practice nets are used in partnership with the local Monbulk Football Netball Club.
title: Monbulk Primary School (School No. 3265; previously known as Dandenong Forest Village Settlement State School 1897 – 1898; Monbulk State School 1898 - 1970)

description:
In December 1940, the Victorian Government appointed George Brown, the Secretary of Mines, as State Coal Controller to regulate, restrict or prohibit the use of coal for domestic or industrial purposes in order to direct existing stock effectively to assist the World War II effort. (At the time much of Victoria’s black coal supply was shipped by sea from New South Wales.) The Commonwealth Government subsequently appointed Judge Davidson as the Commonwealth Coal Commissioner with power to control supply throughout Australia. He established the Victorian State Coal Committee, with Mr Brown as Chairman, on 18 March 1941 under the National Security (Coal Control) Regulations.

The Victorian committee consisted of representatives of suppliers, transporters and consumers of coal, including the shipping lines. In addition to the Secretary for Mines as the original chairman, the Chairman of the Melbourne Harbor Trust Commissioners was also a committee member and over time the committee was enlarged by the inclusion of representatives of Victorian Railways, the State Electricity Commission and the gas industry.

The Committee’s initial priorities were to ensure that Victoria’s limited supply of black coal was distributed to vital war industries, public utilities and hospitals. The use of black coal by less essential industries were either rationed or deprived altogether. The Committee also appointed technical advisers to stimulate the production and use of brown coal as an alternative supply and to advise boiler engineers on adapting or converting their plants to use raw brown coal.

The Committee continued to operate after the war to deal with the ongoing shortage of black coal. It made recommendations to the Victorian Government and made arrangements about augmenting supplies from overseas and overseeing allocations and distribution. The Committee was also responsible for ensuring the distribution of coal during any emergencies in the immediate post war period that threatened supplies such as during strike action.

Although the Committee did not possess any legislative basis to continue after war time control regulations had expired, the committee continue to operate until the level of NSW black coal and Victorian brown coal production had increased to accommodate demand in addition to the increased usage of oil and gas sources. The Committee was abolished in August 1957.
title: State Coal Committee

description:
The Office of the Director of Public Transport (VA 5263) was established under the Rail Corporations (Further Amendment) Act 1998. It was a statutory office under the Department of Infrastructure (VA 3971) from 1998 - 2008 and the Department of Transport (VA 4853) from 2008 - 2013. The Director of Public Transport the head of the Public Transport Division (PTD) within the respective departments. It was responsible for public transport services. It inherited the remaining planning and performance management functions of the Public Transport Corporation (PTC) (VA 2984) following the privatisation of delivery of public transport services.  It was responsible for contract management of transport operators and liaising between the transport operators and state and local Government. 

In 2011, the Office was abolished under the Transport Legislation Amendment (Public Transport Development Authority) Act 2011 and its functions absorbed by Public Transport Victoria (VA 4968).
title: Office of the Director of Public Transport

description:
Beaumaris High School (School No. 7570) (VA 5624) was a co-educational secondary school located in the suburb of Beaumaris, in Melbourne’s south-east.

It first opened in 1958 in temporary accommodations, with Form I and II students attending classes at the local Methodist Church Hall and the Beaumaris Yacht Club. In November that year, students were able to move into a completed portion of the new school building on Reserve Rd. 

The school saw increasing enrolments and additions to the school buildings over the next few years included a cookery centre, a needlework centre, a library, and two further wings with rooms for art and craft, music and needlework. In 1964, Beaumaris High School had its first matriculation class of 45 students and in 1967, a large science block was also added to the school. 

At the end of 1987, Beaumaris High School was closed and merged with Sandringham Technical School (School No. 7320), Highett High School (School No. 7915) and Hampton High School (School No. 7890) to form the new Sandringham College (School No. 8739). At this time, the Beaumaris High School site became the Beaumaris campus of Sandringham College. 

In December 2015, Sandringham College closed its Beaumaris campus and the facilities were demolished. A new school was approved to be built on the same former Beaumaris High School site, with works completed by the start of 2018.
