The new Beaumaris Secondary College (School No. 7566) opened for the start of the 2018 school year.
title: Beaumaris High School (School No. 7570)

description:
Maryborough Education Centre (School No. 8845) (VA 5625) was established in July 2005, through the amalgamation of four Government schools: Maryborough East Primary School (School No. 2828), Maryborough Primary School (School No. 404), Maryborough Specialist School (School No. 5250) (VA 5308) and Maryborough Regional College (School No. 8825).   

The co-educational Prep to Year 12 and Specialist School located in the Central Goldfields region of Victoria had been discussed locally for decades, with momentum building during the 1990s when widespread school closures and mergers were introduced under the Kennett government. Early discussions between local residents and the Central Goldfields Shire (VA 3680) led to the acquisition of a vacant site in 2004, which was given the interim name Maryborough Community Education Precinct.  The name was changed to Maryborough Education Centre (MEC) in 2005. 

Following the amalgamation of the schools in July 2005, MEC operated as five separated campuses for the remainder of 2005.  At the commencement of 2006, this reduced to three campuses, with the Primary and Specialist parts of the school moving to the new site in Balaclava Road.  The remaining two Secondary campuses moved into the new facilities on Balaclava Road in 2007.

MEC remains in operation in 2025, and consists of approximately 18 buildings, including classrooms and administration areas, a Trade Skills Centre, Hairdressing Salon, Library, and Performing Arts Theatre. Funding from the 2025–26 State Budget was allocated to support an Upgrade and Modernisation Project, which is planning to deliver a new administration and technology building subject to further funding.

MEC also operates a Sister School Program with Osaka Business Frontier High School in Osaka, Japan. Every two years, students have the opportunity to host visiting students and to travel to Japan for a ten-day exchange.
title: Maryborough Education Centre (School No. 8845; also known as MEC; previously known as Maryborough Community Education Precinct 2005 – 2005)

description:
Moorabbin Primary School (School No. 1111) (VA 5626) is a coeducational primary school located in Melbourne’s south-eastern suburbs.

The school first opened in 1872, replacing Moorabbin Common School (School No. 422) which closed in September 1872. It was known at this time as South Brighton, or Brighton South, State School. The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) and the school accordingly became Brighton South State School in 1873. The school name was changed to Moorabbin State School in 1909.

From 1962, Moorabbin State School became a designated training school for Toorak Teachers’ College, and subsequently for Frankston Teachers’ College as well. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Moorabbin Primary School. 

As of 2026, Moorabbin Primary School continues to operate.

Moorabbin Primary School (School No. 1111) should not be confused with Moorabbin Common School (School No. 422), which operated from 1854 to 1872, or Tucker Road Bentleigh Primary School (School No. 4687) (VA 5649), which was known as Moorabbin Primary School until 2002.
name.official_title.title: Moorabbin Primary School (School No. 1111; previously known as South Brighton Common School 1872 – c.1873; South Brighton State School c.1873 – c.1909; Moorabbin State School c.1909 – c.1970)
title: Moorabbin Primary School (School No. 1111; previously known as South Brighton Common School 1872 – c.1873; South Brighton State School c.1873 – c.1909; Moorabbin State School c.1909 – c.1970)

description:
Dergholm Primary School (School No. 1729; VA 5628) opened in 1876 as Dergholm State School. It was a co-educational primary school serving a rural district north of Casterton in southwestern Victoria.

Classes were first held in a solid cement and stone building. Enrolments were small. From 1904 to 1905 the school operated part-time with Poolaijelo State School (School No. 2978; VA 3867). One teacher served both schools, dividing time between the two sites.

In 1926 the school moved to a new location, where a new building was constructed. During the 1960s, population growth in the district brought increased enrolments. The school recorded its highest enrolment in 1964, with 39 pupils.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Dergholm Primary School. 

The school closed permanently in 1979.
title: Dergholm Primary School (School No. 1729; previously known as Dergholm State School 1876 – 1970)

description:
Wandella State School (School No. 3331) (VA 5629) was a small rural primary school located in the Loddon region of north-central Victoria.

A school first opened in Wandella in 1886, but it was destroyed by fire in 1900. A replacement building with a teacher’s residence attached was removed from Rodborough State School (School No. 1765) and re-erected in Wandella, and Wandella State School was officially opened as a new school later in 1900.

In 1930, Wandella State School was closed, likely due to low enrolments. In 1932, the school building was removed to Koorangie State School (School No. 4273), and in 1933 the former Wandella residence was also removed to Woorinen North State School (School No. 4148) (VA 3893).

In 1951, a school building was removed from Leaghur State School (School No. 2592) (VA 4613) and re-erected for use as Wandella State School, and the school was re-opened from 1953, though not for many more years. 

Wandella State School was closed for the last time in 1959, and in 1960 the Department of Education (VA 714) put the former school buildings and site up for sale.
title: Wandella State School (School No. 3331)

description:
Fairley Primary School (School No. 3991) (VA 5630) opened in 1919 as Fairley State School. The co-educational primary school was established on donated land at Fairley, in northwestern Victoria. The school initially operated from a single-room weatherboard building relocated that year from Boort State School (School No. 1796) (VA 3195). Ten students were enrolled at the time of opening.

In 1964, a new school building and associated outbuildings were erected on the site.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Fairley Primary School.

Fairley Primary School permanently closed in December 1973. The school building was transferred to Tresco Primary School (School No. 3868) (VA 3656) in 1975.
title: Fairley Primary School (School No. 3991; previously known as Fairley State School 1919 – 1970)

description:
Ararat Technical School (School No. 7008) (VA 5632) was a technical secondary school in the town of Ararat, in the Central Highlands region of Victoria. 

Ararat Technical School originally emerged out of Ararat High School (School No. 7520) (VA 5639), when in 1947, the Education Department (VA 714) introduced technical subjects into the high school at third form (Year 9).

In 1968, it was proposed that a separate technical school be established as its own entity, under the Technical Division of the Education Department. Accordingly, in 1969 Ararat Technical School opened, initially in temporary accommodation on the Ararat High School site, with 222 boys enrolled as students. In 1972, a new purpose-built technical school site was opened on Elizabeth Street. 

In 1991, the decision was made to merge Ararat Technical School and Ararat High School, coming together as a new multi-campus Ararat Secondary College (School No. 8753). The high school site on Barkly Street became Campus 1 of the new secondary college, and the technical school site on Elizabeth Street became Campus 2. 

In August 1997, Ararat Secondary College consolidated on the Barkly Street site and the former technical school site ceased to be used for schooling.
title: Ararat Technical School (School No. 7008)

description:
This school first opened as Ardno State School, School No. 2397 (VA 5633), in a leased building on 30th of May 1881. Average attendance for the first year was 13 students. The school site was gazetted in September 1882, and the name changed to Kaladbro State School. The school number was retained.

During 1883, a portable wooden schoolhouse was removed from Nelson West State School (School No. 1615) and re-erected for Kaladbro, accommodating 30 students. From 1883 to 1884 the school ran half-time with Strathdownie West State School (School No. 2293). 

Kaladbro State School  closed on 17 January 1898, and in September the same year the building was moved to Sandford State School (School No. 1654) (VA 3451) to become an infants’ room.
title: Kaladbro State School (School No. 2397; previously known as Ardno State School 1881-1882)

description:
Murrungowar State School (School No. 3692) (VA 5636) was a coeducational primary school located in the Orbost district of east Gippsland.

The school first opened on 17th July 1911, operating out of a small building on Murrungowar Rd. The first head teacher was Thomas Kidman. Due to declining enrolments, Murrungowar State School was officially closed in 1946, after 33 years of operation.
title: Murrungowar State School (School No. 3692)

description:
Stavely State School (School No. 3472) (VA 5638) was a coeducational primary school located in the small rural locality of Stavely, near Glenthompson in south-western Victoria.

The school first opened in 1904 as Lalkaldarno State School, out of a weatherboard building erected by local residents. Frank W. Kemp was the first head teacher. It may have closed for a period in 1905, when no suitable accommodation could be found for a female teacher, but otherwise continued to operate in this fashion until 1940, when a building was moved to a more central site. At the same time as this move, the school name was changed to Staveley State School.

Staveley State School became unstaffed in 1948 and officially closed in 1949.
title: Stavely State School (School No. 3472; previously known as Lalkaldarno State School 1904 - 1940)

description:
The Ararat High School began in 1912 as the Ararat Higher Elementary School. On Wednesday, 25 June 1913, it was proclaimed Ararat High School (VA 5639) and assigned School No. 7520 (VA 5639).

The school occupied a stone building in Barkly Street, Ararat. The building had a long history. It first served as Laby’s Flour Mill, was destroyed by fire in 1902, and was restored in 1909 as Ararat Grammar School. It was later adapted for use as Ararat High School.

By 1943, enrolments had reached 233 students. After the Second World War, demand for secondary education increased. The introduction of the school bus service brought more students from surrounding districts, and enrolments rose sharply.

In 1947, the Education Department (VA 714) approved the introduction of a third form (Year 9), which included technical subjects for boys. A technical wing was opened soon after. In 1950, a Bristol prefabricated building was added to the site. Another classroom followed in 1952, relocated from Armstrong State School (School No.784). By 1954, enrolments had grown to 413 students.

Growth continued through the 1960s. In 1966, the school was renamed Ararat High and Technical School to reflect the expanding technical program. By 1968, enrolments had reached 820 students, and major remodelling and additions were carried out.

In 1969, the technical section separated and moved to a new site in Elizabeth Street, becoming Ararat Technical School (School No. 7008) (VA 5632). The original school resumed the name Ararat High School and continued operating under the original School No. 7520.

In January 1990, Ararat High School and Ararat Technical College amalgamated to form Ararat Community College (School No. 8753), later known as Ararat Secondary College. After the merger, the former high school site became Campus 1, and the former technical school site became Campus 2.
title: Ararat High School (School No. 7520; previously known as Ararat High and Technical School 1966 – 1968)

description:
Elingamite Primary School (School No. 1424) (VA 5640) opened in July 1874 as Lake Elingamite State School. The school first operated from a leased house on the banks of Lake Elingamite, near Cobden in Victoria’s Corangamite region.

In 1881, the school moved to a permanent site after a local landowner donated one acre of land on the Cobden–Warrnambool Road. The donor also gave the school the right to buy nearby land for a teachers’ residence. A combined schoolhouse and two-roomed teachers’ residence was built on the site. By the end of that year, 21 students were enrolled.

In 1892, the school name was shortened to Elingamite State School. During the 1890s, enrolments fell due to a typhoid outbreak. The school began operating part-time with Ecklin South State School (School No. 2647) (VA 3577). The two schools shared one teacher, who divided time between both sites. Elingamite closed between 1895 and 1897. In 1904, low enrolments continued, and local parents paid £12 per year to keep the school open.

By 1918, enrolment had risen to 48 students. In the late 1930s, numbers fell again. Enrolment dropped from about 45 to 19 students after new schools Elingamite North (School No. 4551) (VA 3579) opened in 1938 and Glenfyne (School No. 4571) in 1940. In 1939, the original building was declared unsafe and demolished. A new school building was then constructed. In 1953, land was donated on the south side of the school for a teachers’ residence, which was built across the road from the school.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Elingamite Primary School. 

The old school site was formally revoked, as gazetted on 29 September 1982. Elingamite Primary School permanently closed in 1987. The site was sold at public auction in 1988.
title: Elingamite Primary School (School No. 1424; previously known as Lake Elingamite State School 1874 – 1892; Elingamite State School 1892 – 1970)

description:
Nathalia Secondary College (School No. 8140) (VA 5641) is a coeducational secondary school located in the rural township of Nathalia, 40 kilometres north-west of Shepparton in northern Victoria. 

The school first opened in 1959 as Nathalia High School. The local primary school, Nathalia State School (School No. 2060), had been operating as a Higher Elementary School since 1919 and in 1957 a craft centre for cookery and woodwork was erected on the site proposed for the new high school.  

In 1990, the school underwent a name change to Nathalia Secondary College following the Change of School Name and Reclassification of Schools Executive Memorandum No 314 from the Ministry of Education (VA 1112).   

As of 2026, Nathalia Secondary College continues to operate.
title: Nathalia Secondary College (School No. 8140; previously known as Nathalia High School 1959 - 1990)

description:
Oberon High School (School No. 8210) (VA 5642) is a secondary school located in Armstrong Creek, Geelong.

Established in 1963 in the Geelong suburb of Belmont, classes initially began in two rooms of the former Belmont Migrant Hostel until additional classrooms became available in August of the opening year. The first two stages of construction comprised accommodation for sixteen classes. By February 1968, a further nine specialist rooms, a gymnasium, and a canteen had been completed.

Enrolment was 70 students in 1963 and grew rapidly to 618 students by 1968.

In 2021, Oberon High School relocated to Armstrong Creek.  In 2024, there were 1,043 students enrolled. 

As of 2026, the Oberon High School remains in operation. Facilities include an administration and library building, three learning community buildings, a science, arts and technology building, a performing arts and physical education building, as well as four outdoor multipurpose courts and a sports oval.
title: Oberon High School (School No. 8210)

description:
Strathdownie Primary School (School No. 2883) (VA 5643) was a co-educational primary school located on Old School Road in the Parish of Werrikoo, in the western district of Victoria. 

It first opened in 1889 as Strathdownie State School, also known as the Werrikoo School, out of a leased building. In 1889 it was worked part-time with Strathdownie West State School (School No. 2239) and sometime after 1914 it was worked part-time with Wilkin State School (also known as Strathdownie East State School) (School No. 2359). 

In 1948, a new school building was erected on a new site, west of the originally leased building, with a single weatherboard classroom coming from the closed Wurt Wurt Koort State School (Chool No. 3728). A second classroom, brought from the closed Vasey State School (School No. 4072), was added in 1954, and a school residence was erected in a reserve beside the school in 1957.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term “State school” to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use “primary school” in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Strathdownie Primary School. 

Due to declining enrolments, at the end of 1996 Strathdownie Primary School was officially closed and merged with Casterton Primary School (School No. 2058) (VA 5482) on the Casterton school site.
title: Strathdownie Primary School (School No. 2883; also known as Werrikoo School; previously known as Strathdownie State School 1889 – c.1970)

description:
Timor West State School (School No. 949) (VA 5644) was a small rural primary school located in the Central Goldfields region of Victoria.

The school first opened in 1869, as Lower Wareek Common School, in response to local families’ request for a common school in the area. 

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked a change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming a State School. At a similar time, the school name was changed to Timor West State School in with the name changed of the local post office.  Some sources suggest that the school name was later changed to Wareek and Timor State School, however the names may have been used interchangeably and the exact details remain subject to further research. 

Timor West State School closed in 1942 due to low enrolments, with the remaining students transferring to Timor State School (School No. 1207) (VA 5836). 

Timor West State School (School No. 949) should not be confused with Wareek State School (School No. 953) which operated from 1867 to 1893, Wareek Primary School (School No. 1419) (VA 4665) which operated from 1874 to 2002, or Timor Primary School (School No. 1207) (VA 5836) which opened in 1873 and continues to operate as of 2026.
title: Timor West State School (School No. 949; previously known as Lower Wareek Common School 1869 – c.1874; also known as Wareek and Timor State School)

description:
Tubbut Primary School (School No. 4593) (VA 5645) was a co-educational primary school located in East Gippsland. It first opened in 1941 as Tubbut State School, with 11 students enrolled. Due to fluctuating enrolments, the school experience several periods where it closed or was worked part-time with nearby schools during its existence. 

From 1952, Tubbut State School was worked part time with Delegate River State School (School No. 2809). It closed in 1954 before re-opening in 1955, still working part-time with Delegate River. When Delegate River State School closed in 1956, Tubbut was briefly worked full-time until later that year when it joined to work part-time with Lower Bendoc State School (School No. 3267). In 1960, Tubbut State School again briefly closed, re-opening the same year but in a new location, on a room attached to the Tubbut Hall.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Tubbut Primary School.

In 2010, the decision was made to close Tubbut Primary School and merge it with Goongerah Primary School (School No. 4545) (VA 3298) to form a new multi-campus school. Goongerah Tubbut P-8 College (School No. 5547) (VA 5631) was opened accordingly from 1st January 2011, with the Tubbut School site used as Campus 2 of the new school.
title: Tubbut Primary School (School No. 4593; previously known as Tubbut State School 1941 – c.1970)

description:
West Creek Primary School (School No. 4620) (VA 5646) was a small rural primary school located in the west Gippsland region.

An application for a school in the area was first made in 1943. In 1946 the Department of Education (VA 714) erected a timber building of a size to school at least 30 children, and in February 1947 West Creek State School was officially opened. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to West Creek Primary School. 

West Creek Primary School officially closed at the start of 1981.
title: West Creek Primary School (School No. 4620; previously known as West Creek State School 1947 – c.1970)

description:
This school first opened as Blackwood Forest State School (School No. 4342) (VA 5650) in 1927, with an initial enrolment of 25. Located in Ryanston, north of Wonthaggi, classes were held in the local public hall until 1929, when a new school building was established on land at the corner of the Lock-Wonthaggi Road and Koetsvelt Road. The building was likely a timber construction standard for schools of the time, with one classroom that could accommodate approximately 32 students. A school residence was built in 1952.

At some stage, the name changed from State to Primary. This likely occurred in 1970, as there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name.

By 1967 enrolment had fallen to 16. By 1981 it had further decreased to 7, with few potential pupils left in the area. Due to the low attendance, the school was unstaffed for this year. It closed in 1982.
​​​​​​​
title: Blackwood Forest Primary School (School No. 4342; previously known as Blackwood Forest State School (1927 - c. 1970)

description:
The Victorian Electrolysis Committee (VEC) was established on 30 August 1927 (originally as the Melbourne Electrolysis Committee) to manage and mitigate the effects of electrolysis corrosion on buried post and telegraph lines and other infrastructure. The Postmaster-General owned this infrastructure and argued that the electrified railways and tramways was causing damage to their assets by electrolysis. Electrolysis is the effect of stray electrical currents that cause corrosion to buried metal structures.

The creation of the VEC was a recommendation of the Electrolysis Investigation Board, which had been established temporarily by the State Electricity Commission Victoria (VA 1002), with representatives from the Melbourne and Metropolitan Tramways Board (VA 2694) and Victorian Railways (VA 3121), to examine international methods of electrolysis mitigation and come up with an approach to the problem for Victoria. The VEC was founded to operate as an advisory committee on electrolysis matters to the Government.  

The VEC Main Committee met four times per year to review of all the electrolysis issues within the state. Its initial membership comprised one representative per related industry:
  • State Electricity Commission of Victoria
  • Melbourne and Metropolitan Tramways Board
  • Victorian Railways Department
  • Melbourne and Metropolitan Board of Works
  • Metropolitan Gas Company
  • Postmaster-General’s Department
  • Melbourne City Council Electricity Department (from October 1929).

The original constitution of the VEC provided for a Main Committee, consisting of senior members of the authorities represented, and a Technical Sub-Committee, comprising technical representatives to direct the field investigations. The Technical Sub-Committee was created on 11 October 1927.

Although the VEC initially had no direct legislative powers, it obtained a degree of indirect power under the State Electricity Commission Cathodic Protection Regulations 1970. The current Regulations, updated in 2009, provide powers through the Electricity Safety Act 1998 relating to the operation of cathodic protection systems. The Regulations were later amended to also include traction drainage bonds. 

The VEC is now formally constituted under part 9 of the Electricity Safety Act 1998, and has eight ministerially-appointed members representing relevant public offices and industry groups as outlined in the Act. Its functions under the Act are:
  • Establish and maintain standards for systems for cathodic protection and for the mitigation of stray current corrosion
  • Provide advice to Energy Safe Victoria, on any matter related to electrolysis and the regulations relating to cathodic protection and to the mitigation of stray current corrosion, when requested to do so by Energy Safe Victoria
  • Encourage the development of new methods and technology to increase the efficiency of systems for the mitigation of stray current corrosion.

The SECV was the VEC’s superior agency at the time of its formation until the SECV was abolished in 1994. From 1994 – 2005 the VEC was administered by the Office of the Chief Electrical Inspector (VA 4207). In 2005 that office was combined with the Office of Gas Safety (VA 4209) to form Energy Safe Victoria (VA 4827), which is the current superior agency to the VEC as at 2025.
name.official_title.title: Victorian Electrolysis Committee
title: Victorian Electrolysis Committee

description:
Warrandyte High School is a coeducational secondary school located on the corner of Warrandyte and Alexander Roads in the Inner East Suburb of Warrandyte.

Prior to its establishment, Warrandyte had only one school – Warrandyte Primary School (No. 12). When children finished Grade 6, they travelled to Norwood Secondary College (School No. 8185) in North Ringwood. By 1972, Norwood was extremely overcrowded, with over 900 students enrolled in a campus designed to accommodate 600. Warrandyte children were then refused admission to Norwood due to this overcrowding and were taken in by Maroondah Secondary College (School No. 8017) in West Croydon where they were temporarily accommodated in a tent.

The Warrandyte Primary School Committee took the matter to the local government and began several years of campaigning backed by local community members. Warrandyte High School was eventually opened in February 1978 in temporary portables. The school’s buildings and grounds were not completed at the time of opening, however, with the site being described as “not so much a school as a shambles”. Due to safety concerns, parents were given the option of taking their children home or leaving them at the school while the grounds were worked on; two-thirds decided to pull their children from the school.

Initial enrolment was 43 Form 1 (Year 7) students, who were temporarily housed at Warrandyte Primary School.

Plans for permanent buildings progressed slowly, and the school was run out of the original portables for the first 9 years of its existence. The new permanent buildings officially opened on 11 April 1987. The school site now comprises these two main buildings, several semi-permanent portables built in the 1990s, and various additional structures, gardens, and sporting grounds.

During the 2000s several construction works were undertaken. The library was upgraded and extended in 2005, in 2008 outdoor sporting fields were expanded and improved, and in 2009 the Doig Learning Centre was constructed, providing a modern and flexible learning space accommodating entire year levels. The gymnasium underwent extensive remodelling in 2011, and the school’s 250-seat theatre was re-fitted in 2013.

In the 2021-22 State Budget, Warrandyte High School was allocated $3.54 million to upgrade and modernize the arts and crafts building and complete landscaping works.

School enrolment has fluctuated over the years. In 1994, 490 students were enrolled. By 2000, the number had grown to 691, and in 2003 it peaked at 750, where it remained for several years. As of 2025, enrolment is approximately 330.

Warrandyte High School is still in operation as of 2025.
title: Warrandyte High School (School No. 8437)

description:
Ballarat North Primary School (School No. 4690) (VA 5654) is a co-educational primary school located on Landsborough Street, Ballarat North.

The school was first proposed in 1923, as a means of relieving pressure on Macarthur Street Primary School (School No. 2022) (VA 5387). In 1953 it eventually opened as Ballarat North State School, operating out of a Bristol pre-fabricated building with six classrooms. Additional classrooms and facilities were added in the following years, and additional frontage on Ligar St was purchased to allow for expansion of the site. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Ballarat North Primary School.

As of 2025, Ballarat North Primary School continues to operate, with an enrolment of approximately 390 students. 

Ballarat North Primary School should not be confused with Invermay Primary School (School No. 822) or Ballarat Primary School (Urquhart Street) (School No. 2103), which were also called Ballarat North State School at times.
title: Ballarat North Primary School (School No. 4690; previously known as Ballarat North State School 1953 – c.1970)

description:
In 1924 a 6 ¼ acre site in Brunswick known as Ogden’s Paddock was purchased by the Education Department (VA 714) for £5000 to establish a new school in the area, which was experiencing a building boom. Over 1926-1927 a two and three-storied redbrick school building (following the same design as Bell State School (School No. 4309)) was constructed, consisting of 12 classrooms, a sewing room, a staff room, a Head teacher’s office, and various storerooms.

Brunswick South West State School (School No. 4304) (VA 5655) was officially opened in November 1927.

By 1929, the school was so overcrowded that some classes taught as many as 90 children at a time. Two pavilion classrooms were constructed on the site to provide some relief, with two additional classrooms (Bristol units) added in the late 1940s. In 1967, four new classrooms were built and fitted at the cost of nearly $100,000.

In approximately 1970, the school’s name was changed to Brunswick South West Primary School, following a state-wide change to naming convention.

In the decades since, the school has grown to incorporate four main buildings; this includes the original school building, which was newly refurbished during 2018-2020 school building works. In addition to this is a hexagonal library and classroom building, with an outer ring of classrooms and specialist rooms; a purpose-built hall/indoor basketball court with stage, kitchen facilities, bathrooms and storage; and an additional modern building containing four classrooms. The school site also features two playground areas, an oval, a tennis court, a native butterfly garden, a kitchen garden, and an orchid.

This school is still in operation as of 2025.
title: Brunswick South West Primary School (School No. 4304; previously known as Brunswick South West State School 1927 – circa 1970)

description:
Kilberry Valley Primary School (School No. 5350) (VA 5656) is a coeducational primary school located in Hampton Park, in Melbourne’s outer south-east suburbs. The school first opened in 1998, as part of significant residential growth in the area in the 1980s-90s. 

As of 2026, Kilberry Valley Primary School continues to operate with an enrolment of around 400 students.
title: Kilberry Valley Primary School (School No. 5350)

description:
Mahogany Rise Primary School (School No. 4939) (VA 5657) is a coeducational primary school located in Frankston North, in Melbourne’s south-east suburbs. 

The school first opened in 1965 as Monterey State School, one of several primary schools built around that time to service a new Housing Commission in the area.  

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Monterey Primary School. 

In 2003, due to declining enrolments, Monterey Primary School merged with Pines Forest Primary School (School No. 4872). The school retained the number 4939 but commenced operations under the new name Mahogany Rise Primary School on the former Monterey Primary School site, while the Pines Forest Primary School site closed.  

As of 2026, Mahogany Rise Primary School continues to operate.
title: Mahogany Rise Primary School (School No. 4939; previously known as Monterey State School 1965 – c.1970; Monterey Primary School c.1970 - 2003)

description:
Newstead Primary School is a co-educational government primary school located in the rural town of Newstead, approximately 16 km from Castlemaine in central Victoria.

The school opened as a National School in 1858. The original red brick school building was constructed on the west side of Daylesford Road.

In 1862, the school became recognised as a Common School under the Board of Education (VA 713). Following the introduction of the Education Act of 1872, which established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714), the school became known as Newstead State School in 1873.

The school commemorated its centenary in 1959 with a “Back to Newstead” event attended by the Minister of Education, the Hon. John S. Bloomfield. An office and storeroom were added to the site in 1964.

In 1970, a statewide change in terminology extended the use of the term ‘State School’ to all government schools. Primary schools subsequently adopted the term ‘Primary School’, and the school name was changed to Newstead Primary School around this time.

An Arts and Technology Centre was constructed in 2007.

Enrolment in 2024 was 73 students. As of 2026, Newstead Primary School remains in operation, with the original red brick school building continuing to be in use.
title: Newstead Primary School (School No. 452; previously known as Newstead National School 1858 – 1862; Newstead Common School 1862 – 1873; Newstead State School 1873 – 1970)

description:
Parkdale Secondary College (School No. 8225) (VA 5659) is a coeducational secondary school located in Mordialloc, in Melbourne’s south-east. 

The school first opened in 1964 as Parkdale High School. The Education Department (VA 714) purchased a site for the school on Warren Road, Mordialloc, however Parkdale High School initially operated out of temporary accommodations in the grounds of Mordialloc-Chelsea High School (School No. 8075). It started to occupy its permanent buildings from 1965 and moved into additional facilities as they continued to be added to the site over the next few years. 

In 1990, the school underwent a name change to Parkdale Secondary College following the Change of School Name and Reclassification of Schools Executive Memorandum No 314 from the Ministry of Education (VA 1112).    

As of 2026, Parkdale Secondary College continues to operate on the Warren Road site.
title: Parkdale Secondary College (School No. 8225; previously known as Parkdale High School 1964 - 1990)

description:
Silvan Primary School (School No. 1801) (VA 5660) is a coeducational primary school located in the rural township of Silvan, on the eastern side of the Dandenong Ranges. 

The school first opened in 1876 as South Wandin Yallock State School, reflecting the name of the district at that time. It may have also been referred to as South Wandin State School during this period. 

In 1906 a bushfire destroyed much of the village and damaged the school. A new school was built in 1908 and the name was changed to Silvan State School in 1913.  

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Silvan Primary School. 

As of 2026, Silvan Primary School continues to operate.  

Silvan Primary School (School No. 1801) should not be confused with Silvan South Primary School (School No. 4259) (VA 3876), years active 1926 to1992, or Wandin Yallock Primary School (School No. 1033), years active 1870 to present (as of 2026).
title: Silvan Primary School (School No. 1801; previously known as South Wandin Yallock State School 1876 – 1913; Silvan State School 1913 – 1970; also known as Wandin South State School 1876 - 1913)

description:
Wandin North Primary School (School No. 3892) (VA 5661) is a coeducational primary school located 50 kilometres east of Melbourne. 

The school first opened in 1915 as Wandin North State School, as part of an attempt to ease overcrowding at other schools in the area.  

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Wandin North Primary School around this time.   

As of 2026, Wandin North Primary School continues to operate.
title: Wandin North Primary School (School No. 3892; previously known as Wandin North State School 1915 – c.1970)

description:
Baulkamaugh North State School (School No. 2336) (VA 5662) opened with an enrolment of 28 students in 1881. The school was situated on a two-acre site approximately two miles east of the junction between Waaia, Yalca, Uluna and Baulkamaugh parishes in northern Victoria. Classes were held in a small newly built weatherboard building with a partition separating the classroom and teacher’s two-roomed residence.

Initially called Baulkamaugh State School, its name had changed to Baulkamaugh North by the early 1900s. By around 1886 enrolment had reached 46 and it became necessary to remove the partition within the building to provide more accommodation for the students. A new classroom was erected in 1890.

In 1892 a fire destroyed the teacher’s residence and an unused school and quarters from Marionvale State School (School No. 2515) was moved to the site. Pupil accommodation remained cramped, however, with complaints of overcrowding in the 1910s.

The highest attendance during its existence was 50 students, but for a period it was conducted as a half time school with the Baulkamaugh South State School (School No. 2920). The school attendance declined during the 20th century and Baulkamaugh North State School was permanently closed in April 1948.
title: Baulkamaugh North State School (School No. 2336; previously known as Baulkamaugh State School 1881 – c.1890)

description:
Beveridge Primary School (School No. 1476) (VA 5663) opened in 1874, replacing Beveridge Common School (School No. 711), a Catholic school first recognised in July 1863 when the Board of Education (VA 713) first granted financial assistance, and which closed in 1874.  The new Beveridge State School operated from a bluestone building constructed on Arrowsmith Street, Beveridge in Melbourne’s northern fringe.  Enrolment on opening was 66, with an average attendance of 28.

In 1875, 17 students left to attend the recently opened Catholic School and Beveridge became half-time with Upper Plenty (School No. 1244).  In 1887, the school was closed for two months before re-opening part-time with Meriang (School No. 437) in September and became full time again in January 1888.  In 1889 a four-room teachers’ residence was added to the site. 

In 1962, a shelter pavilion was added and a pine plantation was established which was likely later milled under the School Endowment Pine Plantation scheme for school profit.  The teachers’ residence was sold and removed.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Beveridge Primary
School around this time. 

By 2018, the school was operating from approximately 11 relocatable buildings, with the original bluestone building used for Out of School Hours Care. 

Enrolments grew from 45 students in 2007 to 207 in 2014 and 472 by 2022. To address this rapid growth on Melbourne’s northern fringe, the 2017–18 State Budget provided funding to purchase land for a new campus. Construction was completed in 2020, and the Ambrosia Way Campus opened for Grades 3 to 6, while the original Arrowsmith Street site became the Foundation to Grade 2 campus. 

As of 2025, Beveridge Primary School remains in operation.

Beveridge Primary School (School No. 1476) should not be confused with the former Beveridge Common School (No. 711), which operated from 1863 to 1874. It was originally a Catholic school and became a public school in 1863 when it received financial assistance from the Board of Education.
title: Beveridge Primary School (School No. 1476; previously known as Beveridge State School 1874– c.1970)

description:
Edithvale Primary School (School No. 3790) (VA 5664) is a coeducational primary school located in Edithvale, a beach suburb 28 kilometres south-east of central Melbourne. 

The school first opened in 1913 as Aspendale State School, taking its name from the larger neighbouring area of Aspendale. When Edithvale railway station opened in 1921, the school name was changed to Edithvale State School to match.  

Increasing enrolments meant that additional facilities were built over the years, however the buildings also suffered damage from a fire during general repairs in 1940. Classes were held in temporary accommodations until new buildings were completed in 1942. 

From 1960, it became a training school for Frankston Teachers College.  

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Edithvale Primary School. 

In 2013 the school celebrated its centenary year. 

As of 2026, Edithvale Primary School continues to operate.
title: Edithvale Primary School (School No. 3790; previously known as Aspendale State School 1913 – 1921; Edithvale State School 1921 – c.1970)

description:
Strathmore Primary School (School No. 4612) (VA 5665) is a coeducational primary school located in the Moonee Valley region of north-western Melbourne.

The school was first opened in 1944 as Strathmore State School, in response to growing urban development to the north of Essendon. The school building was constructed throughout 1943 and 1944 however it burnt down in a fire in November 1945. Students were accommodated across state schools in Essendon, North Essendon and Pascoe Vale until the rebuilding of the school was finished in December 1946. 

To meet increasing enrolment demands, several additional standard and infant classrooms were built in the 1940s and 50s, however the school still faced overcrowding. In 1953, some students were conveyed to Flemington State School (School No. 250) and in 1958, Strathmore State School stopped accepting students younger than six. Some students were accommodated at the Methodist Hall and upon opening in 1961, the new Strathmore North State School (School No. 4821) took 106 students. Enrolments eventually began to decline when housing was demolished to make way for the Tullamarine Freeway in 1967-68. 

In 1959, Strathmore became a training school for Melbourne Teachers College.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Strathmore Primary School. 

In 2019, construction was completed on new administration facilities and a competition-grade sports stadium, containing specialist spaces for arts and community activities, as well as refurbishments of the school’s learning spaces. 

As of 2025, Strathmore Primary School continues to operate. 

Strathmore Primary School (School No. 4612) should not be confused with Strathmore State School (School No. 1106) which operated in the Glenelg region of south-western Victoria between 1871 and 1917.
title: Strathmore Primary School (School No. 4612; previously known as Strathmore State School 1944 - 1970)

description:
Chelsea Primary School is a co-educational government primary school located in the bayside suburbs of south-eastern Melbourne.

The school opened in January 1912 as Chelsea State School, initially operating from Hoadley’s Hall on Main Road, near the Nepean Highway. Enrolment at opening was 65 students. In 1915, the school relocated to a new brick building on Argyle Avenue.

During the influenza epidemic of 1919–1920, the school building was used as a hospital. During this period, students were accommodated at the Congregational Church Hall. A two-storey wing was added to the school in 1921, followed by an additional wing in 1927.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Chelsea Primary School around this time. 

In 1995, the Social Adjustment Centre building was relocated from Coomoora Primary School (School No. 5108) to Chelsea Primary School, where it operated as the Chelsea Social Adjustment Centre. The centre closed in December 1997 and, from January 1998, was transferred to Wallarano Primary School (School No. 5055), where it became the Wallarano Social Adjustment Centre.

In 2010, a senior building was constructed. In 2011, renovations to the second floor of the main building resulted in the establishment of the Bunjil Centre. A further school building was opened in 2015; additional details are subject to further research.

Enrolment was approximately 348 students in 2024. As of 2026, the school remains in operation.

Chelsea Primary School should not be confused with the nearby Chelsea Heights Primary School (School No. 3341), which opened in 1896 and continues to operate in 2026.
title: Chelsea Primary School (School No. 3729; previously known as Chelsea State School 1912 - c.1970)

description:
Wangala Primary School (School No. 4983) (VA 5667) is a co-educational government primary school located in Belmont, approximately three kilometres from the centre of Geelong.

The school opened in February 1971 as Oberon South Primary School. The original school site was located in Pickett Crescent, Belmont, and initially operated from a brick veneer building comprising seven classrooms. Opening enrolment was 170 students.

In 2021, the school changed its name to Wangala Primary School. “Wangala” is a Wadawurrung name. In the same year, the school relocated to a new site on Kidman Avenue, Belmont, which formed part of the former Oberon High School (School No. 8210) (VA 5642) site.

The new school site includes purpose-built facilities comprising several classrooms, two library and communal spaces, an art room, kitchen, STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts And Mathematics) room, music room, and gymnasium.

As of 2026, Wangala Primary School remains in operation. Enrolment in 2024 was reported as 83 students.
title: Wangala Primary School (School No. 4983; previously known as Oberon South Primary School 1971 - 2021)

description:
Koroit and District Primary School is a co-educational government primary school located in the rural town of Koroit, approximately 18 kilometres north-west of Warrnambool in western Victoria.

The school opened in 1857 as Tower Hill Lake National School with an enrolment of 25 students. It initially operated from a brick building located on the site of Victoria Park Recreation Reserve. The building comprised two wings and a central section. The east wing was used for teaching, while the west wing and centre section provided accommodation for the teacher. The west wing was later converted into an additional classroom, and a detached kitchen was constructed at the rear of the building.

In 1862, through the Common Schools Act, the Victorian Parliament abolished the two existing centralised boards and created a single Board of Education (VA 713).  With the passing of this act, the school was re-named Tower Hill Common School.

Following the introduction of the Education Act of 1872, which established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714), the school name was changed to Koroit State School in 1874. Around this time, the school relocated to a new site on Boundary Road, where a new school building was constructed. The original stone building was converted into a teacher’s residence before being transferred for use as a police residence the following year. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Koroit Primary School around this time.

A new classroom was added to the school in 1977. In 1994, the school name was changed to Koroit and District Primary School.

In 2024, the school had an enrolment of 174 students. As of 2026, Koroit and District Primary School remains in operation.
title: Koroit and District Primary School (KDPS) (School No. 618; previously known as Tower Hill Lake National School 1857 – 1863; Tower Hill Common School 1863 – 1873; Koroit State School 1874 – 1970; Koroit Primary School 1970 – 1994)

description:
Emerson School (School No. 4918) (VA 5669) is a specialist government school located in the south eastern Melbourne suburb of Dandenong. The school caters for students with mild intellectual processing difficulties.

The school opened on Heatherton Road in 1973 with an initial enrolment of 100 students.  The school name at time of opening was Dandenong Special School. 

By 1983, the School Council considered the school's existing name to have a stigmatising effect on community attitudes and expectations. In response, a new name was proposed and officially approved by the Office of the Place Names Committee,
Department of Crown Lands and Survey (VA 538), on 2 April 1984. The school was renamed Emerson School in honour of Les Emerson, Director of Special Services at the Education Department (VA 714).

Enrolment continued to grow over subsequent decades, reaching 200 students in 1995, 300 students in 2003 and 400 students in 2013.

To accommodate increasing enrolments, a second campus for middle school students was established in January 2012 on the former site of Greenslopes Primary School (School No. 4891), located approximately 600 metres from the Heatherton Road campus.

In 2024, Emerson School had an enrolment of 360 students. As of 2026, the school continues to operate.
title: Emerson School (School No. 4918; previously known as Dandenong Special School 1973 – 1984)

description:
Galaquil East State School (School No. 3318) (VA 5670) was a small rural primary school located in the Mallee region of north-western Victoria. 

The school first opened in 1898 at Rosevale, however declining enrolments due to drought meant the school closed in 1908. In 1921, the school building was removed 4 miles away to Galaquil East where it was reopened, likely changing name at this time to Galaquil East State School. The exact date of the name change remains subject to further research. 

Galaquil East State School briefly closed again in 1935 before moving to a new building in 1936, where it operated until its final closure in 1956. 

Galaquil East State School (School No. 3318) should not be confused with Galaquil State School (School No. 3083; previously known at Batchica North 1891 - 1902) (VA 5342), which operated from 1891 to 1950, or with Batchica State School (School No. 3191) which also operated in Galaquil East from 1893 to 1956.
title: Galaquil East State School (School No. 3318; previously known as Rosevale State School 1898 – c.1921)

description:
Waratah Special Developmental School (School No. 5144) (VA 5671) is a coeducational school for children with an intellectual disability aged 5 to 18 years. It is located in the suburb of Bellfied, in Melbourne’s north-east.  

The school first opened in 1976 as Brunswick Special Developmental School, at a site on Wales Street, Brunswick West. In 2011, the school was moved from Brunswick West to its current site on Banskia St, Bellfied, and the name was changed to Waratah Special Developmental School.  

As of 2026, the school continues to operate.
title: Waratah Special Developmental School (School No. 5144; previously known as Brunswick Special Developmental School 1976 – 2011)

description:
Kaneira West State School (School No. 3887) (VA 5672) was a primary school located in the rural village of Culgoa, in north-west Victoria. Culgoa was previously known as Kaneira but the name was changed in 1921 when the railway authority sought to remove the confusion caused by Kaneira sounding like Kaniva. It appears that the school retained the name Kaneira West despite this change. 

Kaneira West State School first opened in 1915, operating out of a single room building provided by parents before a school building was erected by the Department of Education (VA 714) in 1922. The school closed in 1933 and the school building was removed to Sunny Cliffs State School (School No. 4416). 

In 1938 the school was reopened in the old, renovated shelter shed, however teaching ceased once more in 1948 and in October 1949 the school was closed for the last time. The school building became part of the Pioneer Settlement air museum in Swan Hill.
title: Kaneira West State School (School No. 3887)

description:
Koonung Secondary College (School No. 7954) (VA 5677) is a coeducational government secondary school located in Mont Albert North, in Melbourne's eastern suburbs.

The school was established in 1964 as Box Hill North High School when the secondary department of Mont Albert Central School (School No. 3943) was separated to form a new government secondary school. The newly established school was assigned School No. 7954 and initially operated from five classrooms and two portable classrooms on the shared site of the former Mont Albert Central School (subsequently known as Mont Albert State School). Opening enrolment was 168 students.

Later in 1964, the school name was changed to Koonung High School. In December 1965, the school relocated to a new site on Elgar Road. Enrolment had increased to 276 students by this time and rose to 462 students by 1966. The new school facilities included science, domestic arts and woodwork rooms, together with general classrooms, staff rooms and an administration block. Enrolment increased to 785 students by 1969.

In June 1977, the Koonung Centre, comprising a hall, theatre and library complex, was officially opened.

In 1982, a fire destroyed the administrative core of the school, including the staff rooms, bursar's office, canteen and mathematics rooms.

In 1990, the school was renamed Koonung Secondary College following the implementation of the Change of School Name and Reclassification of Schools Executive Memorandum No. 314 issued by the Ministry of Education (VA 1112).

In 1992, the college celebrated its 20th anniversary of the Box Hill-Matsudo Sister City relationship established between students at Koonung High School and Matsudo Municipal Senior High School in Matsudo City, Chiba, Japan.

In the 2019–20 State Budget, the school received funding to demolish the former multipurpose block and construct a new classroom wing. The project was completed in 2022. An inclusive learning space was added to the site in 2023.  Further works are planned for the Library, Gym and Creative Arts precinct. 

Enrolment in 2024 was 1,175 students. As of 2026, Koonung Secondary College remains in operation.
title: Koonung Secondary College (School No. 7954; previously known as Box Hill North High School 1964 – 1964; Koonung High School 1964 – 1990)

description:
Riachella State School (School No. 4331) (VA 5674) was a coeducational government primary school located in the rural locality of Riachella in western Victoria (north of Stawell and Grampians National Park).

The school opened in January 1929 and operated from a single wooden classroom.

Riachella State School permanently closed in December 1954 due to low enrolment.

Riachella State School should not be confused with the earlier former Riachella State School (School No. 2674) which operated from 1885 – 1893.
title: Riachella State School (School No. 4331)

description:
Simpson Primary School (School No. 4895) (VA 5675) is a coeducational primary school located in the small township of Simpson, in Victoria’s western district, halfway between Colac and Port Campbell. Situated within a dairying area, the school serves the local rural community.

The school opened on 2 February 1972.  In 2016, the school had a student population of 86 students. Facilities include five learning areas, a multi-purpose room, and a library. As of 2026, Simpson Primary School continues to operate.
title: Simpson Primary School (School No. 4895)

description:
Inglewood Primary School (School No. 1052) (VA 5676) is a coeducational primary school located approximately 45 kilometres north-west of Bendigo. 

The school first opened in 1870 as Inglewood Common School, replacing the previous Inglewood Common School (School No. 456) which had operated on the same site since 1860.  

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked changes to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Inglewood State School in 1873. 

In 1912, the school became a designated Higher Elementary School. It served as both a primary and secondary school until 1982 when it transitioned to purely primary education, changing its name to Inglewood Primary School.  

As of 2026, Inglewood Primary School continues to operate, with the original school building still in use. 

Inglewood Primary School (School No. 1052) should not be confused with the following similarly named schools: 
  • Inglewood National School (School No. 318), years active 1861 to 1863 
  • Inglewood Catholic Church School (School No. 335), years active 1860 to 1863  
  • Inglewood Common School (School No. 456), years active 1860 to 1870 
  • Inglewood Common School (School No. 914), years active 1867 to 1875
title: Inglewood Primary School (School No. 1052; previously known as Inglewood Common School 1870 – 1873; Inglewood State School 1873 – 1912; Inglewood Higher Elementary School 1912 - 1982)

description:
Hoddles Creek Primary School (School No. 2541) (VA 5678) is a coeducational primary school located in Upper Yarra.

The school dates back to 1875 when it was established on a half-time basis with Warburton State School (School No. 1485), sharing Warburton’s school number and known as Hoddles Creek – Warburton State School. In 1886 Hoddles Creek State School received its own number of 2541 and moved to work part-time with Launching Place State School (School No. 2599) (VA 5733).

In 1891 Hoddles Creek State School closed and the school building was later removed to Yarraburn State School (School No. 3248).

In 1912 Hoddles Creek State School reopened on a part-time basis with Beenak State School (School No. 3460), operating out of a leased weatherboard church.  It resumed full-time operation in 1913 and in 1916 a new building was opened.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Hoddles Creek Primary School.

As of 2026, Hoddles Creek Primary School continues to operate, with just three students enrolled.
title: Hoddles Creek Primary School (School No. 2541; previously known as Hoddles Creek – Warburton State School 1875 – 1886; Hoddles Creek State School 1886 – c.1970)

description:
Kyneton High School (School No. 7970) (VA 5679) opened with 62 pupils on the 26th of February 1912 in Kyneton, Macedon Ranges Shire. The school was initially held in a converted market building on the corner of Ebden and Piper Streets, shared with the Kyneton Technical School that had operated there since 1888. The Technical School was absorbed into the High School in 1917.

A purpose-built school building was later constructed on a new site on Epping Street in 1927. The school was officially opened on this site in November 1928, although it had been in use since its construction the previous year. An assembly hall/community hall was added in 1928. This was a joint project by the Department of Education and local residents, who were to contribute £200 a year for five years towards the build. The assembly hall was equipped to enable cinematic projection and was an early example of a combined-use community centre, used as a community cinema, a performance space and an assembly hall for the school.

The main school building was surrounded by various established gardens cared for by students and teachers. While the gardens on either side were subsequently built over, a landscaped garden at the rear and a war memorial rose garden at the front had undergone only minor changes as of 2026.

After World War II, several temporary and permanent buildings were added to the site. In 1957 a Domestic Arts Classroom and a Manual Arts Classroom were put up in Bristol buildings. In 1960 six prefabricated timber classrooms were erected. 

From 1966 the school offered technical subjects from Form 1 in a joint High School-Technical School cooperative programme. Trade school buildings were added to the west of the site in 1969 at a cost of $106,238. A Commonwealth Science block was opened in 1969. A Community Leisure Centre funded jointly with Kyneton Shire Council was opened in 1977 and a new library was established in 1978. Extensive new buildings were opened in 1991.

The school’s name changed to Kyneton Secondary College in 1990 but returned to its original name in 2019. Between 2018 to 2023, a significant program of capital works upgraded existing classrooms and provided additional learning areas such as a new library and a ‘trades hub’ for specialist learning.

In 2024 enrolment was 603. Kyneton High School is still in operation as of 2026.
title: Kyneton High School (School No. 7970; previously known as Kyneton High School 1912 – 1990; Kyneton Secondary College 1990 – 2019)

description:
Moreland City College (School No. 6244) (VA 5680) opened in 1997 following the merger of Coburg East Primary School (School No. 4260) (VA 5377) and Coburg Preston Secondary College (School No. 8822) (VA 5605).

The government coeducational school catered for students from Prep to Year 12. It was located on Alma Grove in the northern Melbourne suburb of Coburg, occupying part of the former Phillip Institute of Technology Coburg campus. The remaining buildings on the site were used by the Education Department (VA 3098) and its successors.

Moreland City College permanently closed in December 2004. Following its closure, the site became the location of Coburg Senior High School (School No. 8849), later known as Coburg High School.
title: Moreland City College (School No. 6244)

description:
The Tambo Water Board (VA 5681) was formed from the amalgamation of the Bruthen Waterworks Trust (VA 2072), Buchan Waterworks Trust (VA 2073), Lakes Entrance Sewerage Authority (VA 1998), Lakes Entrance Waterworks Trust (VA 2113), and Metung Waterworks Trust (VA 2131), effective from 1 October 1984.

The Tambo Water Board together with the Orbost, Mitchell and Mallacoota Water Boards were merged to form the East Gippsland Region Water Authority (VA 4237), effective from 1 January 1995.
name.official_title.title: Tambo Water Board
title: Tambo Water Board

description:
Safe Transport Victoria (STV) was established on 1 July 2022 (Victoria Government Gazette No. S 315, 24 June 2022).

Safe Transport Victoria was established after the merger of Commercial Passenger Vehicles Victoria (VA 5010) and Transport Safety Victoria (VA 5695). The functions of both agencies were combined to create a single transport safety regulator. It manages accreditation and safety regulation for buses, maritime vessels, and commercial passenger vehicles. 

STV was established by way of Transport Restructuring Order (Establishment of Safe Transport Victoria) No.1/2022 made by the Governor-in-Council pursuant to the Transport Integration Act 2010 (TIA). STV is an entity constituted by a single member, that person being its Chief Executive (Victoria Government Gazette No. S 316, 24 June 2022).

STV is a ‘transport body’ under the TIA. As such, STV must have regard for the ‘transport system objectives’ and the ‘decision-making principles’ set out in Part 2 of the TIA when exercising its powers, performing its functions, and making decisions.

STV’s primary functions and powers are set out in Division 1 of Part 7 of the Transport Integration Act 2010, Division 1 of Part 8.1 of the Marine Safety Act 2010, the Bus Safety Act 2009 (powers of the ‘Safety Director’), Division 3 of Part 5 of the Transport Integration Act 2010, and the Commercial Passenger Vehicle Industry Act 2017 (powers of the ‘Commercial Passenger Vehicle Commission’, ‘licensing authority’ or ‘regulator’).

STV regulates the commercial passenger vehicle, bus and maritime industries in accordance with various acts and regulations including the: 
  • Transport Integration Act 2010
  • Commercial Passenger Vehicle Industry Act 2017
  • Commercial Passenger Vehicle Industry Regulations 2018
  • Transport (Compliance and Miscellaneous) Act 1983
  • Road Safety Act 1986
  • Road Safety (Driving Instructors) Regulations 2010
  • Bus Safety Act 2009
  • Bus Safety Regulations 2020
  • Transport (Safety Schemes Compliance and Enforcement) Act 2014
  • Marine Safety Act 2010
  • Marine Safety Regulations 2023.
title: Safe Transport Victoria

description:
Sunbury West Primary School (School No. 5006) (VA 5683) is a coeducational primary school located in the satellite township of Sunbury, 35 kilometres north-west of Melbourne towards Bendigo. 

The school first opened in 1971, during a period of rapid suburban growth. The population of the area and school has continued to grow over the years, and many additional buildings and facilities have been added to the school accordingly. 

In 2021, Sunbury West Primary School celebrated its 50th anniversary and as of 2026 continues to operate.
title: Sunbury West Primary School (School No. 5006)

description:
Manor Lakes P-12 College (School No. 8848) (VA 5684) is a co-educational Prep to Year 12 school, located in Wyndham Vale in Melbourne’s western suburbs.

A site for a new Prep to Year 12 school in the area was first acquired by the State government in 2004. At the time, the registered name of the future school was Wyndham Vale P-12 College (School No. 8848). Building commenced in 2007, the school name was changed in December 2008 to Manor Lakes P-12 Specialist College, and in 2009, it was officially opened. 

It seems that it was intended that Manor Lakes P-12 Specialist College would include a separate Special Campus, offering specialised learning facilities. The building of this separate campus was delayed and appears to have been cancelled entirely, though this remains subject to further research. In 2011, the school name was officially changed to Manor Lakes P-12 College.

In 2019, the school buildings were expanded and upgraded, with additions including a secondary centre with new classrooms and administrative facilities, a new café and student lounge, facilities for trades learning, and new health hubs for sport and outdoor learning. In 2024, additional work was undertaken to replace temporary facilities with permanent buildings. 

As of 2025, the school continues to operate, with approximately 2890 students enrolled. Plans are underway for a kindergarten to be built at Manor Lakes P-12 College, due to open in 2026.
title: Manor Lakes P-12 College (School No. 8848; previously known as Manor Lakes P-12 Specialist College 2009 - 2011)

description:
Tallangatta Primary School (School No. 1365) (VA 5685) is a small rural primary school located in north-east Victoria, east of Wodonga.

The school was officially established as Tallangatta State School in 1874. It had been preceded by Tallangatta Rural School No. 82, which had been operating since 1869. The Education Department (VA 714) purchased the rural school building to use for the new Tallangatta State School. 

In 1970, there was a statewide change in the use of the term “State school” to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use “primary school” in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Tallangatta Primary School. 

In 1989, Bullioh Primary School (School No. 2495) (VA 3212) closed and merged with Tallangatta Primary School. 

As of 2026, Tallangatta Primary School continues to operate.
name.official_title.title: Tallangatta Primary School (School No. 1365; previously known as Tallangatta State School 1874 – c.1970)
title: Tallangatta Primary School (School No. 1365; previously known as Tallangatta State School 1874 – c.1970)

description:
Elwood Primary School (School No. 3942) (VA 5686) is a coeducational government primary school located in Elwood, an inner bayside suburb of Melbourne.

The school opened as Elwood Central School in June 1917. It initially operated from a two storey brick building containing twelve classrooms and opened with an enrolment of 450 students.

In 1926, an infants block was constructed on a separate site opposite the school. Additional classrooms and adjoining land were acquired over subsequent years to accommodate increasing enrolments, which at times exceeded 1,000 students.

In 1956, Elwood Central School was separated into primary and secondary schools. The primary school became known as Elwood State School.

In 1970, there was a statewide change in the use of the term “State school” to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use “primary school” in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Elwood Primary School around this time. 

In 2014, the school had an enrolment of 740 students. In 2018, a new modular building was constructed to replace older classrooms. Enrolment in 2024 was approximately 650 students.

The school forms part of the Elwood Learning Hub, an education precinct comprising Poets Grove Family and Children's Centre, Elwood Primary School, and Elwood College (School No. 7810) (VA 5726).

As of 2026, Elwood Primary School remains in operation.
title: Elwood Primary School (School No. 3942; previously known as Elwood Central School 1917 – 1956; Elwood State School 1956 – circa 1970)

description:
Maldon Primary School (School No. 1254) (VA 5687) was established in August 1873 as Maldon State School. It replaced several church and private schools that had operated in the district since the late 1850s. Classes were initially held in the Church of England and Methodist school buildings, with an enrolment of 300 students.

In 1875, the school relocated to a permanent brick building comprising five large classrooms, three smaller classrooms, and an administrative office. The building was designed to accommodate 750 students.

From 1910 to 1920, the operation of deep gold mines in the district contributed to an increase in enrolment, with attendance reaching 640 students. Enrolments later declined following the end of the gold mining period, before increasing again during the 1950s in association with the construction of the Cairn Curran Reservoir. A teachers' residence was added to the site in 1954 and sold in 1962.

In 1970, a statewide decision was made to broaden the use of the term 'State School' to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use 'Primary School' in their names. The school was accordingly renamed Maldon Primary School around this time, when attendance was approximately 120 students.

In 2024, the school had an enrolment of 83 students.  In 2026, Maldon Primary School continues to operate from its original brick school building.
title: Maldon Primary School (School No. 1254; previously known as Maldon State School 1873 – circa 1970)

description:
Research Primary School (School No. 2959) (VA 5688) is located in semi-rural surroundings on the north eastern outskirts of Melbourne, within the Shire of Nillumbik.

The school was established in 1889 and was first known as Research Gully State School during the gold mining period. It initially operated from a leased four room cottage with 37 students. In March 1891, the school moved to a permanent site purchased by the Education Department (VA 714), where a new wooden building was erected.

Following the Second World War, enrolments increased in the area and additional rooms were added to the school. In 1964, a portable classroom was relocated from Koonung Heights State School (School No. 4727) (VA 3607) and re-erected on the Research State School site. Further classroom additions were made in 1970, at which time enrolment was recorded at 247 students.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Research Primary School around this time

In 2022, an upgrade and modernisation project was completed, replacing and refurbishing earlier classrooms and facilities to provide contemporary learning spaces. The school facilities include purpose built learning spaces across two buildings, an administrative and arts building, a gym, and a library portable building.

In 2025, the school continues to operate with a census enrolment of 244 students.
title: Research Primary School (School No. 2959; previously known as Research Gully State School 1889 – 1891; Research State School 1891 – circa 1970)

description:
Menzies Creek Primary School (School No. 2457) (VA 5689) is a coeducational primary school located in in the Dandenong Ranges, east of Melbourne. 

The school first opened in 1882 as Menzies Creek State School, on land donated by a member of the local community.  In 1917, the school name was changed to Aura State School, before reverting back to Menzies Creek State School in 1923. Following a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name, the school became known as Menzies Creek Primary School. 

Over its years of operation, Menzies Creek Primary School has seen a number of changes. Due to periods of low enrolments, significant illness in the community and damage from both floods and fires, the school has been closed and reopened several times, and has on occasion been worked as a part-time school. 

In 1935, the school was destroyed in an accidental fire. Classes were held in the nearby St Cuthbert’s Church until the school was rebuilt in 1936. Since that time, a number of additional rooms have been added to the site, and additional land acquired, included four new classrooms, library and community rooms in 2009. A new junior school and library were completed in 2012, when Menzies Creek Primary School celebrated its 130th birthday. 

As of 2026, Menzies Creek Primary School continues to operate.
