description:
Gembrook Primary School (School No. 2506) (VA 5690) is a co-educational primary school located in the West Gippsland Region of Victoria, about 20km Northeast of Pakenham, and about 20km Southeast of Belgrave.

Gembrook Primary School first opened in 1883, as Gembrook North State School. Prior to this, a Gembrook North State School operated half time with Emerald State School, both under the School No. 2110. In 1880, Emerald State School became a full-time school, and Gembrook North State School operated part time with Gembrook South State School (School No. 2155). In 1883, Gembrook North State School officially separated from Gembrook South State School and renumbered School No. 2506, operating out of an original leased bark hut off Mountain Road.

Gembrook North (School No. 2506) and Gembrook South (School No. 2155) State Schools were again worked half-time from 1885 until 1889, when Gembrook North regained full-time operations with an average attendance of 26 students. In 1909, Gembrook North State School was renamed Gembrook State School.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school’s name was changed to Gembrook Primary School.

The Uniting church in Gembrook was used as a school building from 1884 until 1906. In 1900, the Puffing Billy Railway Line opened which increased settlement and moved the centre of the town nearby the station. The school then moved to a purpose-built hall in Main Street, into the town centre in 1906. A second room was added in 1922 where the school closed for one week to accommodate building works. A third room was added in 1957, and a fourth in 1968.

As of 2026, Gembrook Primary School continues to operate in the same location near the railway station in the centre of town. 

Gembrook Primary School (School No. 2506) should not be confused with Gembrook North State School (School No. 2110), which operated from 1878 to 1883, or Gembrook South State School (School No. 2155) (renamed Pakenham Upper State School in 1916), which operated from 1876 until 1952.
title: Gembrook Primary School (School No. 2506; previously known as Gembrook North State School 1878 - 1909 and Gembrook State School c. 1909 – 1970)

description:
Darraweit Guim Primary School (School No. 878) (VA 5693) is a small rural primary school located in the Macedon Ranges, approximately 60 kilometres north of Melbourne. 

The school was first opened in 1866 in a building owned by the Wesleyan Church, before officially becoming Darraweit Guim Common School under the Board of Education (VA 713) in 1867. In 1870, a single-room bluestone school building was erected. 

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Darraweit Guim State School.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Darraweit Guim Primary School.

As of 2026, Darraweit Guim Primary School continues to operate. While the school site has changed and developed over the years, sometimes in response to flooding and fires in the region, the original bluestone building is still in use.

description:
The Director, Transport Safety, operating as Transport Safety Victoria (TSV), was established on 1 July 2010. It was established under the Transport Integration Act 2010.

The Director, Transport Safety was the successor in law to the Director, Public Transport Safety (VA 5699) and the Director of Marine Safety (VA 5696) (Transport Integration Act 2010, S. 171(3)). Their bus and maritime vessel regulation functions were transferred to the new office of TSV to create a single transport safety regulator.

Under the Act, “[t]he primary object of the Director, Transport Safety is to seek the highest bus safety and marine safety standards that are reasonably practicable consistent with the vision statement and the transport system objectives”.

The functions and powers of TSV were outlined in S. 173 and S. 174 of the Transport Integration Act 2010. It also had powers under the Bus Safety Act 2009 and the Marine Safety Act 2010.

The Director, Transport Safety was one of two transport safety offices in Victoria as established in the Act, the other being the Chief Investigator, Transport Safety.

TSV was abolished when its functions were combined with those of Commercial Passenger Vehicles Victoria (VA 5010) to form Safe Transport Victoria (VA 5695) on 1 July 2022 (Victoria Government Gazette No. S 315, 24 June 2022). This was enacted under the Transport Restructuring Order (Establishment of Safe Transport Victoria) No.1/2022 made by the Governor-in-Council pursuant to the Transport Integration Act 2010.
name.official_title.title: Director, Transport Safety (operating as Transport Safety Victoria)
title: Director, Transport Safety (operating as Transport Safety Victoria)

description:
On 7 February 2002 the Director of Marine Safety was established under the Marine (Further Amendment) Act 2001. The Director of Marine Safety replaced the Marine Board of Victoria (VA 1424) and was to perform all the functions that had been performed by the Board. The office traded as Marine Safety Victoria (MSV).

Marine Safety Victoria was responsible for the administration of the Marine Act 1988 and the Marine Regulations 1999. Its objectives were to: 
  • facilitate efficient and safe operation of marine vessels 
  • facilitate navigation safety 
  • improve community awareness of boating safety 
  • improve and simplify vessel registration and operating requirements 
  • ensure an effective response to oil pollution incidents. 

MSV was responsible for: 
  • setting standards for the design, construction and equipment of commercial vessels to maintain structural integrity and seaworthiness
  • setting standards related to recreational vessels and for operating and zoning rules
  • licensing of pilots and harbour masters and determining standards for the training of pilots, pilot exempt masters and harbour masters
  • determining standards and procedures for navigation and maritime safety on state waters
  • developing appropriate standards for the provision and maintenance of navigational aids for state waters
  • developing appropriate standards for dredging and maintenance of channels
  • enforcing and monitoring compliance with prescribed standards
  • developing, reviewing, coordinating and managing the Victorian Marine Pollution Contingency Plan
  • providing authoritative advice, commissioning research and promoting education and training in marine safety matters.

MSV was abolished when the Director, Transport Safety (VA 5695) was established on 1 July 2010 under the Transport Integration Act 2010. The bus and maritime vessel regulation functions of MSV and the Director, Public Transport Safety were transferred to the new office of Transport Safety Victoria (VA 5695) to create a single transport safety regulator.
title: Director of Marine Safety (trading as Marine Safety Victoria)

The Omeo Waterworks Trust (VA 5698) was constituted on 4 August 1890. The Omeo District was proclaimed an Urban District on the 28th January, 1892.

Abolition
The Omeo Waterworks Trust was abolished and its function was transferred to the Shire of Omeo Water Board (VA 2247) in 1983.
title: Omeo Waterworks Trust

description:
Tecoma Primary School (School No. 3356) (VA 5700) is a coeducational government primary school located in Tecoma, in Melbourne's eastern suburbs at the foothills of the Dandenong Ranges.

The school opened in 1900 as Upper Ferntree Gully State School. It initially operated as a part time school with Menzies Creek State School (School No. 2457) (VA 5689) from a two room shack known as "The Pines". The two schools shared a single teacher, who divided their time between both locations.  During its early years, the school operated from leased premises and alternated between part time and full time operation. The school relocated to its permanent site in 1916.

The school name was changed to Upwey State School in 1903, Belgrave State School in 1908, and Tecoma State School in 1961.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Tecoma Primary School around this time.

In 1972, a new classroom, furnace room and toilets were added to the site.

In 2015, the original school building was refurbished and converted for administrative use.
Enrolment in 2024 was 394 students. At that time, the school comprised a Prep Learning Centre, BER building, six portable classrooms and a Senior School block. Other facilities included an administration building, art room, library and music room, and a multipurpose hall.

As of 2026, Tecoma Primary School remains in operation.

Tecoma Primary School should not be confused with the separate Upper Ferntree Gully State School (School No. 3926), which opened in 1916, or Upwey State School (School No. 4530) (VA 5737), which opened in 1934, despite Tecoma Primary School previously operating under both names.
title: Tecoma Primary School (School No. 3356; previously known as Upper Ferntree Gully State School 1900 – 1903; Upwey State School 1903 – 1908; Belgrave State School 1908 – 1961; Tecoma State School 1961 – circa 1970)

description:
Tyabb Railway Station Primary School (School No. 3544) (VA 5707) opened in 1907 as Tyabb Railway Station State School in the semi-rural township of Tyabb on the Western Port side of the Mornington Peninsula. The school began as an adjunct to Tyabb State School (School No. 3129), with an initial enrolment of 11 students.

The school was subject to periods of temporary closure. In 1913, Tyabb Railway Station School and Tyabb State School began operating from a new weatherboard building under the administration of a shared Head Teacher. In 1917, Tyabb State School closed owing to the enlistment of a junior teacher. The schools remained combined until 1921, when they separated and resumed operation as two distinct schools.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Tyabb Railway Station Primary School around this time.

As of 2017, the school facilities consist of the original weatherboard building, a large multi-function room and administration area.  In 2024, the school enrolled 167 students. In 2026, the school continues to operate.
title: Tyabb Railway Station Primary School (School No. 3544; previously known as Tyabb Railway Station State School 1907 – circa 1970)

description:
Briar Hill Primary School (School No. 4341) (VA 5709) is a coeducational primary school located in the suburb of Briar Hill, in Melbourne’s north-east. 

The school first opened in 1927 as Briar Hill State School, for which the Education Department (VA 714) acquired a two-acre site and erected a two-room school building. Additional rooms were built to meet increasing demand in the following decades. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Briar Hill Primary School. 

As of 2026, Briar Hill Primary School continues to operate, offering a Steiner Influenced Curriculum alongside the Victorian Curriculum.
name.official_title.title: Briar Hill Primary School (School No. 4341; previously known as Briar Hill State School 1927 – c.1970)

description:
Footscray North Primary School (School No. 4160) (VA 5710) is a coeducational primary school located in Melbourne’s inner western suburbs. 

The school first opened in 1924 as Footscray North State School, out of a large brick building erected on a site the Education Department (VA 714) had purchased in 1920. 

Additional rooms were added to the site in the following years, including a caretaker’s residence in 1928, two classrooms in 1943, and two rooms for specialised learning in 1949. The latter rooms were subsequently transferred to the adjacent Footscray North Special School (School No. 4792; later known as Rosamond Special School) (VA 5310) when it was taken over by the Education Department in 1957. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Footscray North Primary School. 

As of 2026, Footscray North Primary School continues to operate. 

Footscray North Primary School (School No. 4160) should not be confused with Rosamond Special School (School No. 4792) (VA 5310), which was known as Footscray North Special School from 1943 to 1977.
name.official_title.title: Footscray North Primary School (School No. 4160; previously known as Footscray North State School 1924 – c.1970)
title: Footscray North Primary School (School No. 4160; previously known as Footscray North State School 1924 – c.1970)

description:
Tylden Primary School (School No. 621) (VA 5712) is a coeducational primary school located in the Macedon Ranges, approximately 70 kilometres north of Melbourne.

The school first opened in 1861 as Tylden National School. In 1862, through the Common Schools Act, the Victorian Parliament created a single Board of Education (VA 713). With the passing of this act, the school was re-named Tylden Common School and was given the number 621. In 1864 the land for a new school was bought, with a one room brick schoolhouse completed in 1871.

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Tylden State School.

In the 1960s, a number of schools in the area closed and the students transferred to Tylden Primary School. The closed schools included East Trentham State School (School No. 943), North Blackwood State School (School No. 1636), Chanter’s Lane State School (School No. 923) and Spring Hill State School. An extra classroom was built in 1968 to accommodate the additional students. 

Following a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name, the school became known as Tylden Primary School. 

As of 2026, Tylden Primary School continues to operate. New buildings have been erected over the years, including a new brick building in 2004, but the original building also remains in use as an art studio. 

Tylden Primary School (School No. 621) should not be confused with Tylden Presbyterian School (School No. 630), which operated from 1861 to 1864, or Tylden South School (School No. 633), which operated from 1858 to 1894.
title: Tylden Primary School (School No. 621; previously known as Tylden National School 1861 – 1862; Tylden Common School 1862 – 1873; Tylden State School 1889 – c.1970)

description:
Wahgunyah Primary School (School No. 644) (VA 5713) is a coeducational primary school located in the small rural town of Wahgunyah, on the Murray River in north-eastern Victoria. 

The school was first established in 1858 as Wahgunyah National School, to meet the needs of farming families in the district. Children had been previously privately tutored, until a parcel of land was donated by local John Foord to erect the building for Wahgunyah National School on the corner of McDonnel and Victoria Streets.

In 1862, through the Common Schools Act, the Victorian Parliament created a single Board of Education (VA 713). With the passing of this act, the school was re-named Wahgunyah Common School and was given the number 644.

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Wahgunyah State School. In 1878, a new school building was erected to meet growing enrolments.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Wahgunyah Primary School. 

As of 2026, Wahgunyah Primary School continues to operate. A new school building was erected in 2011, however the 1878 building continues to be used as a library, music room and kitchen.
title: Wahgunyah Primary School (School No. 644; Wahgunyah National School 1858 – 1863; Wahgunyah Common School 1863 – c.1872; Wahgunyah State School c.1872 – c.1970)

description:
Establishment 

The Mount Buller and Mount Stirling Alpine Resort Management Board was established on the 1 November 2004 (Victorian Government Gazette, G 41, 7 October 2004) when the Mount Buller Alpine Resort Management Board (VA 5827) was merged with the Mount Stirling Alpine Resort Management Board (VA 5828). The new board subsumed responsibility for the management of both Alpine resorts. 

The Board was established as a statutory authority under the Alpine Resorts (Management) (Amendment) Act 2004 (the Act). It reported to the Minister responsible for environment and Crown land management. The Board was to consist of not less than three and not more than four members appointed by the Minister.

Function 

Functions as per the Act included: 
  • To act as a committee of management of any Crown land deemed to be permanently reserved under the Crown Land (Reserves) Act 1978 in the resort
  • To contribute to the overall promotion of alpine resorts.
  • To develop a tourism and marketing strategy and to collect and expend voluntary contributions from commercial undertakings in the resort for this purpose.
  • To provide the following services - garbage disposal, water supply, gas, drainage, sewerage, electricity, roads, fire protection, snowmaking - and to charge contributions for the provisions of those services.
  • To provide transport services in the resort.
  • To collect fees prescribed by the regulations for the resort.
  • to attract investment for the improvement of the resort.

The Board was responsible for the development, promotion, management and use of the Mount Buller and Mount Stirling Alpine Resorts. All functions and operations of the Resorts had to be performed on a sustainable basis and in a manner that is compatible with the alpine environment, having regard to environmental and ecological considerations (in particular, climate change), economic considerations, and cultural heritage considerations (in particular, Indigenous cultural heritage considerations). 

Further to this, the Board was required to contribute to the development of the Alpine Resorts Strategic Plan and other strategic planning for alpine resorts as a whole, which was managed, monitored and coordinated by the Alpine Resorts Co-ordinating Council. 

Abolishment

As of the 1 October 2022 (Victorian Government Gazette, S 371, 26 July 2022), The Mount Buller and Mount Stirling Resort Management Board was abolished under the Alpine Resorts Legislation Amendment Act 2022, along with all other Alpine Resort Boards. In its place, the Act established a new body known as Alpine Resorts Victoria (VA 5736) that subsumed management of all Alpine Resorts as well as the functions of the Alpine Resorts Co-ordinating Council.
name.official_title.title: Mount Buller and Mount Stirling Alpine Resort Management Board
title: Mount Buller and Mount Stirling Alpine Resort Management Board

description:
Bungeeltap State School (School No. 1751) (VA 5718) was a coeducational primary school located in what was the small farming community of Bungeeltap, approximately 16 kilometres from Ballan, west of Melbourne. 

The school first opened in 1876, however it struggled to maintain sufficient enrolments to stay full-time and open for much of its history.

It seems that from January 1882, Bungeeltap State School became worked part-time with Ingliston State School (School No. 1690) and by 1891 it had closed. In 1910, Bungeeltap State School was likely reopened, only to be possibly closed again at the end of 1918. 

From 1922, it seems likely that Bungeeltap State School was open and working part-time with a range of local schools at different times over the following years, including Mount Wallace State School (School No. 1018) (VA 4628), Bungal State School (School No. 1155) (VA 3215), Morrisons State School (School No. 2086) (VA 3384) and Beremboke State School (School No. 1017) (VA 3185). 

The exact details of closures and part-time arrangements with other schools remain subject to further research.

Bungeeltap State School closed for the last time in 1936.
title: Bungeeltap State School (School No. 1751)

description:
The Victorian Prison Industry Commission was established under the Victorian Prison Industries
Commission Act 1983, which came into operation on 4 July 1984. Its functions were to manage prison business sites and farms, provide work for prisoners and trainees, and oversee their employment. The Act governed industries operated by prisons, including manufacturing, production, services and farming, for the purpose of providing training and employment to prisoners. In this context, trainees were persons detained in a Youth Training Centre, which were sometimes known as Juvenile Detention Centres and later as Youth Justice Precincts.

The Commission was abolished when the Act was repealed by the Corrections (Amendment) Act 1996. Responsibility for prison industry management was then transferred to the Secretary of the Department of Justice (VA 3085) and subsequent departments. Following a departmental review and restructure of correctional administration between 1994 and 1996, this function was assigned to CORE—the Public Correctional Enterprise (VA 4367). During this restructure, the Commission traded as Correction Enterprises.
name.official_title.title: Victorian Prison Industries Commission
title: Victorian Prison Industries Commission (trading as Correctional Enterprises c.1994-1996)

description:
Establishment

Alpine Resorts Victoria (ARV) was established on the 1 October 2022 under the Alpine Resorts Legislation Amendment Act 2022. The Act abolished the previous Alpine Resort Management Boards and transferred all assets and liabilities to ARV. It also abolished the Alpine Resorts Co-ordinating Council and transferred all assets and liabilities to the Secretary. 

ARV subsumed responsibility for the following Management Boards:
  • Falls Creek Alpine Resort Management Board (VA 4879)
  • Southern Alpine Resort Management Board (VA 5826)
  • Mount Buller and Mount Stirling Alpine Resort Management Board (VA 5714)
  • Mount Hotham Alpine Resort Management Board (VA 5825)

Board of Directors was established that consists of not less than three and not more than nine directors appointed by the Minister of Environment, to whom the Board reports. The ARV Board has four committees being:
  • Finance, Risk and Audit Sub Committee
  • First Nations and Stake holder Engagement Sub Committee 
  • People, Culture and Remuneration Sub Committee
  • Strategic Planning, Asset Management and Commercial Operations Sub Committee

Functions

ARV is responsible for the management, development, promotion and use of alpine resorts having regards to environmental and ecological considerations (including climate change), economic considerations, and cultural heritage and landscape considerations (including indigenous cultural heritage). 

Under the Alpine Resorts (Management) Act 1997, ARV must perform their duties while considering the following Principles: 
  • protecting the unique environmental, social, cultural, and economic characteristics of each alpine resort; and 
  • planning for and managing all alpine resorts in a coordinated manner that adapts to and responds to the impacts and risks of climate change; and 
  • the ongoing impact of the use of the alpine resorts on natural and cultural features and the ecology of the alpine resorts; and 
  • respecting, protecting, and promoting Aboriginal self-determination, cultural values, practices, heritage, and knowledge in the alpine resorts; and 
  • partnering with traditional owners in policy development, planning, and decision-making in the alpine resorts; and 
  • protecting and enhancing the amenity, access, and use of each alpine resort, for the benefit and enjoyment of current and future generations of all Victorians; and
  • promoting investment in a diverse range of tourism and recreation experiences, for all seasons, in each alpine resort.
name.official_title.title: Alpine Resorts Victoria
title: Alpine Resorts Victoria

description:
Her Majesty's Prison, Barwon, commonly known as Barwon Prison, is a maximum-security prison for men located in Lara, Victoria. It opened in January 1990 to replace HM Prison, Geelong (VA 1003) and HM Prison, Pentridge (VA 863). Until 2025, it was the only maximum-security prison outside the Melbourne metropolitan area.

The prison was constructed between 1986 and 1989 and was the first prison in Victoria to be built to a modern unit-management design. It accommodates maximum-security, high-security, and protection prisoners in a number of units, including:
  • Acacia: a high security management unit for high-risk prisoners
  • Banksia: a management unit for prisoners requiring close supervision or protection
  • Cassia: a reception unit for mainstream prisoners
  • Diosma: a mainstream unit for prisoners with short- to medium-term sentences
  • Eucalypt: a mainstream unit for older prisoners with long-term sentences
  • Hoya: a protection unit for prisoners considered as at risk if housed with mainstream prisoners
  • Grevillea: a youth justice centre for prisoners aged 16 and 17
  • Illawarra: a remand unit for prisoners awaiting conviction or sentencing
  • Melaleuca: a high-security unit for high-risk prisoners.
  • Olearia: a maximum-security unit.

The Grevillea unit was opened in April 2003 and housed protection prisoners until mid-2015, when prisoners were relocated elsewhere to make room for prisoners involved in the 2015 Metropolitan Remand Centre Riots. In early 2016, the unit was reclassified as a restricted-regime unit used to transition prisoners from high-security units to mainstream units. Later in 2016, it became a youth justice unit to relieve overcrowding at Melbourne Youth Justice Centre (VA 5086), following the 2016 riot.

The Illawarra unit was initially a medium security unit, but was reclassified as a remand unit in 2016. Other units constructed since the prison's opening include the Melaleuca unit, which opened in 2007, and the Olearia unit, which opened in August 2016. The Olearia unit is considered a 'supermax' unit because it is separated from the rest of the prison and has its own visit centre and medical wing. As of 2025, the prison had the operational capacity of 427.
name.official_title.title: Her Majesty's Prison, Barwon
title: Her Majesty's Prison, Barwon

description:
HM Prison, Loddon, also known as Loddon Prison or the Loddon Prison Precinct, is a medium-security men's prison in Castlemaine, Victoria. Construction began in February 1988, and the prison opened in August 1990, replacing HM Prison, Castlemaine (VA 1008). Accommodation includes four-bedroom self-contained units and single-bed cell blocks.

In July 2014, the Middleton restricted minimum-security unit was constructed within the prison complex. The Middleton facility comprises self-catered, cottage-style accommodation, where prisoners are responsible for cooking their own meals.

As of 2025, the prison had an operational capacity of 704.
name.official_title.title: Her Majesty's Prison, Loddon
title: Her Majesty's Prison, Loddon

description:
Dame Phyllis Frost Centre is a maximum security prison for women located in Deer Park, Victoria. The facility includes single cells with ensuite facilities, self-contained units and specialist accommodation for protection prisoners. Medium-security units accommodate 10 prisoners in separate rooms and minimum-security units accommodate 5 prisoners. Unit include kitchen and dining facilities, and prisoners are required to undertake their own meal preparation and other domestic tasks. Shared activity and quiet areas are also provided. As of 2025, the operational capacity was 568.

The prison was established in July 1996 as the Metropolitan Women's Correctional Centre, Deer Park, replacing HM Prison, Fairlea (VA 926). It was initially operated by Corrections Corporation of Australia, the Australian arm of Corrections Corporation of America, known as CoreCivic as of 2025.

On 3 October 2000, the prison was transferred to public ownership under section 8F of the Corrections Act 1986, following significant controversy over prison operations and public pressure. The prison was renamed 'Dame Phyllis Frost Centre' in February 2001.

The centre is named after Dame Phyllis Frost, a philanthropist, welfare worker and advocate for women prisoners. In the 1950s, she was instrumental in the establishment of the Consultative Council for Female Prison Reform. She continued to advocate for improved conditions, rehabilitation and education for women in prisons until her death in 2004.
name.official_title.title: Dame Phyllis Frost Centre
title: Dame Phyllis Frost Centre (previously known as Metropolitan Women's Correctional Centre 1996 - 2001)

description:
Hopkins Correctional Centre (HCC) is a medium-security prison near Ararat, Victoria. It accommodates  sentenced prisoners, including those with protection requirements. The prison operates under the 'Better Living Model' of prison design and prisoner reform. The aim of this operating model is to reduce reoffending rates through reintegration, educational, and employment programs. Prisoners assessed as capable of work are employed full-time in an allocated industry. 

Established in 1967 as Ararat Prison, HCC replaced Ballaarat Gaol (VA 633), which closed in 1965. The prison was built at an initial cost of $1.25 million and was soon expanded in 1970, and again in 1972. It was renamed Her Majesty's Prison, Ararat under the Corrections Act in 1986. The prison site underwent extensive redevelopment from 2006 to 2012, and was renamed Hopkins Correctional Centre when this work was completed.

HCC includes single-, double- and triple-bed accommodation, cottage accommodation, a unit for aged and medically infirm prisoners, and eight beds for offenders on continued detention. As of 2025, its operational capacity was 738.
name.official_title.title: Hopkins Correctional Centre
title: Hopkins Correctional Centre (previously known as Ararat Prison 1967-1986; Her Majesty's Prison, Ararat 1986-2012)

description: Her Majesty's Prison, Tarrengower, also known as Tarrengower Prison, was established in January 1988 as a minimum-security for women, replacing the minimum-security unit at HM Prison, Fairlea (VA 926). It was built on a former farm near Maldon, Victoria. The prison comprises 15 self-contained units with single-room accommodation and shared kitchen and living areas. It also has facilities for pregnant women and young children. As at 2025, Tarrengower Prison was the only minimum-security women's prison in Victoria, and had an operational capacity of 72.
name.official_title.title: Her Majesty's Prison, Tarrengower
title: Her Majesty's Prison, Tarrengower

description:
Beechworth Correctional Centre (BCC) is a minimum-security prison for men near Beechworth, Victoria. It typically accommodates prisoners serving the latter part of their sentences and offers work programs that aims to support their transition back into the community. BCC was opened in January 2005, replacing HM Prison, Beechworth (VA 939).

The prison comprises 22 group accommodation units, in addition to 14 self-catering units and 50 two-person units. Prisoners housed in the self-catering units are given a weekly budget to purchase groceries and prepare their own meals. As of 2025, the has the operational capacity of 210.
name.official_title.title: Beechworth Correctional Centre
title: Beechworth Correctional Centre

description:
Woodford Primary School (School No. 648) (VA 648) is a coeducational primary school located in south-western Victoria, nine kilometres north of Warrnambool.

The school first opened in 1854 as Woodford School, under the National School Board (VA 919). It operated out of the home of the first Head Teacher, Abraham Lauder, which was converted into classrooms. 

In 1862, through the Common Schools Act, the Victorian Parliament abolished the two existing centralised boards and created a single Board of Education (VA 713).  With the passing of this act, the school was re-named Woodford Common School and was assigned the number 648.  

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Woodford State School.  At a similar time, a new teacher’s residence was built, and in 1874 a new sandstone school was constructed. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Woodford Primary School. 

As of 2025, Woodford Primary School continues to operate, with the early sandstone school still in use as the office/administration building.

Woodford Primary School (School No. 648) should not be confused with Woodford State School (School No. 681), which operated from 1857 to 1874.
title: Woodford Primary School (School No. 648; previously known as Woodford School 1854 – c.1862; Woodford Common School c. 1863 – c. 1873; Woodford State School c. 1873 – 1970)

description:
Yinnar South Primary School (School No. 2730) (VA 5777) is a small rural coeducational primary school located in the Latrobe Valley in the Gippsland region of south-eastern Victoria.

The school first opened in 1886 as Yinnar South State School, operating for the first two years out of a private house. In 1887, the school transferred to a portable building. 

Due to a growing number of schools in the district, and a subsequent dip in individual school enrolments, Yinnar South was worked part-time from 1894 to 1898 with Hazelwood Ridge State School (School No.  1768). In February 1898, a bushfire destroyed the Yinnar South school building. Schooling was held in temporary premises until 1924, when a new building was constructed on a site four kilometres south of the original school.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Yinnar South Primary School. 

As of 2025, Yinnar South Primary School continues to operate.

Yinnar South Primary School (School No. 2730) should not be confused with Yinnar Primary School (School No. 2419), which has operated since 1881.
title: Yinnar South Primary School (School No. 2730; previously known as Yinnar South State School 1886 – c.1970)

description:
Tullamarine State School (School No. 2613) (VA 5778) was a coeducational primary school located Melbourne’s north-west suburbs.

Tullamarine State School was established in 1884, as the result of an amalgamation between Seafield State School (School No. 546) and the previous Tullamarine State School (School No. 632). It opened in a new building on a site midway between the two former schools. 

Tullamarine State School closed in 1961. In 1963 the site was bought by the Commonwealth Government. 

Tullamarine State School (School No. 2613) should not be confused with the following similarly named schools:
  • Tullamarine Common School (School No. 735), years active 1864 to 1868 
  • Tullamarine National School (School No. 619; also known as Tullamarine Island School), years active 1859 to 1882
  • Tullamarine State School (School No. 632), years active 1858 to 1884
  • Tullamarine Primary School (School No. 4852) (VA 5764), years active 1959 to present (as of 2025)

The Integrity and Oversight Committee (VA 5790) is a Joint Investigatory Committee of the Parliament of Victoria. The Committee was established in under s. 189 Integrity and Accountability Legislation Amendment (Public Interest Disclosures, Oversight and Independence) Act 2019, which amended the Parliamentary Committees Act 2003. The Committee was an amalgamation of the Accountability and Oversight Committee (VA 5330) and the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission Committee (VA 5333). 

The Committee is responsible for the monitoring and reviewing the performance of the following agencies:
  • Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC, VA 5212)
  • Integrity Oversight Victoria (IOV) 
  • Office of the Victorian Information Commissioner (OVIC)
  • Parliamentary Workplace Standards and Integrity Commission (PWSIC)
  • Victorian Ombudsman (VO, VA 1037)

The Committee can also undertake inquiries into issues related to the work of these agencies and make recommendations for improvements. However, it does not have the power to investigate complaints against these agencies and is prohibited from reconsidering any decisions, findings or recommendations they have made.

Joint Investigatory Committees

Joint Investigatory Committees are groups of members appointed by the Legislative Council and Legislative Assembly to conduct investigations and make recommendations about topics of particular interest to Parliament. Some committees have ongoing functions to scrutinise legislation and finances, and others conduct inquiries into specific subject matters. A key feature of committee work is the taking of evidence from the public and expert witnesses as part of the inquiry process. Committee investigations result in reports to Parliament.

Joint committees have between five and ten members of whom at least one is a member of the Council, and one is a member of the Assembly. Joint committees can inquire into matters referred to it by a resolution of either House or by order of the Governor-In-Council. They may also inquire into, consider, or report to Parliament on any annual report or document relevant to its functions laid before either House. Recommendations made joint investigatory committees are not automatically accepted by Parliament. The responsible Minister must however, table a report stating action to be taken regarding the recommendations within six months of the tabling of the Committee’s report.

The functions of the Committee, as defined in the Public Health and Wellbeing Act 2008, were to review pandemic orders and other instruments made by the Minister for Health to ensure compliance with legislation and the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities.

On 12 October 2022 the pandemic declaration expired and the Committee became inactive. Although the the Committee remains as established Joint Committee according to the Parliamentary Committees Act, it is only required to be active while a pandemic declaration is in force.

description:
Newport Lakes Primary School (School No. 113) (VA 5799) is a coeducational primary school located in the suburb of Newport, in Melbourne’s inner west, directly north of Williamstown.

The school first opened in 1856 as Cambridge National School, under the National School Board (VA 919). It was the first national vested school to be established in the Williamstown area. It moved sites several times in its early years and was likely known as the Geelong Junction School and the Williamstown Junction School based on its location at those times. The school also became known colloquially for many years as Kohry’s School, after Samuel George Kohry, who taught at the school from 1866 to 1893.

In 1862, through the Common Schools Act, the Victorian Parliament created a single Board of Education (VA 713). With the passing of this act, the school was re-named Cambridge Common School and was given the number 113.  

The Education Act of 1872 established the Victorian Education Department (VA 714) which marked further change to school naming conventions, with the school becoming Cambridge State School.  

In 1886, the Newport train station was built. The school adopted the name of Newport State School that same year, moving to a permanent site on Elizabeth Street, Newport. 

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to change the use of the term ‘State School’ to refer to all primary, secondary and technical schools instead of just primary schools, and for all primary schools to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Newport Primary School. In 2000, the school name was changed again to Newport Lakes Primary School. 

The school was significantly damaged by a fire in 1967, with eight classrooms destroyed and many records lost. The school was rebuilt in 1968.

As of 2026, Newport Lakes Primary School continues to operate, and is the oldest continually operating government primary school in the Western Metropolitan Region of Melbourne.
title: Newport Lakes Primary School (School No. 113; previously known as Cambridge National School 1856 – c.1863; Cambridge Common School c.1863 – c.1873; Cambridge State School c.1873 – 1886; Newport State School 1886 – c.1970; Newport Primary School c.1970 - 2000; also known as Kohry’s School; Geelong Junction School; Williamstown Junction School)

description:
Seymour College (School No. 8884) (VA 5806) is a coeducational Foundation (Prep) to Year 12 and Special Education school located in the town of Seymour, north of Melbourne.

The school first opened in Term 3 2010, the result of the closing and merging of four existing schools in the area: Seymour Primary School (School No. 547), Seymour East Primary College (School No. 4957), Seymour Technical High School (School No. 8315) and Seymour Special School (School No. 5149).

It was initially known by the interim name Seymour P-12 College, before officially changing to Seymour College in September 2011. At the time of opening, the school operated across multiple campuses, continuing to occupy the original sites until mid-2013, when schooling consolidated onto the main campus at 29-47 Stewart Street. 

In 2019, the City of Mitchell (VA 3704), with funding from the Victorian Government Shared Facilities Fund, built an integrated community/learning hub at Seymour College, consisting of two early learning rooms, two maternal and child health rooms and two consulting rooms. It is used by allied health professionals to early childhood intervention services, family services, counselling, occupational therapy and speech therapy. 

As of 2026, Seymour College continues to operate.
title: Seymour College (School No. 8884; previously known as Seymour P-12 College 2010 - 2011)

The Court at Cassilis was established by the Governor on 26 July 1904 (Victoria Government Gazette 104, p. 2463, 3 August 1904).

It was established as a Court of Petty Sessions, with the fourth Wednesday of the month at 11am to be the scheduled sitting day.

The Order establishing the Court at Cassilis was revoked on 17 August 1915 under Section 62 of the Justices Act 1890 (Act No. 1105) (Victoria Government Gazette 104, p. 3045, 25 August 1915).

It appears that following its abolition, the records of the Court of Petty Sessions at Cassilis were transferred to the custody of the nearby Court in Omeo (VA 5287).

Cassillis Courts includes:
  • Court of Petty Sessions (1904 - 1915)
  • Children's Court (1907 - 1915)

District and Circuit Court Systems

In the mid-19th to early 20th century, courts and court districts were established across Victoria of various levels. This practice remained until either the court was abolished, or a state-wide court entity was established. Once a state-wide court was established, hearings continued in regional centres using a circuit court system.

Under the district system, courts largely administered themselves, with major decisions such as the appointment of judicial officers and court locations, as well the development of court rules, procedures and jury lists passed down by Governor in Council. Additionally, judicial officers, registrars and clerks were appointed to specific court locations. These functions were largely taken over by the primary court and their respective chief judicial officer once the primary court was established. Likewise, judicial officers were no longer appointed to specific court locations, but rather to the primary court then assigned to hearings according to the scheduled circuit.

Both district courts and circuit courts commonly used their own recordkeeping systems to manage cases until centralised recordkeeping systems were gradually introduced from the late 20th century. Administrative resources were often shared between the different levels of court when operating from the same location.

Court of Petty Sessions/Magistrates’ Court (1838 – Present)

Courts of Petty Sessions were established to hear criminal and civil cases of minor offences and disputes. Courts of Petty Sessions were appointed to be held in population centres. These courts were renamed Magistrates’ Courts in 1971. Under the Magistrates’ Court Act 1989, the Magistrates’ Court of Victoria (VA 5113) was constituted as the primary body, while the various courts were grouped into regions with the largest in each appointed as a headquarter venue. Magistrates and other Judicial Officers were assigned to regions to hear cases in each location according to the scheduled circuit. Each region is managed by a regional coordinating magistrate and a senior registrar. Individual Magistrates’ Courts continue to maintain their own case registries. As of 2023, there are 51 courts in 13 regions. The Court has several divisions including Koori Court, Drug Court, Assessment and Referral Court as well as several specialist family courts. These divisions are appointed to locations within regions, usually the headquarter court.

Children’s Court (1907 – Present)

Children’s Courts were established to hear and to inquire into charges against children. During the 1930s, these courts also began hearing other cases involving children such as child neglect. Children’s Courts were appointed to be held at locations that already held Courts of Petty Sessions or Magistrates’ Courts and operated as a division of the Magistrates’ Court until the Children's Court of Victoria (VA 4190) was established in 2000. As such, Children’s Courts operated under the Magistrates’ Court district system until 1989 and continue to mirror the Magistrates’ Court’s regional system. Like the Magistrates’ Court, when the Children’s Court of Victoria was constituted as the primary and independent body, courts were grouped into regions, and Judicial Officers and Support Services staff were assigned to these regions. Judicial officers were assigned to hearings according to each region’s circuit schedule. Individual courts continue to maintain their own case registries and often share administrative resources with the Magistrates’ Court registries. As of 2025, there are 33 courts in 6 regions. The Court has a Family division, and Criminal division, as well as a Children’s Koori Court for criminal matters.

description:
Myrrhee Primary School (School No. 2677) (VA 5848) is a government primary school situated on 100 acres of bushland in the rural Myrrhee Valley in Victoria’s High Country.

The school initially operated from a bark-roofed building on a local resident’s property. The building had originally been erected for church services by various denominations. The date on which the school first commenced operation remains subject to further research. In its early years, the school operated part-time with Willow Bank School, formerly Boggy Creek Upper School (School No. 2676). The two schools likely shared a single teacher, who divided their time between both sites.

A school building was constructed around 1876. In October 1885, the school was officially opened by the Department of Education (VA 714).

A fire swept through the district in 1901, destroying both the school building and the teacher’s residence. The school temporarily operated from Tyrrell’s hop shed until a replacement school building was completed and opened on a new site in 1903.

A teacher’s residence was added to the site in 1952. In 1963, a new school building comprising two classrooms, a long corridor and an entrance area was constructed.

In 1970, there was a statewide decision to broaden the use of the term ‘State School’ to include all government schools, rather than referring exclusively to primary-level schools. Subsequently, all primary schools began to use ‘Primary School’ in the name. Accordingly, the school name was changed to Myrrhee Primary School around this time.

In January 1997, Fifteen Mile Creek Camp opened as an alternative education setting and campus of Myrrhee Primary School. On 19 January 2010, the campus became part of Bogong Outdoor Education Centre, subsequently known as Outdoor School (School No. 7618).

As of 2024, Myrrhee Primary School formed part of the King Valley Cluster, a network of rural primary schools comprising Moyhu Primary School (School No. 1335), Myrrhee Primary School, Whitfield Primary School (School No. 2441), Greta Valley Primary School (School No. 5398), and Broken Creek Primary School (School No. 862) (VA 5782).

Enrolment in 2024 was 35 students. As of 2026, the school remains in operation.
title: Myrrhee Primary School (School No. 2677; previously known as Boggy Creek Upper School; Myrrhee State School 1885 – circa 1970)
